en: Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha.
Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men.
And likewise to the goddess Sarasvatī; thereafter, one should utter the word "Victory" (jaya).
O you whose hair-ends are like molten gold, whose eyes are like a blazing fire,
whose touch of the claws exceeds that of a diamond— O divine lion, homage be to you!
May the tips of the claws and tail of Narasiṃha protect you—
those which are crimson with the mire of blood from the field of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s chest.
All the high-souled sages dwelling in the Himalayas, who had mastered the Vedas,
were knowers of the three periods of time and residents of the Naimiṣa forest.
Those who delight in the Arbuda forest, those who dwell in the Puṣkara forest,
those who delight in Mount Mahendra, and those who reside in the Vindhya mountains;
And those who delight in the forest of Dharma, those who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, those who are devoted to Śrīśaila, and those who reside in Kurukṣetra; // NsP_1.6 //
Those who dwell on Mount Kaumāra and those who reside at Pampā—
these and many other stainless sages, together with their disciples, [are present].
In the month of Māgha, they came to the holy site of Prayāga to bathe;
having bathed there according to the rules and performed their rites, such as recitation and so forth.
Having bowed to the god Mādhava and performed the libations for the ancestors,
he beheld Bharadvāja there, a resident of that holy pilgrimage site.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, and being well-honored by him in turn,
they sat down in due order upon various seats, such as those conducive to virility.
Seated upon seats provided by Bharadvāja, all those ascetics,
centered on Kṛṣṇa, then spoke among themselves.
Then, at the conclusion of the discourses of those sages of purified souls,
the highly intelligent Sūta of great splendor arrived there.
The disciple of Vyāsa, known as Lomaharṣaṇa and well-versed in the Purāṇas,
having bowed to them according to tradition, was in turn honored by them.
Having sat down appropriately according to the opinion of Bharadvāja,
Bharadvāja then questioned Lomaharṣaṇa— the disciple of Vyāsa who was seated comfortably— in the presence of the sages.
Bharadvāja said: O Sūta, the Saṃhitā known as the Vārāha was previously heard by us and by these others at the great sacrificial session of Śaunaka.
"Now, O Sūta, I desire to hear from you the Purāṇic compendium known as the Nārasiṃha; these others are also standing here, desirous of hearing it."
Therefore, O Sūta, I ask you this question in the presence of these great-souled ṛṣis, at dawn, O Great Sage.
From what has this world, with its moving and unmoving beings, arisen? By whom is it sustained? Or into what does it dissolve? (NsP 1.18)
What is the measurement of the earth, O Nṛsiṃha, and by what action, O illustrious and high-minded one, are you satisfied? Tell me that.
And how might there be a beginning of creation, and how might there be an end?
How is the calculation of a yuga made, or what indeed constitutes the four yugas?
What is the distinction among them here, and what is the state of affairs in the Kali age?
How is the god Narasiṃha propitiated even by those who are not human?
Which fields are meritorious, and which mountain peaks are meritorious?
And which rivers are supremely meritorious, auspicious, and removers of the sins of men?
How did the creation of the gods and others occur, as well as that of Manu and his Manvantara?
Likewise, how did the creation of the Vidyādharas and others come about in the beginning?
O highly fortunate one, tell me all of this in due order: which kings were performers of sacrifice, and who attained supreme perfection?
Sūta said: O you whose wealth is austerity, through the grace of Vyāsa I know the Purāṇas;
having bowed down to him, I shall proclaim the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa.
I bow always to the son of Parāśara, the Supreme Person, the sole source of all the gods, possessed of knowledge, the bestower of vast intelligence, known through the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs;
eternally tranquil, having stilled the objects of the senses, of pure and expansive luster, the arranger of the Vedas, free from all impurity, and the burner of all suffering.
Homage to that Blessed One Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
by whose grace I shall relate this narrative of Vāsudeva.
This great question which you have proclaimed is well-determined;
it cannot be answered by anyone without the grace of Viṣṇu.
Nevertheless, by the grace of Narasiṃha alone, I shall now proclaim this [account] of great merit; O Bhāradvāja, listen to me.
"Let all the sages who are present here with their disciples listen;
I shall proclaim the Purāṇa of Narasiṃha exactly as it is."
From Nārāyaṇa this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has arisen;
by him alone is everything protected through forms such as Narasiṃha.
In the same way, at the end, it dissolves into Hari, whose nature is light.
Listen as I explain how the Lord creates; hear that.
For this verse is known to be common to all the Purāṇas;
O Sage, having heard it, listen to it from me in its entirety.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
I shall describe, in brief and in due order, the primary creation, the secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manus, and the accounts of the dynasties.
O twice-born ones, I shall indeed first relate the great primordial creation,
from which the conduct of the gods and of kings has proceeded.
And the eternal Supreme Self is known along with its secret doctrine:
O best of the twice-born, prior to creation and after dissolution, nothing at all existed.
There was a single light known as Brahman, the cause of all,
eternal, stainless, peaceful, devoid of qualities, and perpetually pure.
He is the pure ocean of bliss which those seeking liberation desire;
he is omniscient because his nature is knowledge, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
But when the time for creation had arrived, that leader of knowers, having recognized the latent transformation, proceeded to bring it forth.
Therefore, the Pradhāna manifested, and from that the Mahat arose;
the Mahat is threefold: consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is Tāmasa—
this threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) was born from the principle of Mahat.
For as the Great One (mahat) is enveloped by the Primal Nature (pradhāna),
so too is the Origin of Elements (bhūtādi) transformed from that [Great One], resulting in the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra).
From the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), he emitted space, which is characterized by sound;
that Bhūtādi then completely enveloped both the subtle element of sound and space.
But space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch;
it became the powerful wind, and touch is considered its quality.
Space, as the subtle element of sound, likewise enveloped the subtle element of touch;
then the air, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of form.
Light arises from wind, and it is said to have the quality of form;
indeed, wind, which consists of touch alone, envelops that which consists of form alone.
And light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste;
from that, the waters arise, which serve as the support for taste.
The waters, undergoing transformation, enveloped the subtle element of form;
and the waters, as they transformed, produced the subtle element of smell.
From that, this earth was born, which possesses the qualities of all elements;
from that, the aggregate is produced, and its quality is considered to be odor.
Because they consist of that alone in each respective case, they are known as "tanmātras" (subtle elements).
The tanmātras are non-specific (aviśeṣa), whereas the others are specific (viśeṣa) according to their functions.
This creation of the gross elements and the subtle elements from the tamasic ego has been described by me to you in brief, O Bharadvāja.
The thinkers declare that the ten sense organs are derived from the *taijasa* [ego], while the gods are the *vaikārika* [ego]; herein, the eleventh, the mind (*manas*), is also proclaimed among them.
In this context, there are five organs of perception and five organs of action;
I shall describe them and their functions to you, O purifier of your lineage.
The ear, the two eyes, the tongue, the nose, and the skin as the fifth—
these five are indeed joined with the intellect for the sake of accomplishing the cognition of sound and the other sense objects.

The anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech as the fifth, O Bharadvāja— these, along with emission, bliss, craftsmanship, movement, and speech, are traditionally known as action (karma).
Space, air, fire, water, and earth,
O Brahmin, are endowed with successive qualities beginning with sound.
Possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, they were unable to create progeny without a collective union, having failed to come together in their entirety.
Having come together through mutual conjunction and by way of reciprocal dependence,
they are characterized as a single aggregate, having attained complete unity.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of Pradhāna,
those [evolutes] beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the Egg.
O one of great intelligence, that [embryo], having gradually increased, remained like a bubble of water; from the elements, a vast cosmic egg was formed, resting upon the waters.
The primordial, unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, whose form is Brahman, exists there;
in that place dwells Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, the Sovereign, whose nature is unmanifest.
Abiding by himself, having assumed the very nature of Brahman,
Meru became his amnion and the mountains his chorion;
the oceans were the fetal waters of that Great Soul.
Mountains, islands, and oceans, along with the light and the collection of worlds—
all that, including gods, asuras, and humans, existed within that egg.
The supreme Lord Hari himself, endowed with the quality of rajas,
assumes the form of Brahmā and proceeds with the creation of the world.
And having created [the world], he protects it age after age until the dissolution of the kalpa;
then, in the form of Narasiṃha and others, or in the form of Rudra, he shall withdraw it.
Desiring to protect the entire world, Ananta creates it all in the form of Brahmā;
taking on forms such as Rāma, he protects it, and then, becoming Rudra, he brings about its destruction.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 1.
Sūta said:
Having become Brahmā for the creation of the world, Narasiṃha proceeds [with his task];
O Bharadvāja, listen to me as I shall describe this to you.
O learned one, the Lord known as Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is said to have been born; yet he is eternal by way of metaphorical designation.
By its own measure, its lifespan is recorded as one hundred years;
that is called a *parā*, and half of that is designated as a *parārdha*.
O sinless one, understand from what I have told you regarding the nature of Viṣṇu as Time how his measurement is established.
And also of all other beings, both moving and unmoving—
of the earth, the mountains, the oceans, and so forth, O best of beings, without exception.
I shall now tell you the knowledge of numbers regarding human beings; listen to me.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* are proclaimed to be one *kāṣṭhā*.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are to be known as one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute one *muhūrta*.
A human day and night is recorded as consisting of thirty such *muhūrtas*.
That many days and nights constitute a month consisting of two fortnights;
six such months form a solstice (*ayana*), and there are two solstices: the southern and the northern.
The southern course is the night of the gods, and the northern is their day;
the two courses together are proclaimed here as a year for mortals.
A month of humans is declared to be a day and night of the ancestors;
a year of humans is remembered as a day and night of the Vasus and other gods.
A cycle known as Tretā and the others consists of divine thousands of years;
understand from me the division of that set of four ages (caturyuga) according to its twelve [thousand-year] units.
Those who know the past have stated that in the Kṛta and subsequent ages, the [lifespans] are respectively four, three, two, and one thousand divine years.
The preceding twilight (saṃdhyā) is ordained there as being equal in measure to one hundred [years] of that [yuga],
and the transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśaka) immediately following the yuga is indeed equal to that.
O twice-born one, that period which exists between the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the twilight-interval (saṃdhyāṃśa) is to be known as the "yuga," designated by names such as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages;
a thousand of such cycles, O twice-born one, is declared to be a single day of Brahmā.
O Brahman, during the day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus;
hear now their duration as determined by time.
The seven ṛṣis, Śakra, Manu, and those who are his sons,
are indeed created at one time and withdrawn in the same manner as before.
The duration of a Manvantara, O twice-born one, is seventy-one cycles of four yugas plus a little more; this is the time of the Manu and also of Śakra and the others.
By divine reckoning, it is recorded as eight hundred thousand,
plus another fifty-two thousand additional [years].
O twice-born one, they are reckoned by calculation to be a full thirty crores,
as well as sixty-seven other hundred-thousands (niyutas), O great sage.
O twice-born one, twenty thousand years, plus an additional period,
is the reckoning of a *manvantara* by human years.
Indeed, this period of fourteen [ages] is recorded as a day of Brahmā;
at the beginning of the universe, he created with a well-disposed mind both the gods and the ancestors.
Gandharvas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, and likewise guhyakas;
sages, vidyādharas, and also humans and animals.
Having created birds, stationary beings, ants, and serpents, as well as the fourfold social order, he appointed them to their respective duties in the sacrificial rites.
Furthermore, at the end of the day, having withdrawn the three worlds,
that immutable Lord rests upon the couch of Ananta for as long as that night.
At its conclusion occurred the great aeon renowned as the Brāhma,
in which there was the incarnation of the Fish and the churning of the great ocean.
In the same way, the third is conceived as the Varāha-kalpa,
wherein Viṣṇu himself, being praised by the great seers, assumed the form of a boar out of affection in order to lift up the goddess Earth.
Having created the world and the immeasurable beings who move through the sky, and likewise having created all living creatures,
the Lord Hari, the primordial God, withdraws everything into the dissolution known as the occasional (naimittika) and rests.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Composition of Creation," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. NarP 2.
Sūta said:
O illustrious one, while the Lord was sleeping there, a great lotus appeared from his navel;
upon that lotus dwelt one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Born from Brahmā, he was addressed by him: "O high-minded one, create progeny.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Nārāyaṇa vanished.
Having said "So be it" to that god Viṣṇu, Brahmā then remained reflecting;
he did not perceive even the slightest seed of the world.
At that moment, great wrath arose within the high-souled Brahmā;
from that wrath, a child was born upon his lap.
Weeping and restrained by that Brahmā of manifest form, he was told, "Give me a name"; thus, he gave him the name Rudra.
Thus addressed with the words "Release this world again," he,
being unable to do so, immersed himself in that water, devoted as he was to asceticism.
When he had submerged into the water,
Prajāpati Brahmā, the Lord of Beings, created another [self] from his right thumb.
Then, from his left thumb, Dakṣa’s wife was born;
in her, the Lord produced Manu Svāyambhuva.
Therefore, the creation of living beings was then brought forth by Brahmā.
Thus has this creation been described by me to you, O best of sages.
What more do you wish to hear regarding him as he was creating the world?
Bharadvāja said:
O Lomaharṣaṇa, you have related that to me in brief;
now, O high-minded one, tell me again in detail about the primary creation.
Sūta said:
In the same way, at the end of the kalpa, the Lord Brahmā, having risen from his night-slumber and overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), beheld the world as empty.
Nārāyaṇa is supreme and inconceivable, the progenitor even of the ancients;
the Lord, whose nature is Brahman, is beginningless and the source of all.
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god whose nature is Brahman and who is the source of the world: NsP_3.13 // [Verse follows]
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*;
since they were his first abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*.
As he was contemplating creation as it had been in the past at the beginning of the kalpas,
darkness then manifested before him without the intervention of conscious thought.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and that which is called andhatāmisra—
this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Self.
The creation presided over in five ways by the one who meditates, being devoid of awakening,
without light within or without, with its nature concealed and consisting of immobile things—
this is to be known as the primary creation (*mukhya-sarga*) by those expert in the accomplishment of creation. (NsP 3.17)
Furthermore, as that Brahmā was meditating, the *tiryaksrotas* (the downward-streaming) came into being; therefore, it is traditionally taught that from him the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) arose.
Those who are well known as cattle and the like, and those who follow wrong paths—
even considering them to be ineffective, the Four-faced One [Brahmā] entered the womb of an animal.
The third, however, was the upward-streaming (ūrdhvasrotas), which arose as a sattvic one;
then the Lord, being satisfied, indeed reflected upon another creation.
Then, as that Prajāpati was contemplating the expansion of creation,
human beings known as "accomplishers" (sādhaka) arose, characterized by downward-flowing currents (arvāksrotas).
They abound in illumination yet are joined with darkness and dominated by passion;
therefore, they experience much suffering and act again and again.
These many creations have been described to you, O best of sages:
the first is the creation of the Great Principle (mahat), and the second is that of the subtle elements (tanmātras).
The third creation is known as the Vaikārika, pertaining to the senses;
the fourth is the Mukhya creation, and the "principal" ones are indeed remembered as the stationary beings (plants).
And he who is called *tiryaksrotas* is said to be born in the animal womb;
after that, the sixth [creation] among those of upward-streaming (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is remembered as the divine creation (*devasarga*).

Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, known as the human; the eighth is the creative outpour of grace (anugraha-sarga), which is declared to be characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
The ninth is the creation of Rudra; thus there are nine creations of Prajāpati.

These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations, while those three are known as the primary (prākṛta) ones. The primary and the modified, along with the ninth, the Kaumāra creation, are thus recorded.
Both the primary and the secondary causes of the world,
which were described by me as having arisen when Brahmā was creating the creation, [are these].
The infinite Supreme Lord, assuming Māyā, creates each respective transformation;
he is the unmanifest form known as the Supreme Self, who, being impelled, is to be known by all souls.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Manner of the Creation of the World," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 3)
Bharadvāja said: A ninefold creation arose from Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
O Sūta, tell me now how that [creation] increased.
Sūta said: First, Marīci and the others were created by Brahmā—
namely Marīci, Atri, as well as Aṅgiras, Pulaha, and Kratu.
And Pulastya of great splendor, Pracetas, and Bhṛgu;
Nārada was the tenth, and Vasiṣṭha of great intelligence.
Sanaka and the others were appointed to the dharma known as *nivṛtti*,
while Marīci and the others were appointed to the dharma known as *pravṛtti*, with the exception of the sage Nārada alone.
That other Prajāpati, named Dakṣa, who was born from the limbs [of the primordial being],
by means of the lineage of his daughter's sons, [created] this world of moving and unmoving things.
The gods, the dānavas, as well as the gandharvas, uragas, and birds—
all these were born from the daughters of Dakṣa, and they were supremely righteous.
For the four kinds of beings, both immobile and mobile,
having thus increased, they arise again at the beginning of each creation.
O highly fortunate one, the authors of the Anusarga are the great sages beginning with Marīci and ending with Vasiṣṭha, who were born from the mind of Brahmā.
At the time of creation, however, the Great-Souled One creates all things—the elements, the intellect, and the sense-objects;
subsequently, that same Infinite One, assuming the form of the four-faced Brahmā and the form of a sage, performs the act of creation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 4.
Bharadvāja said:
O great-minded one, tell me in detail about the creation of Rudra;
furthermore, how did all those beginning with Marīci create once again?
O high-minded one, how could Vasiṣṭha be the son of Mitra and Varuṇa,
given that he was previously born from the mind of Brahmā?
O best of beings, I shall proclaim the creation of Rudra and his various emanations;
listen as I describe in detail the successive creations of the sages.
Then, at the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord was meditating upon a son equal to himself,
a youth named Nīlalohita appeared on his lap.
With a body half-female and half-male, he was fierce and possessed of an immense form;
by his splendor, he illuminated all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Seeing him blazing with splendor, Prajāpati replied:
"O high-minded one, divide yourself today at my command."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, O Brahmin, the powerful Rudra then assumed the state of womanhood and the state of manhood separately.
He divided his manhood into ten parts and one part;
O best of the twice-born, listen as I tell you their names.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Kapālī, and Rudra;
as well as Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Aparājita.
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata—
these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
In the same way, Rudra divided his female nature into ten parts and then into one;
Uma alone, as his wife, remained established in many forms.
When he had previously emerged from the water after performing severe austerities,
then the powerful god Rudra created [the world] there.
O best of Brahmins, by the power of his asceticism, he [created] various beings,
as well as Piśācas and Rākṣasas with the faces of lions, camels, and crocodiles.
He [subdued] spirits headed by Vetālas, as well as thousands of others,
and thirty-five million of the fierce Vināyakas.
And with another purpose in mind, he created Skanda as well;
such is that Lord Rudra whom I have described to you.
Listen to me as I describe the secondary creation (anusarga) of Marīci and the others:
all beings, from the gods down to the stationary plants, were created by the Self-born One.
When all his subjects did not multiply,
that wise one then created mental sons who were like himself.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, and the high-minded Bhṛgu.
"These are the nine Brahmās, as established in the Purāṇas;
Agni and the Pitṛs are indeed the two mind-born sons of Brahmā."
At the time of creation, O Brahmin, those two illustrious ones, Svāyambhuva and Śatarūpā, emerged;
having created the maiden Śatarūpā, he gave her to Manu.
And from that Puruṣa, the goddess Śatarūpā gave birth to Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, and a daughter named Prasūti.
Manu Svāyambhuva gave his daughter Prasūti to Dakṣa;
and then Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters upon Prasūti.
He created those maidens; now hear their names from me:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and likewise Kriyā.
The Lord Dharma took as his wives for the sake of offspring the daughters of Dakṣa: Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Siddhi, Kīrti, and the thirteenth.
From his wives, Śraddhā and the others, were born sons such as Kāma;
through the sons, grandsons, and descendants of Dharma, the lineage of Dharma was greatly expanded.
I shall proclaim the names of those remaining younger daughters:
Sambhūti, Anasūyā, Smṛti, Prīti, and Kṣamā.
O best of the twice-born, Saṃnati, Satyā, Ūrjā, and Khyāti were likewise;
and he had two highly fortunate sons, Mātariśvan and Satyavān.
Then Svāhā is to be known as the tenth, and Svadhā is remembered as the eleventh;
these were given by Dakṣa to the sages of purified souls.
I shall now tell you of those who were the sons of Marīci and the others: Saṃbhūti was the wife of Marīci, and she gave birth to the sage Kaśyapa.
Smṛti was the wife of Aṅgiras, and she likewise gave birth to daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati.
Likewise, Anasūyā bore to Atri three stainless sons:
Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya.
O twice-born one, from that Agni— who is the presiding deity of fire, the son of Brahmā, and the first-born— Svāhā obtained three sons of noble vigor.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Śuci, and also Jalāśin—
there are forty-five others in their lineage.
And these fires are said to be the father and his three sons;
thus, forty-nine fires are proclaimed.
The Pitṛs, who were created by Brahmā and described to you by me, from them was born Svadhā; she gave birth to Menā and likewise Dhāriṇī.
O best of beings, hear from me how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-born One to "create progeny," brought forth all living creatures.
For in the beginning, the sage Dakṣa created all beings by means of the mind alone—
the gods, the ṛṣis, the gandharvas, the asuras, and likewise the pannagas.
O twice-born one, when those [beings] born from his mind did not multiply,
that sage Prajāpati, having reflected for the sake of creation, [proceeded further].
Desiring to create various offspring through the very law of sexual union,
he married Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa.
We have heard that Dakṣa begot sixty daughters by Vīraṇī;
he gave ten to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Twenty-seven [verses] are for Soma, four for Ariṣṭanemi,
two for Bahuputra, and likewise two for Aṅgiras.
Two [daughters] were born to the wise Kṛśāśva; hear from me about their offspring:
Viśvā gave birth to the Viśvedevas, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas.
In the Muhūrta named Marutvatī, the Marutvants are remembered as the Vasus; in Bhānu, the Bhānus are the gods; and in Muhūrtā, the gods born of the Muhūrtas [are the presiding deities].
From Lambā was born the one named Ghoṣa; Jāmī gave birth to Nāgavīthī;
and from Arundhatī was born everything pertaining to the realm of the earth.
And from Saṃkalpā, O high-minded one, was born a son named Saṃkalpa;
as for those gods who have many riches and vital breaths, with Jyotis at their head—
The Vasus are declared to be eight; hear their names from me:
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dharma, Anila, and Anala.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus;
their sons and grandsons are by the hundreds and thousands.
Many offspring have been mentioned, as well as his sons by the thousands.
Now hear from me the names of those who were the wives of Kaśyapa: Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, and Khasā.
O knower of dharma, Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, and Muni— listen now to me regarding their offspring.
Twelve beautiful sons were born to Kaśyapa by Aditi;
I shall name them for you—listen as I speak.
Bharga, Aṃśu, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Vivasvat, O high-minded one. (NsP 5.51)
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as Indra, and Viṣṇu is said to be the twelfth;
we have heard that two sons were born to Diti from Kaśyapa.
Hiraṇyākṣa, who possessed a massive body and was slain by the Boar,
and Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was slain by the Man-Lion.
Furthermore, many other Daityas and Dānavas, the sons of Danu, were born;
likewise, from Kaśyapa, the Gandharvas were born of Ariṣṭā.
Then, on Surasā, the sage Kaśyapa begot many hosts of Vidyādharas; indeed, he procreated those [beings] upon Surabhī.
To Vinatā were born two renowned sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa;
of these, Garuḍa became the vehicle of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Out of affection, Aruṇa became the charioteer of the Sun and his mount.
Now learn from me of the six sons born to Tāmrā from Kaśyapa. NsP_5.57 //
Horses, camels, donkeys, elephants, gayals,
and deer were likewise born from Krodhā, as were those wicked species that exist upon the earth.
From Irā were born trees, creepers, climbing plants, and the species of hemp;
from Khasā came the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, and likewise from Muni, the Apsarases.
The twenty-seven great nāgas who are the sons of Kadrū, who are venomous biters with fierce poison, are said to be the wives of Soma, sharing his vows.
O twice-born one, the sons of those wives were the great beings beginning with Budha;
these were the sixteen offspring of Ariṣṭanemi’s wives in this world.
The four Vidyuts are remembered as the daughters of the wise Bahuputra;
they were the eminent sons of Pratyaṅgiras, sages honored by the seers.
The gods and the sages are the sons of the divine seer Kṛśāśva;
indeed, at the end of a thousand yugas, these very same beings are born once again.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been proclaimed according to the dharma of the Lord Narasiṃha, who abides in his established state.
O Brahmin, these manifestations have been proclaimed by me to you;
I have also described to you the lineage of the offspring of Dakṣa’s daughters.
One who possesses faith should recollect this; he shall come to possess a noble lineage.
I have related to you in brief the primary and secondary creations for the sake of the expansion of creation.
Those men who, devoted to Viṣṇu, always recite this, O twice-born ones, become pure.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Account of Creation," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 5)
Sūta said: O twice-born one, I have related to you the creation of this world by Viṣṇu,
and how the gods, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and others were born from that Great Soul.
Regarding that which you previously asked me in the presence of the sages— namely,
how Vasiṣṭha came to be the son of Mitra and Varuṇa.
I shall now relate this ancient narrative concerning merit;
listen with a one-pointed mind, O Bharadvāja, especially so.
He who knows the reality of the meaning of all phenomena, the best among those who know all the Vedas,
one who has reached the further shore of all sciences, was the Prajāpati named Dakṣa.
By him, thirteen auspicious daughters with lotus-like eyes, endowed with all the auspicious marks, were given to Kaśyapa.
I shall now declare their names; listen to me:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Muhūrtā, Siṃhikā, and Muni.
Irā, Krodhā, Surabhi, Vinatā, Surasā, Khasā,
Kadrū, and Saramā, who is known as the dog of the gods.
These daughters of Dakṣa he gave to Kaśyapa;
among them, O twice-born one, the eldest and most excellent was Aditi by name.
Aditi gave birth to twelve sons whose splendor was equal to that of fire;
I shall state their names—listen as I speak them.
By these [deities] this day and night always proceed in succession:
Bhaga, Aṃśu, Aryaman, Mitra, and likewise Varuṇa.
O Great-minded One, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vivasvat,
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as Indra, and Viṣṇu is recorded as the twelfth.
And these twelve Ādityas both scorch and cause rain;
and his middle son is named Varuṇa by name.
Known as Lokapāla, he is celebrated in the western quarter;
he shines in the direction of the western ocean.
There stands a glorious mountain named Jātarūpamaya,
possessing peaks composed of every kind of jewel and endowed with flowing streams of mineral ores.
The auspicious Śaileśa mountain shines, composed of various jewels,
with its great caves and grottoes resounding with the roars of lions and tigers.
Frequented by siddhas and gandharvas in various secluded lands,
when that sun has departed, the world is filled with darkness.
On its peak is a great, divine, auspicious, and beautiful palace made of Jāmbūnada gold,
constructed by Viśvakarman with pillars made of jewels.
There was a city named Viśvāvatī, flourishing with all means of enjoyment;
in it dwelt the Āditya Varuṇa, blazing with his own splendor.
Appointed by Brahmā himself, he protects all these worlds while being worshipped by Gandharvas as well as by hosts of Apsarases.
Once Varuṇa, his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments,
went to the forest accompanied by Mitra.
In the auspicious and delightful Kurukṣetra, which is always frequented by Brahman-sages,
endowed with various flowers and fruits, and crowded with various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having taken refuge at that sacred ford, which abounds in flowers, fruits, and water, where the hermitages of sages with sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) are seen.
Wearing garments of bark and black antelope skins, they were practicing supreme austerity;
there, in a certain region of the forest, was a beautiful pool with pure water.
It was overgrown with many shrubs and creepers, frequented by various birds,
covered by various groves of trees, and adorned with lotus ponds.
There is a lake known as Pauṇḍarīka, frequented by fish and tortoises;
then the two brothers, the gods Mitra and Varuṇa, wandering at will as forest-dwellers, arrived at that place.
Then, in that secluded forest, those two beheld the excellent Apsaras Urvaśī,
that lady of beautiful countenance, bathing together with her companions,
singing and laughing, and feeling entirely at ease.
Gaurī has a luster like the interior of a lotus, with glossy black hair;
her large eyes are like lotus petals, her lips are red, and she speaks softly.
With teeth as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, closely set and even;
with beautiful eyebrows, a fine nose, a lovely face, and a handsome forehead, she was wise and high-minded.
With subtle and well-proportioned limbs like a lioness, she has full thighs, hips, and breasts;
she is skilled in sweet speech, slender-waisted, and possesses a charming smile.
Holding a red lotus in her hand, slender-limbed, with beautiful feet and endowed with modesty,
the young maiden resembles the full moon and moves with the gait of an elephant in rut.
Having seen her form— with its laughter, dance, smiles, and grace— those two gods were filled with wonder.
And by a gentle breeze, cool, fragrant, and accompanied by the songs of intoxicated bees and the cries of male cuckoos; (6.32)
O best of sages, both of them were pierced by Urvaśī’s sweet song in a melodious voice and by her sidelong glance; then,
due to the curse of Nimi, they departed from their own bodies.
"O Vasiṣṭha, you are the son of Mitra and Varuṇa," so said the Viśvedevas upon their arrival;
for one-third of that seed had fallen into the lotus, according to the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā). Thus it was said regarding Vasiṣṭha.
The seed divided into three ways: upon the lotus, on the ground, and in the water.
Upon the lotus was born Vasiṣṭha, that best of sages;
on the ground Agastya came into being; and in the water, the highly effulgent Matsya.
Born there, the wise Vasiṣṭha was in the jar, while Agastya was in the water as a fish;
for that semen of Mitra and Varuṇa fell equally upon those three places.
At that very time, however, Urvaśī departed for heaven;
having approached those sages, the two gods returned once more to their own hermitage,
while the twins continued to perform intense and supreme austerity.
Desiring to attain the supreme, eternal light through austerity,
those two best of gods were performing penance when Brahmā approached them and spoke as follows.
O gods Mitra and Varuṇa, you who possess sons and great splendor,
there shall indeed be for you once again the Vaiṣṇava perfection.
"Remain now in your respective offices, with the world as your witness.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā vanished; the two of them remained in their respective offices.
Thus, O Brahmin, have I told you of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha’s and the wise Agastya’s status as the sons of Mitra and Varuṇa.
This narrative concerning Pūṃsīya belongs to Varuṇa and destroys all evil.
Any men who, desiring sons and observing pure vows, listen to this, will obtain sons before long; of this there is no doubt.
The best of the twice-born who constantly recites this during offerings to the gods and the ancestors,
his deities and progenitors go to supreme bliss, being fully satisfied.
That person who, having risen early in the morning, should constantly hear this,
rejoices happily upon the earth and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus has this ancient narrative been told by me, as proclaimed by those who know the Vedas;
whoever shall read or always hear it, being purified, goes straightway to the world of Hari.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Puṃsavana," in the glorious Nārasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 6)
The venerable Bharadvāja said:
"O Sūta, tell me this which was previously indicated by you: how was death conquered by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya?"
Sūta said: O Bharadvāja, listen to this great narrative from me;
let these sages also listen as I relate this ancient history.
At the highly meritorious Kurukṣetra, at the excellent hermitage of Vyāsa’s seat,
[they approached] the best of sages, the seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, as he sat there.
Having performed his ablutions and his silent recitations, surrounded by the disciples of the sage,
he was a knower of the true essence of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, and an expert in all the scriptures.
Having prostrated according to the proper rule, the most righteous Śuka,
with palms joined in reverence, questioned him regarding this very matter.
"Regarding that which we have been asked by you here in the presence of the sages,
[we shall speak] as a devotee of Narasiṃha who has made his dwelling at a sacred ford."
Śrī Śuka said:
"O father, tell me now how death was conquered by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya; I desire to hear this from you."
Vyāsa said:
O child of great intelligence, listen as I shall relate to you how death was conquered by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
"Let these sages listen, and let my disciples also listen, as this great and supreme narrative is now being told by me."
To Bhṛgu, by Khyāti, was born a son named Mṛkaṇḍu;
and the wife of that high-souled Mṛkaṇḍu was indeed named Sumitrā.
To her, who was knowledgeable in the Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, and intent on serving her husband,
was born a son, the high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya.
The highly fortunate grandson of Bhṛgu, though still a child, was possessed of great intelligence;
having performed his rites there, the boy grew up as a favorite of his father.
As soon as he was born, a certain seer declared:
"When his twelfth year is completed, his death will occur."
O Great-minded One, upon hearing that, his mother and father became sorrowful; their hearts were consumed with grief as they gazed upon him.
Nevertheless, his wise father then performed all the rites for him with effort at the proper time; having been initiated, he [the son] resided in the house of his guru.
He remained engaged in the study of the Vedas, intent on serving his teacher;
having mastered the Vedas and the Shastras, he returned home once again.
Having paid homage at the feet of his parents with humility,
the wise and great sage Mārkaṇḍeya remained there in that house.
Beholding that high-souled one, who was possessed of true wisdom and discernment,
his mother and father there were deeply afflicted by grief.
Seeing them fallen into such distress, the high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya spoke these words there: "For what reason is there such sorrow?"
O mother, you always do this together with my wise father;
you ought to tell me the cause of my sorrow as I ask you.
Thus addressed by her son, the mother of that great-souled one related everything that Āgamī had said.
Having heard that, the sage spoke again to his mother and father:
"O mother, you must not feel even the slightest bit of grief along with your father."
"O sir, I shall overcome death through asceticism; there is no doubt in this.
I shall perform such penance that I may become long-lived. (NsP 7.23)
Having spoken thus and consoled his parents,
he went to the forest named Vallīvaṭa, which was frequented by various sages.
There, the high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya beheld his own grandfather Bhṛgu, the knower of dharma, seated together with the sages.
Having saluted the sages according to the proper custom,
that righteous and self-controlled man stood before them with his palms joined in reverence.
Then, seeing that his young grandson’s life had come to an end,
the high-minded Bhṛgu spoke to the illustrious child Mārkaṇḍeya.
"Why have you come here, my son? Is all well with your father, your mother, and your kinsmen? What is the reason for your arrival?"
Thus addressed by Bhṛgu, the high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya then related to him the entire instruction of Ādeśin.
Having heard the words of his grandson, Bhṛgu spoke again:
"O one of great intelligence, this being so, what action do you intend to perform?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I now desire to conquer death, which carries away all beings;
I have come to you for refuge, so tell us the means to achieve that."
Bhṛgu said:
"O son, without propitiating Nārāyaṇa through great austerity, who would be able to conquer death? Therefore, worship him with austerity."
Go with devotion for refuge to that infinite, unborn Viṣṇu, the infallible Supreme Person, the beloved of his devotees, and the best among the gods.
O child, it was to that very Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment, that the sage Nārada formerly went for refuge through great asceticism.
O highly fortunate one, by his grace, Nārada, the son of Brahmā,
having quickly conquered old age and death, prospers happily with long life.
O child, apart from that lotus-eyed Janārdana, who is the Man-lion (Nārasiṃha),
what man could effect the warding off of the power of death?
Constantly go for refuge to that infinite, unborn Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, the victorious one, the Lord of Śrī, Govinda, the Lord of the cows, the God.
O child, if you always worship Narasiṃha, the Great God, you will constantly conquer death; there is no doubt about this.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by his grandfather Bhṛgu,
the greatly resplendent Mārkaṇḍeya spoke again to his own grandfather with humility.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O dear one, you have described Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, as the one to be propitiated.
But how and where, O Teacher, must I perform the worship of Acyuta?"
By this, he will indeed be pleased with me and will immediately remove my death.
Bhṛgu said:
"O child, having installed Keśava at Bhadravaṭa on that river known as the Tuṅgabhadrā which flows from the Sahya mountain,"
Worship the Lord of the World with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order,
having placed the collection of senses within the heart and restraining the mind according to reality.
O child, meditating with a one-pointed mind upon the Lord of Gods in the lotus of the heart— He who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace— practice the twelve-syllable mantra.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva!
For the Soul of the Universe becomes pleased with one who recites this mantra of the God of Gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, by which he shall ward off death.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to him and then departed for the forest of asceticism.
On the excellent bank of the Bhadrā, which rises from the foot of the Sahya mountain,
there is a place filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with diverse flowers.
In that place, which was filled with thickets, bamboos, and creepers, and crowded with various groups of sages,
he installed Viṣṇu and worshipped him in due order with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya worshipped the Lord of Gods;
having worshipped Hari there, he performed most difficult austerities.
There, the sage remained without food for one year, unwearied;
and when the day close to the time mentioned by his mother had arrived, that high-minded one [remained there].
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and likewise performed the worship of Viṣṇu,
one should withdraw the collection of senses into the heart with a purified inner self.
Having assumed the svastika posture and performed the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma),
the wise one, by the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*, causes the heart-lotus to blossom.
In the center of that, having arranged the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire in their proper order,
one should establish there the eternal seat (pīṭha) of Hari.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, who wears yellow garments and holds the conch, discus, and mace,
with the flowers of devotion, one should then fix the mind upon Him.
Meditating upon Hari in the form of Brahmā, he then uttered the mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva."
Vyāsa said: As the wise Mārkaṇḍeya was meditating in this manner,
his mind became firmly fixed upon that very Lord of gods, the Master of the world.
Then, at the command of Yama, the messengers of Yama arrived there with nooses in their hands; however, they were struck down by the messengers of Viṣṇu as they sought to lead him away.
Being struck by spears, they then departed, leaving the twice-born one behind, saying, "We shall go back; death itself will come."
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"Where the name of our Lord, the Protector of the World, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is heard—
who there is Yama, or Death, or Time, the best among those who reckon?"
Vyāsa said: Death himself came into the presence of the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya and wandered about, suspecting him to be an attendant of Viṣṇu.
Raising their iron clubs quickly, those servants of Viṣṇu stood firm, resolved:
"By the command of Viṣṇu, we shall slay Death this very day."
Then the high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya, his mind dedicated to Viṣṇu,
bowed down and offered praise to Janārdana, the God of gods.
With that well-spoken hymn which had been uttered by Viṣṇu himself into the ear of the high-souled one,
he praised Mādhava with a devout mind.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-eyed, the lotus-navelled, the ancient one, Hṛṣīkeśa; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in Govinda, the lotus-eyed, the infinite, the unborn, and the imperishable Keśava; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, sun-colored and beyond the senses;
what can death do to me? O Dāmodara!
I have taken refuge in the Lord who bears the conch and the discus, the imperishable one who conceals his true form;
what can death do to me? (NsP 7.66)
I have taken refuge in Vārāha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, Janārdana, and Mādhava; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Puruṣa, the meritorious Puṣkara, the seed of security, the Lord of the world, and the Protector of the worlds; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Great Soul, the self of all beings, the source of the universe, who is not born from a womb; he is the universal form—what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the thousand-headed God, the eternal, who is both manifest and unmanifest, the Great Yoga; what can death do to me?
Having heard this hymn uttered by that great-souled one,
Death departed from there, tormented by the messengers of Viṣṇu.
Thus was Death conquered by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya;
when the lotus-eyed Nṛsiṃha is propitiated, nothing is difficult to attain.
This meritorious and auspicious hymn to Mṛtyuñjaya, which pacifies death,
was indeed spoken by Viṣṇu himself for the benefit of Mārkaṇḍeya.
For that man who, being self-controlled and pure, recites this with devotion three times a day,
there shall be no untimely death, as his mind is fixed on Acyuta.

Having meditated upon the ancient Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, the eternal primordial God, shining even more brilliantly than the sun within the center of the heart-lotus, that yogi has conquered death at that very moment.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Mārkaṇḍeya’s Victory over Death," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
Śrī Vyāsa said:
Mortality and his servants, having been tormented by the messengers of Viṣṇu,
went to their own king to report the matter and wailed bitterly.
The servants of Death said:
"Listen, O King, to our words which we speak before you.
At your command, we went and stationed Death at a distance."
And [he went] into the presence of the Brahmin Bhṛgu’s grandson, O best of beings,
who was meditating with one-pointed mind upon some deity.
O Mahāmati, we were all unable to go to his side;
meanwhile, we were struck by men of massive stature wielding clubs.
Seeing that we had turned back, Death went there again;
having reviled us, he was struck there with clubs by those men.
Thus, O Lord, we ourselves are truly unable to bring that brahmin, who is established in asceticism, here along with Death.
Therefore, O illustrious one, tell me what is the Brahman of a Brāhmaṇa;
which god does the wise man meditate upon, and who are they by whom we have been slain?
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by all the servants and by Death, O high-minded one,
the immensely wise Yama, son of Vivasvat, meditated for a moment and then spoke.
Yama said: "Listen, all you servants, as well as Death and the others, to my words.
I shall proclaim this truth, the knowledge derived from the path of yoga."
The highly fortunate and great-minded Mārkaṇḍeya, the grandson of Bhṛgu,
having realized that his own time had come today, departed with the desire to conquer death.
Following the path taught by Bhṛgu, that wise man performed supreme austerity,
propitiating Hari while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.
With a one-pointed mind, he constantly meditates on Keśava within his heart while engaged in yoga; O servants, he is a sage indeed.
"O servants, I see no other power for that great sage than the strength of his initiation into the meditation on Hari when his time has come."
When the lotus-eyed Lord, who is ever affectionate toward his devotees, dwells within the heart,
who indeed, beholding him as Viṣṇu himself, would not take refuge in Keśava?
Those men by whom you have been severely struck are indeed [servants] of Viṣṇu;
henceforth, you must not go where the Vaiṣṇavas reside.
I do not consider being beaten there by those great-souled ones to be remarkable;
rather, it is your life itself that is remarkable, having been granted by the compassionate yakṣas.
Who would dare to look upon that Brahmin who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa?
And as for the effort made by you great sinners to bring Mārkaṇḍeya, the beloved of Hari— it was not a wise thing to do.
By my command, you must not go near those men who worship Narasiṃha, the Great God.
Śrī Vyāsa said: Having thus addressed his servants and having looked at Mṛtyu standing before him, as well as the person staying in hell who was being tormented, Yama [spoke].
Endowed with supreme compassion and especially with devotion to Viṣṇu, he spoke these words for the sake of favoring living beings; listen to them.
To one being cooked in hell, Yama said:
"Why was the god Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, not worshipped by you?"
If even water cannot be obtained when there is a lack of material goods, why was that Lord—
who gives his own world— not worshipped by you?
Narasiṃha, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose eyes resemble lotuses—
he who grants liberation to men through mere remembrance— has he not been worshipped by you?
Having spoken thus to all the denizens of hell, Yama Vaivasvata himself, endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, spoke again to his servants: NsP_8.24.
The imperishable Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, spoke thus to Nārada,
having constantly heard it from other perfected beings (siddhas) devoted to Viṣṇu.
Out of affection for you, I shall proclaim this unsurpassed word of Hari;
O servants, all of you listen with devotion for the sake of instruction, bowing down before Hari.
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa!"— whoever remembers me thus constantly,
I lift them out of hell, just as a lotus rises having pierced through the water.
"O lotus-eyed one, Lord of Gods, Narasiṃha, Trivikrama!
May you rescue him who has come to you for refuge, saying, 'I have reached you for protection.'"
"I have come to you for refuge, O God of gods, Janārdana"—
whosoever has thus sought refuge, I deliver him from suffering.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words spoken by Hari and by Yama, the denizens of hell cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Narasiṃha! (8.30)
To whatever extent the denizens of hell chant the name of Hari here,
to that same extent they carry devotion for Hari and spoke this:
The denizens of hell said: Oṃ, homage to that Blessed One, the great-souled Keśava, by the chanting of whose name the fire of hell is instantly extinguished. (NsP 8.32)
Salutation to the God who is dear to his devotees, to the Protector, to Hari;
to the Lord of the worlds, to the Peaceful One, to the Lord of sacrifice, to the Primordial Form.
Homage to you, the infinite and immeasurable Narasiṃha;
homage to the Teacher Nārāyaṇa, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Salutations again and again to the one who loves the Vedas, to the Great One, to the one of great valor;
salutations to the Boar-form, the inconceivable, the limb of the Vedas, and the upholder of the earth.
Homage always to the radiant one, homage again and again to the Brāhmaṇa;
homage to the dwarf, the possessor of great knowledge, who upholds the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Salutations to you, the protector of the Vedas, who are skilled in binding Bali;
salutations to Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, the all-pervading Supreme Self.
Salutations to you, the four-armed, the pure one, whose substance is purity;
salutations to Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, the bringer of destruction to the wicked kṣatriyas.
Salutations to you, the great-souled one, the end of Rāvaṇa, for the sake of Rāma;
lift us up, O Govinda, we who are foul-smelling; salutations be to you!
Vyāsa said:
When Viṣṇu had been thus glorified with devotion by the denizens of hell,
that infernal torment then vanished for those great-souled ones.
All of them assume the form of Kṛṣṇa, adorned with divine garments,
their limbs anointed with divine perfumes, and decorated with divine ornaments.
Having placed them upon divine celestial chariots and having threatened the messengers of Yama, the attendants of Hari led them to the abode of Keśava.
And when all those in the hells had been led away by the attendants of Hari to the world of Viṣṇu, Yama then again paid homage to Hari.
I always bow down to that divine Narasiṃha, my guru, by the chanting of whose name even those in hell have gone to the abode of Keśava.
Salutations again and again even to those who offer obeisance to that Narasiṃha Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
Seeing that the fierce fire of hell had become tranquil and that all the mechanical instruments and such were overturned,
Yama himself then set his mind to speak to his own messengers once more for the sake of instruction.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Song of Yama," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 8)
Śrī Vyāsa said:
Beholding his own servant with a noose in hand, Yama indeed whispers into his ear:
"Avoid those who have taken refuge in Madhusūdana; I am the master over other mortals, but certainly not over the Vaiṣṇavas."
I have been appointed as Yama by the Creator, who is honored by the hosts of immortals, to oversee what is beneficial and harmful for the world;
I govern those mortals who turn their backs on Hara and Śiva, while I pay homage to those prostrate at the feet of Hari.
I too desire a happy rebirth, O Vāsudeva, for my inner self is established in the Bhāgavata;
yet I am subject to the slaying of Madhu and am not independent, for Kṛṣṇa has power even over my restraint.
For one who is turned away from the Blessed One, there is no accomplishment; that poison becomes nectar—this is not so.
Even if it were being smelted here for a hundred years, iron never attains the state of gold.
For the moon, though its luster is marred by a hare, never ceases to be nor does it ever lose its nature as the moon;
and likewise, a person whose mind is fixed on the Blessed Lord Hara shines brilliantly, even if he is exceedingly impure.
Even after thoroughly investigating the principles of the world, there is no attainment without the worship of the Blessed One;
therefore, for the sake of liberation from the heat of worldly existence, remember those two feet of Hari, which bestow the very firm grace of the Preceptor of the Gods.

Having obtained this auspicious human state through hundreds of virtuous deeds, one who delights in the objects of the senses for their sake in vain does not cultivate the path to liberation; it is like burning sandalwood quickly for the sake of ashes.

Salutations to the First-born, whose lotus feet are constantly worshipped by the lords of the gods with hands folded like buds; he who, for the sake of unimpeded progress, takes birth in this world for the sake of the Eternal One.
Whoever recites or hears this meritorious *Yamāṣṭaka* is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, this supreme speech of Yama, which increases devotion to Hari, has now been told by me to you;
I shall further relate the ancient story of what was performed in the past by the grandson of Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 9.
Śrī Vyāsa said:
Having thus conquered his own death through austerity, the high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya, whose vows were praised, went to the house of his father.
Having performed the marriage according to dharma, specifically following the particular instruction of Bhṛgu,
he begot a son named Vedaśiras in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having worshipped Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, who is free from affliction, with sacrifices;
having honored the ancestors with a śrāddha rite; and having gratified guests with the gift of food.
Having reached Prayāga and bathed again in that most excellent sacred ford,
the immensely radiant Mārkaṇḍeya performed austerities at the foot of a banyan tree.
Desiring to behold that deity by whose grace he had formerly conquered his own death, he performed supreme austerity.
Subsisting on air for a long time, drying his body through asceticism,
the highly effulgent and wise Mārkaṇḍeya once [did this].
Having propitiated the god Mādhava with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
he stood before Him with a focused mind, recollecting Him in his heart,
and praised the one who has the Garuda as His banner and holds the conch, discus, and mace in His hands.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: I bow to Viṣṇu, the ancient Puruṣa— Nara, Nṛsiṃha, the Lord of Men, Acyuta, with long arms and eyes as broad as lotuses, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the lords of the earth.

I bow to Govinda, the Lord of the universe, whose abode is the ocean of milk; who holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand, who is worshipped by hosts of sages, the husband of Śrī, the upholder of prosperity, the Sovereign, the Supreme Lord, and possessed of infinite splendor.

With devotion, I bow to Hari, the unborn, the most excellent, the destroyer of the suffering of beings, the Guru, the Ancient One, the Supreme Person, the Lord, who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns, the Infallible, the Primordial Ādhamava.

I bow to Hari, the witness of the deeds of the three worlds, the lord of the earth, the lord of the world, and the lord of creatures; the supreme goal of the meritorious, the foremost even among the foremost, and the ultimate cause.

In ancient times, the Lord Keśava, the primordial creator, indeed lay upon the ocean of milk, which is an infinite storehouse of enjoyments; I bow down to that Śrīnivāsa, who is moistened by the water of a mere droplet from the waves of the Ocean of Milk.

I bow constantly to that great god Viṣṇu, the enemy of Mura, who assumed the form of Narasiṃha, who brought about the end of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and who removes the suffering of all the worlds; I bow perpetually to him.

I perpetually bow with devotion to Janārdana, who is infinite, unmanifest, beyond the senses, all-pervading, and who abides by himself in his own respective forms; he who is always saluted even by the masters of yoga.

I bow to Hari, the Lord who is dear to his devotees— the one blissful, stainless, and conscious Self, the abode of Vṛndāvana worshipped by yogis alone, subtler than the subtlest, undecaying, and imperishable.
Śrī Vyāsa said: At the conclusion of this hymn, an incorporeal voice spoke to the highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya, who was established in asceticism at the sacred ford.
O Brahmin, why do you weary yourself for one who is not even seen? [Only] when you have performed ablutions in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) will Mādhava appear.
Thus addressed, the high-minded one, having bathed in all the sacred fords, said:
"By repeatedly bathing in every sacred ford, the bath is indeed accomplished.
Tell me that out of affection; who you are, he you are—salutations be to you!"
Vāc said:
"O best of Brahmins, O observer of noble vows, praise the Lord Nārāyaṇa with this hymn;
otherwise, you shall not obtain the fruit of all the sacred fords."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Blessed One, tell me that very hymn which bestows the fruit of sacred fords (tīrtha),
by the recitation of which one may obtain the entire fruit of bathing in all the sacred fords.
Speech said: Victory, victory to you, O God of gods! Victory to you, Mādhava Keśava!
Victory to you, lotus-petal-eyed one! Victory to you, Govinda, Lord of the cows!
Victory, victory to Padmanābha! Victory to Vaikuṇṭha and Vāmana!
Victory to Padma and Hṛṣīkeśa! Victory to Dāmodara and Acyuta!
Victory to you, O infinite Lord of Padmā; victory, O Teacher of the World!
Victory to you, O wielder of the conch and mace; victory to you, the Boar who upholds the earth!
Victory, O Lord of Sacrifice, Varāha! Victory, O Upholder of the Earth, Protector of the World!
Victory, O Lord of Yoga, Knower of Yoga! Victory, O Originator of Yoga!

Victory to you, O initiator of yoga! Victory to you, O initiator of dharma! Victory, victory to you who have performed what is dear! O Lord of sacrifice, victory to you, O limb of sacrifice! NsP_10.24 //
Victory to you, O venerable one honored by the virtuous twice-born; victory to you, O bestower of perfection upon Nārada!
Victory to you, O abode of the meritorious; victory to you, O vessel of the Vedas!
Victory, victory to you, O four-armed one! Victory, O God! Victory to you, the bringer of fear to the Daityas!
Victory, O omniscient one, O soul of all! Victory, O Śaṅkara, O eternal one!
Victory to you, O Viṣṇu, Great God! Victory to you eternally, O Adhokṣaja!
Grant your grace, O Lord of Gods, and reveal today your own form.
Vyāsa said: When this had been thus proclaimed by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya,
the Blessed Lord Janārdana, clad in yellow garments, appeared.
Holding the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands, adorned with all ornaments,
the eternal Viṣṇu illuminates all directions with his splendor.
Upon suddenly seeing him— the sight of whom he had long desired—
that descendant of Bhṛgu, submissive through devotion, prostrated himself on the ground with his head.
Falling down and rising up again and again, the high-minded one,
with his limbs intact and his hands joined in prayer, stood before Govinda and offered praise.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

"Homage be to you, O God of gods, O Great-Minded One, O Great-Body, O Great-Wise One, O Mahādeva, O You of Great Renown! O You whose pair of feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Candra, and Rudra; O You who hold the glorious lotus in Your hand; O You who have crushed the bodies of the Daityas; O You upon whose entire body the coils of Ananta are spread as a couch; O You whose true nature of liberation is incessantly meditated upon by Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, and other yogis whose eyes are fixed on the tip of their noses."
His divine glory is sung day after day by gandharvas, vidyādharas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and kimpuruṣas.
O Nṛsiṃha, Nārāyaṇa, Padmanābha, Govinda, dweller in the cave of Govardhana, Lord of Yogins, Lord of Gods, Lord of Waters, Great Lord! NsP_10.35 //

O bearer of yoga, bearer of the great illusion, bearer of knowledge, bearer of glory, bearer of fame, abode of the three qualities, bearer of the three principles, bearer of the three sacrificial fires! NsP_10.36 //
He is the possessor of the three Vedas, the one with three abodes, the one who recites the *trisuparṇa* hymn, and the bearer of the triple staff.

O you who shine with a splendor honored like that of glossy clouds, wearing yellow garments, illuminating all directions with the radiance of the gems from your crown, bracelets, armlets, and necklaces; NsP_10.38.
O Madhusūdana, whose cheeks are adorned with earrings of gold and jewels, O you who possess the universal form!

O Lord of the World, Lord of Sacrifice, lover of sacrifice, composed of splendor, lover of devotion, Vāsudeva, you who are to be propitiated for the removal of misfortune, Supreme Person—homage be to you!
Vyāsa said:
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Blessed Janārdana,
the God of gods, with a gracious soul, spoke to Mārkaṇḍeya.
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with you again, my child, by virtue of your great austerity;
O one of great intelligence, through these hymns as well, you are now cleansed of sin."
"Choose a boon, O best of Brahmins; I stand before you as a granter of boons.
O Brahmin, I cannot be easily seen by one who has not performed austerities."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Lord of Gods, I have now achieved my purpose through the sight of you.
O Lord of the World, grant me unwavering and singular devotion to you."
O Blessed One, Mādhava, Śrīpati, Hṛṣīkeśa, if you are pleased with me, grant me long life so that I may worship you for a long time.
The Blessed One said:
Death has been conquered by you previously, and you have obtained long life.
May your devotion to me, the Vaiṣṇava devotion that bestows liberation, remain unwavering.
"O highly fortunate one, this sacred ford shall attain renown by your name;
furthermore, you shall indeed behold me again reclining in yoga within the Ocean of Milk."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one vanished on the spot;
and the righteous Mārkaṇḍeya, too, remained there, meditating upon Madhusūdana.
Worshiping the Lord of the gods of gods, reciting the pure [mantra], and bowing down,
he likewise studies the meritorious Vedas, the Shastras, and all the Puranas.
That best of beings, whose wealth was his asceticism, meditated upon the verses of the sages,
the sacred histories, and the true nature of the ancestors.
Then, at one time, remembering the words spoken by Puruṣottama, that sage of fierce splendor, the most eminent among those who know the scriptures,
while wandering, went to see Hari, the Lord of the gods, across the ocean.

Endowed with diligence through long-term exertion and bearing devotion to Hari, that grandson of Bhṛgu reached the Ocean of Milk and beheld Hari, the Lord of the Gods, asleep upon the coils of the king of serpents.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Life of Mārkaṇḍeya," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 10.
Vyāsa said:
Having prostrated before Hari, the Lord of the World and the teacher of all that is moving and unmoving,
Mārkaṇḍeya offered praise to Him who reclines upon His serpent-couch.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Be gracious, O Blessed Viṣṇu; be gracious, O Supreme Person.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods; be gracious, O You whose banner is Garuḍa.
Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, Lord of Lakṣmī; be gracious, O Upholder of the Earth.
Be gracious today, O Lord of the World; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
Be gracious, O Lord of all gods; be gracious, O lotus-eyed one;
be gracious, O upholder of Mount Mandara; be gracious, O slayer of Madhu.
Be gracious, O beloved of the fortunate; be gracious, O Lord of the world!
Be gracious today, O Mahādeva; be gracious to me, O Keśava!
Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! Victory to the inconceivable! Victory to Viṣṇu! Victory to the imperishable!
Victory to the universe! Victory to the unmanifest! Victory to Viṣṇu! Homage be to you!
Victory, O God! Victory, O Unconquerable One! Victory, O Truth! Victory, O Imperishable One!
Victory, O Time! Victory, O Lord! Victory, O All! Homage be unto You!
Victory, O Lord, Master of Sacrifice! Victory, O All-pervading Lord of the Universe! Victory, O Protector, Lord of Beings! Victory, O All-pervading Lord of All!
Victory to you, O Lord of the Universe, O Protector! Victory to you, O Skillful One; let there be homage to you!
Victory to you, O Infinite One who removes sin! Victory to you, the dispeller of birth and old age!
Victory, O Bhadra, Lord of the exceedingly auspicious! Victory, O Bhadra, homage be to you!
Victory, O granter of desires, descendant of Kakutstha! Victory, O giver of honor, Mādhava!
Victory to you, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods! Victory to you, O Lord of Śrī! Salutations be unto you!
Victory to you, who shine with the hue of saffron! Victory to you, whose eyes are like lotuses!
Victory to you whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste! Victory, O Rāma! Homage be to you!
Victory, O God, Lord of the World! Victory, O Son of Devakī!
Victory to you, O universal teacher, O object of knowledge! Victory to you, O Śambhu; let there be homage to you!

Victory to you, O beautiful one with the luster of a lotus! Victory to you, O beloved of the beautiful woman! Victory to you, O one whose every limb is beautiful! Victory to you, O venerable one; let there be homage to you!
Victory to you, O Giver of All, Lord of All! Victory to you, O Eternal Bestower of Bliss!
Victory to you, O Granter of Desires to devotees! O Sovereign One, homage be unto you!
Homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the one garlanded with lotuses.
O Lord of the World, let there be homage to you; O Vīrabhadra, let there be homage to you.
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, the Master of the universe in four forms;
homage to the God of gods, homage to you, O Nārāyaṇa!
Homage to you, Vāsudeva; homage to you, clad in yellow garments;
homage to you, the Man-Lion; homage to you, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Homage to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and homage to the one whose weapon is the discus;
homage to the auspicious God, and homage to you, O Lord of the World!
Salutations to the one known through the Vedānta; salutations to the infinite Viṣṇu.
Salutations to you, O sovereign of all; salutations to you, O Śrīdhara, O Acyuta.
O Overseer of the World, O Supreme Self worthy of worship by the universe, homage be to you!
You are the mother of all worlds; you alone are the father of the world.
You are the friend and ally of the distressed; you are beloved; you are the great-grandfather;
you are the teacher, you are the refuge, you are the witness, you are the lord, and you are the ultimate resort.
You are the eternal, you are the utterer of *vaṣaṭ*, you are the oblation, and you are the consumer of the oblation;
you are Śiva, you are the Vasu, the Ordainer, you are Brahmā, and you are the Lord of the gods.
You are Yama, you are Ravi, you are Vāyu, you are water, you are the Lord of Wealth;
you are Manu, you are day and night, you are the night, and you are the maker of night;
you are fortitude, you are prosperity, you are splendor, you are patience, and you are the upholder of the earth.
You are the creator and the Lord of the worlds; you are the slayer, O Madhusūdana;
you alone are the protector of the entire universe, O You who encompass all that is moving and unmoving.
You alone, O Supreme Lord, are the instrument, the cause, and the agent;
O Mādhava, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, please deliver me!
O beloved one with eyes like lotus petals, I constantly bow with devotion to you alone, the Supreme Person, reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa as your couch.
O Lord, I bow to your body, marked with the Śrīvatsa, the seed of the universe, dark-hued, lotus-eyed, and the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age.
Lakṣmīdhara, whose limbs were noble, adorned with divine garlands,
possessing a beautiful back and mighty arms, was decorated with exquisite ornaments.
Padmanābha has wide eyes with pupils like lotus petals,
a long and prominent high nose, and resembles a dark blue cloud.
Long-armed, with well-guarded limbs, his chest radiant with a necklace of jewels;
possessing beautiful eyebrows, forehead, and crown, with glossy teeth and lovely eyes.
Hari, the bearer of Śrī, has beautiful arms and lips as red as copper; his earrings blaze with jewels, his neck is well-rounded, his shoulders are broad and full, and he is full of vitality.
He was eternally youthful, with dark, curly hair;
he had high shoulders, a broad chest, and eyes that extended as far as his ears.
To Hari, whose face is like a golden lotus, the abode of Indirā, the Lord, the creator of all worlds, and the remover of all sins; NsP_11.33.
Viṣṇu, the infallible Lord, the infinite Supreme Person, endowed with all auspicious marks and delightful to all sentient beings.
I am born with my mind ever devoted to Nārāyaṇa, who is free from affliction,
the granter of boons, the fulfiller of desires, the beloved, the infinite, the truthful, and the auspicious.
O Viṣṇu, ever compassionate toward your devotees, I bow my head to you always in this terrible, single ocean, turbulent and agitated by the wind.
Upon a couch of infinite splendor, adorned with a thousand hoods,
a beautiful and variegated bed served by a gentle breeze.
Now, in this world, I have beheld you entirely with my mind— you who are served by Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus, and who are embraced by her five arms.
But now, afflicted by great suffering and deluded by your illusion,
[I am lost] where there is but a single body of water, where there is no support, and where all things mobile and immobile have perished.
In the empty, dark, and impassable mire of suffering, which is devoid of any refuge and is perpetually afflicted by cold, heat, old age, disease, grief, thirst, and the like; (NsP_11.40)
"I am greatly afflicted, O Father, for a very long time, O Acyuta;
seized by the planet of grief and delusion, I have been wandering in the ocean of existence."
Today, here in the presence of your lotus feet, I have arrived by destiny;
I am afflicted by suffering in this most terrible and difficult-to-cross single ocean.
Exhausted by long wandering, I have today come to you for refuge;
be gracious, O Viṣṇu of great illusion, lotus-eyed one!
O Source of the Universe, O Wide-Eyed One, O Soul of the Universe, O Origin of the Universe!
Therefore, O Delighter of Your Clan, [look upon] me who have come to you with no other refuge.
Save me, O Kṛṣṇa, out of compassion, for I am distressed and have come to you for refuge;
salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, O ancient Supreme Person!
O You who have the luster of collyrium, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O You who consist of māyā, homage be to You!
Lift me up, O mighty-armed one, for I am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.

O Govinda, O giver of boons, lift me up— me who am helpless, wretched, miserable, and fallen into the ocean of existence, which is a deep abyss difficult to cross, afflicted by suffering, and infested with the great crocodiles of the afflictions; homage be to you!
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, to Hari, and to the Upholder of the Earth!
O God of gods, homage be to you; O Beloved of Śrī, homage be to you!
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, you are compassionate; you are the refuge for those who have no other resort.
Be gracious, O Madhusūdana, toward us who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
I [bow] to You alone—the primordial, ancient Puruṣa, the Lord of the universe, the cause, the infallible Master;
Janārdana, the destroyer of the afflictions of birth and old age, the Lord of the gods, the beautiful husband of Indirā.
I bow to Hari, the eternal Lord— of broad arms, dark and tender, auspicious, with a beautiful face and eyes like lotus petals, his long locks of hair curling like waves, most lovely to behold.
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which is offered to You.
Only those two hands are truly praiseworthy which perform Your worship.
O Govinda, by the chanting of "Vāsudeva," may you take away that sin which has been committed by me throughout thousands of previous births.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, Viṣṇu,
the soul of the universe whose banner bears Garuḍa, being well-pleased, spoke to that sage.
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with your asceticism and your hymn of praise, O Brahmin, descendant of Bhṛgu!
Choose a boon—may it be well with you; I shall grant you whatever boon you request."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Lord of Gods, grant me perpetual devotion to your lotus feet;
if you are pleased with me today, I choose one other boon.
O Lord of Gods, O God, Lord of the World, grant eternal residence in the heavenly realm to whoever constantly praises you with this hymn.
That long life which was granted to me by you in the past while I was performing austerities—
all of that has now become fruitful through the sight of you.
"O Lord of Gods, O Blessed One, I desire to dwell right here, eternally free from birth and death, while worshipping your lotus feet."
The Blessed One said:
"O best of the Bhṛgus, let there be unswerving devotion toward me.
Through devotion, O most virtuous one, liberation shall indeed come to you in due time."
But he who recites this hymn of praise to you in the evening and in the morning,
having established firm devotion toward me, rejoices in my world.
"O best of the Bhṛgus, wherever you may be stationed, whenever you remember me, there I shall come; for I am self-controlled and subject to my devotees."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to that best of sages, Mārkaṇḍeya, Mādhava ceased speaking;
he saw Viṣṇu everywhere, here and there.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you the life story of that wise sage Mārkaṇḍeya, which was told to me by him himself in the past.
Those who daily recite this ancient narrative concerning the grandson of Bhṛgu, out of devotion to Viṣṇu,
are liberated from sin and dwell in the world of Narasiṃha, being honored by devotees.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Life of Mārkaṇḍeya," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 11)
Sūta said: Having heard this nectar-like, meritorious [account] which destroys all sins,
the righteous Śuka, still not satiated, addressed Vyāsa.
Śrī Śuka said:
Oh, how extraordinary is the ascetic practice of the wise Mārkaṇḍeya,
by whom Hari was seen in person and by whom death was conquered!
