"I am not yet satiated, my dear, having heard this meritorious and sin-destroying narrative of Viṣṇu; therefore, tell me something else."
O Great-minded One, tell me that merit which has been proclaimed by the sages for men of firm resolve who do not perform what ought not to be done in this world.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, listen as I describe to you that merit which belongs to men of firm resolve, both in this world and in the next. NsP_12.5 //
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Yama and the high-souled Yamī.
Vivasvat was the son of Aditi; his two sons were of great splendor:
Yama was born, and Yami was also born as the younger sister.
There, in their father’s excellent palace, they both grew up, playing according to their nature, moving about with complete freedom.
Yamī, having approached her brother Yama, spoke to him.
A brother should not desire a sister who desires him;
for what is he to his sister if, as her brother, he does not become her husband?
He should be known as if unreal, and not real in any way,
he who does not protect his own sister, who is without a protector and seeks one.
O best of sages, that man who does not desire his brother— who longs for him as his protector and lord—
is not called a "brother" in this world.
Or perhaps another woman might become his wife; what is the use of her?
But as he gazes [upon her], his sister is consumed by passion for her brother.
Whatever task I desire, you alone must surely desire that very thing;
otherwise, longing for you and deprived of my senses, I shall die.
"O brother, is the suffering of desire indeed unbearable that you do not desire it?
I am being intensely tormented by the fire of desire; O dear one, let me dissolve [into you] without delay."
O beloved, become subject to the will of this woman afflicted by desire; do not delay.
You ought to unite your body with my body.
Yama said: "O sister, what is this dharma you speak of that is loathed by the world?
O auspicious lady, what man of sound mind here would perform such an improper act?"
O beautiful woman, I shall not unite my body with your body;
a brother does not grant his desire to a sister afflicted by passion.
They say that he who approaches his own sister commits a mortal sin;
O auspicious lady, this would be the law for animals belonging to the animal kingdom.
Yamī said:
"Just as our union in one place previously was not blameworthy,
so too this union of ours within the mother's womb is not blameworthy."
"O brother, do you not desire me, though I am unprotected?
The Rākṣasa Nirṛti constantly consorts with my sister."
Yama said:
Even the Self-Existent One might censure a loathsome worldly practice;
yet this world follows that which has been practiced by the Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Therefore, the supreme person should practice blameless dharma and should strive to avoid what is blameworthy; this is the characteristic of dharma.
Whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows it.
"O fortunate one, I consider your words to be exceedingly evil;
they are contrary to all dharmas and especially to the ways of the world."
If there should be someone other than me who is indeed superior to you in beauty and character, rejoice with him; I shall not be your husband.
"O blessed lady, firm in my vows as I am, I do not touch your body with my own,
for the sages declare that he who seizes his sister commits a sin."
Yama said: "I consider such a form as this to be truly rare to behold in this world;
where on earth are both such beauty and such youth established?"
I do not understand your mind; whereon is it established?
You do not desire one who is deluded, though she is endowed with the beauty and virtues of your own self.
Like a creeper clinging to a tree, having truly come for refuge to you,
I, of pure smiles, dwell here embracing you with my arms.
Yama said:
"O fair-hipped goddess with dark eyes, take refuge in another god,
for your mind has fallen into delusion through the infatuation of desire."
O woman of excellent complexion, you shall become the goddess of that god.
Men praise her as the most excellent among all beings, desired by all;
they describe Subhadrā as one whose every limb is beautiful and who is perfectly refined.
Even for that purpose, the very wise will not offer criticism;
O lady of great wisdom, I, firm in my vows, shall feel no remorse.
"O auspicious lady, my mind is stainless and is established in both Viṣṇu and Rudra;
therefore, being firm in my vows and possessed of a righteous mind, I do not desire sin."
Vyāsa said:
Although he was addressed in this manner by her repeatedly, Yama, firm in his vow, did not perform that task; by that [steadfastness], he attained the state of a deity.
For those men of firm resolve who do not commit such evil, they say the fruit is infinite; for them, there shall be the fruit of heaven.
This ancient account concerning Yami, which occurred in the past, is meritorious and removes all sins; it should be heard with a mind free from malice.
The Brahmin who constantly recites this during offerings to the gods and the ancestors,
his forefathers remain fully satisfied and do not enter the abode of Yama.
Whoever recites this constantly shall become free from debt to the ancestors;
he is liberated from the fierce torments of Vaivasvata.

I have related to you this unsurpassed ancient narrative, which is determined by the meaning of the Vedic words, always removes the sins of men—tell me, what else shall I speak to you today? NsP_12.40.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Yamī and Yama," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 12.
Śrī Śuka said:
"O dear one, this wonderful Vedic narrative told by you to me is marvelous;
tell me other meritorious stories that destroy all sins."
I shall relate to you an unsurpassed ancient account,
the conversation between a certain celibate student and a devoted wife.
There was a brahmin named Kaśyapa, known as Nītimān, who had mastered the Vedas,
understood the true meaning of all the śāstras, and was fully proficient in exposition.
Devoted to the duties of his own dharma and turning away from the dharma of others,
he approaches his wife only during her fertile period and is dedicated to the maintenance of the sacred fire.
O illustrious one, having offered oblations into the fire morning and evening, gratifying the twice-born, honoring guests who arrive at his home, and worshipping Narasiṃha; NsP_13.5 //
His wife was highly fortunate, known by the name Sāvitrī;
she was devoted to her husband, illustrious, and dedicated to her husband’s pleasure and welfare.
By the very service of her husband for a long time, that blameless,
auspicious woman, esteemed for her virtues, attained knowledge of what was beyond her sight.
Together with her, that righteous and highly intelligent one, dwelling in Nandigrāma in the Middle Country, remained wise and devoted to his own religious observances.
Now, there was a highly intelligent Brahmin named Yajñaśarman from Kauśala;
he had a virtuous wife known by the name Rohiṇī.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and devoted to the service of her husband,
that blameless woman gave birth to one son from that husband.
Having become one who follows the *yāyāvara* mode of life once his son was born, the wise man then performed the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) for his son after bathing and reciting the sacred mantras.
On the twelfth day, the wise man, having had the auspicious day proclaimed for him, gave him the name Devaśarman according to the prescribed rite.
And he carefully performed the ceremony of going out of the house in the fourth month,
as well as the first feeding of solid food in the sixth month, according to the prescribed rites.
Then, when the year was complete, that knower of dharma performed the tonsure ceremony;
and in the eighth year from conception, he performed the initiation into the vows.
Having been brought up according to the rules, he studied the Veda under his father;
but once a single Veda had been mastered, the father departed to the world of the gods.
When his father had passed away, that wise son was initially distressed along with his mother;
however, being urged by virtuous men, he regained his fortitude.
Having performed the funeral rites for his son, Devaśarman went to excellent holy places such as the Gaṅgā and bathed there according to the prescribed rules.
O high-minded one, having reached that very village where that devoted wife resided,
that renowned celibate student then arrived there.
Having gone on his alms-round and reciting the Veda without weariness,
and performing the fire-rituals, he remained in Nandigrāma.
When her husband had died and her son had gone forth into homelessness, she,
lacking a protector, fell inevitably from sorrow to greater sorrow.
Then, having bathed in the river, the celibate student, restraining his speech, should spread out his own cloth on the ground to dry it while remaining seated in silent recitation.
The crow and the crane, having seized that garment, departed quickly;
seeing them, the brahmin Devaśarman then rebuked them.
Having cast off the excrement upon his garment, they departed because of his rebuke;
however, as they were flying through the sky, he glared at the two birds with rage.
Burned by the fire of his wrath, the two birds fell to the ground;
seeing that the two birds had reached the earth, he was filled with wonder.
Thinking, "There is no one on the surface of the earth who is my equal in asceticism," he went straight to the village to wander for alms.
Wandering among the houses of Brahmins, a celibate student, proud of his asceticism,
O child, entered that house where a devoted wife resided.
Seeing him, even though he was begging for alms, the devoted wife—
having previously understood her husband’s intention and carried out his instruction— remained silent.
She washed his feet again with warm water;
having comforted her husband, she then proceeded to give him alms.
Then the student, his eyes red with anger, desiring to burn the devoted wife by the power of his asceticism, looked at her again and again.
But Sāvitrī, looking at him thus, said to him while smiling: NsP_13.29.
I am neither a crow nor a crane; rather, it was through your anger that those two died on the riverbank today. O wrathful one, if you so desire, take alms from me.
Having been addressed thus by Sāvitrī, he took alms and went before her,
reflecting in his mind upon her power that perceives distant objects.
Having come to the hermitage and carefully placed the alms-bowl in the monastery,
[he should wait] until the devoted wife has eaten and the householder husband has departed.
Returning once more to her home, he spoke to that devoted wife.
The student said:
"O highly fortunate one, explain this to me as I ask it, according to the truth."
"How did your cognition of this distant object become so swift?
Thus addressed by him, that virtuous Sāvitrī, devoted to her husband, replied.
Having come to his house, he spoke to that celibate student who was questioning him:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmin, to that which you ask me."
I shall explain that to you, augmented by one's own duty (*svadharma*):
for women, service to the husband is established as their primary duty.
O Mahāmati, I would always do that very thing and nothing else;
day and night, without doubt, I would satisfy him with faith. (NsP 13.37)
While I was performing it, there arose for me a vision of distant objects;
furthermore, I shall tell you another thing—listen, if you so desire.
His father was a pure Yāyāvara; having studied the Veda under him, and after his father had died, he performed the funeral rites and returned here.
Having abandoned his mother— who is aged, miserable, ascetic,
helpless, and widowed— he remains here constantly devoted only to nourishing his own belly.
O Brahmin, having abandoned her who formerly bore you in her womb, protected you, and cherished you, do you not feel shame as you practice dharma in the forest?
O Brahmin, what would become of you wandering in the forest if you were to abandon that sorrowful woman at home, she by whom, in your childhood, the removal of your impurities was performed?
Because this face of yours was fashioned by your mother, it has become foul-smelling due to her suffering;
since it was prepared by your father as well, this power has arisen.
O evil-minded one of wicked soul, the bird has now been burnt in vain;
in vain was the bath, in vain the pilgrimage site, in vain the recitation, and in vain the oblation.
O Brahmin, he whose mother is deeply distressed lives in vain;
whereas he who, being devoted to his mother, constantly protects her with devotion, truly lives.
O Brahmin, by those supreme men who have fulfilled their mother’s word, everything has been accomplished here and the fruit [of that action] is indeed attained both in the next world and in this one.
They are to be honored and they are to be saluted both in this world and in the next;
therefore, go today to that place where your mother resides.
Protect her while she still lives; her protection is your supreme austerity.
Abandon this anger, which destroys both the seen and the unseen.
"O Kuru, for the sake of the purification of those two birds and for my own purification,
I have related all of this to you exactly as it happened."
"O celibate student, perform [this] if you desire the goal of the virtuous.
Having spoken thus to the son of the twice-born, the devoted wife then fell silent.
He also spoke to Sāvitrī once more, seeking her forgiveness:
"O woman of excellent complexion, forgive me for the sin committed through ignorance."
O illustrious one, devoted to your husband, forgive whatever harm I have done to you by looking at you with anger; it was spoken for your own benefit.
Having gone there, O you of auspicious vows, tell me what deeds must be performed by me so that I may attain a happy rebirth.
Thus addressed by him, that devoted wife also spoke to him as he questioned her:
"Listen to the tasks and duties which I shall describe to you."
O Brahmin, your mother must be supported by you there through the practice of begging for alms; whether here or there, you must also perform an expiation for the two birds.
"The daughter of Yajñaśarman shall become your wife;
take her according to the law, for he will give her to you when you have departed."
"A son shall be born to you from her, one who will increase your lineage;
your livelihood shall be like that of your father, through the wealth of the Yāyāvaras."
Furthermore, when your wife has died, you shall become a *tridaṇḍin*;
by means of the duties of the ascetic stage (*yatyāśrama*) performed according to the instructions,
and through the grace of Narasiṃha, you will attain the station of Viṣṇu.
This which must be cultivated has indeed been told by me to you who asked;
do not consider this to be false, for carry out all my words.
The Brahmin said:
"O devoted wife, I am going this very day for the sake of protecting my mother;
having gone there, O lady of auspicious eyes, I shall carry out all your words."
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, Devaśarman then departed in haste,
having carefully protected his mother and being freed from anger and delusion.
Having performed his marriage and begotten an auspicious son who would continue his lineage,
he— whose wife had died and who had renounced the world— regarded a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
and through the grace of Narasiṃha, he attained supreme perfection.
This power of yours as a devoted wife has been aroused, and the supreme duty is the protection of one's mother;
having struck down the tree of worldly existence and severed its bonds, a human being attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Religious Student," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 13)
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O child of great intelligence; let these disciples also listen to this supreme narrative being told by me, which destroys all sins.
Long ago, a certain excellent brahmin, learned in the Vedas and the Śāstras,
whose wife had died, went to a sacred ford and performed his ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Having performed intense austerities in solitude, free from desire for marriage,
subsisting on alms, he set out on his journey, devoted to silent recitation and ritual bathing.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, the holy Sarasvatī, Vitastā, and Gomatī,
and having reached Gayā while satiating his fathers and grandfathers, he went to Mahendra.

There, too, on the mountain, the high-minded one bathed in the sacrificial pits, beheld the best of the descendants of Bhṛgu, and likewise offered satisfaction to his ancestors; then, departing, he entered the sin-destroying forest.
Having devoutly received upon his head that great, falling torrent from the mountain peak dedicated to Narasimha,
that brahmin then became one whose body was completely purified, as all his sins were destroyed.

Having worshipped with auspicious flowers born of the mountain Ananta, the Infallible One (Acyuta), who is ever stationed on the Vindhya mountain and eternally honored by devotees and the lords of sages, he remained right there, longing for spiritual perfection (siddhi).
Nārasiṃha, pleased by his long-term worship, spoke to that devotee who had fallen into a deep sleep:
"The cause of the destruction of your home was indeed your lack of belonging to any stage of life (āśrama); therefore, O twice-born one, accept the highest stage of life."
"O twice-born one, even if you have mastered the Vedas, I do not grant my favor here to one who is without an āśrama;
nevertheless, O best of men, having observed your steadfastness, I have spoken thus because I am pleased with you."
Having been addressed thus by the Supreme Lord, the twice-born one reflected upon those words with his intellect;
acknowledging the command of Hari in the form of Narasiṃha as insurmountable, he became an ascetic.
Holding the triple staff, the wooden bowl, and the ring of kusha grass in his hands, he stands after bathing in water that removes all evil;
constantly reciting the Sāvitrī mantra which dispels defects, he remembers Hari, the Lord, within his heart.
Having obtained vegetables by any means whatsoever, he was content with alms and dwelt as a forest-dweller;
having worshipped Viṣṇu in the form of Narasiṃha, he constantly meditated in his heart upon the pure, primordial One.

Having settled in a secluded and spacious place upon a seat of kusha grass, one should dissolve within the heart of this [deity] all external qualities of the senses, along with every distinction, into the infinite Blessed Lady.
Having contemplated that which is to be known— the blissful, unborn, vast, consisting of truth, the state of security, and the most excellent—
he abandoned his body therein and became liberated, having the nature of the Supreme Self.
Those who recite this discourse, which is devoted to liberation as it has been told, while remembering Narasiṃha,
obtain the fruit that comes from bathing at the sacred ford of Prayāga and go to the great abode of Hari.

Thus has been told to you, my son, who asked, this ancient, most meritorious, and purifying account—the supreme destroyer of the tree of saṃsāra. Now, tell me what further desired object you wish for.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 14.
Śrī Śuka said:
O Father, I now desire to hear, together with the sages,
about this entire tree of worldly existence by which all this revolves.
"O dear one, you ought to explain this to me, which was previously indicated by you;
for no one else, O illustrious one, knows the characteristics of the ascent through saṃsāra."
Sūta said: Thus addressed by his son, who stood in the midst of his disciples,
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke concerning the characteristics of the tree of worldly existence.
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, all you disciples; my child, listen with a purified mind.
I shall describe the tree of saṃsāra, by which this entire world is enveloped."
Having its origin in the unmanifest (avyakta), it thus arises at the beginning;
it consists of the intellect (buddhi) as its trunk, and has the sense-faculties (indriya) as the hollows of its sprouts.
The great elements are its trunk, and it possesses branches and leaves through specific qualities;
merit and demerit are its beautiful flowers, and the arising of pleasure and pain are its fruits.
The eternal Brahma-tree is the means of subsistence for all beings;
it is both this [world] and the supreme Brahman, for that is the tree of Brahman.
Thus, my dear child, has been described the characteristic of the tree of saṃsāra;
embodied beings who have climbed this tree fall into delusion.
Constantly wandering here in this world, endowed with pleasure and pain,
ordinary mortals for the most part turn their backs on the knowledge of Brahman.
Having severed this, the skillful proceed; those who know Brahman do not [proceed].
O one of great wisdom, neither ritual action nor its performance, nor evil deeds, can sever this.
Having cut and split this [bond] with the supreme sword of knowledge,
they then attain immortality, from which there is no returning again.
Even one firmly bound by the fetters of body and wife is liberated;
knowledge alone is the supreme desired good for men, the means of pleasing Narasiṃha; a man devoid of knowledge is but a beast.
Food, sleep, fear, and sexual intercourse—these are common to humans and animals alike.
Indeed, knowledge is the distinguishing excellence of humans in this world; those devoid of knowledge are equal to animals.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 15.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having climbed the tree of worldly existence, which is bound by hundreds of firm snares of dualities and fettered by sons, wealth, and power, he has fallen into the ocean of birth.
He who is tormented by desire, anger, and greed, as well as by sense objects, and is bound by his own secondary karmas such as the longing for sons, wives, and possessions; ||| NsP_16.2 |||
By what means does he swiftly cross over the difficult-to-cross ocean of existence?
O Father, answer my question: how may his liberation come to be?
The venerable Vyāsa said: Listen, O child of great wisdom, to that which, once known, one shall attain liberation;
I shall declare that divine truth to you, which was heard by Nārada in the past.
Deprived of both dharma and knowledge, those who have reached the terrible Raurava hell in the abode of Yama experience great suffering there due to their own past actions.
Seeing that sinful people had encountered a terrible and great evil,
Nārada went quickly to where the Three-eyed Lord was.
Having prostrated according to the prescribed rites before the god Mahādeva, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, Śaṃkara, the wielder of the trident, Nārada questioned him.
Nārada said:

He who is bound in this world by the great dualities, by desires and enjoyments, both auspicious and inauspicious, by the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest, and is tormented by the six waves; ||| NsP_16.8 |||
"How indeed may one be swiftly liberated from the ocean of death and saṃsāra?
O Blessed One, Śaṅkara, tell me the truth; I wish to hear it."
Having heard those words of Nārada, the three-eyed Śambhu, Hara, with a gracious countenance, spoke to that ṛṣi.
Maheśvara said:
O best of sages, I shall speak of the nectar of knowledge, which is secret and esoteric; listen, for it destroys suffering and removes the fear of all bonds.
By whose Māyā the entire world— the fourfold collection of beings from blades of grass up to the four-faced Brahmā, including all that is moving and unmoving— is plunged into deep sleep.
If anyone awakens through the grace of that Viṣṇu,
he crosses over saṃsāra, which is difficult even for the gods to cross.
Intoxicated by the pride of wealth and power, and turned away from the knowledge of reality,
he sinks like an old cow in the vast mire of saṃsāra.
But for one who binds themselves with actions like a silkworm in its cocoon,
I do not see liberation even in hundreds of millions of births.
Therefore, O Nārada, one should always properly worship Viṣṇu, the imperishable God of all gods, and meditate upon him with a concentrated mind.
He who always meditates upon that Viṣṇu— who is all-pervading, without beginning or end, the primordial source, established within his own self, omniscient, and stainless— is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Vāsudeva— the unborn Viṣṇu, who is free from conceptual construction, spaceless, beyond phenomenal proliferation, and untainted— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon the stainless, supreme, peaceful, and infallible one— the creator of beings, the divine embryo, the all-pervading Viṣṇu— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is liberated from all evil, immeasurable, devoid of characteristics, and the sinless Nirvāṇa— one is released.
By constantly chanting the names of Amṛta, Paramānanda, Sarvapāpavivarjita, Brahmaṇya, Śaṅkara, and Viṣṇu, one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the Lord of Yoga, known as the Ancient One, bodiless, dwelling in the cave of the heart, measureless, and immutable— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is free from the auspicious and the inauspicious, who transcends the six waves, who is all-pervading, inconceivable, and stainless— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is liberated from all dualities, devoid of all suffering, inconceivable, and unborn— one is released.
The nameless and lineage-less, non-dual, supreme fourth state—
by constantly meditating upon that Viṣṇu who dwells within the hearts of all, one is liberated.
By constantly meditating with one-pointed mind upon Viṣṇu— who is formless, whose resolve is truth, who is pure like space, and supreme— one is liberated.
Constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the embodiment of all selves, abiding in his own nature, whose form is the consciousness of the Self, pure, and the single syllable— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is inexpressible, unknowable, beyond the syllable *akṣara* and the like, unborn, unique, and ever-new— one is liberated.

By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the primordial source of the universe, the protector of the universe, the consumer of the universe, the granter of all desires, and the one who transcends the three states— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Hari, Viṣṇu— the destroyer of all suffering, the bringer of all peace, and the remover of all sins— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, who is served by Brahmā and the other gods, by Gandharvas, by sages, by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and by yogis, one is liberated.
The universe is established in Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is established in the universe;
by glorifying Viṣṇu, the unborn Lord of the universe, one is indeed liberated.
Desiring liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra and wishing to abandon desire entirely,
one is liberated by constantly meditating with devotion upon Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons.
Vyāsa said:
In former times, when he was thus questioned by Nārada, that bull-bannered god spoke to him;
what he then said has been related by me to you.
Meditate constantly on that very same seedless, absolute Brahman;
O dear one, you will surely attain the eternal, imperishable state.
Having heard from the Lord this preeminence of Viṣṇu among the gods and ṛṣis,
he properly worshipped Viṣṇu and attained supreme perfection.
And whoever recites this with their mind fixed on Nṛsiṃha,
even the sin committed by them throughout a hundred lifetimes is utterly destroyed.
Having bathed in the morning, one should daily recite this meritorious hymn to Viṣṇu proclaimed by Mahādeva; he attains immortality.
Those who constantly meditate upon the infinite and infallible One within the centers of their heart-lotuses, and those who praise Him—
the supreme Lord and Master of worshippers— they indeed attain the highest Vaiṣṇava perfection.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Śrī Narasiṃha Purāṇa, in the description of the King of Hymns to Viṣṇu. (NarP 16)
Śrī Śuka said:
O father, what should one who is constantly devoted to Viṣṇu recite to be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra? Tell me this, O father, for the benefit of all.
Vyāsa said:
I shall proclaim the eight-syllabled mantra, the supreme among mantras;
by reciting which, a mortal is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra.
Having meditated with one-pointed mind upon Viṣṇu, who stands in the center of the heart-lotus and holds the conch, discus, and mace, the twice-born should perform the recitation.
Having fixed Viṣṇu in his mind, he should indeed recite the eight-syllable mantra in a solitary place, in a secluded spot, before an image of Viṣṇu, or near water.
For this eight-syllable mantra, the seer is Nārāyaṇa himself;
the meter is the divine Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Supreme Self.
The syllable Oṃ is white in color, and the syllable Na is said to be red;
the syllable Mo is black in color, and the syllable Nā is said to be red.
The syllable *rā* has the luster of saffron, while the syllable *ya* is said to be yellow;
the syllable *ṇā* has the luster of collyrium, and the syllable *ya* possesses many colors.
"Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa"—this mantra accomplishes all aims.
For those devotees who recite it, O dear one, it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation.
This eternal mantra is perfected by means of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) of the Vedas.
The glorious eight-syllable mantra, which removes all sins and is the most excellent among all mantras— one should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa while reciting it.
By constantly performing this at the conclusion of the twilight prayers, one is forever liberated from all sins;
this indeed is the supreme mantra, this indeed is the supreme austerity.
This alone is the supreme liberation; this is declared to be heaven.
This essence has been extracted from all the secret teachings of the Vedas.
Indeed, in ancient times, Viṣṇu [taught] this for the benefit of his devotees among men;
having understood this, the brahmin should then meditate upon this eight-syllabled mantra.
Having bathed and become pure, one should recite [the mantra] in a clean place for the purification of sins;
likewise during recitation, giving, fire-offerings, walking, and at the stages of meditation.
One should recite the mantra of Nārāyaṇa both before and after the ritual action;
having become pure and composed, one should recite it a thousand or a hundred thousand times.
But every month on the twelfth day, that best of the twice-born who is a devotee of Viṣṇu,
having bathed and become pure, should recite "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" one hundred times.
He who recites this while worshipping Viṣṇu with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings shall go to the supreme god, the healthy Nārāyaṇa.
Even one joined with great sins is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter—provided that he holds Lord Hari in his heart and recites this mantra.
With his self purified of all evil, he shall go to the supreme goal;
indeed, by the first hundred thousand [recitations], the purification of the self will occur.
By the second hundred thousand [recitations], however, one shall attain the accomplishment of humans;
by the third hundred thousand, moreover, one shall attain the heavenly world.
By the fourth hundred thousand [recitations], one attains proximity to Hari;
by the fifth hundred thousand, however, one attains stainless knowledge.
Likewise, by the sixth hundred thousand [recitations], the mind becomes fixed upon Viṣṇu;
but by the seventh hundred thousand, one attains his true form.
But by the eighth hundred thousand, one attains nirvāṇa;
the best of the twice-born should perform the recitation conjoined with his own specific dharma.
This eight-syllable mantra brings success to one who is unwearied;
[it protects against] bad dreams, asuras, piśācas, serpents, and brahmarākṣasas.
Thieves, petty criminals, and afflictions do not approach one who recites the mantra with a one-pointed and undistracted mind— a devotee of Viṣṇu firm in his vows.
One should recite the mantra of Nārāyaṇa, which removes the fear of death;
it is the supreme mantra among mantras and the deity among deities.
The eight syllables beginning with Oṃ are the supreme secret among secrets;
they bestow long life, wealth, sons, cattle, knowledge, and great fame.
By reciting this, a person attains virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
this is the truth and the righteous path, as demonstrated by the Vedic scriptures.
This form of mantra brings success to men, without a doubt;
[it is worshipped by] the seers, the ancestors, the gods, the siddhas, and the asuras and rākṣasas.
Having recited this very [mantra] alone, others have attained supreme perfection from here;
but he who, knowing his own time of death according to the prescriptions of other scriptures,
recites it at the time of his end, goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
"Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa"—this alone is the true mantra for destroying the terrible poison of saṃsāra.
Listen, you of auspicious minds, joyful and hastening! With my arms raised high, I shall teach this most exalted [mantra]. (NsP 17.30)
Raising my arms, I now speak with truth as my foundation:
"O son, O disciples, listen! There is no mantra superior to the eight-syllabled one."
Truth, truth, and again truth—raising up my arm, I declare:
there is no scripture superior to the Veda, and no god higher than Keśava.
Having examined all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this one conclusion is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times.
Thus, all this has been told to you for the merit of your disciples;
various stories have also been narrated by me. Worship Janārdana.
O son of great intelligence, if you desire accomplishment, recite this eight-syllable mantra which destroys all suffering.
Those men who recite this hymn, which has issued from the mouth of Vyāsa, at the three junctions of the day,
cross over the ocean of saṃsāra without fear, like royal swans with their wings washed white.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Eight-Syllable Mantra," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 17)
Sūta said: Having thus heard these various meritorious stories that destroy all sins from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana once again, O best of sages, [they were filled with wonder].
O high-minded one, in former times the illustrious Śuka Bharadvāja,
accompanied by other perfected beings, was devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Brahmin, these various stories of Mārkaṇḍeya and others, which destroy sin, have been told by me to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Bharadvāja said: You have previously described to me the creation of Vasu and the others;
however, you have not yet told the origin of the Aśvins and the Maruts—please speak of that.
Sūta said: O high-minded one, the origin of the Maruts and the city was previously described in detail by Vāyu, the son of Śakti, in the Purāṇa known as the Vaiṣṇava.
The creation of the two divine Aśvins has already been described in great detail;
now I shall tell you this creation in brief—listen to it from me.
Diti was the daughter of Dakṣa;
from Aditi, Āditya was born as a son. To him, Tvaṣṭṛ gave his daughter, a maiden named Saṃjñā.
He too, having obtained the beautiful and charming daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, took his pleasure with her.
After some time, unable to endure the heat of her husband Āditya, she went to her father’s house.
Beholding her daughter, the father said: "Daughter, what of it? Is your husband Sūrya protecting you out of affection, or is he harsh?"
Having heard these words of her father, Saṃjñā replied to him:
"I am consumed by my husband's fierce heat."
Having heard this, her father said to her: "Go, daughter, to your husband's house."
"For young women, the service of their husband alone is the highest duty.
I too shall return after a few days and remove the heat from my son-in-law, who is like the sun."
Having been told this, she returned to her husband's house and, after some days, gave birth to three children—Manu, Yamī, and Yama—from the Sun.

Then, unable to endure his heat, she created a double of herself (Chāyā) by the power of her own intelligence for the sake of her husband’s enjoyment; having established her there and departed for the Northern Kurus, she became a mare and roamed about.
Āditya, thinking, "This too is Saṃjñā," begot three more offspring upon her as his wife.
Seeing Chāyā—who was devoted to her own offspring with partiality—along with Manu, Śanaiścara, and Tapatī, Yama said to his father, "This is not our mother. (NsP 18.15)
The father, having heard that, said to his wife:
"Let her behave equally toward all her children."
Furthermore, seeing the shadow proceeding again out of affection for their own offspring, Yama and Yamī spoke to it in many ways thus;
however, due to the presence of Āditya, they remained silent.
Then their shadow cast a curse upon them:
"O Yama, you shall become the King of the Dead; O Yamī, you shall become the river named Yamunā."
Then, out of anger, Āditya also pronounced a curse upon the two sons of Chāyā: "O son Śanaiścara, you shall become a planet with a cruel gaze and slow movement; you too shall be a malefic planet."
"O daughter, become a river named Tapatī. Then, Āditya, having entered into meditation, reflected: "Where has Saṃjñā gone?"
Having seen her roaming about in the form of a mare in Uttarakuru by means of his eye of meditation,
he himself went there in the form of a horse and engaged in union with her.

From that very [chariot], the Aśvins were born from Āditya; when they, who possessed exceedingly beautiful forms, arrived, Prajāpati himself came and granted them divinity, a share in the sacrifice, and the primary status of physicians among the gods, and then departed.
And Āditya, having abandoned his horse-form and taken his wife Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ—who had assumed her own form—back with him, resumed his own form and went to heaven.
Then Viśvakarman, having arrived and praised the Sun with various names, diminished his excessive heat and scorching power.
Thus, O brahmins, the supreme origin of the Aśvins has been narrated to you—
meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin, O high-minded Bharadvāja.
Having heard of the birth of those two physicians, the sons of Āditya, who shine with divine forms, a man on earth shall become handsome and rejoice in heaven.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Birth of the Aśvins," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 18)
Bharadvāja said:
O Sūta, I desire to hear those names by which Savitṛ was praised by that Viśvakarman; tell me [the names] of Vivasvat.
Sūta said:
Listen to those names by which Savitṛ was praised by Viśvakarman; I shall declare them to you, for they remove all sins.
Āditya, Savitṛ, Sūrya, Khaga, Pūṣan, Gabhastimat, Timironmathana, Śambhu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mārtaṇḍa, and Āśuga.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Kapila, Tapana, Bhāskara, Ravi,
Agnigarbha, the son of Aditi, Śambhu, and the destroyer of darkness.
Aṃśumān, Aṃśumālī, Tamoghnas, Tejasāṃnidhi,
Ātapī, Maṇḍalī, Mṛtyu, Kapila, and Sarvatāpana.
Hari is the universe, possessed of great splendor, the source of the luster of all jewels;
he wears a garland of rays, destroys darkness, and is permeated by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
The revealer of the vital breath, Mitra, the excellent lamp, swift as thought,
the Lord of sacrifice, the Lord of cattle, the glorious one, the knower of beings, and the destroyer of afflictions.
The slayer of enemies, the auspicious one, the swan, the leader, the one of pleasing appearance,
the pure one, the radiant one, the long-haired one, the thousand-rayed one, and the subduer.
Dharmaraśmi, Pataṅga, Viśāla, Viśvasaṃstuta,
Durvijñeyagati, Śūra, Tejorāśi, and Mahāyaśas.
Radiant, the lord of lights, victorious, the creator of the universe;
the powerful, whose nature is luminosity, a mass of knowledge, the maker of light.
The Sun, the all-seeing, the performer of sacrifice, the leader, the bringer of glory,
the stainless, the heroic, the Lord, the knower of yoga, and the one who contemplates yoga.
Śiva is the essence of immortality, eternal, most excellent, the bestower of boons, and the Lord;
he is the giver of wealth, the giver of life, the most eminent, the granter of desires, and the wearer of forms at will.
The Savior, the Eternal, the Teacher, the Knower of Scriptures, the Scorching One, the Reclining One;
He whose womb is the Veda, the Pervasive, the Hero, the Peaceful, the Beloved of Sāvitrī.
He is the one to be meditated upon, the Lord of the Universe, the Sustainer, the Protector of the World, the Great Lord;
he is Mahendra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Divākara.
When the Sun had been praised with these names by that high-souled one,
the blessed Lord Ravi, being pleased, spoke to Viśvakarman.
"Having placed me upon a lathe here, cut away my mandala;
I know that which resides in your mind, and thus this heat shall come to rest."
Thus addressed, O twice-born one, Viśvakarman did exactly so;
the sun, with its cool and warm rays, became the daughter of that Viśvakarman.
And when Saṃjñā had departed, O Brahmin, Bhānu spoke to Tvaṣṭṛ:
"Since I have indeed been praised by you with eight hundred names..."
"Choose a boon from me; therefore, O sinless one, I am the giver of boons to you.
Being thus addressed by Bhānu, Viśvakarman then spoke these words:
"O God, if you are a granter of boons, grant me this boon:
that man who shall constantly praise you with these names," (NsP 19.20)
O Sun-god, bring about the destruction of the evil of this devotee.
Having been addressed thus by him, the Maker of Day, the Sun, said "So be it" to Tvaṣṭṛ and fell silent;
then, having reassured Saṃjñā who remained within the solar orb and having propitiated Ravi, he departed.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 19.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the origin of Māruta;
formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, by the gods led by Indra against the sons of Diti...
The sons having been defeated and Diti having lost her children, she, desiring a son who would humble the pride of Mahendra, propitiated her husband, the sage Kaśyapa.
Satisfied by that asceticism, he performed the rite of conception with her,
and spoke to her once again as follows:
"If you, being pure, shall carry this embryo for a hundred autumns, then a son will be born who shall be the destroyer of the pride of Mahendra.
Having been addressed thus, she carried that embryo.

Indra, having learned of this, came in the guise of an old brahmin and stood by Diti's side. When the hundred years were nearly complete, Diti, without having washed her feet, ascended her bed and fell asleep. (NsP 20.5)
Vajrapāṇi, having found his opportunity, entered her womb and split that embryo into seven pieces with his vajra;
as he was being thus cut apart, it wept.
Saying "Do not weep," Indra cut each of them into seven pieces.
When they were all born, he said to them, "Do not cry," and thus divided them into seven groups;
these gods known as the Maruts became the companions of Mahendra.
Thus, O Sage, has this creation of the gods, asuras, humans, nāgas, and rākṣasas, as well as those headed by Viyat, been described by you.
Whoever recites or hears this with devotion goes to the world of Hari.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 20.
Bharadvāja said:
You have described to me the secondary creation and the primary creation in various ways;
now tell me about the genealogies, the Manvantaras, and the histories of the dynasties.
Sūta said: The lineage of kings has been proclaimed at length in the Purāṇas;
I shall describe that lineage and the Manvantaras to you in brief.
And now listen, O wise brahmin, to the history of the dynasties;
and let these sages who have come here to listen and stand before you also hear it.
First, Brahmā [arose]; from Brahmā, Marīci;
from Marīci, Kaśyapa; and from Kaśyapa, Āditya.
From Āditya came Manu;
from Manu, Ikṣvāku; from Ikṣvāku, Vikukṣi;
from Vikukṣi, Dyota; from Dyota, Vena; from Vena, Pṛthu; and from Pṛthu, Pṛthāśva.
From Pṛthāśva came Asaṃkhyātāśva;
from Asaṃkhyātāśva came Māndhātṛ.
From Māndhātṛ came Purukutsa; from Purukutsa came Dṛṣada; and from Dṛṣada came Abhiśambhu.
From Abhiśambhu came Dāruṇa, and from Dāruṇa, Sagara.
From Sagara came Haryaśva; from Haryaśva came Dhārīta.
From Hārīta came Rohitāśva; from Rohitāśva came Aṃśumat;
and from Aṃśumat came Bhagīratha.
From Bhagīratha came Saudāsa, and from Saudāsa came Śatruṃdama.
From Śatrudaman came Anaraṇya; from Anaraṇya came Dīrghabāhu; and from Dīrghabāhu came Aja.
From Aja came Daśaratha;
from Daśaratha, Rāma; from Rāma, Lava; and from Lava, Padma.
From Padma came Anuparṇa; from Anuparṇa came Vastrapāṇi.
From Vastrapāṇi comes Śuddhodana;
from Śuddhodana comes Budha;
from Budha, the Solar Lineage (Ādityavaṃśa) ceases.
Those who were born of the Solar dynasty have been proclaimed as the principal ones;
by those Kṣatriyas this earth was formerly enjoyed in accordance with righteousness. O Sage, the lineage of the Sun has been recounted by me, from which the lords of men arose in ancient times.
Now, with a concentrated mind, listen as I describe the unsurpassed kings in the lineage of the Moon.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Solar Lineage," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 21)
Sūta said: Now listen, O great sage Bharadvāja, to the lineage of Soma;
though it has been described in detail in the Purāṇas, I shall now relate it in brief.
First, there was Brahmā;
from Brahmā was born his mind-born son Marīci, and from Marīci, through Dākṣāyaṇī, was born Kaśyapa.
From Kaśyapa and Aditi came Āditya;
from Āditya and Suvarṇalā came Manu.
From Manu and Surūpā was born Soma;
from Soma and Rohiṇī was born Budha; and from Budha and Ilā was born Purūravas.
From Purūravas came Āyu;
from Āyu, through Rūpavatī, came Nahuṣa.
From Nahuṣa and Pitṛvatī was born Yayāti;
from Yayāti and Śarmiṣṭhā was born Pūru.
From Pūru, in the lineage of Vaṃśa, came Saṃpāti; from Saṃpāti, in the lineage of Bhānudattā, came Sārvabhauma;
and from Sārvabhauma, in the lineage of Vaidehī, came Bhoja.
From Bhoja, through Liṅgā, came Duṣyanta;
from Duṣyanta, through Śakuntalā, came Bharata.
From Bharata and Nandā was born Ajamīḍha;
from Ajamīḍha and Sudevī was born Pṛśni; and from Pṛśni and Ugrasenā was born Prasara.
From Prasarā and Bahurūpā was born Śantanu; from Śantanu and Yojanagandhā was born Vicitravīrya;
and from Vicitravīrya and Ambikā was born Pāṇḍu.
From Pāṇḍu and Kuntīdevī was born Arjuna;
from Arjuna and Subhadrā was born Abhimanyu.
From Abhimanyu and Uttarā was born Parīkṣit;
from Parīkṣit and Mātṛvatī was born Janamejaya;
and from Janamejaya and Puṇyavatī was born Śatānīka.
To Śatānīka, by Puṣpavatī, was born Sahasrānīka;
to Sahasrānīka, by Mṛgavatī, was born Udayana;
and to him, by Vāsavadattā, was born Naravāhana.
From Naravāhana, Kṣemaka was born at the horse sacrifice;
from Kṣemaka came the Pāṇḍavas, and thus the Lunar dynasty comes to an end.
Whoever should constantly hear this unsurpassed royal lineage,
with his soul purified of all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whoever constantly recites this, or causes the ancestors to hear it during a *śrāddha* ceremony,
that meritorious proclamation of the lineage becomes an inexhaustible gift to the ancestors.
O twice-born one, I have thus related to you this genealogy of the kings of Soma’s lineage, which destroys all sins;
now listen, O chief of brahmins, as I describe the fourteenth Manvantara as well.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Lunar Lineage," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 22.
Sūta said: First, the Svāyambhuva Manvantara has been described; its nature was told.
At the beginning of creation, the second Manu was named Svārociṣa.
In that Svārociṣa Manvantara, the lord of the gods was named Vipaścit;
the gods were the Pārāvatas and the Tuṣitas.
Ūrjastamba, Suprāṇa, Danta, Nirṛṣabha, Varīyān, Īśvara, Soma, and the seven sages (saptarṣayaḥ), as well as Kimpuruṣa and others, are the sons of Svārociṣa Manu who become kings.
The third Manu is named Uttama;
his gods are the Sudhāmans, the Satyas, the Śivas, the Pratardanas, and the Vaṃśavartins.
These five constitute the twelve groups.
Indra is their perfect peace.
The Seven Sages became worthy of veneration;
here, Paraśu, Citra, and others were the sons of Manu.
The fourth Manu is named Tāmasa.
In that Manvantara, there are three groups of twenty-seven deities each: the Parās, the Satyas, and the Sudhiyas.
There, the lord of gods named Bhṛśuṇḍi,
the god Hiraṇyaroman, Devaśrī, Ūrdhvabāhu, Devabāhu, Sudhāman, Parjanya, and Muni— these are the seven seers (saptarṣis).
Jyotirdhāmā, Pṛthu, Kāśya, Agni, and Dhanaka—these were the kings who were the sons of Tāmasa Manu.
The fifth Manu is named Raivata.
During his interval, there are fourteen groups of divine beings consisting of the Amitās, the Niratās, the Vaikuṇṭhas, and the Sumedhasas.
The lord of the gods is named Asurāntaka.
The sons of Manu, beginning with Saptaka, indeed became kings.
Śānta, Śāntabhaya, Vidvān, Tapasvī, Medhāvī, and Sutapas became the seven ṛṣis.
The sixth Manu was named Cākṣuṣa;
his sons were kings headed by Puruṣatadyumna.
Suśāntas, Āpyas, Prasūtas, Bhavyas, and Prathitas—these five groups of eight, known as the Lekhas and others, were the gods of great power there.
Among them, Indra is Manojava;
Medhā, Sumedhā, Virajas, Haviṣmān, Uttama, Matimān, and Sahiṣṇu by name—these are the seven ṛṣis.
The seventh Manu, Vaivasvata, is currently reigning;
his sons, beginning with Ikṣvāku, are Kṣatriyas who rule the earth.
The gods here are Āditya, Viśvavasu, Rudra, and others; among them, Devendra is Puraṃdara.
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama, Viśvāmitra, and Bharadvāja are the seven ṛṣis.

The future Manvantaras are now being described. To wit: the Manu previously mentioned who was born to Āditya by Saṃjñā is the first; however, the second Manu, who was produced by Chāyā, belongs to the eighth Sāvarṇika Manvantara of his elder brother Sāvarṇa—listen to that.
The eighth Manu will be Sāvarṇa; there, the groups of gods beginning with Sutapas will appear, and Bali will be their Indra.
The seven sages will be the radiant one named Gālava, as well as Kṛpa, Droṇa, Vyāsa, and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Virāja, Urvarīyān, Nirmoka, and others will be the kings who are the sons of Sāvarṇa Manu.
The ninth Manu will be Dakṣasāvarṇi.
Dhṛti, Kīrti, Dīpti, Ketu, Pañcahasta, Nirāmaya, Pṛthuśravas, and others will be the kings who are the sons of this Manu Dakṣasāvarṇi.
The Marīcigarbhas, Sudharmans, and Haviṣmants are the deities there;
their Indra is Adbhuta.
Savana, Kṛtimān, Havya, Vasumedha, Atithi, and Jyotiṣmān—these are the seven ṛṣis.
The tenth Manu will be Brahmasāvarṇi;
Viruddha and others will be the gods there,
and Śānti will be their Indra.
Haviṣmān, Sukṛti, Satya, Tapomūrti, Nābhāga, Pratimoka, and Saptaketu—these are the seven ṛṣis.
In the *Sukṣetra* kalpa, there will be kings such as Bhūriṣeṇa and others, the sons of Brahmasāvarṇi.
In the eleventh Manvantara, the Manu will be Dharmasāvarṇika.
The hosts of gods such as the Siṃhasavana and others;
their lord of heaven is Indra.
Nirmoha, Tattvadarśin, Nikampa, Nirutsāha, Dhṛtimat, and Rucya—these will be the seven sages (ṛṣis).
Citrasena, Vicitra, and others will be the kings, the sons of Dharmasāvarṇi.
Rudrasāvarṇi will be the twelfth Manu.
There, Indra has made his abode; the gods are the Haritas, the Rohitas, the Sumanas, the Sukarmans, and the Sutapas.
Tapasvī, Cārutapas, Tapomūrti, Taporati, Tapodhṛti, Jyotis, and Tapa—these are the seven ṛṣis.
Devavān, Devaśreṣṭha, and others will be the sons of that Manu, who will become kings.
The thirteenth Manu shall be named Ruci;
the hosts of gods shall be Sragvin, Bāṇa, Sudharmā, and others;
their Indra shall be named Ṛṣabha.
Niścita, Agnitejas, Vapuṣmat, Dhṛṣṭa, Vāruṇi, Haviṣmat, and Nahuṣa—the Bhavya—will be the seven ṛṣis.
Sudharmā, Devānīka, and others will be the sons of that Manu, the lords of the earth.
Bhauma will be the fourteenth Manu;
Suruci will be the Indra there;
and the Cakṣuṣmantaḥ, Pavitrāḥ, and Kaniṣṭhābhā will be the classes of gods.
Agnibāhu, Śuci, Śukra, Mādhava, Śiva, Abhīma, and Jitaśvāsa—these are the seven ṛṣis;
Urugambhīra, Brahmā, and others are the sons of that Manu, who were kings. (NsP 23.35)
Thus have those fourteen Manvantaras been described,
as well as the kings by whom this earth is protected.
In each Manvantara, there arise Manu, the seven ṛṣis, the gods, the kings who are the sons of Manu, and the Śakras who hold authority.
O twice-born one, when these fourteen Manvantaras have passed,
a period of time equivalent to a thousand yugas elapses as a single day.
O best of beings, the night thereafter is of that same duration;
during it, the Lord Nṛhari himself, the soul of all, reclines assuming the form of Brahmā.
O Brahmin, the Lord Janārdana, the primordial creator and omnipresent one, having assumed all forms and resorted to his own māyā, has swallowed the entire triple world.
Then the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, having awakened, once again establishes the system of the ages (yugas) and performs creation, just as before.

These Manus, the immortals, the sons, the kings, and all the sages whom you have mentioned—know, O Brahmin, that they are all manifestations of Him who remains established in His own state; indeed, everything is He alone.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 23.
Śrī Sūta said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the auspicious history of the dynasties,
which destroys the sins of those who hear it, and which consists of the lineages of the Sun, the Moon, and kings.
Listen to me as I recount the life of that protector of the earth named Ikṣvāku, who was born of the solar dynasty and was previously mentioned as the son of Manu.
O fortunate one, there was on earth a divine and most beautiful city named Ayodhyā, situated upon the banks of the Sarayū.
Surpassing Amarāvatī, it spanned thirty yojanas and was filled with throngs of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, as well as trees radiant like the wish-fulfilling kalpavṛkṣa.
It shone everywhere with walls, watchtowers, and gateways radiant with golden luster,
its crossroads well-apportioned.
It possesses many-storied palaces on various levels, excellent markets for numerous goods,
and is graced by ponds filled with the pure waters of lotuses and water-lilies.
It was adorned with divine shrines for the deities and the sounds of Vedic recitations,
and endowed with the most excellent sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums.
It was adorned with *śāla*, *tāla*, and coconut trees, as well as with breadfruit, *āmalaka*, and *jambū* trees, and likewise with mangoes, *kapittha*, and others, along with *aśoka* trees.
It is endowed with various groves everywhere filled with fruit-bearing trees,
such as the *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jāti*, *pāṭalā*, *nāga*, and *campaka*.
It was adorned with *karavīra*, *karṇikāra*, and *ketakī* flowers;
in some places it was beautifully graced by plantains, *lavalī*, *jāti*, *mātuluṅga*, and large fruits, as well as by *nāraṅga* oranges and the fragrance of sandalwood.
It was filled with wealthy men and women who were delighted by constant festivities and skilled in song and instrumental music, and who were intent upon the beauty of forms and wealth.
It was crowded with people from various regions, adorned with banners and flags,
and filled with princes possessing a splendor equal to that of the gods.
She was surrounded by beautiful women of equal form, like celestial nymphs,
and attended by Brahmins who were excellent poets and possessed a splendor equal to that of Bṛhaspati.
She was accompanied by merchants and citizens, as well as by the best of wish-fulfilling trees,
by horses equal to Uccaiḥśravas, and by elephants like the elephants of the quarters.

Having seen that city, which through its various wonders was equal to Indrapurī, Ayodhyā, Nārada recited this verse in the midst of the assembly: NsP_24.15: "Having seen that [city], which through its various wonders was equal to Indrapurī, Ayodhyā, Nārada recited this verse in the midst of the assembly."
Indeed, for the lotus-born one who was creating heaven, it would have been in vain,
since Ayodhyā had already come into being as superior to heaven and endowed with all objects of desire.
Having been consecrated, that mighty lord of the earth dwelt in Ayodhyā,
having conquered all kings through righteousness.
The feet of that [king], made calloused by the prostrations of kings and regional lords adorned with crowns of rubies, were pressed down by them out of both devotion and fear.
Ikṣvāku, whose strength was unimpaired and who was learned in all the scriptures,
was like Indra in splendor and possessed the majesty of Manu’s son.
Righteous in soul, he protected this earth as far as the oceans, accompanied by Brahmins who were learned in the Vedas and possessed of both dharma and justice.
The powerful one conquered all the kings in battle with his missiles;
having utterly defeated them, he then seized their realm with his exceedingly sharp weapons.
O Brahmin, the powerful King Ikṣvāku conquered the worlds beyond through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees and various kinds of gifts.
With his two arms he supported the earth, with the tip of his tongue Sarasvatī,
with his chest Padmā, and with his heart devotion toward Mādhava.
Having had the stainless form of Hari standing, Mādhava seated,
and Ananta lying down depicted upon a pure cloth, ||| NsP_24.24 |||
Having worshipped the three forms of the high-souled Viṣṇu three times a day with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, she constantly took delight in beholding Hari upon the cloth-painting.
He saw him even in his dreams— Kṛṣṇa, who has the luster of a dark cloud, who dwells upon the king of serpents, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who is clad in yellow garments.
The king conceived a high regard for that cloud of such color,
and he felt partiality toward that deer of its name and toward a lotus of that same appearance.
O best of beings, an unprecedented and intense longing arose in that king to behold the divine form of Hari directly before his eyes.
But when his craving had awakened, the wise king, by means of his mind alone, reflected upon the enjoyment of sovereignty as being devoid of essence.
In this world, there is no one equal to him who, preceded by dispassion and knowledge, has renounced his home, wife, children, and fields— all of which are sources of suffering.
Having reflected thus, with his mind intent upon asceticism,
he questioned his domestic priest Vasiṣṭha regarding the means to achieve it.
O Sage, by the power of asceticism I wish to behold the unborn Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods; tell me the means for that.
Thus addressed, Vasiṣṭha— knower of all dharmas and ever devoted to his welfare— spoke to the king whose mind was intent on asceticism.
If you desire, O Great King, to behold the supreme Nārāyaṇa,
propitiate Janārdana here through well-performed austerity.
The God of gods, Janārdana, can never be seen by anyone who has not performed austerities; therefore, worship him with austerity.
O King, on the bank of the Sarayū river in the south-eastern quarter,
there is the hermitage of the sages headed by Gālava.
A distance of five yojanas from here is a place that purifies;
it is filled with various trees and creepers and abounds with diverse flowers.

O twice-born one, having entrusted the burden of his own kingdom to his minister Arjuna— who was highly wise, possessed of statesmanship, and a king— [he devoted himself] even to the ritual portion [of the Veda].
Having praised and propitiated Gaṇādhyakṣa Vināyaka, depart from here;
seeking the perfection of your asceticism, perform your penance there.
Assuming the garb of an ascetic and subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits,
meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa and constantly recite this mantra.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva!
This mantra known as the twelve-syllabled one brings about accomplishment;
by reciting it, the ancient sages attained supreme perfection.
The planets, such as the sun and the moon, return again and again;
yet those who contemplate the twelve-syllable mantra do not return even to this day.
O King, having fixed the external senses in the heart and the mind upon the subtle Supreme Self, while silently reciting that mantra, Madhusūdana is to be beheld.
Thus have I explained to you the means for performing austerities to attain Hari;
now, if you so desire, do that which you ask further.
Thus addressed by the sage, that king, having entrusted the sovereignty of the earth to his chief minister,
praised Gaṇeśa, honored him with flowers, and departed from his own city, firm in soul for the sake of asceticism.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Life of Ikṣvāku," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 24)
Bharadvāja said:
O high-minded one, tell me how the Lord of the Gaṇas was praised by that great-souled king, and how he performed his ascetic penance.
Sūta said: O twice-born one, on the fourth day, having bathed at the three periods of the day, the king,
wearing red garments and anointed with red perfumes, [proceeded].
Then he worshipped Vināyaka with pleasing, deep-red flowers,
preceded by a ritual bath with red sandalwood water, according to the prescribed rule.
Having smeared [the image] with red sandalwood paste, he worshipped it with red flowers;
then he offered incense mixed with ghee and sandalwood,
as well as an offering of turmeric-colored food soaked in jaggery, sugar-candy, and clarified butter.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka according to the proper rite, he then praised him.
Ikṣvāku said:
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, I shall praise that Vināyaka.
To Mahāgaṇapati, the heroic, the unconquered, the increaser of wisdom,
who has one tusk, two tusks, and four tusks, and who possesses four arms.
The three-eyed one, holding a trident in his hand, with red eyes and bestowing boons;
the son of Ambikā, with ears like winnowing baskets, the fierce Vināyaka.
Likewise, one who is reddish-brown, carries a staff, has a face like fire, and is fond of oblations—
such a person, if not honored, creates obstacles for men in all their undertakings.
I bow to that leader of the Gaṇas, the formidable and fierce son of Umā,
the three-eyed one intoxicated with joy, who wards off obstacles for his devotees.
I pay homage to Vināyaka, who resembles ten million suns, whose radiance is like crushed collyrium, who is bound [in mudrā], perfectly pure, and peaceful.
Homage be to the elephant-faced one; homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas;
homage to him whose form is like Meru and Mandara; homage to the dweller of Kailāsa.
Homage be to you, O Virūpa; homage to you, the practitioner of celibacy;
homage to you, the God praised by devotees; homage to you, O Vināyaka!
In ancient times, for the sake of accomplishing the task of the former gods,
you assumed the form of an elephant and terrified all the dānavas.
Since your leadership over the sages and the deities has been revealed,
you are therefore worshipped first by the gods, O Son of Bhava.
Having propitiated you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, the omniscient one who can assume any form at will,
with red flowers and water mixed with red sandalwood paste for the sake of accomplishing his purpose.
Having put on red garments, one should worship and recite [the mantra] on the fourth lunar day;
one should perform the worship three times a day or once a day, while maintaining a restricted diet.
One shall bring under control the king, the prince, or even the royal minister,
as well as the kingdom together with its realm, O Lord of All Obstacles.
"O Vināyaka, grant that my asceticism be free from obstacles; I bow to you.
Thus praised with devotion and especially worshipped by me, [he granted his favor].
Whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices,
one obtains that fruit in its entirety by praising the god Vināyaka.
For him there shall be no adversity, nor shall he suffer defeat;
no obstacle shall arise for him, and once born, he shall remember his past lives.
Whoever recites this hymn shall obtain a boon within six months;
and within a year, one attains spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). Of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having thus praised the Lord of the Gaṇas in former times,
the king assumed the guise of an ascetic and went to the forest to perform penance.
Having cast aside his costly garment, which resembles the skin of a serpent,
that best of kings wears instead a rough, tree-bark girdle around his waist.
Likewise, having cast aside divine jewels and bracelets,
one should take up a rosary as an ornament, beautiful with lotus seeds.
Likewise, having cast off the crown adorned with jewels and gold from his head, the king should wear a mass of matted hair for the sake of asceticism.
Having thus assumed the attire for asceticism as instructed by Vasiṣṭha,
he entered the penance grove and performed austerities, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
During the summer, that great ascetic practiced heat by standing in the midst of five fires;
during the rainy season, he remained without shelter; and during the winter, he stayed within the waters of a lake.
Having again restrained all the senses within the heart and having absorbed the mind into Viṣṇu, one should indeed [recite] the twelve-syllable mantra.
As that high-souled king was muttering prayers while subsisting on air alone,
the Blessed Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, appeared before him.
Then, beholding the four-faced one born from the lotus who had arrived,
he prostrated with a spirit of devotion and gratified him with hymns of praise.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, the creator of the world, the Great Soul;
homage to you, the four-faced one, who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras.
Thus praised, Brahmā, the creator of the world, spoke to the best of kings.
Devoted to austerity, peaceful, having renounced the kingdom, he possessed great happiness.
Brahmā said:
O King, the Sun, the illuminator of the worlds, is your grandfather.
Manu, the father, is always to be honored even by all the sages;
he and his grandfather formerly performed intense austerities.
"For what purpose, O best of kings, have you abandoned all royal enjoyments and perform such severe penance? Tell me, O high-minded one."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the king bowed to him and spoke these words:
"I wish to behold Madhusūdana through the power of my ascetic practice."
"I am indeed performing such penance, O Brahmin, for the sake of the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace.
Thus addressed, the lotus-born one spoke to the king as if smiling.
The all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa cannot be seen by you through asceticism;
nor can Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, be seen even by those like me.
I shall relate an ancient and meritorious tale; listen to me.
At the end of the night, at the time of universal dissolution, the lotus-eyed Lord, having led the worlds [to their rest]—
O high-minded one, Hari has entered into yogic sleep upon his couch of infinite enjoyments,
while being praised by Sanandana and other sages.
While he was thus asleep, O King, a great lotus was born from his navel;
upon that auspicious lotus, I was born in the past as one who knows the Vedas.
Then, casting his gaze downward, he beheld the lotus-eyed Hari,
resembling crushed collyrium, seated upon a couch formed by the coils of Ananta.
Having the luster of an *atasī* flower, reclining, clad in yellow garments, his limbs variegated with divine jewels, and resplendent with a crown; NsP_25.42 //
O Mahāmati, it has a form resembling a jasmine flower or the moon, and is infinite;
it is exceedingly radiant with jewels situated in the midst of its thousand hoods.
Having seen him for only a moment, I did not see him there again;
overcome by great sorrow, O best of kings, I became [distraught].
Then, out of curiosity to behold that healthy Nārāyaṇa, I descended from there, taking hold of a lotus stalk.
Then, O Indra among kings, having searched along the edge of the water and not seeing him,
I again approached that very same lotus while meditating upon the Lord of Śrī.
He performed great penance in order to behold that form of Vāsudeva;
then, a bodiless voice from the sky spoke to me.
"O Brahmin, why do you distress yourself in vain? Now follow my word;
the Lord Viṣṇu cannot be seen by you even through great asceticism."
If you wish to see him here, then, being thus commanded,
perform the creation [of the visualization] of Him who reclines upon the serpent-couch, resembling pure crystal.
O Mahāmati, that form of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow which was seen, possessing a luster like crushed collyrium, appeared as a fixed form stationed upon a celestial chariot.
"Worship [Him] constantly and without indolence; then you shall behold Mādhava.
O King, having been thus urged by her, he abandoned his ascetic heat at every moment.
Having created the creation of the elements of the world and having established that which was created,
Viśvakarman, the Lord of Creatures, appeared within his mind.
By him, two auspicious forms, Ananta and Kṛṣṇa, were manifested;
O King, they were seen by me in the water as before, stationed in a celestial chariot.
Having likewise worshipped Hari there with devotion, I remained;
by His grace, I attained supreme austerity and unsurpassed knowledge.
And having attained liberation, I behold the bliss of unchanging activity;
that I shall declare to you for your benefit, O Lord of the best of kings.
"O King, having relinquished this severe austerity, go to your own city;
for the protection of subjects is the duty of kings, as is austerity."
"I shall dispatch a celestial chariot accompanied by hosts of perfected twice-born ones;
there, propitiate the Lord of Gods with all auspicious external offerings."
O tiger among kings, worshiping Nārāyaṇa— who lies upon the one called Ananta— with sacrifices, remain free from desire and protect your subjects with righteousness.
"O King, through the grace of Vāsudeva, your liberation shall come to pass.
Having spoken thus to him, the Grandfather then departed for the world of Brahmā.
O twice-born one, as Ikṣvāku sat reflecting upon the words of the Lotus-born One,
that celestial chariot appeared before the king.
Having seen that auspicious [image] of Mādhava and Ananta accompanied by Brahmā and the twice-born, and having bowed with supreme devotion to Puruṣottama; ||| NsP_25.61 |||
Having bowed to the sages and the brahmins, he took that [gift] and went to the city,
where he was beheld by the citizens, the people, and women endowed with splendor.
And as they scattered parched grain, the king was led to his own home;
within his spacious palace stood a beautiful Vaiṣṇava celestial chariot.
Having established [the image], he propitiated Hari, who was worshipped by those twice-born men;
meanwhile, the beautiful queens, having ground yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), [prepared the paste].
Having fashioned a garland rich with fragrance, his joy increased greatly;
meanwhile, the citizens [offered] camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and likewise aloe-wood.
Having brought them, they gave the king an entire, especially fine cloth, guggulu resin known as mahiṣa, and flowers suitable for Viṣṇu.

Having worshipped Hari seated in his celestial chariot with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order, at the three junctions of the day, with supreme devotion through recitations and Vaiṣṇava hymns; ||| NsP_25.67 |||
With songs, clamorous sounds, and the resonance of conchs and musical instruments,
as well as with spectacles prescribed by the scriptures and joyful vigils throughout the night.
Having gratified Hari, who embodies all the gods, with sacrifices, he caused a supreme festival for Hari to be held for a very long time.
Free from desire, through the practice of giving and righteousness, he attained supreme knowledge;
performing sacrifices, protecting the earth, and worshipping Keśava.
Having procreated sons for the sake of his ancestors and abandoned his body through meditation, he,
contemplating only Brahman, indeed attained the state of Viṣṇu.

Then, having abandoned the cycle of existence with its endless suffering, the king went to that state of Viṣṇu, which is unborn, free from sorrow, stainless, pure, peaceful, and eternally composed of the nature of blissful consciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*, in the account of Ikṣvāku's deeds. (NarP 25)
Śrī Sūta said:
Ikṣvāku had a son named Vikukṣi.
When his father had attained perfection, he was consecrated by the great seers and, while righteously protecting the earth, [saw] one seated in a celestial chariot.
Having propitiated Acyuta, who reclines upon the infinite serpent Śeṣa, and having worshipped the gods with sacrifices, he consecrated his own son Subāhu in the kingdom and ascended to heaven.
From the radiant Subāhu, Udyota is said to have descended.
Having protected the earth with its seven islands according to Dharma, and having shown supreme devotion to Nārāyaṇa like Brahmā,

he worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice with rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, with a mind free from desire; and having meditated upon the eternal, stainless, undifferentiated, supreme light— the immortal, imperishable form of the Supreme Self— he [attained] Hari and the infinite Supreme.
Having propitiated [him], he went to the heavenly world.
Yuvanāśva was his son, and Māndhātṛ was the son of Yuvanāśva.

Having been consecrated by the great seers, he was a devotee of Viṣṇu by his very nature; worshipping Acyuta, who reclines upon the infinite [ocean], with devotion and having performed various sacrifices, he protected the earth consisting of seven continents and then ascended to heaven.
Regarding him, this verse is sung:
"From the time the sun rises until it sets,
all that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva."
His son was Purukuśya, by whom the gods and the brahmins were satisfied with sacrifices and gifts.
From Purukuśya came Dṛṣada; from Dṛṣada came Abhiśambhu; from Abhiśambhu came Dāruṇa; and from Dāruṇa came Sagara.
From Sagara came Haryaśva; from Haryaśva, Dhārīta; from Dhārīta, Rohitāśva;
and from Rohitāśva, Aṃśumān.
From Aṃśumat came Bhagīratha,
by whom, through great asceticism, the Gaṅgā— the destroyer of all impurities and the bestower of the four goals of human existence— was brought down from heaven to earth in ancient times;
and the ancestors known as the Sagaras, who had been reduced to skeletal fragments and consumed by the great seer Kapila, were raised to heaven once they were touched by the waters of the Gaṅgā.
From Bhagīratha came Saudāsa; from Saudāsa came Satrasava.
From Satrasava came Anaraṇya, and from Anaraṇya came Dīrghabāhu.
From Dīrghabāhu was born Aja, and from Aja came Daśaratha;
in his house, for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa, Nārāyaṇa himself descended as Rāma.
Following his father’s command, he went to the Daṇḍaka forest accompanied by his brother and wife and practiced austerities.

There, his wife having been abducted by Rāvaṇa, he became sorrowful along with his brother; then, with the assistance of Sugrīva—the leader of many tens of millions of monkeys—he built a bridge across the great ocean, went to Laṅkā with them, and slew Rāvaṇa, that thorn in the side of the gods, together with his kinsmen.
Having taken Sītā back to Ayodhyā and being consecrated there by Bharata, he bestowed the kingdom of Laṅkā and a celestial chariot upon Vibhīṣaṇa and sent him forth.
That Supreme Lord, seated in the chariot and being escorted by Vibhīṣaṇa, did not wish to dwell even in Laṅkā, the city of the Rākṣasas; instead, he established a sacred forest there.
Having observed this, the Blessed One lay down right there upon the couch of the great serpent’s coils;
Vibhīṣaṇa, too, being unable to lead that celestial chariot away from there, returned to his own city at his word.
Due to the presence of Nārāyaṇa, it became a great Vaiṣṇava sacred field (kṣetra), which is visible even today.
From Rāma came Lava; from Lava, Padma; from Padma, Ṛtuparṇa; from Ṛtuparṇa, Astrapāṇi;
from Astrapāṇi, Śuddhodana; and from Śuddhodana, Buddha.
The lineage ceases with the Buddha.
These rulers of the earth born of the solar dynasty have been described to you according to their preeminence,
those mighty ones by whom the earth was protected in ancient times through sacrificial rites, O kings who dwell among the gods.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Account of the Solar Dynasty," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 26)
Sūta said:
Now, the history of the kings born of the Lunar dynasty (Somavaṃśa) is told in brief.
First of all, having placed the entire triple world within his belly, [he rests] upon the bed of the serpent's coils in the great waters of the single ocean.
The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, who consists of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda, entered into yogic sleep.
As he slept, a great lotus was born from his navel;
upon that lotus, the four-faced Brahmā came into being.
Atri was the mind-born son of that Brahmā. From Atri and Anasūyā was born Soma.
Having taken the thirty-three daughters of the Prajāpati Dakṣa, beginning with Rohiṇī, as his wives, he—his mind especially pleased by his eldest beloved—beheld a son, Budha, in Rohiṇī.
He generated [it].
Budha, who was learned in all the śāstras, resided in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna;
he begot a son named Purūravas upon Ilā.
To him, who was endowed with extraordinary beauty, Urvaśī became his wife for a long time, even after she had abandoned the enjoyments of heaven.
Āyu was born as the son of Purūravas by Urvaśī;
having ruled the kingdom according to dharma, he ascended to heaven.
From Āyu, Rūpavatī bore a son, Nahuṣa,
by whom the status of Indra was attained.
From Nahuṣa, in turn, Pitṛmatī bore Yayāti.
From his lineage were born the Vṛṣṇis;
from Śarmiṣṭhā, Yayāti’s son Pūru was born.
To Pūru, in the lineage of Vaṃśa, Saṃyāti was born as a son;
for him, all desires were fulfilled upon the earth.
From Saṃyāti and Bhānudattā was born Sārvabhauma.
While he was protecting the entire earth with righteousness, he propitiated the Blessed One Narasiṃha through sacrifices and gifts, and thereby attained perfection.
From that universal monarch, through Vaidehī, was born Bhoja;

in whose lineage, long ago in the battle between the gods and the asuras, Kālanemi—struck by Viṣṇu’s discus and having become Kaṃsa—was slain and brought to his destruction by Vāsudeva, who was born of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
The son of that Bhoja was Duṣyanta in Kaliṅga.
He, having propitiated the Lord Narasiṃha and, by His grace, having ruled a kingdom free from thorns according to dharma, attained heaven.
The son of Duṣyanta through Śakuntalā was Bharata; he, ruling the kingdom according to dharma, performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.

Having propitiated the Blessed One, who embodies all the deities, and having fulfilled his office, he became intent on the meditation of Brahman and attained absorption into the supreme Vaiṣṇava light.
From Bharata, by Ānandā, was born Ajamīḍha.
