He was a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu; having propitiated Narasiṃha and obtained a son, he ruled the kingdom with righteousness and ascended to the city of Viṣṇu.
Vṛṣṇi was born as the son of Ajamīḍha by Sudevī.
He too, ruling the kingdom righteously for many years, brought the seven continents under his control by suppressing the wicked and protecting the virtuous.
To Vṛṣṇi, by Ugrasenā, a son named Pratyañca was born.
He too, protecting the earth according to dharma, performed the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice every year and attained nirvāṇa. From Pratīca, through Bahurūpā, Śāntanu was born.
For that Devadatta, mounting the chariot became impossible at first, but then possible.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Lineage," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 27)
Bharadvāja said:
How was Śāntanu previously incapable of mounting a chariot, and how did he later become capable? Tell us that truly.
Sūta said: O Bharadvāja, listen; I shall relate to you this ancient account, for that life-story of Śāntanu removes all the sins of men.
In former times, Śāntanu was a devotee of Narasiṃha;
according to the ritual prescribed by Nārada, he worshipped Mādhava.
O Brahmin, because that excellent chariot had been stepped over by King Śāntanu as if it were the remains of an offering (nirmālya) to the god Narasiṃha, [it was seized].
At that moment, he became unable to mount Devadatta and thought:
"Why has this movement of mine suddenly failed with respect to the chariot?"
While he was thus reflecting on his sorrow, Nārada arrived;
being asked, "O King, why do you stand here despondent? Śāntanu replied.
"Nārada, I do not know the cause of this interruption in my progress.
Having been addressed thus, Nārada meditated and then, having understood the cause of that, [spoke].
Standing there with humility, he spoke to King Śāntanu:
"O King, wherever you may be, [you must certainly provide for] this lion among men."
Therefore, O Great King, because he was bypassed as unworthy of the floral offerings, his progress was broken during the act of mounting the chariot;
hear now the reason for this.
O King, in former times there was a certain high-minded gardener named Ravi within the sacrificial altar; by him Vṛndāvana was established.
And various groves were indeed well-fashioned for the sake of flowers,
consisting entirely of *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jāti*, *bakula*, and other such blossoms.
Having made his own wall high and wide upon its foundation,
and both impassable and impenetrable, he constructed his own residence.
O best of beings, having entered the house, that door shall not be found elsewhere;
such was the case for the wise garland-maker as he lived there.
That forest was in full bloom, its fragrance perfuming the quarters of the sky;
day after day, he would gather flowers together with his wife.
Having fashioned garlands for Narasiṃha constantly according to the prescribed rule,
she gave some to the twice-born and supported herself by selling others.
He made his wife and others live together with himself;
then, having come down from heaven in a chariot, the son of Indra indeed arrived.
Accompanied by a host of Apsarases, he would gather flowers at night;
desiring their fragrance, he would go about picking and bringing all of them.
Day after day, as his flowers were being taken away, even the gardener thought:
"There is no other entrance to this forest, for its high wall is insurmountable."
"Indeed, I see no power in men to steal the entire collection of flowers at night; what then could this be? Let me investigate."
Having reflected thus, the wise man remained awake in the forest at night;
then, that man returned in the same manner, gathered the flowers, and departed.
Seeing him, the garland-maker became exceedingly distressed in the forest;
then, having fallen asleep, he saw that man-lion in a dream.
Having heard those words, he said: "O my dear son, having brought this flower-offering (nirmālya), let it be quickly cast near the flower garden."
"Against this wicked son of Indra, there is no other means of restraint," having heard these words of the wise Narasiṃha Hari.
Having understood this, he brought the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and acted exactly as instructed;
he too returned as before in an unobserved chariot.
Having descended from his chariot and gathering flowers,
the son of Indra, acting inauspiciously, stepped over the withered garlands lying upon that ground.
Then he would have no power for the act of mounting the chariot;
and thus the charioteer spoke regarding your mounting of the chariot.
"There is no fitness for one to step over the remains of Narasiṃha's offerings.
I shall go to heaven itself; you remain on earth, do not ascend."
Having been addressed thus by him, the wise son of Hari said to him:
"In this matter, tell me that action by which there may be an expulsion of my sin."
"Having said that, O charioteer, go quickly from us to heaven."
The charioteer said:
"At Kurukṣetra, during Rāma’s twelve-year sacrifice, it occurred constantly."
"By removing the remnants of the twice-born's meal, you shall attain purity";
having said this, the charioteer went to heaven, which is frequented by the gods.
The son of Indra, having reached Kurukṣetra on the bank of the Sarasvatī,
should likewise perform the cleansing of the remnants of the twice-born at Rāma’s sacrifice.
When the twelfth year was complete, the twice-born, filled with suspicion, said to him:
"Who are you? Tell us, O fortunate one, why are you constantly wiping away the leavings?"
"If you do not eat at our sacrificial session, we would have great cause for suspicion.
Having been addressed thus, he related the events in their proper sequence.
The son of Hari quickly went to the third heaven by means of that chariot;
therefore, O protector of the earth, you too [should partake] with reverence of the remnants of the Brahmins.
Perform the purification for Rāma during his twelve-year sacrificial session;
there is nothing superior to [giving] to the Brāhmaṇas, which is the supreme remover of all sins.
"O protector of the earth, when Devadatta has thus been made to mount the chariot, your own course will be successful once the expiation has been performed. (NsP 28.36)
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, do not step over the floral remains (nirmālya) of the god Narasiṃha, nor those of other celestial dwellers.
Thus addressed by him, Śāṃtanu performed the wiping away of the Brāhmaṇa’s remnants for twelve years, and then he mounted that chariot.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, there was previously a lack of power for the king to mount the chariot;
afterwards, power arose for him in that very same way.
Thus, O Brahmin, the fault in stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) has been told to you;
likewise, the merit for the twice-born in sweeping up the remnants (ucchiṣṭa) has been declared.
The man who, being pure and with a well-composed mind, wipes away here the leavings of a twice-born with devotion,
casts off the bond of sin and, remaining in heaven, enjoys the fruit of the gift of cows.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Life of Śāntanu," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 28)
Śrī Sūta said:
To Śaṃtanu and Yojanagandhā was born Vicitravīrya.

Residing in Hastināpura, he protected his subjects according to their own dharma; having gratified the gods with sacrifices and the ancestors with śrāddha rites, and having fathered sons, he ascended to heaven.
To Ambālikā, the wife of Vicitravīrya, Pāṇḍu was born as a son.
Having ruled the kingdom according to dharma, he too, upon abandoning his body due to a sage’s curse, attained the world of the gods. To that Pāṇḍu, Arjuna was born by Kuntīdevī.

Having gratified Śaṅkara through great austerity and obtained the Pāśupata weapon, he slew the Nivātakavaca Dānavas, the enemies of the lord of heaven; having offered the Khāṇḍava forest to Agni according to his desire, he received divine boons from the satisfied Fire-god; and then, though his kingdom had been seized by Suyodhana, he remained accompanied by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Nakula, Sahadeva, and Draupadī.

Having lived in concealment in the city of Virāṭa, and having defeated Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Duryodhana, Karṇa, and others during the cattle-raid and recovered the entire herd of cows, he— honored by King Virāṭa along with his brothers and accompanied by Vāsudeva—
engaged in battle at Kurukṣetra against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and their vast forces, including Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, Karṇa, and the rest.

Together with many princes of great prowess who had come from various lands, he slew Duryodhana and the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, regained his own kingdom, and having protected the realm according to dharma, ascended to heaven in joy along with his brothers.
From Arjuna and Subhadrā was born Abhimanyu,
by whom, having penetrated the wheel-array (cakravyūha) in the Bhārata war, numerous kings were brought to their death.
From Abhimanyu and Uttarā was born Parīkṣit;
having been consecrated by the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) as he departed for the forest, that prince ruled the kingdom and, having attained heaven, rejoiced.
From Parīkṣit, Janamejaya [received it] through Mātṛvatsya;
by him, for the purpose of warding off the sin of killing a Brahmin, the *Mahābhārata* was heard from beginning to end from Vaiśampāyana, the disciple of Vyāsa.
Having ruled the kingdom according to dharma, he ascended to heaven;
from Janamejaya and Puṣpavatī was born Śatānīka.

While ruling his kingdom with righteousness, he became disenchanted with the suffering of *saṃsāra*; through the instruction of Śaunaka and by means of *kriyā-yoga*, he propitiated Viṣṇu, the Lord of all worlds, and, being free from desire, attained the station of Viṣṇu.
To that Śatānīka was born Sahasrānīka in Phalavatī.
He was consecrated while still a child and became exceedingly devoted to Narasiṃha;
his life story will be told further below.
From Sahasrānīka, by Mṛgavati, was born Udayana;
he too, having ruled the kingdom according to Dharma and having propitiated Nārāyaṇa, attained that city.
From Udayana and Vāsavadattā was born Naravāhana;
having ruled the kingdom according to dharma, he attained heaven.
From Naravāhana and Aśvamedhadattā was born Kṣemaka.
And he, while established in kingship, having protected his subjects, resorted to Kalāpagrāma through the power of his knowledge when the world was overwhelmed by barbarians.
He who, full of faith, recites or hears this account of the kings' devotion to Hari,
shall obtain a lineage, perform pure deeds, and, having attained heaven, shall dwell there happily for a long time.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Śantanu’s Lineage," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*.
Śrī Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, hereafter I shall describe the terrestrial globe (bhūgola) in brief, with its mountains and rivers on all sides.
There are seven continents known as Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmala, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara.
Starting from Jambudvīpa, which measures one hundred thousand yojanas, each successive continent is double the size of the preceding one.

These continents are encircled by seven oceans—known as the Salt Ocean, the Sugarcane Juice Ocean, the Wine Ocean, the Clarified Butter Ocean, the Curd Ocean, the Milk Ocean, and the Clear Water Ocean—which are each double the size of the continent they surround and are shaped like rings.
That son of Manu named Priyavrata became the sovereign of the seven continents;
he had ten sons, beginning with Agnīdhra.
Three of them went forth as renunciants. To the remaining seven, their father gave the seven continents.
Among them, nine sons were born to Agnīdhra, the sovereign of Jambudvīpa.
Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta,
Ramya, Hiraṇyaya, Kuru, Bhadra, and Ketumān.
Having divided [his kingdom] into nine regions, the father, as he was entering the forest, gave them to his sons:
the Agnīdhrīya region, called Himavat,
whose sovereign lord was Nābhi, whose son was Ṛṣabha.
From Ṛṣabha came Bharata; because it was protected by Bharata for a long time through righteousness (*dharma*), this became known as Bhārata-varṣa.
In the center of Ilāvṛta is Meru, made of gold; its height is eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, and it is also submerged sixteen thousand [yojanas] below.
Twice that [measurement] is the width at the crown of the head.
In the center of that [world] is the city of Brahmā;
in the eastern direction is Indra’s Amarāvatī;
and in the southeastern direction is Agni’s Tejovatī.
In the south is Yama’s Saṃyamanī;
in the southwest is Nirṛti’s Bhayaṃkarī;
in the west is Varuṇa’s Viśvāvatī.
In the northwest is Vāyoḥ Gandhavatī;
in the north is Somasya Vibhāvarī.
Jambūdvīpa is endowed with nine regions, possessed of meritorious mountains and meritorious rivers.
The eight regions beginning with Kiṃpuruṣa are the places of enjoyment for those possessing merit; Bhāratavarṣa alone is a land of action, endowed with the four social classes.
In that very place, by means of their actions, human beings shall attain heaven;
and in this very place, liberation is attained by those free from desire through knowledge and action.
O Brahmin, those who commit evil deeds indeed go from here to a downward state.
Know that those evildoers, numbering in the tens of millions, reside in the hells at the bottom of the netherworld (pātāla).
Now the seven principal mountain ranges are described:
Mahendra, Malaya, Śuktimān, Ṛṣyamūka, Sahya, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—
these are the principal mountain ranges in Bhārata.
The Narmadā, Surasā, Ṛṣikulyā, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇāveṇī, Candrabhāgā, and Tāmraparṇī—these are the seven rivers.
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kāverī, and Sarayū—these are the great rivers that destroy sin.
This auspicious Jambudvīpa is renowned by the name of Jambu;
this excellent Bhārata is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
In the auspicious regions such as Ṛkṣadvīpa,
those who are free from desire and worship the Lion among Men according to their own dharma dwell there;
and through the exhaustion of their karmic authority, they attain liberation.
There are seven oceans, beginning with the Jambu-ocean and ending with the ocean of sweet water;
beyond that is the golden earth, and beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain. This is the world of the earth (bhūrloka).
Above this is the world of the atmosphere;
delightful is that realm of sky-dwellers, and above that is the heavenly world.
Understand that which is being proclaimed: the abode of heaven, a place of great merit, the very dwelling even of the gods for those who have performed meritorious deeds in Bhārata.
In the center of the earth stands the king of mountains, the radiant, golden Meru,
rising eighty-four thousand yojanas in height.
The mountain-dweller has entered sixteen [yojanas] below the earth;
the earth surrounding that mountain is of the same extent on all sides.
Upon its summit are three peaks where heaven is established;
it is filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with diverse flowers.
Meru indeed has three peaks: the middle, the western, and the eastern.
The middle peak is made of crystal, and it consists of lapis lazuli gems.
The eastern part is said to consist of sapphire (indranīla), and the western part of ruby (māṇikya);
it measures fourteen million and one thousand yojanas.
The middle peak is elevated, where the triple-heaven of Svarga resides;
it stands upon the summit like a parasol, unobstructed by light.
Between the northern peaks and the central one, on the back of the vault of heaven, is Triviṣṭapa; there dwell the blissful Apsarases.
Then Ānanda and Pramoda are on the middle Svarga-peak;
likewise Śveta, Pauṣṭika, Upaśobhana, and Manmatha.
Āhlāda is indeed the king of heaven on the western peak of heaven;
he is free from possessiveness, free from egoism, auspicious, and exceedingly pure.
And the heavens, O best of the twice-born, are situated upon the eastern peak;
indeed, twenty-one heavens are established upon the summit of Meru.
Those people, who were practitioners of non-violence and charity, as well as performers of sacrifices and austerities,
dwelt among them, free from anger.
In the case of entering water, there is bliss; in the daring act of entering fire, there is joy; and in leaping from a precipice, there is both happiness and for him a stainless victory in battle.
One who dies while practicing renunciation through fasting shall go to Triviṣṭapa;
one who performs seasonal sacrifices goes to the vault of heaven, and an Agnihotrin attains final liberation.
The twice-born who constructs tanks and wells obtains nourishment;
the giver of gold attains good fortune, and through the fruit of austerity, he reaches heaven.
The man who kindles a great fire during the cold season for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings shall attain heaven and the company of apsarases.
Indeed, by the gift of gold and cows, one attains freedom from ego;
through the pure gift of land, one obtains the state of peace.
By the gift of silver, a man attains the stainless heaven;
by the gift of a horse, an auspicious day; and by the gift of a maiden, prosperity.
Having offered libations to the twice-born and having given garments with devotion,
one attains the white heaven, reaching which one does not grieve.
By the gift of a tawny cow, one is glorified in the ultimate sense;
by the gift of a bull, one shall attain heaven and the fulfillment of desires.
One who bathes in a river during the month of Māgha, likewise one who gives a cow made of sesame seeds,
and one who gives an umbrella and sandals, goes to the most splendid heaven.
Having established a shrine for the deities, likewise serving the twice-born,
and being devoted to pilgrimages to sacred fords, one is glorified in the kingdom of heaven.
The mortal who eats only once a day, who always eats only at night,
and who observes fasts of three nights and so forth, being tranquil, shall attain auspicious heaven.
One who bathes in rivers, has conquered anger, lives as a celibate student, and is firm in his vows,
attains the stainless heaven, being devoted to the welfare of beings as they truly are;
through the gift of knowledge, the wise man shall attain freedom from egoism.
For by whatever disposition a person bestows whatever gift,
he attains that very heaven which he desires.
There are four supreme gifts: a maiden, a cow, land, and Sarasvatī;
these rescue one from hell by means of victory, conveyance, and milking.
But he who bestows all kinds of gifts upon the Brahmins shall reach the peaceful and healthy heaven and never return from it.
On the western peak, Brahmā himself is stationed;
on the eastern peak, Viṣṇu himself, and in the center, Śiva is stationed.
Beyond this, O best of Brahmins, hear about this path to heaven,
which is stainless, vast, and enlightened, situated higher and higher.
In the first [section] stands Kumāra, in the second the Mothers;
in the third are the Siddhas and Gandharvas, and in the fourth the Vidyādharas, O twice-born one.
On the fifth [path] is the King of Nagas, while on the sixth is the son of Vinata;
on the seventh are the divine ancestors, and likewise Dharmarāja on the eighth;
on the ninth is Dakṣa, and on the tenth path is Āditya.
The sun moves one hundred thousand yojanas above the Bhūrloka;
from there, at a distance of two thousand yojanas, is the Viṣṭambhana mountain.
The solar disc is three times its diameter in circumference according to its measurement;
when the sun is at midday in the city of Soma during the night,
then the Maker of Light stands in Amarāvatī, the city of Mahendra.
When the sun is at midday in Amarāvatī,
it is then seen rising in Saṃyamana, the realm of Yama.
Circumambulating Meru, the Sun always shines;
likewise, rising with Dhruva as his support, he is praised by the Vālakhilyas and others.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Earth-Globe," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 30)
Bharadvāja said:
Who was this Dhruva? Whose son was he, and how did he become the support of the sun?
O Sūta, having reflected upon this, tell me quickly; may you live for a hundred years!
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, Svāyambhuva Manu had a son named Uttānapāda;
that lord of the earth had two sons born to him.
Uttama was the eldest son of Suruci, while Dhruva was another, born of Sunīti;
once, as the king sat in the midst of his assembly, [Dhruva] entered.
Appointed by Sunīti for service at the royal court, her son Dhruva was adorned with ornaments and, intent on disciplined conduct, lived together with the sons of the nurses.
Having gone there, he prostrated before the king Uttānacaraṇa,
seeing that Uttama was indeed seated upon the lap of his father.
And having approached the king seated upon the throne, Suruci, observing that he desired to climb up due to childish impulsiveness, certainly said this: ||| NsP_31.6 |||
Suruci said: "O son of ill fortune, you who are born from the womb of an unfortunate woman, why do you, a child of childish intellect, desire to climb onto the lap of the lord of the earth?"
What meritorious deed have you performed to be worthy of sitting upon this lion-throne?
If there were any merit in you, why were you born in the womb of one so unfortunate?
By this very inference, understand your own meager store of merit.
"Even though he has become a prince, he does not adorn my womb;
behold this supreme and unsurpassed one born from my virtuous womb."
It was placed upon the knee of the king of the earth, augmented by his pride.
Sūta said:
Thus rebuked as "a mere child" in the midst of the royal assembly, he—
With tears falling from his eyes, that king, out of fortitude, said nothing at all—
neither what was appropriate nor what was inappropriate.
Restrained by the weight of his queen’s good fortune,
he suppressed his grief through his outward actions and dismissed the assembly.
Having bowed to the king with childlike innocence, that infant went to his own residence; then Sunīti, beholding the boy who was the abode of policy, [was filled with wonder].
By the very beauty of her face, he surely knew that the king had been insulted;
then, he saw Sunīti, a resident of the inner apartments, in private.
Having embraced him, he sighed deeply and wept aloud;
Sunīti, having comforted him and wiped his face, [spoke].
Fanning him with her soft hand and the hem of her dukūla garment,
the mother asked her son, "Tell me, what is the cause of your weeping?"
While the king was still alive, by whom was the child insulted?
Dhruva said:
"O Mother, I ask you; explain it correctly before me."
And since the status of being a wife is common to both, how is it that Suruci is the beloved,
and how is it, O Mother, that you are not the beloved of the king?
How did the son of Suruci attain such supremacy as to be called "the Best," while I,
despite being equally a prince, am called "the Unsurpassed"?
"How is it that you are unfortunate, while Sukukṣi and Suruci are so favored?
How is it that the royal throne is suitable for the supreme one, yet not for me?"
Hearing these words of that wise youth— "How may my own trivial merit become supreme, and how may the supreme [merit] of the Supreme One be attained?"— Sunīti [reflected].
Sighing slightly and slowly for the sake of soothing his grief for the child,
he began to speak words naturally sweet.
Sunīti said:
"O dear father of great intellect, with a pure inner self, I declare everything to you; do not set your mind on contempt."
Everything she said was indeed true and not otherwise,
for that queen was exceedingly beloved by the king among all his queens.

Accompanied by the accumulations of great merit, he, who was most excellent and worthy of the lion-throne of kings, dwelt within the womb of that most excellent woman, which was itself most excellent.
A parasol with the luster of the moon, two auspicious fly-whisks, a lofty throne, and elephants intoxicated with rut; NsP_31.27.
Swift horses, fleet steeds, a life free from mental anguish and physical disease,
and a prosperous kingdom without rivals— these are to be obtained through the grace of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
Having heard these faultless words of his mother Sunīti,
Dhruva, the son of Sunīti, took up speech to speak this reply.
Dhruva said:
"O mother Sunīti, listen to my composed words.
O auspicious lady, it is my conviction that there is nothing other than Uttānapāda."
"O Mother, my purpose is accomplished if there exists anyone who grants the desires of those who take refuge;
for today itself, having propitiated that Lord of the World, the one to be worshipped by all."
Know that each step I have attained is difficult for others to reach;
O Mother, you alone ought to grant me your assistance.
Grant me permission so that I may worship Viṣṇu.
Sunīti said:
"I cannot grant you permission, O son of Uttānapāda."
"My son, you are about seven or eight years old and fit for play; my dear child, you are her only son, and she lives solely depending upon you."
You were obtained through many hardships after I had fervently prayed to the gods; yet,
dear son, whenever you go outside even three or four steps to play, my very life-breath follows after you.
Dhruva said:
Until today, you were my father and mother, as was the powerful Uttānapāda;
from this day forward, Viṣṇu alone is my mother and father—of this there is no doubt.
Sunīti said: "O good son, I do not restrain you from the worship of Viṣṇu;
were I to restrain you, O dear one, my tongue would split into a hundred pieces."
Having thus received, as it were, permission, Dhruva circumambulated and prostrated at his mother’s lotus feet, and then departed for asceticism.
And having woven that garland of blue lotuses with the thread of her composure and with great skill, she presented it there as an offering to Dhruva.
Then, for the sake of protecting that path, his mother offered more than a hundred blessings, which were accepted by him; their flow could not be obstructed by others.
May Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, the all-pervading Lord and ocean of compassion, protect you everywhere, my son.
Sūta said:
Having emerged from his own palace, that boy of youthful prowess entered the forest,
his path revealed by a favorable breeze.
Familiar only with the royal highway because his mother was his deity, that prince did not know the path through the forest; for a moment he reflected.
Having reached the city garden, that boy reflected:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Who might become my helper?"
Thus, as soon as Dhruva opened his eyes and looked,
he beheld the Seven Sages in the forest, moving with an inconceivable gait.
Then, seeing the seven seers, possessing the splendor of the seven suns,
as if drawn and brought near by the threads of destiny, he rejoiced.
Their noble foreheads were marked with *tilaka*, their fingers held blades of *kuśa* grass,
they were seated upon black antelope skins, and they were adorned with sacred threads (*brahmasūtra*).
Approaching with his shoulders bowed and his palms joined in reverence,
Dhruva made this request after bowing down, speaking these charming words:
Dhruva said: "O best of sages, know me to be Dhruva, born from the womb of Sunīti,
the son of Uttānapāda, whose mind is filled with world-weariness."
Sūta said:
Having seen that boy, full of vital energy, whose form was naturally sweet, whose priceless eyes were beneficial to behold, and who spoke with words that were soft yet profound—
Having seated the child, they, greatly astonished, said to him:
"O child, even now we do not know the cause of your world-weariness."
Detachment arises in men who have not attained their desires;
how then is it that you, the prince of a king who rules over the seven continents, are likewise [disenchanted]?
"What indeed must be done by us? What is your desire?"
Dhruva said:
"O sages, he who is my kinsman is the most excellent and the most supreme of the supreme."
"O you of excellent vows, that supreme auspicious seat was indeed given to her by her father;
for I desire this assistance rendered by you."
How could that state be attained, which has never been enjoyed by another king, which rises far above all others,
and which is difficult even for Indra and the other gods to reach?
Having heard these words of the boy, Marīci and the other sages then replied to Dhruva with words that were indeed exactly as they were.
Marīci said:
One who has not tasted the essence of the pollen from the lotus feet of Govinda cannot realize the abundant fruit that transcends the path of one's desires.
Atri said:
How could one who has not honored the feet of Acyuta attain that station which is difficult for even Indra and others to reach, and which is very hard for human beings to approach?
Aṅgiras said: Indeed,
for one who cultivates with a virtuous disposition the lotus-feet of the Beloved of Kamalā, the state of all perfections is not far off in this world.
Puṣṭya said:
By the mere remembrance of whom the succession of great sins reaches the supreme end— that Viṣṇu is the eternal bestower of all.
Pulaha said:
That which they call the Supreme Brahman, beyond both Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
by whose Māyā all this is created— he is celebrated as Viṣṇu, the bestower of goals.
Kratu said:
What would Janārdana Viṣṇu— the Lord of Sacrifice, who is to be known through the Vedas,
and the inner self of this world— not bestow when he is satisfied?
Vasiṣṭha said:

O Prince, when one has propitiated that Hṛṣīkeśa, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) that abide in the dance of the world are attained; the fourfold goal of human existence (caturvarga) is not far off.
Dhruva said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have spoken the truth regarding the propitiation of Viṣṇu. How is that Blessed Lord to be worshipped? Let that procedure also be taught."
He who indeed gives abundantly would become most difficult to propitiate; [he thinks:
"I am a child, I am a prince; suffering is simply not tolerable for me."
The sages said:
Whether standing or walking, whether sleeping or waking, whether lying down or sitting, Nārāyaṇa is always to be known.
A mortal who mutters the name of Vāsudeva undoubtedly obtains everything— sons, wife, friends, kingdom, heaven, and liberation.
Who has not attained perfection by meditating on the four-armed Viṣṇu and reciting the twelve-syllable mantra, which consists of Vāsudeva?
And this great mantra was also practiced by your grandfather Manu,
O prince, when he, a devotee of Viṣṇu, desired sovereignty.
You too, O best of beings, become devoted to Vāsudeva by means of this mantra; you will swiftly attain whatever prosperity you desire.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, all those high-souled lords of sages vanished;
and Dhruva, having fixed his mind upon Vāsudeva, departed for ascetic penance.
Chanting the mantra that grants all goals, Dhruva performed austerities in Madhuvana on the bank of the Yamunā, following the path pointed out by the sage.

Through the power of his asceticism, the prince, endowed with faith while muttering prayers, beheld the Lord of the Heart as if visibly present before him, lotus-eyed and of divine form; thereupon, he immediately began to mutter them again with joy.
Hunger, thirst, rain, dense clouds, wind, the great heat of the day, and so forth—the multitude of physical sufferings—did not affect him at all;
for with his mind immersed in an incomparable ocean of bliss, the king’s infant did not even perceive the condition of his body.
And indeed, the obstacles created by the gods out of apprehension became fruitless for that youth of intense asceticism;
for localized impediments are truly not able to overcome a sage who is permeated by Viṣṇu, just as cold, heat, and the like cannot affect him.

Then the Lord Hari, who is dear to his devotees, the giver of boons whose vehicle is the king of birds, having been propitiated by the child through the power of meditation, arrived to behold that kinsman of his.
Adorned with a crown of clusters of jewels and possessing a magnificent complexion of great, shimmering gems,
he appeared like the Black Mountain (Astagiri) holding up the young sun out of envy for the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayagiri).

With a gaze steady and affectionate, he spoke thus to Dhruva, the prince established in asceticism, as if washing the dust from his body with the boundless streams of light-rays from his teeth: NsP_31.78.
"Choose a boon, my child, choose whatever is in your heart; for I am pleased with your asceticism, with your meditation, your restraint of the senses, and your difficult practice of mental control."
Hearing all those profound words, he suddenly opened his eyes and beheld before him that very Brahman whom he had been contemplating within himself, now manifest in bodily form with four arms.
Having seen for a moment the Lord of the Three Vedas, who was worthy of supreme worship, standing before him, the prince, filled with agitation, thought, "What shall I say here?
Or what shall I do? Yet he said nothing at all, nor did he perform any action.
His eyes filled with tears of joy and his limbs covered in horripilation, he cried out loudly, "O Lord of the Three Worlds!
and then fell to the ground before Hari in a prostration like a staff, his eyebrows trembling.
Then, having prostrated like a staff and having rolled about on the ground,
he wept for a long time with joy upon seeing that teacher of the world.
It was heard by Nārada, Sananda, and Sanaka,
as well as by other yogis such as Sanatkumāra and others, from that best of yogis.
The Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), holding him by the hand, certainly raised up that lotus-eyed one who was moistened by the waters of tears of compassion.
Hari, however, touched that body, which was grey with dust, with his two tender hands; having embraced him, Hari said to him:
"Choose a boon, O child, whatever dwells in your mind;
I shall grant it, of this there is no doubt, for there is nothing that cannot be given to you."
Then the royal child requested from Viṣṇu this boon: "May I have the power to praise You.
The God, under the guise of testing his knowledge of forms, touched him on the face with His stainless conch.
Then, his mind—as if perfectly purified by the moon of knowledge bestowed by the divine sage—became truly full for Dhruva;
and as the sun of knowledge born from the touch of Śaṅkha, the teacher of the three worlds, rose within him, he, being overjoyed, praised him most excellently.
Dhruva said:
[O you] whose feet are honored by the multitude of all the sages;
[O you] who bring about the destruction of the wicked!
One whose conduct is impetuous;
one whose foot-water is worshipped by the gods;
one who is dark like a water-bearing cloud.
He who has pacified the abode of Śālva, the lord of Saubha;
he who has brought joy to the hearts of the celestial nymphs, whose senses were captivated by the fresh aesthetic flavors of his exquisite discipline over lovely women;
he who is without beginning or end.
He who was steadfast in rescuing his own friend, the twice-born Aḍhananija;
he who disregarded the factions of the enemies who had sought refuge even with the Lord of the Gods;

and he whose heart bore the burden of the three worlds, which had been distressed by his own ill-repute when it was stolen during the entry into the cave of the King of Bears and later cleansed by the Syamantaka jewel.
Dwelling in Dvārakā;
having manifested supersensuous knowledge through hearing the nectar-like sound of his swift and sweet flute-playing;
wandering on the banks of the Yamunā.
He by whom the twice-born, the cows, and the swarms of bees were made to abandon their respective food;
he who is the boat-like feet for crossing over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of saṃsāra;
and he by whom Kālayavana was consumed by the fire of his own prowess.
Wearing a garland of forest flowers, his ears adorned with excellent jewel-earrings; known by various celebrated names;
he is the object of the minds and the speech of the learned sages of the Vedas.
The Blessed One, clad in saffron-colored silken garments, his chest adorned with the *bhṛgupada* mark and the *kaustubha* gem;

He who is accompanied by His beloved [Rādhā], Kṛṣṇa, His own mother, and the cowherds of Gokula; possessing four arms and adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, as well as garlands of fresh *tulasī* leaves, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and a crown;
His universal form (*viśvarūpa*) worshipped by Sunanda and other devotees.
The Ancient Supreme Person;
He of Exalted Praise;
Vāsudeva, the Abode of the World.
Born from the womb of the illustrious Devakī; whose lotus feet are bowed to by the Lord of Beings (Śiva) and Brahmā;
who dispels the fatigue of the gopīs during his divine sports in Vṛndāvana.

I bow to this exceedingly heart-stealing form of the Lord of All, which constantly fulfills the desires of the virtuous; which bears conchs white as kunda flowers and a face like the moon; which is beautiful and lovely to behold, with a most noble smile, and is worshipped by the wise. Desiring a dwelling place and established in austerity, I have beheld you, the secret of the holy lords of sages.
O Lord, like one searching for a divine jewel among mere glass trinkets, I have attained my purpose; I shall ask for no further boons.
Having seen your lotus feet, never before beheld, O Lord, I shall certainly not abandon them;
I do not beg for sensual desires, for he would be a fool indeed who would seek a mere grain of chaff from the wish-fulfilling tree.

Having taken refuge in you, the seed of liberation, I am no longer able to enjoy external pleasures. O Lord, when you, the mine of jewels, are one's own master, it is not fitting to wear an ornament made of glass.
Therefore, O Lord, I do not ask for any other boon; let there be constant devotion to your lotus feet for me.
O best of gods, grant me this boon; again and again I entreat you for this alone.
Śrī Sūta said:
To him who was thus speaking, having obtained divine knowledge through the vision of the Self, the Blessed One spoke.
The Blessed One said:
"Having propitiated Viṣṇu, what has been gained by this? Let there not be such ill-repute even while eating.
Attain that supreme state which is desired by you; with a purified heart, you shall reach me in due time."
The support of all the planets, a wish-fulfilling tree for all people, and worthy of veneration by everyone—
by my grace, that noble Sunīti, who is your mother, shall be near me.
Śrī Sūta said:
Having thus granted him boons, Mukunda, whose form is visible to all, went to his own abode;
slowly casting off his divine body, he repeatedly turned back to gaze upon his devotee.
And at that moment, the assembly of gods and Siddhas, seeing that gathering of Śrī Viṣṇu and his devotees,
rained down a shower of celestial flowers and joyfully praised Dhruva and the Imperishable One.
This son of Sunīti shines with splendor and self-confidence, being praised even by the gods;
he who, through both his glorification and his sight, increases the lifespan, fame, and fortune of men.
In this way, Dhruva attained that station so difficult to reach through the grace of Hari;
yet this is not surprising, for when He whose banner is the moon is pleased, nothing is unattainable for His devotees.
The lunar mandala is twice the measure of the solar mandala;
two hundred thousand [yojanas] from that is the mandala of the constellations.
The station of Mercury is also two hundred thousand [yojanas] from the circle of the lunar mansions;
and at a distance equal to that same measure, Venus is situated above Mercury.
Aṅgāraka is situated at that same distance from Śukra;
however, the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] from Bhauma.
Saturn is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] above Jupiter;
and one hundred thousand [yojanas] above that Saturn is the sphere of the Seven Sages.
O best of beings, one hundred thousand [yojanas] above the circle of the seven ṛṣis, Dhruva stands as the central pivot for the entire wheel of luminaries.
O best of Brahmins, by its very nature the sun blazes with its rays below and above;
it determines the duration of time for the three worlds in age after age.
O best of the twice-born,
O tiger among sages, through devotion to Viṣṇu, Brahmā increased austerity, truth, and these worlds.
O best of the twice-born, the sun heats with its upward-reaching rays,
and with its downward-reaching, long beams, it illuminates the earthly realm (bhūrloka).
The Sun, the remover of all sins and the creator of the three worlds,
should be viewed as one mandala after another, like a succession of umbrellas.
Beneath the solar disc, the Bhuvarloka is established;
and the sovereignty over the three worlds was granted by Viṣṇu to Śatakratu.
Accompanied by the world-protectors, he protects the worlds according to the Dharma;
that illustrious lord of the gods shall dwell in heaven, O fortunate one.
O Sage, know that below this is the radiant Pātāla;
there the sun does not scorch, nor is there night, nor the moon.
O best of the twice-born, those people dwelling in Pātāla, having assumed divine forms, constantly perform austerities, shining with their own splendor.
Maharloka is situated at a distance of one crore [yojanas] from Svarloka;
it is twice as large in its circumference, increasing by one yojana [at each successive level].
O Brahmin, the fifth world, Janaloka, is situated there, frequented by sages;
above that stands Tapoloka, extending for forty million [yojanas].
Satyaloka, situated above Tapoloka, consists of eight crores [of yojanas];
all [the worlds] situated above the [seven] worlds should be known as having the shape of umbrellas.
The world of Viṣṇu is situated at twice the distance from the world of Brahmā;
its majesty has been described by those who contemplate the worlds in the Vārāha [Purāṇa].
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, the Supreme Person remains;
he stands as the one beyond the cosmic egg, the manifest, untainted Puruṣa.
"One endowed with austerity and knowledge shall be liberated from the bonds of Paśu.
Thus, O sinless one, the structure of the terrestrial globe has been described by me to you;
he who understands this correctly attains the supreme goal.
The immeasurable Viṣṇu, the creator of the world’s structure, the Man-lion, worshipped by men and gods,
assumes a form without beginning in age after age and, as the slayer of the wicked, protects the universe.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 31.
Bharadvāja said:
O high-minded one, I now wish to hear about the incarnations of Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who possesses a thousandfold armies; tell that to me.
Sūta said:
"Indeed, I shall narrate to you the life of that wise Sahasrānīka; listen to me as I describe the incarnations of Hari."
Consecrated in his own kingdom by the best of the twice-born, that prince Sahasrānīka ruled the realm in accordance with righteousness.
While that wise prince was protecting the kingdom,
his devotion was fixed upon Narasiṃha, the lord of gods and the best of deities.
In former times, Bhṛgu came in person to see that devotee of Viṣṇu;
having honored him with offerings of water for the hands, water for the feet, and a seat, the king spoke this to him.
"I have been purified now, O best of sages, by the sight of you;
for those lacking merit, a vision of you is very difficult to obtain in this Kali age."
Having installed Narasiṃha, the eternal God of gods, I wish to worship him; tell me the procedure for that.
I wish to hear of all the incarnations of the God of gods, the wielder of the discus; please tell me about all those meritorious ones as well.
Bhṛgu said:
Listen, O son of a king; indeed, in this Kali age, no one at all performs devotion to Hari, nor is anyone possessed of supreme devotion toward this Nṛsiṃha.
For one who possesses devotion by their very nature toward Narasiṃha, the best of gods,
his enemies perish and the accomplishment of his purpose arises.
"You are an exceedingly devoted follower of Hari and the most excellent among those of the Pāṇḍu lineage;
therefore, I shall tell you everything. Listen with a one-pointed mind."
He who, full of devotion, should construct a beautiful temple for Narasiṃha,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Viṣṇu.
One should have an image of Narasiṃha fashioned, endowed with all the [auspicious] marks;
liberated from all sins, he shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
O tiger among men, he who performs the consecration of Narasiṃha according to the prescribed rite,
being free from desire, is liberated from the affliction of the body.
The man who, having installed Narasiṃha, performs worship,
his desires shall be fulfilled and he shall attain the supreme state.
In ancient times, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, attained their respective positions by worshipping Viṣṇu through the grace of Keśava.
O King, those various excellent monarchs, headed by Māndhātṛ,
having propitiated Viṣṇu, departed from here for the heavenly world.
But he who constantly worships Narasiṃha, the Lord of the gods, shall partake in heaven and liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Therefore, having become single-minded, by means of worshipping Narasiṃha with a vow for as long as you live, you shall obtain that which you desire.
O King, he who causes Janārdana to be fashioned and installs him according to the prescribed rites shall never depart from the world of Viṣṇu.

Having installed that Nṛsiṃha of infinite prowess, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by gods and asuras, a person should worship him with devotion according to the prescribed rites; he shall go directly to Hari, the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the *Śrīnarasiṃhapurāṇa*, in the account of Sahasrānīka. (NarP 32)
The King said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear in truth the meritorious ritual for the worship of Hari;
by your grace, O Lord, explain it to me in detail."
Whatever merit a man who sweeps the temple of Narasiṃha obtains,
a man who smears it with plaster gains that same merit.
Whatever merit may arise from bathing Keśava with pure water,
whatever merit arises from bathing him with milk, and likewise with curd and honey,
whatever merit arises from bathing him with ghee, or that which arises from the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); [all that is attained by this].
When the image has been washed with warm water and then bathed with devotion using a mixture of camphor and agallochum water;

Whatever merit is gained by the offering of the *arghya*, and that which comes from the offering of water for the feet and the rinsing of the mouth, as well as that which arises from bathing with mantras and the gift of clothing; ||| NsP_33.5 |||
What fruit would arise from worshipping with sandalwood and saffron?
And what is the fruit of worshipping with flowers, as well as with incense and lamps?
Whatever fruit has been declared for offerings of food, for performing circumambulations,
for performing prostrations, and for hymns and songs of praise— [all that is obtained by one who performs this rite].
Whatever merit may arise from the gift of a palm-leaf fan and a chowrie, whatever from the gift of a banner for Viṣṇu, and whatever from the gift of a conch; ||| NsP_33.8 |||
O Brahmin, tell me, who am devoted to Keśava, all this and whatever else has been prompted by ignorance.
Sūta said: Thus urged by that king, the Brahmin Bhṛgu then appointed Mārkaṇḍeya to the narration and departed.
He too, being especially devoted to Hari and filled with joy,
began to speak to the king, having been urged by Bhṛgu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O prince, descendant of the Pāṇḍu lineage, listen to this; I shall describe to you, a devotee of Viṣṇu, the procedure for the worship of Hari in its proper sequence.
And he who constantly undertakes the sweeping of the Narasiṃha [temple],
being liberated from all sins, rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who performs the smearing [of the ground] with cow dung, clay, and water,
having attained imperishable fruit, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In this regard, O best of beings, there is an ancient history of events from the past,
by hearing which one becomes liberated from all sins.
In former times, O Indra among kings, King Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by his five brothers and Draupadī, wandered through the forest.
Then those five Pāṇḍavas emerged from the thorns of their pain,
and Nārada too, having enjoyed this supreme sacred site, departed for heaven.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira set out for that supreme sacred ford,
in order to behold the foremost of sages, the teacher of the dharma of sacred fords.
And the righteous-minded Dānava Bahuroma, free from anger and malice, likewise [thinks thus],
O King Sthūlaśiras.
O Sage, King, seeing the Pāṇḍavas departing, the Dānava, desiring Draupadī,
then assumed the form of a man with thick body hair and went along.
Then, having made his formal vow, he sat upon a seat of kuśa grass,
holding a water-pot at his side and a needle for darbha grass in his hand.
Chanting mantras while holding a rosary and gazing at the tip of his own nose,
he was seen there on the banks of the Revā by the Pāṇḍavas, who were wandering in the forest.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his younger brothers, bowed down to him and, having beheld him, spoke these words: "O great sage, by good fortune you have arrived!"
O Lord, reveal the most secret sacred sites (tīrthas) belonging to the body of Rudra;
O Protector, I have heard of the vision of the sages which imparts the teaching of Dharma.
Just as Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was saying this to the sage,
another sage named Sthūlaśiras arrived, assuming the form of a sage.
Who indeed is the protector here for this person speaking such words while afflicted?
Only he who would protect a living being terrified by fear when that being has come to him for refuge.
The fruit of that [gift] shall indeed be infinite; how much more so for me, the best of the twice-born?
On one side is the gift of the earth, with Mount Meru as the sacrificial fee.
For indeed, one should protect from others those whose lives are in distress, those facing a threat to their very breath,
as well as a twice-born man, a cow, a woman, a child, and anyone being oppressed by wicked people.
But the man who remains indifferent goes to the Raurava hell;
then, when my entire wealth has been seized, I shall be intent on giving up my life.
"Which heroic man protects one who has been defeated by the Dānavas,
having seized my rosary as well as this beautiful water-pot?"
"I have been struck down by blows from his hands; likewise, my charming horse Khāṭa has been killed, and all my possessions have been seized by that evil-minded Dānava."
Having heard these words of the eunuch, the Pāṇḍavas were seized with agitation;
with their hair standing on end, they once again prepared the fire for that sage and departed.
Having set Draupadī down there beside the high-souled sage,
those Pāṇḍavas then proceeded much further away in their agitation.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira said: "What is it that we do not see here?
O Arjuna, turn back and go for the sake of protecting Kṛṣṇā!"
Then Arjuna departed, impelled by the words of his kinsmen;
thereafter, King Yudhiṣṭhira made his word come true.
Then, O Lord, having beheld the orb of the sun in that most dense forest,
[I was sustained] by my truth, my well-performed deeds, and my discourse on dharma.
"May the gods, who partake in my doubt, declare the truth to me.
Then, from the sky, there arose an incorporeal voice to the king:
"O Great King, this is the Dānava, the sage Sthūlaśiras, standing here.
He has not been harmed by anyone; this is merely the illusion of that evil-minded one."
Then Bhīma, becoming exceedingly enraged with fury, struck that Dānava on the crown of his head as he was being destroyed by blows from his hands.
He too, having regained his own fierce and terrifying form, struck him;
there a dreadful battle ensued between the two formidable demons.
Even Bhīma, with great effort, broke off his thick head in the forest;
yet when Arjuna arrived, he did not see that sage at all.
And so, having climbed the tree, Arjuna looked again for Draupadī, the virtuous, beloved, and dear wife.
Having placed her upon his shoulder, the Dānava ran swiftly;
she went along, held by the wicked one, weeping like a female osprey.
Crying out "Terrible! Terrible! and "O son of Dharma!", the hero, seeing her, advanced while making the quarters resound with his shouts.
The trees were violently shattered by the force of the impact of his footsteps;
then the Daitya, too, quickly abandoned that slender woman and fled.
Nevertheless, out of anger toward him, Arjuna did not release the asura;
at that very moment, he fell upon the surface of the earth, now possessing four arms.
Wearing two yellow garments and bearing the conch and discus as weapons, Pārtha, overcome with wonder, bowed down and spoke these words: NsP_33.47.
Arjuna said:
O Blessed One, how was this Vaiṣṇava illusion created by you here?
O Lord, I too have committed an offense; forgive that, for salutations be unto you!
"Surely this terrible deed was committed by me through a state of ignorance;
therefore, O Lord of the World, it must be forgiven. For whence comes consciousness in a human being?"
Caturbhuja said:
"O mighty-armed one, I am not Kṛṣṇa; I am a Dānava with many hairs on my body, who has entered the body of Hari through the power of his past karma."
Arjuna said:
O Bahuroma, tell me truly of your previous birth and its deeds;
by what ripening of karma did you attain the same form as Viṣṇu?
Caturbhuja said:
Listen, O highly fortunate Arjuna, together with my brothers,
to this most wonderful account, which increases the joy of those who hear it.
In former times, I was a king born of the Lunar dynasty,
renowned as Jayadhvaja, and solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
He was constantly devoted to sweeping the temple of Viṣṇu,
intent upon smearing it with plaster, and ever prepared to offer lamps.
There was a virtuous priest known as Vītihotra;
seeing my conduct, that brahmin was filled with wonder.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Once, when that king, who was solely devoted to Viṣṇu, was seated,
Vītihotra, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, questioned him.
O King, supreme knower of dharma, devoted to the worship of Hari,
you are the best among men who possess devotion to Viṣṇu, O bull among men.
O illustrious one, tell me that: what fruit was known by you through being constantly devoted to sweeping and likewise intent upon smearing [the ground] with cow dung?
Indeed, there are other rites that are even more dear to Viṣṇu;
nevertheless, O illustrious one, you are constantly intent upon these two.
O Lord of Men, that great merit is known to you in its entirety;
therefore, if it is not a secret and if you have affection for me, please speak of it.
Jayadhvaja said:
"Listen, O tiger among brahmins, to my own history from the past."
O best of Brahmins, because I remember my past births, I know this which will cause wonder among the listeners:
in a previous life, I was a Brahmin named Raivata.
I was indeed always a priest for those unworthy of sacrifice, a village priest,
a slanderer, a cruel man, and a seller of goods that should not be sold.
Abandoned by his own kinsmen due to the performance of forbidden acts,
he was constantly devoted to great sins as well as to hatred toward Brahmins.
One who lusts after the wives and wealth of others, who harms living beings, who is constantly addicted to drinking liquor, and likewise devoted to hatred for the Veda; NsP_33.65 //
Thus, constantly devoted to evil and repeatedly obstructing the path,
I once acted according to my own whims, having taken the wives of brahmins.
O Brahmin, having reached the empty temple of Viṣṇu at night with offerings and other rites,
how much of it was swept clean by him from the hem of his own garment?
O best of the twice-born, a lamp was placed there for the sake of sexual pleasure;
by that act as well, my evil karma has been entirely brought to destruction.
O twice-born one, while I remained thus in the temple of Viṣṇu out of a desire for enjoyment,
the city guards arrived at that very moment upon seeing the lamp.
Saying, "This is a foreign spy sent for the sake of theft," they struck me down;
having severed my head with a sharp-edged sword, they departed.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot accompanied by the Lord's servants,
I then went to the heavenly world while being sung of by Gandharvas.
Caturbhuja said:
O best of the twice-born, having stayed there for more than a hundred Brahma-kalpas,
endowed with divine enjoyments and possessed of a divine form.
"Indeed, by virtue of my merit, I was born into the Lunar dynasty as a lotus-eyed king known as Jayadhvaja."
There too, having died by the power of time, he attained heaven;
reaching the world of Indra, he then went to the world of Rudra.
As I was traveling from the world of Rudra to the world of Brahmā, I saw the sage Nārada;
I bowed to him, yet out of pride I did not even smile at him.
"O King, become a Rākṣasa!"— thus did that enraged twice-born man utter a curse upon me when I heard it being pronounced by him.
O King, when I had propitiated him at the Revā-maṭha of the wise son of Dharma, O monarch, the sage bestowed his grace upon me.
"For one who carries off his wife, there shall be release from the curse;
I am that very person, O King Arjuna, son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira."
I have attained the same form as Viṣṇu; indeed, today I am going to Vaikuṇṭha.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, he mounted Garuḍa while the son of Dharma looked on.
He went to the abode of Viṣṇu, where Viṣṇu dwells together with Śrī;
there his greatness was described by him through the acts of sweeping and smearing.
If one has attained this prosperity even by performing an action involuntarily,
how much more so through the proper worship of those who are devoted and tranquil?
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, King Sahasrānīka, born of the Pāṇḍu lineage, became devoted to the worship of Hari.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, listen: the imperishable Lord Nārāyaṇa grants liberation to his worshippers, whether [the worship] is performed with knowledge or even without knowledge.
Worship the Lord of the World again and again; this I say to you repeatedly, O twice-born ones, if you desire to cross the difficult-to-traverse ocean of worldly existence.
Those devotees who worship Hari, who removes the suffering of those who bow before him—
those are to be saluted, they are to be honored, and they are especially worthy of prostration.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Fruit of Sweeping and Smearing as Taught by Mārkaṇḍeya," in the *Śrī-Narasimha Purāṇa*, within the narrative of Sahasrānīka.
Śrīsahasrānīka said: O best of the twice-born, O high-minded Mārkaṇḍeya, tell me once again what merit is gained from removing the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Viṣṇu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, having removed the remains of the previous offerings (nirmālya) and having bathed Keśava,
who possesses the form of Narasiṃha, with water, one is liberated from all sins.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), he shall ascend a celestial vehicle and go to heaven;
having reached the abode of Śrī Viṣṇu, he rejoices for an imperishable duration of time.
"Come, O Narasiṃha!"— having thus invoked [the deity] with unbroken rice grains and flowers,
by this much alone, O King of kings, one is liberated from all sins.
Having offered a seat, as well as water for honor, water for the feet,
and water for sipping according to the ritual procedure to the God of gods, one is liberated from all sins.
O lord of men, having bathed Narasiṃha with water and milk,
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who, being pure and pleasing to behold, bathes [the image] once with curd,
attains the world of Viṣṇu, where he is honored by the best of the gods.
The man who performs the worship of Hari, bathing the image with honey,
shall rejoice in the world of Agni and thereafter dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
He who, at the time of the ritual bath, especially performs the bathing of the form of Narasiṃha with ghee, accompanied by the sounding of conchs and kettledrums; ||| NsP_34.9 |||
Having cast off the evil skin like a snake shedding its worn-out slough,
he ascends a divine celestial chariot and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Great King, for him who bathes the Lord of Gods with devotion using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) preceded by mantras, his merit is infinite.
And he who, having rubbed the Lord of the Gods with wheat flour and washed him with warm water, shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
But he who, out of devotion, cleanses the footstool with *bilva* leaves and washes it with warm water, is liberated from all sins.
Having bathed with water and *kuśa* grass flowers, one shall attain the world of Brahmā; with water containing jewels, the world of Savitṛ; with golden water, the world of Kubera;
and having bathed Narasiṃha with camphor and agallochum water.
Having rejoiced in the world of Indra, he shall thereafter dwell in the city of Viṣṇu,
O best of men, after having bathed Govinda with devotion using meritorious water.
Having reached the world of Savitṛ, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
by worshipping with devotion and having clothed Hari in two garments, he attains the state of Hari.
Having delighted in the world of Soma, one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu;
[one who has anointed] the form of Acyuta with pastes of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
O King of kings, by anointing [the deity] with devotion using jasmine, *mālatī*, *jāti*, *ketakī*, *aśoka*, and *campaka* flowers, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million eons.
With *puṃnāga*, *nāga*, and *bakula* trees; with lotuses, various types of water-lilies (*utpala*);
with *tulasī* and *karavīra*; and with *pālāśa* and *anukumbaka* flowers.
With these and other excellent flowers, a person should worship Acyuta; for each flower, one shall obtain the fruit of ten gold pieces.
Having fashioned a garland from these as they may be obtained, one should worship Viṣṇu;
[thereby one dwells] for thousands of koṭis of kalpas and hundreds of koṭis of kalpas.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu—
he who, with devotion, [worships] Narasiṃha with unbroken bilva leaves.
He who worships [the deity] together with flawless *tulasī* leaves shall be liberated from all sins and adorned with every ornament.
One is honored in the world of Viṣṇu by means of a golden celestial chariot;
likewise, one who offers guggulu resin known as māhiṣa, combined with clarified butter and sugar, [attains the same].
O Indra among kings, the devotee who offers incense to Narasiṃha becomes free from all sins through the incense that permeates all directions.
Resplendent in a celestial chariot crowded with hosts of Apsarases,
he rejoices in the world of Vāyu and thereafter proceeds to the city of Viṣṇu.
If a person should light a lamp with ghee or oil for Viṣṇu according to the rules and with devotion, hear now the fruit of his merit.
Having abandoned the mire of evil, he, possessing a radiance equal to the sun,
goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a luminous celestial chariot.
Having offered as oblation to Narasiṃha rice cooked with milk (śālyodana) mixed with ghee and sugar during the day, as well as barley gruel (yāvaka) and milk-rice (pāyasa), ||| NsP_34.29 |||
O King, for as many years as there are grains of rice in that heap,
that devotee of Viṣṇu remains in the world of Viṣṇu, enjoying great pleasures.
Then, being satisfied by that Vaiṣṇava offering, the inhabitants of heaven grant him peace, prosperity, and indeed good health.
O son of a king, listen to the fruit that accrues to men by performing even a single circumambulation of the God of gods with devotion.
Having obtained the fruit of circumambulating the earth, he shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu by him who has indeed performed a prostration with devotion to Mādhava.
By him who praises Madhusūdana before the gods with hymns and recitations, the fruit known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is attained directly.
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
[he who performs] singing, instrumental music, and dance, accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments.
The man who indeed causes [the temple] of Viṣṇu to be built goes to the abode [of the Lord], especially during the time of a festival; he can travel at will and assume any form at will.
And being attended by hosts of apsarases who were skilled in excellent singing,
he shone forth in a celestial chariot resplendent and variegated with highly precious jewels.
Having reached heaven from heaven, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu—
he who offers a banner to Viṣṇu accompanied by Garuḍa.
He too, shining in a celestial chariot adorned with banners,
attains the world of Viṣṇu, where he is attended by hosts of apsarases.
O King, he who worships Viṣṇu with divine golden ornaments— necklaces, armlets, earrings, crowns, and other such finery— [attains the highest state].
Freed from all evil and adorned with every ornament,
the wise one shall dwell in the world of Indra for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
He who, having first propitiated Viṣṇu, bestows a milch cow that is tawny-colored,
whatever [gift] is offered thereafter is most excellent, even if it be merely burnt.
Having given that to Narasiṃha, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
his ancestors rejoice for a long time in Śvetadvīpa, O King.
O King, for that best of men who thus worships Narasiṃha, both heaven and liberation shall be attained; of this there is no doubt.
O King, wherever Viṣṇu Narasiṃha is thus worshipped by men,
there is no fear of disease, famine, kings, thieves, or the like.
Having propitiated Mādhava, the Man-Lion, according to this rite,
one shall enjoy the various pleasures of heaven and shall never again become a suckling at the breast.
In whatever village the daily oblation of ghee with sesame seeds is performed,
no fear shall arise anywhere in that village.
O King, having propitiated Narasiṃha through Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, there shall be for us no drought, no great pestilence, no faults, and no conflagrations.
One should perform a Lakṣahoma sacrifice in the village where the lord of the city resides;
when that which I have described is performed, his fear will not come.
Having perceived the danger of death for both the subjects and oneself,
one should properly propitiate [the deity] in the temple of Narasiṃha.
O lord of men, one should also have a *koṭihoma* performed at a temple of Śaṅkara by restrained Brahmins, provided with meals and ritual fees.
O best of kings, when that has been performed through the grace of Narasiṃha,
the deaths of living beings caused by portents and other calamities are pacified.
Upon seeing a terrible bad dream or when afflicted by planetary disturbances,
by performing a fire-oblation and offering a meal, his misfortune is destroyed.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses,
one should worship Narasiṃha and perform a lakṣahoma sacrifice.
O Indra among kings, there is peace for him and for those dwelling in that place;
O King, the worship of Narasiṃha is endowed with such fruits as these.
O son of the king, perform this if you desire a happy destiny;
there is nothing superior to this for bestowing the fruits of heaven and liberation.
It is easy for kings to perform the worship of the God of gods;
for in the forest there are, indeed, priceless leaves and flowers of the trees.
Water exists as a common element in rivers and ponds;
one should restrain the mind solely upon the practice for the accomplishment of knowledge.
For one by whom the mind is restrained, liberation rests in the palm of their hand.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus has the worship of Acyuta here been described by me at the urging of Bhṛgu. Perform this adoration of Viṣṇu day after day; tell me what else you wish to hear, and I shall speak to you.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Śrī Viṣṇu," in the *Śrī Narasiṃha Purāṇa*, within the narrative of Sahasrānīka. (NarP 34)
The King said:
"Aha! You have described the great fruit born from the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
O tiger among sages, those who do not indeed worship Viṣṇu are truly asleep."
"By your grace, I have indeed heard this sequence for the worship of Narasiṃha;
I shall worship him with devotion. Tell me [the rite] that yields the fruit of ten million fire-offerings (koṭihoma)."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, in former times Śaunaka was questioned about this very matter by his teacher;
what Śaunaka told him, that I shall relate to you.
Bṛhaspati, however, questioned Śaunaka as he sat comfortably.
Bṛhaspati said:
"The ground for a *lakṣahoma* and that which is auspicious for a *koṭihoma*," 35.4cd.
O best of Brahmins, tell me that procedure for the performance of the fire-oblation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been thus addressed by his preceptor, he [then performed] the ritual procedure beginning with the hundred-thousand oblations (lakṣahoma).
Śaunaka began to speak correctly, O best of kings.
Śaunaka said:
I shall explain it to you correctly; listen, O priest of the gods.
The great ground for the Lakṣahoma, its specific purification,
and the supreme characteristics of the ground recommended for the sacrificial rite.
Having dug a pit knee-deep that is well-prepared, level, smooth, and increasingly superior toward the east,
one should especially clean it out.
Having covered it there with clay that is clear on the outside, one should apply a plaster;
the measurement for the pit in all respects is indeed the length of an arm.
One should have it made four-cornered and square with equal cords;
above that, one should fashion a very extensive girdle, also square.
[The ground] should be raised to the measure of four finger-breadths and marked out with threads;
[one should invite] Brahmins who are perfected in the Vedas and endowed with the performance of Vedic rites.
The patron, in particular, should address them according to the rule:
"Those twice-born ones shall observe the vow of celibacy for three nights."
Then, having fasted for a day and night, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times;
they [the practitioners] shall wear white garments, be bathed, and bear fragrances, garlands, and flowers.
Pure, abstaining from food, contented, with their senses restrained,
they sat upon seats of kuśa grass once more with one-pointed minds.
Then, being unwearied, they should diligently undertake the fire-oblation;
having drawn a mandala on the ground and sprinkled it with water, they should carefully establish the fire.
And there, one should perform the oblation according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya texts;
however, one should first offer the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāga portions.
The wise one, with a single-pointed mind, should offer the first oblation mixed with grains and sesame seeds, accompanied by the Gāyatrī mantra and the utterance of "svāhā."
Gāyatrī is the mother of the meters, established as the womb of Brahman;
Savitṛ is its deity, and Viśvāmitra is likewise its seer.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations accompanied by sesame seeds using the *vyāhṛti* mantras,
until the prescribed number is fulfilled— whether it be one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) or ten million (*koṭi*).
During that time, the patron, having first performed the worship of Acyuta, should diligently perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds for the sake of the poor and the helpless.
One should provide food for as long as the fire-oblation (homa) is being performed;
when it is completed, one should, endowed with faith, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests.
Then, according to what is appropriate and not out of greed, one should sprinkle with water of peace especially those who are ill in the midst of the village.
When this is done for the fire-oblation,
O highly fortunate one, there shall always be a pacification that quells all afflictions for the city, the town, the kingdom, the king, and the countryside.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus, O delighter of kings, this procedure for the hundred-thousand-fold oblation and other rites, which bestows great peace upon the kingdom, has been narrated as spoken by Śaunaka.
Whether in a village, a house, or a place outside the city, this rite for the city has been performed with effort by the twice-born;
therein shall there be peace for men, for cattle, for their servants, and for the king as well, O Lord of the Earth.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Lakṣahoma," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 35)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall describe the incarnations of the Discus-bearer, the God of gods;
listen to them, O protector of the earth, for they are purifying and destroyers of sin.
Just as the Vedas were given to the Self-born by means of the form of a fish, and Madhu and Kaiṭabha were brought to their destruction by that Great-souled One; ||| NsP_36.2 |||
Just as Mandara was supported by Viṣṇu in the form of a tortoise, and just as the earth was supported, O King, by the high-souled one in the form of a boar; NsP_36.3 //
O King, it was by that very [means] that the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, possessed of great heroism and a massive body, met his end.
Just as in ancient times, O King, Hiraṇyakaśipu, the enemy of the gods,
was brought to his destruction by the Lord Narasiṃha.
O Prince, just as in the past the great-souled Vāmana bound Bali,
so too was Indra made the sovereign of the three worlds by him.
And how Rāvaṇa, along with his hosts of wondrous Rākṣasas who were thorns to the gods, was slain by Viṣṇu having become Rāma, O King.
Just as in former times the warrior caste was exterminated by Paraśurāma,
and as in former times the Daitya was slain by Balabhadra Rāma.
Just as Kaṃsa and other Daityas, the enemies of the gods, were slain by Kṛṣṇa, so too,
when the Kali age has arrived, the Lord Buddha shall be Nārāyaṇa.
I shall tell you how, at the conclusion of the Kali age, the Mlecchas were struck down once again by assuming the form of Kalkin.
O King, he who with a concentrated mind hears of the prowess of the infinite Hari as it is being told by me,
being liberated from sin, goes to the most exalted abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Sequential Account of the Manifestations of Hari," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 36)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Because of the multiplicity of the incarnations of the high-souled Acyuta, it is not possible to describe them in detail; therefore, I shall speak of them in brief.
In ancient times, it is said, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person and creator of the world,
entered into yogic sleep upon the couch of Ananta’s coils.
Then, O King, as that god of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, lay fast asleep,
two drops of sweat fell from his ears into the water.
From him were born two of great strength named Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
they possessed massive bodies, great heroism, and immense power and prowess.
O best of kings, while Acyuta was asleep, a great lotus arose from the center of his navel; within it, Brahmā was born.
And he was told by Viṣṇu, "O King, O high-minded one, create living beings";
having said "So be it" to the Lord of the World, Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, [departed].
Just as he was preparing to create progeny by the power of the Vedic scriptures,
at that moment both Madhu and Kaiṭabha arrived there.
Having arrived, those two terrible Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, instantly deprived Brahmā of his knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras and departed.
Then, O King, the Lotus-born one became bereft of knowledge in an instant;
distressed, he reflected: "How indeed shall I create the subjects?"
"Commanded by the God to 'create progeny,' how shall I do so, being devoid of knowledge? Alas! A great calamity has arrived. (NsP 37.10)
Having reflected thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, afflicted by grief,
though he recalled the Vedic scriptures with great effort, did not perceive [a solution].
Then, with a dejected mind, he began to praise that god, the Supreme Person, correctly with a one-pointed mind according to the scripture.
Brahmā said:
Oṃ, salutations to the treasury of the Vedas; salutations to the treasury of the scriptures;
salutations eternally to the treasury of higher knowledge and the treasury of ritual actions.
Homage again and again to the Vidyadhara god, the Lord of Speech;
homage eternally to the Inconceivable One, homage again and again to the Omniscient One.
O mighty-armed Adhokṣaja, you are formless, yet you are the embodiment of sacrifice;
today you alone are the embodiment of the Sāman chants, possessing every form at all times.
You are composed of all-knowledge; O Acyuta, you are knowledge itself within the heart.
Grant me that all-knowledge, O God of gods; salutations, salutations!
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus praised by him at that time, the Lord of Gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, said to Brahmā: "I shall grant you supreme knowledge."
Having spoken thus, O King, Viṣṇu then reflected:
"By whom has his knowledge been taken away, and in what form did he assume it?"

O King, knowing that everything had been wrought by Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Janārdana assumed the form of a fish, many yojanas long and many yojanas wide, consisting entirely of all-encompassing knowledge.
Having quickly entered the water, Hari agitated it;
and having entered Pātāla, he beheld Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Having bewildered them with that tumultuous sound, Hari seized that knowledge;
Madhusūdana was praised by the sages as he took up the Vedas and the Śāstras.
O King, having brought that fish and given it to Brahmā, and having abandoned it,
he once again fell under the power of yogic sleep for the welfare of the world.
Then, having awakened and become enraged, both Madhu and Kaiṭabha approached and beheld the imperishable Lord lying there.
"This is that deceitful man who, having deluded us both with his magic,
brought us here and gave us the Vedas and Shastras, and now lies here like a virtuous man."
Having spoken thus, O King, those two most terrible Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
quickly awakened Keśava as he lay sleeping.
"O high-minded one, we have come here for the sake of battle with you;
give us a combat, rise up and fight now!"
O best of kings, having been addressed thus by those two, the Blessed One, the God of gods,
said "So be it," and the Lord then made his Śārṅga bow ready.
With the twanging of his bowstring and the sound of his palms, as well as the blast of his conch, Mādhava effortlessly filled the sky, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate quarters.
And those two of great prowess, O King, then made the twang of their bowstrings;
the most terrible Madhu and Kaiṭabha fought with Hari.
And Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe, fought with those two as if in play;
thus did their battle proceed as they discharged their weapons.
Then Keśava, with arrows resembling venomous serpents released from the Śārṅga bow,
cut all those weapons into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
Having fought with him for a very long time, those two intoxicated Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
were slain by Kṛṣṇa with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow.
O King, the earth was fashioned by Viṣṇu from the fat (medas) of those two;
therefore, this Vasuṃdharā obtained the name Medinī.
O protector of the earth, having thus obtained the Vedas through the grace of Kṛṣṇa,
