Prajāpati created living beings by means of the rites prescribed in the Vedas.
O King, he who constantly hears this account of the manifestation of Hari shall become a knower of the Vedas and a Brāhmaṇa residing in the abode of the Moon.

O protector of the earth, remember that great and terrible fish-form of Viṣṇu, which was like a mountain and composed of knowledge, which he assumed for the welfare of the world and which was then praised by those dwelling in Janaloka.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Fish," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 37)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods were defeated by the daityas;
they all went for refuge to the Lord who is the husband of the daughter of the Ocean of Milk.
O King, all the hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, having propitiated the Lord of the World, praised him with hymns while standing with palms joined in reverence.
The gods said:
Homage to you, the God of gods, the Lord of the world, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
homage to you, the one with a lotus in his navel, the Lord of the world, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Homage to you, O Padmanābha, who removes all suffering;
homage to you, whose form is the universe and who consists of all the gods.
Salutations again and again to Keśava, for the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
"O God, we have been defeated in battle by the powerful Daityas;
O Compassionate One, salutations to you! Please tell us the means for our victory."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus praised then by the gods, Janārdana, the God of gods,
Hari, standing right before them, spoke to those deities.
The Blessed One said: "O all you gods, go there and make peace with the Dānavas;
having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope."
Having gathered all the medicinal herbs and cast them into the ocean, act with haste; joining together with the Dānavas, churn the Ocean of Milk.
And I, O dwellers of heaven, shall provide assistance there;
the nectar will be present there, and by drinking it, you shall become even more powerful.
By the power of the nectar, you shall all in an instant become gods— highly fortunate, most radiant, and possessing valor in battle.
But Indra and the others, possessing great energy, having obtained that supreme nectar, will then indeed be capable of conquering the Dānavas; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, all the deities bowed to the Lord of the World and, returning to their abodes, then made a treaty with the Dānavas.
During the churning of the ocean of milk, O King, everyone made the greatest effort;
and the great mountain named Mandara was lifted up by Bala.
O best of kings, having cast all medicinal herbs into the ocean of milk, he alone was likewise thrown into that sea by the gods and the daityas.
O King, Vāsuki also arrived there at the command of Nārāyaṇa;
and for the sake of the welfare of all the gods, Viṣṇu himself came as well.
Then, having approached Viṣṇu there, all those gods and asuras together took their stand upon the shore of the Ocean of Milk with a spirit of friendship.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
O King, they then began to churn for the sake of the nectar of immortality with great force.
Then Viṣṇu stationed the Dānavas at the head-end for the churning,
while he appointed the gods to the tail-end.
And so, O King, as Mount Mandara sank down into the depths during that churning,
Hari, seeing it suddenly deprived of its support, [acted].
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, he assumed the form of a tortoise;
having entered within himself, he then positioned himself beneath Mount Mandara.
Having entered, Madhusūdana held Mount Mandara;
Keśava stood upon the mountain, having assumed a separate form.
And Janārdana, together with the gods— Janārdana being in the midst of the Daityas with a form invisible to the deities— dragged the King of Serpents.
Then, filled with haste, they churned the Ocean of Milk.
O best of kings, as the gods and asuras exerted their strength,
O monarch, [the following] emerged from that Ocean of Milk while it was being churned.
The poison known as Kālakūṭa, which was utterly unbearable, was taken up by all the nāgas; Śaṅkara took what remained of it.
By the command of Nārāyaṇa, he attained the state of being Nīlakaṇṭha;
furthermore, he became Airāvata, the lord of the nāgas, and Hari, the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
"O King, we have heard that [the first two] were produced from the second turning;
O King, from the third turning the most beautiful Apsarases arose;
and from the fourth, that great tree was born."
For from the fifth [ocean], the moon indeed rose up from the milk-ocean;
O King, Bhava bears it upon his head like a woman wears a svastika.
Various kinds of divine jewels and ornaments,
as well as thousands of gandharvas, have arisen from the Ocean of Milk.
Having seen these [beings] thus arisen, endowed with such great wonder,
all those gods and asuras there became filled with joy.
Then, on the side of the gods, the clouds remain and rain only slightly;
and by the command of Kṛṣṇa, a pleasant breeze blows toward the deities.
O high-minded one, others were slain by the wind of Vāsuki’s poisonous breath; the Daityas became devoid of splendor and stripped of their prowess.
Then, O king of kings, Śrī rose up from that Ocean of Milk holding a lotus,
resplendent with her own radiance in all directions.
Then, having bathed in the waters of the sacred fords, adorned with divine garments,
her limbs anointed with celestial perfumes, and beautifully decorated with flowers and fine ornaments;
O subduer of enemies, having reached the side of the gods and stayed there for a moment,
that lotus-dwelling goddess then arrived at the chest of Hari.
Then, O King, having churned the full jar of nectar from the ocean of milk, Dhanvantari emerged; thereupon the gods were delighted.
O King, abandoned by Śrī, those Daityas became miserable;
yet, taking the full jar of nectar, they departed as they pleased.
Then, O tiger among kings, for the sake of the welfare of the gods, Viṣṇu indeed assumed a female form for himself, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Then the Blessed One went toward the asuras in the form of a woman;
and upon seeing her of divine beauty, those enemies of the gods were infatuated.
O best of beings, having placed that jar filled with nectar there out of delusion,
the asuras were instantly tormented by desire.
Having thus deluded those very Asuras, O lord of the earth,
Hari took the nectar and bestowed it upon the gods.
Having drunk that, by the grace of the God of gods, the deities became powerful and possessed of great heroism; they then went forth against the asuras in battle.
Having conquered the asuras in battle, the gods established their own kingdoms;
this, O King, has been told to you—this manifestation of Hari.
The one called Kūrma bestows merit upon men who hear it or even read it.
This Kaurma [Purāṇa], possessing infinite splendor, was revealed by Nārāyaṇa, the performer of wondrous deeds;
its supreme form, which is indeed purifying, was proclaimed solely for the benefit of the inhabitants of heaven.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation as Kūrma," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 38)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, hereafter I shall relate to you the meritorious manifestation of Hari as the Boar; listen with a concentrated mind.
O best of beings, when the dissolution of the world occurs at the end of Brahmā’s day,
the waters remain pervading the entire triple world.
O Indra among kings, having indeed swallowed all sentient beings whatsoever in the three worlds, Viṣṇu then lies upon those waters of the single ocean.
On a bed of infinite splendor, adorned with a thousand hoods,
the Lord of the World, assuming the form of Brahmā, remains through the night that lasts until the end of a thousand yugas.
We have heard that Diti had a great son born from Kaśyapa,
renowned as Hiraṇyākṣa, who possessed immense strength and prowess.
Dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), that Daitya besieged the gods;
he strove on the surface of the earth to obstruct those who performed sacrifices.
Then, standing upon the earth, mortals shall worship the deities;
by that, their strength, vigor, and splendor shall also increase.
Thinking thus, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa took away that power of the earth to support [beings] which had been established by Brahmā at the time of creation.
O King, he entered into the midst of the waters to the depths of the netherworld;
and the earth, deprived of Śakti, entered the netherworld.
At the end of his sleep, the Soul of All reflected, "Where has the earth gone? and through yoga, he perceived that it had gone to the depths of the netherworld.
Then, O lord of men, he assumed a form consisting of the Vedas, taking on the body of a boar,
with the Vedas as his feet, the sacrificial post as his tusks, and the sacrificial banner as his face.
O lord of men, he had broad shoulders, mighty arms, and a wide face;
his tongue was like fire, his snout was a sacrificial ladle, and his great eyes were the moon and the sun.
There was the hearing of the divine dharma of *pūrta* and *iṣṭa*, accompanied by the sound of *sāman* chants;
it had the *prāgvaṃśa* hall as its body, the sacrificial oblation as its nose, and the *kuśa* and *darbha* grasses as its body hair.
And that [ocean] consists of all the Vedas, with its great mane of meritorious hymns;
it has the constellations and stars for its food and the whirlpools of cosmic dissolution for its ornaments.
Having thus assumed the form of a boar,
O best of kings, Vṛṣākapi entered Rasātala while being praised by Sanaka and the other sages.
And having entered and defeated Hiraṇyākṣa in battle,
Vṛṣākapi then lifted up the earth from the netherworld (rasātala) with the tip of his tusk.
Being praised by the hosts of immortals, he established [the world] as before;
having established all the mountains, he arranged them in their respective places.
Having abandoned his boar-form at the renowned sacred ford of Kokā,
he made that supreme, secret field for the benefit of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Assuming the form of Brahmā, he again performed the work of creation;
as Viṣṇu, he protects the entire world in this manner age after age;
and at the end, Janārdana, taking the form of Rudra, destroys the whole universe.
The person who knows the Vedānta, and the man who hears this story of Vṛṣākapi,
having fixed his firm resolve upon the body of the sacrifice and abandoned all evil, that man shall go to Hari.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vārāha," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 39.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus has the manifestation of Hari as the Boar been described to you;
now I shall speak of the Man-lion (Nārasiṃha); listen to me.
In ancient times, there was a great son of Diti named Hiraṇyakaśipu;
he performed austerities without food for many thousands of years.
As he was performing penance, Brahmā, being well-pleased, said to that Dānava:
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas, whatever dwells in your mind."
Thus addressed by Brahmā in the past, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu,
bowing to the Lord of Gods, Brahmā, spoke with humility.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Blessed One, if you are intent upon granting me boons,
O Brahman, you ought to grant me whatever I choose."
Not by the dry, nor by the moist, not by water, nor by fire;
not by wood, nor by insects, not by stone, nor by wind.
Not by weapon, nor by spear, nor by mountain, nor by humans;
not even by gods, nor by asuras, nor by gandharvas, nor by rākṣasas.
Neither by kinnaras nor by yakṣas, nor by vidyādharas or bhujaṅgas; neither by monkeys nor by wild beasts, nor even by the hosts of mātṛs.
Neither within nor without, nor by any other causes of death,
neither by day nor by night, may my death come to pass, through your grace.
"Thus indeed, O Lord of the gods, I choose a boon from you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by the king of the Daityas, O King, Brahmā spoke to him.
"O Lord of Daityas, I am pleased with your great asceticism; therefore, I grant you these most wonderful boons, though they are difficult to obtain."
"Such has not been given to others, nor have they performed such austerity;
yet, at your request, everything has been granted by me—may all that be yours as well, O Lord of Daityas."
"Go, O mighty-armed one, and enjoy the exalted fruit of your austerities"—
thus [spoke the voice] in the past to Hiraṇyakaśipu, the king of the Daityas.
Having granted the boons, Brahmā departed for the unsurpassed world of Brahmā;
and that Daitya, having obtained the boons, was powerful and arrogant because of his strength.
Having conquered the gods and lions in battle, he brought them down from heaven to earth;
endowed with all powers, he himself established his sovereignty in heaven.
O King, out of fear of him, even the gods, the Rudras, and the sages all wandered upon the earth,
assuming human bodies.
O King of kings, having attained sovereignty over the three worlds, that Hiraṇyakaśipu summoned all his subjects and spoke these words.
"O gods, you must not sacrifice, you must not offer oblations, and you must not give gifts;
for today I alone am the sovereign of the three worlds over all creatures."
"Perform worship for me alone through acts such as sacrifice and charity";
and all of them did exactly so out of fear of the lord of the Daityas, O King.
O best of kings, while these things were being performed in this manner, the entire triple world, including all that is mobile and immobile, became permeated with unrighteousness.
Due to the neglect of their own duties, the minds of all turned toward evil;
when a great deal of time had passed, the gods, together with Indra, [approached] Bṛhaspati.
Endowed with humility, they questioned that knower of policy and knower of all scriptures regarding the destruction of this Hiraṇyakaśipu, O best of sages.
Tell us quickly the means for the slaying of those who captivate the three worlds.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Listen to my words, O gods, for the sake of attaining your own stations."
The great asura Hiraṇyakaśipu was likely one whose merit was exhausted;
for grief destroys wisdom, and grief destroys sacred learning.
Grief destroys the intellect; there is no enemy equal to grief.
The touch of fire can be endured, as can the terrible contact of weapons.
But, O King, it is not possible to endure the suffering born of grief;
we gods perceive the exhaustion of that [suffering] through time and signs.
And all the wise ones, staying everywhere, will constantly say:
"This wicked one shall surely perish very soon through mutual conflict."
The omens tell me of the supreme prosperity of the gods, characterized by their attainment of their own station, as well as the destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Since this is so, therefore, O gods, all of you go without delay to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, where Keśava is sleeping.
The God, being praised by you, will become pleased in an instant;
for once he is pleased, he will declare the means for the destruction of the Daitya.
Thus addressed by him, those gods exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
and, filled with supreme joy, they then made an effort to depart.
On an auspicious lunar day and at a favorable moment, having had the sages perform meritorious rites for well-being and prosperity, those inhabitants of heaven set forth.
O best of kings, for the destruction of the wicked Daitya and for their own prosperity,
they went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, placing Śarva at their head.
Having gone there, all the gods, honoring Viṣṇu, the victorious Janārdana, with various hymns of praise, set forth.
The Blessed Lord Bhava also, with single-minded devotion, praised the Blessed Janārdana, Hari, by means of meritorious names.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Viṣṇu is the victorious, the all-pervading God, the Lord of sacrifice and the protector of sacrifice;
he is the powerful creator, the devourer, the soul of the worlds, and the guardian of the worlds.
Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, the one who is fit [for all things], the cause of all causes,
the performer of action, the Lord Vāmana, Vāsudeva, who is praised by many.
The Primordial Creator, Varāha, Mādhava, Madhusūdana,
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Haṃsa, Viṣṇusena, and Hutāśana.
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Śrīmān, Āyuṣmān, Puruṣottama,
Vaikuṇṭha, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Kṛṣṇa, Sūrya, and Surārcita.
The Man-Lion, the most terrifying, with adamantine fangs and claws as his weapons;
the primordial god, the creator of the world, the lord of yoga, whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Govinda, Gopati, Goptṛ, Bhūpati, Bhuvaneśvara,
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vibhu, Dāmodara, Hari.
Trivikrama, Lord of the three worlds, Lord of Brahmā, Increaser of joy,
Vāmana, Subduer of the wicked, Govinda, Beloved of the cowherds.
Acyuta is fond of devotion, the Truth, whose fame is truth, the Immovable, the Pure,
Compassionate, the Merciful, Vyāsa, the Destroyer of Sin, and the Increaser of Peace.
He is an ascetic who knows the true essence of the scriptures, whose banner is the Mandāra mountain, whose abode is Badarī;
he is peaceful, an ascetic, and possesses the radiance of lightning.
The abode of beings, the dweller in the cave, the abode of Śrī, the Lord of Śrī;
the abode of austerity, the abode of self-restraint, the abode of truth, the eternal one.
The Supreme Person, the Abundant, the Meritorious, the Lotus-eyed, the Great Lord;
the Full, the Fulfillment, the Knower of the Purāṇas, the Knower of Merit, the Increaser of Merit.
He who holds the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the plow, the pestle, and the club;
he who wears a crown, earrings, necklaces, a girdle, armor, and a banner.
The victorious, the conqueror, the great hero, the slayer of enemies, the scorcher of foes; the peaceful, the bringer of peace, the teacher, the benefactor, praised by Śantanu.
He is the charioteer, the one of pure essence, the Lord, the lover of the Sāmaveda, the equanimous,
the means of measurement, the courageous, the being, the one of full portions, and the possessor of prosperity.
The giver of heaven, the giver of desires, the giver of prosperity, the giver of fame, and the destroyer of infamy;
the lotus-eyed one who bestows liberation, whose banner is made from the ocean of milk.
O Lord, praised by gods and asuras, the impeller, the destroyer of sins;
you are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the *oṃ* syllable, and you are the sacred fires.
You are *svāhā*, you are *svadhā*, you are the god, you are the nectar, O Supreme Person! Homage to Viṣṇu, the primordial god of gods and the eternal one!
Homage to you, O Garuḍa-bannered one, who are infinite and immeasurable!
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus was Madhusūdana praised by these divine names.
Having manifested himself, he spoke these words to all the gods.
The Blessed One said:
"O gods, you have praised me with auspicious names alone."
Therefore, I am pleased; what may I do for you?
The gods said:
O God of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Mādhava!
"You alone know, O Hari; why then do you ask?"
The Blessed One said:
"O destroyers of the asuras, I know all about your arrival."
I was praised by Śaṅkara for the sake of destroying Hiraṇyaka;
indeed, I was extolled by Bhava with a hundred holy names.
O Mahāmati, by this which you have spoken to me constantly,
I am perpetually honored by you here, just as if by you [personally].
"I am pleased; go, O Lord, to the auspicious peak of Kailāsa.
Praised by you, O Bhava, I shall slay Hiraṇyakaśipu."
"Go now, O gods; wait for some time until his son, the wise Prahlāda, who is a devotee of Viṣṇu," [is born].

"O King, when that Daitya shall commit treachery against the gods, I will slay him, though he be protected by boons and invincible to both gods and dānavas. Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu [dismissed] the gods; and having bowed to Viṣṇu, they departed.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Hymn of Names of Viṣṇu," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 40)
Sahasrānīka said:
O Mārkaṇḍeya, of great wisdom and learned in all the scriptures,
you ought to recount the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha exactly as it occurred.
"O sinless one, relate the life of Prahlāda to me in detail.
O great yogi, O great sage, by your grace we are truly blessed."
Blessed are we, for we drink the nectar named the discourse of the Lord of Śrī, which is difficult to obtain.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Formerly, as Hiraṇyakaśipu was going to the forest for the sake of performing austerities...
A conflagration and an earthquake occurred for that great-souled one,
even as he was being restrained by his kinsmen, servants, and well-wishing friends.
O King, the birds born there were deformed, and that was not auspicious;
for you are the sovereign of the three worlds, and all the gods have been defeated by you.
"O gentle one, you have no fear; for what purpose do you perform this austerity?
Even though we are endowed with intelligence, we perceive no purpose [for it]."
For he who performs ascetic practice while still possessing deficient desire—
even though being thus restrained by them— is stubbornly arrogant and deluded by pride.
Surrounded by two or three friends, he went to the peak of Kailāsa;
while performing that most difficult penance, he was consumed by fervent austerity.
O protector of the earth, anxiety arose in Viriñci, the lotus-born:
"What shall I do? How can this Daitya be turned away from his asceticism?"
O protector of the earth, while Brahmā was thus overwhelmed with anxiety, the most excellent sage Nārada emerged from his body; having prostrated himself, he spoke.
Nārada said:
"O dear one, why do you grieve, you who are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa? Those in whose minds Govinda dwells truly ought not to mourn."
I shall restrain that son of Diti as he performs his austerities;
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, will grant me his counsel.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus and bowed to his father, that bull among sages set out together with Parvata, keeping Vāsudeva in his heart.
Having become two kalaviṅka birds, they went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains,
where the foremost of the sons of Diti dwelt, surrounded by two or three friends.
Having performed his ablutions there, the sage, perched upon the branch of a tree,
spoke with a deep voice while the Daitya listened.
Having repeated "Namo nārāyaṇāya" three times with a noble mind, Nārada indeed took recourse to silence.
Having heard those words of the kalaviṅka bird with respect,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, filled with rage, took up his bow.
O King, as soon as he fixed an arrow upon his bow and was about to release it at them, Nārada and Parvata flew up and departed.
Then, O Lord of the Earth, Hiraṇyakaśipu, his limbs overwhelmed by anger,
abandoned that hermitage and returned once more to his own city.
His wife, named Kayādhū by name, was one with beautiful hips;
at that time, she had become menstruating, but by the turn of fate, she had already bathed.
At night, during a moment of solitude, he was questioned by her:
"O Lord, when you had gone from your home to the forest to perform ascetic penance..."
Then you said: "For ten thousand years I have performed this austerity;
for what reason, O Great King, have you now abandoned your vow? (NsP 41.22)
"Tell me the truth, O Lord; I ask out of affection, O Daitya."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to my truthful words that destroy one's vows."
O Goddess, on the peak of Kailāsa, in the great forest of supreme bliss, you are the mother of extreme wrath and the increaser of the joy of the gods.
Uttering auspicious speech, saying "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," they spoke these auspicious words two or three times, O blessed one.
"Because of that, O lady of beautiful countenance, an exceeding anger arose in my mind;
O passionate one, I fixed an arrow upon my bow and was about to release it."
Meanwhile, those two birds, being terrified, went to another land; but I, having abandoned my vow, have indeed returned here by the power of what was destined to happen.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While these words were being spoken, there was then a discharge of semen;
and when the time of her season had arrived, a fetus was indeed conceived at that very moment.
Furthermore, as the wise embryo continued to grow within the womb,
he became a Vaiṣṇava through the instruction of Nārada.
I shall relate that further on, O King; be intent upon faith.
He had a son, Prahlāda, who was devoted and a Vaiṣṇava by birth.
Thus he grew up in the family of the Asuras, stainless though his dwelling was defiled,
just as devotion to Hari in the Kali age liberates one from the bondage of saṃsāra.
Growing up with his companions, he shone with devotion toward the stations of the Lord of the Three Vedas;
though a child of small body, that great-souled one appeared resplendent, spreading forth the vast devotion to Viṣṇu.
Just as the fourth age is said to bestow dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation, and indeed to bring fame,
so too he was constantly engaged in childish play with other boys, such as playing riddles and games.
And in the course of conversations, he spoke only of Kṛṣṇa, for that was indeed his nature;
thus, even in childhood, performing such wondrous deeds, he grew up drinking the nectar of the glories of the Lord.
Once, that wicked lord of the Daityas, surrounded by women, beheld that lotus-faced youth with long, wide eyes as he arrived at his preceptor’s house.
Then, having taken his son by the hand, he respectfully placed upon his head a most beautiful turban-band marked with a wheel and inscribed with the name of Kṛṣṇa.
Filled with joy, he called his little son and, caressing him, said:
"My son, your mother is always very wise; she praises you to me."
Now, tell me whatever was learned in the teacher’s house;
having reflected upon that which generates bliss, speak it correctly as it truly is.
Then Prahlāda, whose very birth was Vaiṣṇava, spoke to his father with joy:
"Having bowed to Govinda, the Lord who is worshipped by the three worlds, I shall speak to you."
Having heard this praise of his enemy spoken by his son, the wicked king, though surrounded by women and though enraged, laughed loudly as if delighted in order to deceive him.
Embracing his son, he said: "Listen, my child, to these beneficial words:
'Rāma, Govinda, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, Śrīpati!'"
"All those who speak thus are my enemies, my son; they have now been subdued by me. Where have you heard such words? (NsP 41.42)
Having heard his father’s words, the wise Prahlāda, endowed with fearlessness, said: "O noble one, never speak thus again."
The man who utters the word "Kṛṣṇa"— a mantra that bestows all sovereignty and increases virtue and the other goals— attains the state of fearlessness.
There is no end to the evil arising from the reviling of Kṛṣṇa;
O Rāma, Mādhava, Kṛṣṇa—remember [His name] with devotion for the purification of the self.
I tell this even to my guru, because it is supremely beneficial:
go for refuge to the Lord of All, which brings about the destruction of all sins.
Then the enemy of the gods, his anger manifest, spoke while rebuking his son:
"By whom has this boy been brought to such a wretched state?"
"Fie! Fie! Alas! O wicked son, what great sin have you committed against me? Go away, go away, O man of evil conduct, most sinful, lowest of men!
Having spoken thus, and looking all around, he spoke again to the child's teacher:
"Having learned [this], let him be brought by the cruel Daityas of fierce prowess.
Having heard this, the Daityas then brought him and presented him;
the wise one said to the wicked king, "O Devāntaka, let him be examined."
O Lord, the entire three worlds have been conquered by you with mere ease; indeed, not repeatedly through wrath. Why then are you angry with me, a person of such little account?
Having heard these words of Sāma spoken by the twice-born, the king of the Daityas said:
"O sinner, you have taught even my young son the hymn to Viṣṇu!"
Having spoken thus, the king said to his son, who was preeminent in the Sāman chants:
"What is this dullness in my own son, and what has been done to you by the twice-born?"
O fool, always abandon those who are certainly rogues under the guise of Viṣṇu’s followers;
indeed, abandon association with the twice-born, for association with the twice-born is unwholesome.
The splendor appropriate to our lineage has been obscured by those twice-born ones;
for whatever a person associates with, like a gem, he comes to possess that quality.
Therefore, for the prosperity of his own lineage, the wise man should resort only to his own group,
abandoning that which is suitable for my son but destructive to the followers of Viṣṇu.
O dull-witted one, why are you not ashamed to worship Viṣṇu yourself?
Having become the son of me, the Lord of the Universe, do you seek another as your protector?
Listen, my child, to the true nature of the world: there is no master who is inherently one's own;
he who is brave enjoys prosperity—he is the master, he is the great lord.
That god, the sovereign of all, is the conqueror of the three worlds just as I am;
therefore, abandon your dullness and resort to the heroism befitting your own lineage.
Others will also kill you, and people will say this of you:
"This asura praises the gods, like a cat praising mice."
Like a peacock toward venomous serpents, they treat their enemies with hatred; this is certainly a bad omen.
Even after attaining great sovereignty, those of little intelligence fall into contempt.
"Just as this son of mine praises those who praise him like a lowly person, so do you, O fool, speak of Hari before me even after seeing my sovereignty! (NsP 41.61)
"But this praise of Hari, who is incomparable, is a mockery," having said this to his son, O King, he became filled with wrath and terrifying.
Glancing askance and making his preceptor tremble with rage, he said:
"Go, go, you beast of a brahmin! Teach my son well!"
Saying "I am pleased," that brahmin, who served the wicked king, went home;
having dismissed Viṣṇu, he followed after the Daitya—for what indeed will those greedy for sustenance not do?
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Nṛsiṃha," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 41.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
That son of the lord of the Daityas, adorned with devotion to Hari, was also quickly led by the Daityas to the house of his preceptor;
and in time, that yogi attained boyhood along with the entire mass of sciences.
Generally, having reached youth, people nourish atheism and evil ways;
yet for one established in that age, there arises outward detachment, and toward the Unborn, there has been a wondrous devotion.
Then, on one occasion, the lord of the Daityas summoned Prahlāda, who was fully accomplished in learning and recognized as a knower of the Lord, and spoke to him as he stood bowed before him.
"Excellent! O destroyer of the gods, you have been released from the folly of that ocean of ignorance;
now you shine like the sun emerged from the mist."
In our childhood, O son, we too were deluded by the twice-born into folly just like you;
but as we grew in years, we were thus well-instructed.

Therefore, today, having placed upon you— who are now the leader— the burden of this world which has become thorn-laden, I shall be at ease, beholding your sovereign glory that I have long maintained.
Whenever a father perceives the skill of his son,
at that very moment he casts off his anxiety and attains great happiness.
And my guru described your extreme proficiency before me;
it is no wonder, my son, that my ears long to hear of it.
In his two eyes was the poverty of his enemies; in his two ears, the well-spoken words of his sons;
on his limbs, the wounds of battle; and for the masters of illusion, it was a great festival.
Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, who was skilled in deceit,
the yogi Prahlāda then spoke fearlessly and with reverence to his guru.
O Great King, well-spoken words are truth and a great festival for the ears;
however, one should consider nothing else apart from those words of Viṣṇu.
Policy, wise sayings, and stories worth hearing, as well as poetry worth hearing—
all such speech is that in which Hari is sung of as the fire that consumes the forest of the flood of suffering in saṃsāra.
Where the inconceivable one, who grants the desires of his devotees, is praised with devotion—
what use, my dear, is a treatise on worldly profit (arthaśāstra), wherein there is only the continuous succession of saṃsāra?
O dear one, what is the use of the toil of [studying] other treatises by which the Self itself is destroyed?
Therefore, the literature concerning Viṣṇu should always be heard and practiced.
"If those seeking liberation do not [overcome] the afflictions of existence, they will never be happy"—
hearing these words of his, Hiraṇyakaśipu then [reflected].
The king of the Daityas blazed up even more intensely at Prahlāda’s meritorious words, which destroy the cycle of worldly existence, like clarified butter heated with water.
The base Asura could not endure it, like an owl cannot endure the radiance of the sun;
looking all around, he spoke thus in anger to the Daitya warriors: NsP_42.17.
"Let this crooked one be slain with most terrifying blows of weapons;
let his vital organs be cut away again and again, while Hari himself must be protected!"
Let him now behold the fruit born of praising Hari:
let his body be divided and distributed among crows, vultures, and eagles.
Then, having raised their weapons and threatening with loud roars, those Daityas,
urged by their lord, assailed that beloved devotee of Acyuta.
Prahlāda, too, having bowed to the Lord, took up the vajra of meditation;
he was a devotee of unartificial flavor, thus rendered motionless by meditation.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, the remover of the suffering of his devotees, protected Prahlāda;
then the weapons of the Rākṣasas, failing to find a foothold, struck against his body.
Like fragments of blue lotuses, [the weapons] fell, severed in many ways;
for what can ordinary weapons do against the beloved of Hari?
Indeed, the entire great flood of the three types of suffering fears him;
diseases, demons, and planetary spirits afflict people only so long [as he does not exist].
As long as the mind does not find Viṣṇu, who dwells in the cave of the heart and is subtle,
those [demons] shall be struck down by fragments of shattered weapons rising up from all directions.
Being struck, they turned back immediately, as if from those who grant immediate fruit;
this was not surprising for the wise, but it brought wonder to the ignorant.
Beholding the Vaiṣṇava power, the king certainly felt fear;
that evil-minded one again began to contemplate a means for his destruction.
Having summoned the most venomous serpents, he commanded them:
"This man, who pleases Śiva, is made of stone and is not fit to be slain by weapons."
"Therefore, you must soon slay those whose weapon is poison.
Having heard these words of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
those serpents residing in that region received his command upon their heads with great joy.
Then, with blazing fangs that were fierce and terrifying with their thousand clearly throbbing teeth,
the *akarṣakas*— who drag away the buffalo of Hari— rushed with fury even more swiftly toward the beloved of Hari.
Your weapons, though capable of piercing even the thinnest skin, were insufficient to break through the form of his body which was difficult to pierce due to its innate power and strength;
yet, having merely bitten that lion-bodied one with your own teeth, you have been rendered useless.
Then those serpents, their forms dejected by the flowing poison of their blood, their fangs split apart in wonder,
gathered together and addressed the Lord of the Daityas with sighs, their hoods quivering.
O Lord, even those who were capable of reducing mountains to ashes became powerless at that very moment and were slain;
having been employed for the slaughter of your high-souled son, they were rendered toothless.
Thus, having delivered their harsh message, the double-tongued ones were dismissed by the Lord;
departing without having achieved their purpose, they reflected with great astonishment solely upon the source of Prahlāda’s power.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the lord of the Asuras, having deliberated with his ministers and reached a conclusion that his son could not be subdued by punishment,
summoned him— who was always pure in heart and meritorious— and spoke these words to him as he bowed down with gentleness.
"O Prahlāda, although you are wicked, because you are born of my own body, compassion has arisen within me today that you are not to be slain."
Then, having arrived quickly, the foolish priests of the Daitya king— twice-born men learned in the scriptures— spoke with their palms joined in reverence.
O Lord, as you are filled with desire, the three worlds tremble violently;
yet Prahlāda, being of little strength, does not realize that you are enraged and possessed of great power.
Therefore, O King, enough with anger; you ought to show compassion. A son may become a bad son, but never his mother or father.
Having spoken thus to the Daitya of crooked intellect, the priests of the Daityas took Prahlāda, whose wealth was his wisdom, with his permission and departed.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Narasiṃha," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 42.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, even while residing in the house of his teacher, he— though a master of all sciences, yet with a mind whose merit was fixed on Acyuta—
moved about as if dull-witted in external affairs, constantly beholding the world as consisting of the Infinite.
Once, those young companions living with you in the teacher’s house, having grown weary of their studies, gathered together and said:
"O Prince, this conduct of yours is truly wondrous!
For, O dear one, whenever you reflect upon something in your heart, your hair stands on end; and you always speak of it, provided it is not a secret."
When the sons of the ministers had spoken thus, the king, out of his affection for all beings, said this to them:
"Listen with attentive minds, O sons of the enemies of the gods, to that which I, having no other delight, declare when asked."
This worldly prosperity, which indeed appears delightful through the pleasures of wealth, people, and young women—
wise men should reflect upon it and either resort to it quickly or else abandon it from afar.

First, let this be considered here: that extreme suffering experienced by the mother while [the fetus] is within her womb—[a suffering] endured by those with extremely contorted bodies, scorched by fire, and remembering various previous births.
Like a thief bound in a prison, I am fettered by the fetal membrane within this house of feces, worms, and urine;
even while in the womb, I behold the misery of once again failing to remember the lotus feet of Mukunda.
Therefore, there is no happiness for one dwelling in the womb, nor likewise in childhood, youth, or old age.
Thus, existence is always composed of suffering; O sons of the Daityas, how could it be pursued by the awakened?
While searching throughout this existence, we do not perceive even a minute fraction of a particle of happiness.
The more we investigate thoroughly, the more we recognize it to be increasingly painful;
therefore, the wise do not fall at all into this existence, which, though appearing beautiful, is in truth a source of suffering.
Furthermore, those who do not know reality and are utterly deluded fall like moths into a beautiful fire;
if there is no other refuge for happiness, then this falling into that which appears to be happiness is indeed appropriate.
Alas, those who are emaciated have found no food; for it is indeed fitting that they should consume oil-cakes, chaff, and the like.
Yet there exists the eternal and primordial [bliss], obtainable through the worship of the pair of lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī, which is unborn.
He who, having renounced this great bliss that is to be attained without affliction, should desire other pleasures, is utterly deluded;
like one who, casting away his own kingdom already in his hand, wanders for alms with a dejected mind.
And that pair of lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī is not worshipped with garments, nor with wealth, nor with physical labors;
rather, it is worshipped by a man whose mind is focused on nothing else when he utters the names "Keśava" and "Mādhava."
Having thus understood that existence consists of suffering, O sons of the Daityas, worship Hari well;
in this way a person may obtain the fruit of birth, otherwise he will fall lower and lower into the ocean of worldly existence.

Therefore, in this world, those whose desires have ceased should constantly remember with the yoga of true devotion the Lord Ananta— the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, the giver of boons, Mukunda— who is worthy of praise within their hearts.
Out of compassion and because I am not a nihilist, I shall speak this secret to you who are situated in the ocean of existence:
cultivate a sense of friendship toward all beings, for Viṣṇu is indeed omnipresent.
The sons of the Daityas said: "O Prahlāda, O high-minded one, because of our childhood,
neither you nor we know any friend or teacher other than Śaṇḍa and Marka."
"Where did you learn this? Tell us the truth, free from all ambiguity."
Prahlāda said:
"O father, when my father had departed for the great forest for the sake of asceticism..."
Then Indra, having arrived, besieged his city,
for he had learned that the lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu, was dead.
Indra, having seized my mother and burning with the fire of passion, travels swiftly along the road toward that illustrious lady.
Then, perceiving that I was within the womb, Nārada, whose vision is divine, approached Indra and spoke aloud: "O fool, release this devoted wife!"
"He who is situated within her womb is indeed the most excellent devotee of the Lord.
Having heard those words of Nārada, I prostrated before my mother.
Then, through devotion to Viṣṇu, Hari was liberated and returned to his own abode;
meanwhile, Nārada, firm in his auspicious vows, brought her back to his own hermitage.
O sons of Danu, having been addressed to me, that illustrious lady, this was indeed told at that time;
it has not been forgotten by me at all, due to my practice since childhood.
By the very grace of Viṣṇu and through the instruction of Nārada,
that lord of the Rākṣasas once went out upon a secret mission.
At night in the city, he heard the proclamation, "Victory to Rāma!
and the powerful lord of the Dānavas understood that everything had been done by his son.
Then the lord of the Daityas, blinded by rage, addressed his priests:
"Ho there, you wretched brahmins! You have reached the point of wishing to die."
"This Prahlāda speaks false words and even teaches others [to do so]," the king said, reviling those brahmins as he entered his home panting for breath.
And though his death was near, he did not abandon his resentment toward the one who had killed his son; out of indignation, he reflected upon a single course of action.
Having summoned the Daityas and others, he secretly instructed them on what was indeed an improper act:
"Tonight, while Prahlāda is fast asleep, [seize] that wicked one with your fierce [weapons]."
Having bound him firmly with nāga-nooses and cast him into the middle of the ocean,
they approached him and beheld him, having taken his command upon their heads.
The night-wanderers [approached] him who delights in the night, established in meditative absorption, awakened yet remaining as if asleep,
whose great bonds of passion, greed, and the like had been severed.
Having realized that he was a devotee of the one whose banner bears Garuḍa, those senseless ones bound that high-souled man with serpentine ropes, though they were weak.
Having carried away the one beloved by the one who reclines upon the waters, those powerful Daityas cast him into the mass of water and placed immovable mountains upon him.
They quickly reported that pleasant news to the king, and he in turn honored them;
he also sent for Prahlāda, who was staying in the midst of the ocean like another submarine fire (aurvāgni).
The crocodiles abandoned him, who was blazing with the splendor of Viṣṇu, out of great fear;
and he remained absorbed in the midst of the ocean of undivided consciousness and bliss.
He did not realize that he himself was bound and situated in the midst of the salt ocean;
meanwhile, the sage remained within his own self, which was an ocean of the nectar of Brahman.
Then the waves reached a state of agitation like the ocean upon the entry of a second sea;
yet, having shaken off their distress as if shaking off afflictions from further afflictions, they then attained great serenity.
They were brought to the shore of the ocean, which was like the words of a guru emerging from the depths of the sea;
there, the Lord whose abode is Varuṇa beheld him who had become one with Viṣṇu through meditation.
Having deposited jewels on the shore and come to see him,
the eater of snakes (Garuḍa) arrived there, overjoyed at being commanded by the Blessed One.
Having approached and devoured those who were bound, he departed once more;
then the ocean, with a deep resonance, addressed Prahlāda.
Having prostrated before the beloved of Hari who was established in samādhi, he, possessing a divine form, said:
"O Prahlāda, devotee of the Blessed One, virtuous soul, I am Arṇava."
"Behold me with your eyes, for I have come seeking purification"—
hearing these words from the ocean, that great-souled one, the beloved of Hari, [responded].
Suddenly beholding the god and bowing to him, the son of the asura said: "When did you arrive, O Blessed One? Then the ocean replied.
"O Yogi, you have acted unknowingly; an offense was committed against you by the Asuras.
You were bound by the Daityas in the form of serpents and have indeed been cast upon me today, O Vaiṣṇava."
Then, having quickly placed you on the shore along with those serpents,
the great Garuḍa has just now departed after devouring them.
O Great-Souled One, show favor to me, who seeks the company of the virtuous;
accept these jewels, for you are as worthy of worship to me as Hari himself.
"Even if you have no need for these jewels, I shall nevertheless offer them;
for one who is devoted even to the sun offers lamps."
For even in the midst of terrible calamities, you have indeed been protected by Viṣṇu alone;
there are not many like you whose souls are stainless, just as there are not many suns.
What need is there for much? I have achieved my purpose in that I stand with you; I speak with you even for a moment, for I do not behold this [world] which resembles a mere fruit.
Thus praised by the Ocean with words concerning the majesty of the Lord of Śrī,
Prahlāda, the beloved of the Blessed One, felt both shame and great joy.
Having accepted the jewels, that affectionate one said to the ocean:
"O Great-souled One, truly blessed are you, for that Lord rests within you."
Even at the end of the aeon, having swallowed the entire world, that Great Soul, who is identical with the universe, indeed reclines upon you alone when everything has become a single ocean.
"O Ocean, I wish to see the Lord of the World with my own eyes;
you are ever blessed to behold him, so grant me the means to do so."
Having spoken thus, Sāgara quickly raised up Prahlāda, who was prostrate at his feet, and said: "O lord of yogis, you always behold [the truth] within your heart."
"If you wish to see him with your own eyes, then praise Him who is affectionate toward His devotees.
Having said this, Sindhudvīpa entered the waters of his own lake.
When the lord of rivers had departed, that son of a Daitya remained alone at night and praised Hari with devotion,
thinking that a vision of him was impossible.
Prahlāda said:

How could that which the wise always seek to purify by heating the mind with the flame of dispassion— kindled by the winds of hundreds of Vedāntic statements— for the sake of its fitness to behold [the Truth], ever be within my reach?
My mind is tightly bound by the six powerful fetters—envy, anger, passion, greed, delusion, and pride—layer upon layer; it is blind. Where is Hari, and where am I?

Ah, my hope is that I may behold Him whom the chief of the world-protectors and the gods, seeking peace from their fears, somehow manage to see after approaching the shore of the Ocean of Milk and offering supreme hymns of praise.
Thinking himself unworthy in the sight of the Lord,
and terrified at not attaining him, his mind submerged in an ocean of agitation and sorrow, shedding streams of tears, O King, he fell down in a swoon.
Then, in an instant, the omnipresent one, four-armed and of auspicious form, the sole beloved of his devotees,
that ocean of compassion, embraced the distressed man with his nectar-filled arms and appeared right there before the king.
Then, having regained consciousness, he suddenly opened his eyes from the touch of her body and beheld one with a serene face,
eyes as broad as lotuses, long arms, and a complexion like the Yamunā.

Seeing the Lord standing there, embracing her who was composed of sublime splendor, immeasurable, and marked with the beautiful signs of the mace, discus, conch, and lotus, he trembled with wonder, fear, and joy.
Then, considering it indeed to be a dream, he thought, "Even in a dream I behold Hari, my purpose fulfilled.
With his mind submerged in an ocean of supreme joy, he once again fell into a swoon of bliss.
Then the Lord, the sole kinsman of his own people, having sat down upon the very ground and taken him onto his lap,
gently shook him with his sprout-like hand, touching him repeatedly and embracing him like a mother.
Then, after a long time, Prahlāda, his eyes opening wide,
beheld the Lord of the World with a mind filled with wonder.
Then, after a long time, having perceived that the steadfast one was reclining upon the auspicious Śārṅga bow,
he suddenly rose up with immediate fear and agitation.
Prostrating himself upon the earth and repeatedly saying, "Be gracious," he,
though possessed of great learning, did not recall any other word of homage due to his agitation.
Then the Lord, the ocean of compassion, who holds the mace, conch, and discus, took Prahlāda by his hand with a gesture of fearlessness and established him [in safety].
Then the Lord, gladdening him once more, spoke thus to him consolingly, as his tears flowed from the joy of the touch of the lotus-hand and he trembled with emotion.
"O child, abandon this fear and agitation born of respect for me;
I am not pleased by such behavior toward my devotees; become one who is self-reliant in your affection."
For me, whose every desire is eternally fulfilled, these various births exist for the sake of granting all that is desired by my devotees; therefore, tell me what you wish for.
Then Prahlāda, bowing with palms joined in reverence, made this request to Viṣṇu while gazing at His face with longing and eyes wide with wonder.
Nor is this the time for granting a boon; do not be gracious toward me.
My inner self finds no satisfaction from tasting the nectar of beholding you.
O Lord, even in hundreds of tens of thousands of kalpas, my mind will find no satiety in beholding you alone, who are difficult to perceive even for the gods beginning with Brahmā.
"This is not so; for how could one who is unsatisfied choose anything else after seeing you?
Then, filling his beloved with floods of the nectar of his smile, he spoke further to her.
Joining him with the very fortune of liberation, the Lord of the World said to him:
"My child, truly there is nothing dearer to you than the sight of me."
"Choose whatever you wish for me to give you for the sake of my pleasure.
Then the wise Prahlāda said, "O God, even in future births..."
"May I become your servant, possessing devotion like Garuḍa.
Then the Lord said to Prahlāda, "Indeed, this trouble has been created by you."
"I desire to give myself to you, yet you desire the state of being my servant;
choose other boons, O wise one, son of the lord of the Daityas."
Prahlāda spoke again to Hari, the granter of the desires of his devotees:
"Be gracious, O Lord; let my devotion to you be steady and characterized by goodness (sāttvikī)."
With this [hymn], I now bow to you and always dance, devoted solely to you.
Then the Blessed One, being well-pleased, spoke kindly to the one who speaks kindly.
"My child, whatever you desire, let that be so; be happy.
And when I have vanished from here, O high-minded one, do not grieve."
I shall not depart from your mind, just as one does not leave the beloved Ocean of Milk;
again, in two or three days, you shall see me intent on the destruction of the wicked.

Having spoken thus to Nṛsiṃha, whose form was unprecedented and never before manifested, and who was terrifying to the wicked, he addressed him as he bowed down and gazed upon him with intense longing.
While he remained dissatisfied, Hari, the Lord, concealed himself through his illusory power (māyā);
then, not seeing him anywhere despite searching everywhere, [the sage] realized that the Lord is affectionately devoted to his devotees.
Then, while the sounds of people awakening all around were being heard, he, bathed in tears, cried out "Alas! Alas! and after a long time, offered his salutation.
Rising from the shore of the ocean, the wise Prahlāda went to his own city.
Then the son of the Daityas, having rejoiced for a long time and beholding him all around through the power of his memory,
and seeing clearly that Hari had indeed entered the mortal world, slowly reached his father’s house with his hair standing on end.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Narasiṃha," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 43.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, seeing Prahlāda returned, the Daityas were greatly amazed; they reported to the lord of the Daityas that he had been cast into the great ocean.
Hearing that he had returned healthy, the king of the Daityas was overwhelmed with astonishment; standing on the brink of death, he spoke out of anger, saying, "Let him be summoned!"
Thus, brought there by the Asuras, he who possessed divine vision beheld the lord of the Daityas seated there, whose splendor was exceedingly great, yet whose death was imminent.
His ornaments were covered by the luster of rubies mingled with blue rays;
he stood upon a high throne-altar like a smoke-enveloped fire.
It was filled with Daityas who were like messengers of Yama— fierce with prominent fangs, most terrible, possessing thick complexions, and arrogant, showing the way to evil paths.
Having bowed from a distance to his father, he stood with palms joined in reverence;
then that wicked man, his anger provoked by the failure of the ritual, began to revile his son.
O fool, as if resorting to death itself—the most exalted refuge dear to the Blessed One—listen to my words; this indeed shall certainly be your final one.
"I shall not speak further to you from here; having heard this, do as you wish.
Having said this, he quickly drew his wondrous sword, Candrahāsa.
Gazed upon with alarm by everyone as he shook him, he spoke to him again:
"Where is your Viṣṇu, O fool? May he protect you today!"
"You said that he is indeed everywhere; why then is he not seen in the pillar?
If I were to see that Viṣṇu now, situated within the pillar..."
"In that case, I shall not kill you; otherwise, you will be split in two.
Having seen this, Prahlāda also reflected upon that Supreme Lord.
Remembering those words previously spoken, he bowed with palms joined in reverence;
meanwhile, the pillar was seen to have burst open by the son of the Daitya.
Within the mirror-like form of the Daitya, that which was produced from his sword was established;
in its center, a form extending for many yojanas was seen.
Extremely fierce, with a massive body that strikes terror into the dānavas,
he has large eyes, a large mouth, large fangs, and large arms.
He had great claws and great feet, with a face like the fire of cosmic destruction;
his wide-open mouth reached as far as his ears, making him exceedingly terrifying.
Having thus assumed the form of Narasiṃha, Viṣṇu Trivikrama departed;
and Narasiṃha, emerging from the middle of the pillar, let out a roar.
Upon hearing the roar, the Daityas surrounded Narasiṃha;
having slain them all there by means of his own manly prowess, [he remained].
And he shattered the divine assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu, O King;
then the great warriors, having approached, sought to restrain Narasiṃha.
But they, O King, were slain in an instant by that lion among men;
thereafter, they rained down weapons upon the majestic Narasiṃha.
But in an instant, that Blessed One, having destroyed that army by his might,
let out a great roar, filling the quarters with the sound.
Having learned that they too had died, the great asura again commanded eighty-eight thousand others, who held weapons in their hands.
They too, having arrived, besieged that god from every direction;
having slain them all in battle while fighting, he let out a roar.
Furthermore, having perceived that they too were slain, his eyes bloodshot with rage, he destroyed the splendid assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Then the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu emerged and spoke,
O protector of the earth, to the Dānavas who were arrogant in their strength.
Having slain those who were fighting in battle, that lion among men roared;
thereupon, the remaining Daityas fled in every direction.
While thousands of millions of Daityas were being slain as they fought,
the sun reached the region of the sky.
O King, the exceedingly powerful Narasiṃha, skilled in raining down weapons and missiles, swiftly seized Hiraṇyakaśipu by force.
Standing at the door of his house at twilight and placing that enemy upon his thigh,
he angrily tore open Hiraṇyakaśipu— whose broad chest was like a diamond—
with his claws as if they were sprouts; then that Asura spoke.
There, in battle, the maces from the tusks of Indra’s elephant were shattered; there, the edge of the axe wielded by the wielder of the Pināka bow met with bluntness.
Yet now, that very chest of mine is being torn apart by the claws of the Man-Lion. When fate turns malevolent, even a blade of grass is generally treated with contempt.
While the lord of the Daityas was speaking thus,
Narakesarin tore open the heart of the king of the Daityas, as an elephant rends a lotus leaf.
When the two fragments had vanished into the nail-scratches of the Great-Souled One,
the Lord was greatly amazed, wondering, "Where has that wicked one gone?"
"O King, having looked in every direction, [he thought], 'This labor of mine has been in vain. Thus reflecting, O Indra among kings, the exceedingly powerful Narasiṃha—"
Then, O King, they vigorously shook their hands,
and the two fragments of Hari fell to the ground like dust from the hollows of their fingernails.
Seeing this, the Supreme Lord, his anger having subsided,
laughed while raining down a shower of flowers upon the head of Narasiṃha.
All the gods, together with Brahmā, arrived filled with joy;
having arrived, they worshipped the supreme Lord, the Man-Lion.
And Brahmā consecrated Prahlāda as king of the Daityas;
at that time, all people came to take delight in righteousness.
Indra, too, was established in heaven by Hari along with all the gods;
and the Lord Narasiṃha indeed [was established] for the welfare of all the worlds.
Having reached the peak of Śrīśaila, the renowned one, worshipped by the gods,
remains there for the benefit of his devotees and for the sake of forgiving those who are not devoted.
O best of kings, the man who recites or hears this majesty of Narasiṃha is liberated from all sins.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever hears this supreme narrative is liberated from widowhood, from suffering and grief, and from association with the wicked.
Even a man who is immoral, of evil conduct, having wicked offspring, a performer of harmful deeds,
most unrighteous, and lacking in devotion— by listening [to this], he shall become pure.
Hari, the Lord of the gods, worshipped by the world of men, for the welfare of the world of moving and unmoving beings,
having previously assumed a deformed form through his own power of illusion, tore apart Hiraṇyaka— who caused such suffering— with his claws.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Narasiṃha," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 44)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O King, in brief, to the prowess of Vāmana,
by whom thousands of Daityas were formerly slain at the sacrifice of Bali.
In former times, the son of Virocana, possessed of great strength and prowess,
conquered the gods led by Indra and enjoyed the sovereignty of the three worlds.
Thereupon the gods became even more emaciated, being deprived by him; O best of kings, seeing Indra thus weakened and his kingdom lost, they too grew feeble.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, who had performed supreme austerity,
prostrated before Janārdana and praised him with pleasing words.
Then, highly gratified by the hymn of praise, Janārdana, the God of gods,
Madhusūdana, stood before him and spoke these words.
"O fortunate one, I shall become your son, the binder of Bala," having said this to her, Viṣṇu went to his own abode, and she returned home.
Then, in due time, O King, she conceived a child from Kaśyapa;
that Lord of the Universe was born in the form of the Blessed Vāmana.
When he was born, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
arrived and performed all the rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*).
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, the eternal Lord, being a religious student (*brahmacārī*),
took leave of Aditi and went to Bali’s sacrificial hall.
As he walked, the entire earth trembled with the stamping of his feet;
and the Dānavas did not accept their sacrificial portions from Bala’s sacrifice.
The sacrificial fires there were extinguished and the officiating priests had deviated from the mantras;
seeing this reversal, the mighty Śukra said:
O Sage, why do the great Asuras not accept their portion of the sacrificial oblation?
Why are the fires extinguished, and why, O twice-born one, does the earth tremble?
"And why have all these officiating priests fallen from their mantras?
When Balin had spoken thus, Śukra addressed these words to the lord of the Dānavas:
Śukra said:
O Bali, listen to my words; the gods have been cast out by you.
To restore their kingdom, O Asura, Acyuta [Viṣṇu] has entered into Aditi.
The God of gods, the source of the universe, has been born in the form of a dwarf;
he is coming to your sacrifice, [the earth] trembling at the imprint of his foot.
"O Lord of Asuras, this entire earth is trembling today because of him;
due to his presence, the Asuras do not accept the sacrificial oblation at the sacrifice."
Indeed, O Bala, even your fires have become extinguished because of Vāmana’s arrival;
furthermore, neither the officiating priests nor the sacrificial mantras shine forth now.
"The prosperity of the gods destroys the splendor of the asuras; this is the supreme fortune of the gods.
Having been told this, Bali spoke to Śukra, the best among those possessed of political wisdom.
Listen, O Brahmin, to my words now that the sacrifice has come to Vāmana;
hear what must be done by me today for this wise Vāmana.
Tell me that, O illustrious one, for you are our supreme teacher.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus urged by King Bali, O monarch, Śukra—
He spoke these words to Bali: "Listen now to me as well, for the sake of assisting the gods and for the destruction of you all."
He will surely come to your sacrifice, O Bala; of this there is no doubt.
When the god Vāmana has arrived, you must [offer] to that great-souled one.
"One should not even make a formal promise, saying 'I give this to you'";
having heard these words of his, Bali, the best among the powerful, [reflected].
He spoke these auspicious words to Śukra, his own domestic priest:
"O Śukra, now that the dwarf Madhusūdana has arrived at my sacrifice..."
"O Teacher, I cannot refuse to give even to other living beings; this is what I have now said to you regarding giving."
But what need is there to speak of Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, when he has arrived?
O twice-born one, you must not create an obstacle here when Vāmana has come.
"Whatever object anyone requests, that very object I shall give;
I am fulfilled, O best of sages, if Vāmana comes."
While he was speaking thus, that dwarf arrived at the sacrificial hall and entered; he then praised the sacrifice of Bali.
O King, having seen him suddenly, Bali, the king and lord of the Daityas,
honored him with hospitable rites and spoke these words.
"O God of gods, whatever wealth or anything else you request from me, I shall give all of that to you; ask me for it today, O Vāmana."
Thus addressed by Bali there, O lord of men, Vāmana, the Lord of Gods, then requested: "Give me three paces of land."
"I have need for this for the purpose of a fire-sanctuary; I have no personal use for it.
Thus addressed by Vāmana, Bali then spoke to Vāmana.
"If you are satisfied with three paces, then the three paces have been given by me.
When this was said by Bali, Vāmana spoke to Bali:
"Let water be given into my hand if the three steps have been granted," thus was Bali himself addressed there by the God of gods.
Rising with devotion and taking up a golden pitcher filled with water,
he approached the dwarf to offer the water into his hand.
At that moment, O best of beings, Śukra, who was contained within the water-pot, blocked the stream of water; then Vāmana, becoming enraged, [struck him] with the tip of his sacrificial grass-broom.
In the water, at the opening of a jar, he pierced his white eye;
then, O best of men, the semen was discharged and one eye was pierced.
Again, a stream of water fell into the hand of Vāmana;
as the water fell upon his hand, Vāmana grew in an instant.
With one step he strode across the entire earth;
with the second, the intermediate space; and with the third, the heavens, O best of beings.
Having slain numerous Dānavas and having seized the three worlds from Bali,
he gave the triple-world to Purandara and spoke to Bali.
"Since water was given by you today with devotion into my hand,
therefore this excellent netherworld (pātāla) is now granted to you."
Having gone there, O illustrious one, enjoy [the fruits] through my grace;
when the Vaivasvata interval has passed, you shall become Indra once again.
And having prostrated and then departed, he attained enjoyment upon the ground.
O King, Śukra too, having ascended to heaven through the grace of Vāmana,
returned to the three worlds accompanied by the gods.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should remember this story of Vāmana,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O King, in former times Hari, having assumed the form of a dwarf, took away the three worlds from Bali;
and having bestowed favor upon the lord of the gods and granted him the three worlds, he departed for the great ocean.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vāmana," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 45)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the auspicious manifestation of Hari as the son of Jamadagni, by whom the kṣatriyas were formerly exterminated; listen.
O King, in former times Viṣṇu was praised by the hosts of gods and by the highly fortunate ṛṣis while in the Ocean of Milk; he then became the son of Jamadagni.
That Lord, renowned throughout all the worlds as Paraśurāma,
descended to the surface of the earth to subdue the wicked.
In ancient times, the illustrious Kārtavīrya was the son of Kṛtavīrya;
having propitiated Dattātreya, he attained the status of a universal emperor (cakravartin).
Once that illustrious one went to the hermitage of Jamadagni;
and Jamadagni, seeing him accompanied by a fourfold army, [was amazed].
He spoke these sweet words to Kārtavīrya, the best of kings:
"Let your army be dismissed here; you have arrived as a guest.
O high-minded one, eat the forest produce and other offerings given by me, and then depart."
Having dismissed his army out of respect for the words of the sage, the high-minded king remained there;
then the sage of unassailable fame took leave of the king and milked that milch-cow.

O King, there were various stables for elephants and horses, and variegated houses with ornamental arches for men— auspicious dwellings fit for vassals and lovely groves desired by those seeking pleasure.

"Furthermore, having milked this most excellent house with its many stories, which is endowed with the implements and qualities of the virtuous, and having fashioned it for the king, the Sage said: 'O King, enter here this house that has been made for you.'"
And let these eminent ministers and people quickly enter their divine dwellings;
let the noble elephants and horses enter their stables, and let the servants reside in humble houses.
As soon as the sage had spoken thus, that king entered his most excellent palace;
yet, even though there were other houses available, the sage spoke again to the monarch.
"O King, these one hundred excellent women have been prepared by me for the purpose of providing you with a bath;
bathe here today as you desire, just as the Lord of the Gods does in heaven amidst dance and song."
Having bathed there like the lord of the gods, the king was [honored] with sweet sounds of song and musical instruments;
and as soon as he had bathed, O King, the sage gave him two auspicious garments, beautifully adorned.
Having put on his lower garment and prepared his upper robe, and having performed his ritual duties, he performed the worship of Viṣṇu;
and that sage, having churned a great mountain of food consisting of milk, gave it to the king and his servant.
While that king was eating together with his attendants, the sun went down behind the mountains;
and at night, engaged in the diversions of song and other arts, the king lay down in the house constructed by the sage.
Then, at the clear dawn, having seen a certain stretch of ground that seemed as if obtained in a dream, the king began to reflect upon it.
"O highly fortunate priest, tell me: is this the power of the asceticism of this great-souled sage, or is it that of Surabhi?"
Thus addressed by Kārtavīrya, the domestic priest said to him:
"O King, the sage possesses such power, for this cow is indeed a supernatural attainment."
Nevertheless, O lord of men, she must not be taken by you out of greed;
for whoever should wish to take her away, his destruction will certainly come to pass.
Then the excellent minister, a Brahmin beloved by Brahmins, said:
"He does not indeed perceive the affairs of the king, because he is occupied solely with nourishing his own faction."
O King, various dwellings, as well as golden vessels, beds, and women, all abide in you.
O Indra among kings, having obtained that cow, we saw our possessions dissolving there at that very moment; let that excellent cow be led away.
"O Indra among kings, O high-minded one, she is worthy of you alone; if you so desire, I shall go and bring her back. Grant me your command, O lord of the earth."
Thus addressed by the minister, the king, O best of monarchs, said, "So be it.
Then the minister went there and began to seize Surabhi.
Jamadagni restrained his minister on all sides, saying:
"O Brahmin, O high-minded one, give this [bow] suitable for a king to the king."
"But you subsist on vegetables and fruits; what need have you for a cow?
Having said this, the minister seized her by force and proceeded to lead her away.
Again, that sage, together with his wife, restrained the king;
then, O King, that extremely wicked-minded minister killed the sage.
The slayer of a Brahmin began to carry her away through the path of the wind;
she departed, and the king, with an agitated heart, went to the city of Māhiṣmatī.
O King, the sage’s wife, afflicted by great sorrow and weeping bitterly at that time,
struck her own belly twenty-one times.
Hearing that, Rāma then arrived, having taken up his axe;
and having gathered flowers and other offerings from the forest, he spoke to his mother.
"Enough, mother, with striking me; I have understood it from the omen.
I shall slay the ill-behaved Arjuna, that wicked counselor."
"Since my womb was struck by you twenty-one times—
three times seven— I shall therefore slay the kings upon the earth."
Having thus made his vow and taken up his axe, he went forth;
reaching the city of Māhiṣmatī, he then challenged Kārtavīrya.
Then he arrived for the sake of battle, accompanied by many akṣauhiṇīs;
there, a terrible and hair-raising battle took place between the two of them.
Then there arose Paraśurāma, possessed of great strength and prowess, who brought joy to the flesh-eating folk and was crowded with hundreds of weapons and missiles.
Viṣṇu, the supreme light whose nature is inconceivable, the embodiment of the primal cause,
[destroyed] the entire army of Kārtavīrya along with many kṣatriyas.
Having struck him down and felled him to the ground, the one of most wonderful prowess,
filled with rage, lopped off the forest of Kārtavīrya’s arms;
once that forest of arms was severed, Bhārgava cut off his head.
Having met his death at the hand of Viṣṇu, that sovereign king,
assuming a divine form, became glorious, adorned with divine fragrances and unguents.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot,
even Paraśurāma, possessed of great strength and prowess, attained the world of Viṣṇu through his anger.
Twenty-one times indeed he struck down the earthly kings upon the earth;
by that slaughter of the Kṣatriyas, the burden of the earth was removed.
And the entire earth was given to the high-souled Kaśyapa;
thus has this manifestation known as Jāmadagnya been described by me.
And whoever should hear that with devotion is liberated from all sins.

Having descended to the earth, O King, this Hari himself, having slain the rulers of the land twenty-one times and having distributed the kṣatriya splendor, remains even today as Rāma on Mount Mahendra.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Paraśurāma," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 46)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the auspicious manifestation of Hari,
by whom Rāvaṇa, that thorn in the side of the gods, was slain along with his hosts.
The great sage Pulastya was the mind-born son of Brahmā;
his son was named Viśravas, from whom the Rākṣasa was born.
Born from him was the great hero Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out;
endowed with mighty ascetic power, he oppressed the worlds.
O King, by him the gods along with Indra were conquered, as were the Gandharvas and Kinnaras;
likewise, the Yakṣas and Dānavas were utterly defeated by him.
And beautiful women were carried off by that evil-minded one,
O best of kings, as well as various jewels belonging to the gods and others.
Having defeated Kubera in battle, Rāvaṇa, arrogant in his strength,
seized his city Laṅkā as well as the Puṣpaka aerial chariot.
In that city, Daśagrīva became the sovereign of the rākṣasas;
and he had many sons of immeasurable prowess.
And relying upon him, O King, there dwell in Laṅkā many tens of millions of Rākṣasas who possess great strength and prowess.
Then they cause the gods, the ancestors, humans, the hosts of vidyādharas,
and even the yakṣas— all of them— to be slain day and night.
O lord of men, because of that very fear, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings became terrified;
it became utterly overwhelmed by suffering.
At that very time, however, the gods led by Indra, the great seers,
the Siddhas, the Vidyādharas, as well as the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, [gathered there].
The Guhyakas, Bhujagas, Yakṣas, and others who dwell in heaven,
O lord of men, having placed Brahmā and Śaṅkara at their head.
Having lost their prowess, they went to the excellent shore of the Ocean of Milk;
there, having propitiated Hari, the gods then stood with palms joined in reverence.
And Brahmā, having propitiated Viṣṇu with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
stood with palms joined in reverence and praised Vāsudeva.
Brahmā said:
Homage to Viṣṇu, who dwells in the ocean of milk, who reclines upon the serpent-couch,
and whose divine feet are touched by the hand of Śrī.
Salutations to you who are the sleep of yoga, and who are absorbed within yoga;
salutations again and again to the divine Govinda, whose seat is Tārkṣya.
Homage to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who was touched merely by the waves of the Ocean of Milk;
homage to Viṣṇu, the lotus-navelled one, whose feet are like lotuses.
Salutations indeed to the one whose feet are worshipped by devotees, to the lover of yoga;
salutations again and again to the one of auspicious limbs, the beautiful-eyed Mādhava.
Salutations again and again to the one with beautiful hair, beautiful eyes, and a beautiful forehead; to the wielder of the discus, who has a beautiful face and beautiful ears, the bearer of Śrī.
Salutations indeed to the one with a beautiful chest, to the one with a beautiful navel, to the lotus-navelled one;
salutations to the one with beautiful eyebrows, to the one with a lovely body, to the one with beautiful teeth, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Salutations again and again to the divine Keśava of beautiful shanks;
salutations to the one with excellent teeth, the perfectly peaceful, the possessor of true knowledge, the wielder of the mace.
Homage again and again to the god who loves the Dharma, to Vāmana;
homage again and again to the slayer of Asuras, to the fierce one, to the slayer of Rākṣasas.
Homage to the one who performs terrifying deeds for the destruction of the gods' distress;
homage to you, the Lord of the World; homage to the one who brings about the end of Rāvaṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus praised by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), Hṛṣīkeśa was pleased;
having revealed his true form, he spoke to the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
"For what purpose, O Grandfather, have you come here together with the gods?
Tell me, O Brahmā, what is the task for which you have been praised by me?"
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, the powerful God of gods,
Brahmā, together with all the hosts of deities, spoke to Janārdana.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord, the entire world has been destroyed by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa;
Indra and the other gods have been defeated many times by that Rākṣasa."
Mortals were devoured by the rākṣasas and even the sacrifices were desecrated;
by him, celestial maidens were forcibly abducted by the hundreds of thousands.
O lotus-eyed one, since even the gods are not capable of the slaying of Rāvaṇa without you, therefore, you must effect his destruction.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu spoke this to Brahmā:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmā, to these beneficial words that I speak."
There was a glorious and heroic king on earth born of the solar dynasty, renowned by the name Daśaratha; I am his son.
O best of beings, for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, all the hosts of deities, by means of their own portions in the form of monkeys, [manifested] as four parts.
"O Architect of All, let them proceed so that the destruction of Rāvaṇa may come to pass";
thus was Brahmā, the Grandfather of the Worlds, addressed by the God of Gods.
Then those gods, having bowed down, went to the summit of Mount Meru;
and by means of their own portions in the form of monkeys, they descended to the surface of the earth.
