Then King Daśaratha, being childless, had the sages who had mastered the Vedas perform a sacrifice intended to procure him a son.
Then, taking the sacrificial offering of milk-rice contained in a golden vessel,
the Fire-god indeed rose up from the fire-pit, surely impelled by the Lord.
Taking the two auspicious morsels of food consecrated by mantras from the mantra, the sages gave one each to Kauśalyā and Kaikeyī.
O Mahāmati, at the time of consuming the alms-food, they gave very small portions of food to Sumitrā, the fortunate one.
Then those queens ate the rice-balls prepared by the gods according to the prescribed ritual; having eaten them, those blameless women conceived embryos.
Thus, O Lord of the World, Viṣṇu was born from Daśaratha through his own portions in his three wives,
appearing fourfold solely for the welfare of the world.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna,
having received the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) performed by the sages, [attained their respective stations].
Having attained mastery through the power of the mantra-piṇḍa, they moved about like children;
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa wandered together constantly.
O King, having received the sacraments beginning with birth, those two of great prowess, who were the ornaments of the Vedas and their terminology, grew up bringing joy to their father.
O King, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, lived with his brother in the palace;
O best of monarchs, he mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, as well as the science of weaponry.
At that very time, however, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic,
began to sacrifice to Madhusūdana according to the prescribed ritual.
In the past, that sacrifice was repeatedly obstructed by Rākṣasas;
he had come there for the purpose of leading away Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to serve as sacrificial victims.
Viśvāmitra went to the auspicious palace of his father, that best of kings;
and the high-minded Daśaratha, seeing him, rose up to meet him.
He honored Viśvāmitra according to the rites of *arghya*, *pādya*, and so forth;
thus honored, the sage spoke to the king in the presence of the assembly.
Listen, O King Daśaratha, to the purpose for which I have come;
O tiger among kings, I shall declare that task before you.
"My sacrifice has been destroyed many times by unassailable Rākṣasas;
for the sake of protecting my sacrifice, give me Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
O King, having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, King Daśaratha,
with a dejected countenance, spoke to Viśvāmitra.
"What need will you have for my two young sons?
I myself, having come with you, shall protect your sacrifice to the best of my ability."
Having heard the king's words, the sage said to the king:
"O King, Rāma is indeed capable of destroying them all."
"O King, these Rākṣasas can indeed be overcome by Rāma alone, but not by you;
therefore, give Rāma to me, for you ought not to harbor anxiety."
Having been addressed thus by that wise sage Viśvāmitra,
the king remained silent for a moment and then spoke to the best of sages.
O best of sages, listen to what I say with a gracious mind:
I shall give you Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses, along with his younger brother.
"But, O Brahmin, his mother will die if she does not see him;
therefore, O Sage, I have come together with my fourfold army."
"Having arrived, I shall slay the Rākṣasas"—this is what remains fixed in my mind.
Viśvāmitra spoke thus again to the king of immeasurable luster.
O best of kings, Rāma is not ignorant; he is omniscient, equanimous, and patient.
These two sons of yours are Śeṣa and Nārāyaṇa; of this there is no doubt.
O lord of men, there is no doubt that they have descended into your house for the sake of subduing the wicked and protecting the virtuous.
"O King, neither your mother nor you should feel even the slightest grief in this matter;
O Great King, I shall entrust your two sons to me as a deposit."
Having been addressed thus by the wise Viśvāmitra, Daśaratha,
fearing his curse, spoke in his mind, "Let him be taken."
O King, having taken Rāma along with his younger brother, who had been released from his father's hardship with great difficulty,
that Kauśika then set out for Siddhāśrama.
Then, seeing him set out, King Daśaratha followed after him and spoke these words at that time.
"O Brahmin, formerly I was childless; but now, O best of beings, through the grace of the sage and by means of many rites performed for specific desires, I have become possessed of a son."
"But I shall not be able to endure separation from him even in my mind, especially so;
you yourself know this, O Sage—take him and give him back to me quickly."
Having been addressed in this manner, Viśvāmitra spoke again to the king:
"Once the sacrifice is completed, I shall take Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa back with me."
"I shall give you my word of truth; you need not worry.
Having been addressed thus, he dispatched Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Although the king did not desire it, out of fear of the sage’s curse,
King Viśvāmitra took the two of them and went slowly toward Ayodhyā.
O king of kings, having reached the bank of the Sarayū, as Kauśika was departing,
he first bestowed the two sciences upon them out of affection.
The high-minded one [taught] Valā and Ativalā, along with the mantras and the compendium, as well as [the methods] for removing hunger and thirst.
Having then instructed them in the entire collection of weapons,
as well as in the divine hermitages of the sages of purified souls, they [departed].
Having shown himself and having dwelt in sacred places,
the Best of Beings crossed the Gaṅgā and reached the western bank of the Śoṇa.
Beholding the sages, the righteous, and the perfected ones, and having received boons from the seers, the two princes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were led away by him.
O best of kings, when he had gone to that terrible forest of Tāṭakā, which was like another mouth of Death, Viśvāmitra of great ascetic power [remained there].

He spoke these words to Rāma, whose actions are effortless: "O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! A rākṣasī named Tāṭakā dwells in this great forest by the command of Rāvaṇa. By her, many humans, sons of sages, and likewise deer [have been slain]."
"They have been slain and even devoured; therefore, O best of beings, slay her!
Having been addressed thus by the sage, Rāma spoke to that sage.
For how could I, O Great Sage, commit the murder of a woman today?
The wise declare that the killing of a woman is a great sin.
Having heard these words of Rāma, Viśvāmitra said to him:
"O Rāma, because of her death, all the people have become free from distress."
"Therefore, her killing constantly yields merit.
While the sage Viśvāmitra was speaking thus, the night-stalker—
The most terrible Tāṭakā arrived with her mouth wide open;
seeing her with her mouth agape, Rāma was urged on by the Sage.
Beholding her with one arm raised like a staff and a girdle of human entrails hanging from her hips, Rāghava cast away his compassion for the slaughter of a woman along with his arrow.
O King, having fixed an arrow with great force, he split her chest into two; she fell down and died.
Having thus caused her to be slain and brought those two back,
the sage led them to that place frequented by various ṛṣis.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers,
rich with the waters of many waterfalls, and situated within the Vindhya mountains.
Having specially instructed both of them and established them there for the sake of protection, he left his own divine hermitage, which was endowed with vegetables, roots, and fruits.
Then the great ascetic Viśvāmitra commenced the sacrifice;
and when the high-souled sage Viśvāmitra had entered the initiatory rite (dīkṣā), [the following occurred].
When that sacrifice was spread out, the officiating priests,
Mārīca, Subāhu, and many other rākṣasas performed the ritual acts.
Having been dispatched by Rāvaṇa to destroy the sacrifice, they arrived;
and the lotus-eyed Rāma, perceiving that they had come, [acted accordingly].
With an arrow he struck Subāhu down to the surface of the earth,
and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) he struck Mārīca, who was raining forth streams of blood.
Having struck him, he drove him into the ocean like a leaf by the wind;
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa then slew the remaining night-stalkers.
The highly illustrious Viśvāmitra, whose sacrifice had been protected by Rāma,
completed the ritual according to the rules and honored the officiating priests.
Having honored the members of the assembly as was appropriate, O subduer of enemies,
he also worshipped Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with devotion.
Then, O best of men, the host of gods, gratified by their share of the sacrifice,
rained down a shower of flowers upon the head of Rāmadeva.
Having warded off the fear of the rākṣasas and having caused that sacrifice to be performed,
Rāma, accompanied by his brothers, listened to various meritorious stories.
He led that self-disciplined man to where Ahalyā was staying;
for she had previously been cursed by her husband, the great Indra, on account of her infidelity.
O Indra among kings, by the sight of that Rāma, Ahalyā— who had become like a stone— was released from her curse and went back to Gautama.
Then Viśvāmitra reflected there for a moment:
"Now that I am married, the lotus-eyed Rāma must be led by me."
Having reflected thus, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra took them both and,
surrounded by many disciples, set out toward Mithilā.
Then, from various countries, princes of great heroism who had previously desired Sītā arrived at Janaka’s residence.
Having seen them and honored them according to their merit,
Janaka [recounted] that great bow of Maheśvara which had been produced for Sītā.
Having honored it with perfumes and garlands, he placed that bow upon a vast and spacious stage endowed with delightful splendor.
And King Janaka spoke loudly to all the monarchs:
"O princes, by whomsoever this bow has been broken through drawing it..."
"Sītā, beautiful in all her limbs, is his wife by right of dharma"—
thus was it declared by that high-souled Janaka.
O Lord of the Earth, having taken them up one by one in succession, they all then attempted to string that bow, but were struck down by it one after another.
Shaken off and fallen there, O King, those monarchs were filled with shame;
when they had been broken, Janaka [approached] that bow of Tryambaka, O King.
Having established himself there, the hero remained waiting in expectation of Rāma’s arrival;
then Viśvāmitra arrived at the house of the lord of Mithilā.
And Janaka, seeing Viśvāmitra arrived at his home accompanied by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, and followed by his disciples, [welcomed him].
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites— the wise one who follows the Brahmins,
as well as Rāma, the Lord of the Raghus, who is endowed with qualities such as beauty— Nārada spoke.
Having honored the high-minded Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with virtue, conduct, and good qualities, according to tradition, Janaka was delighted in his heart.
Then, to Viśvāmitra, who was seated comfortably on a golden throne and surrounded by his disciples from both the east and the west, he said: "What should be done by me?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of his, the sage spoke to the lord of the earth:
"O great king, this Rāma is Viṣṇu himself, the sovereign of the world."
Born as the son of Daśaratha for the protection of the worlds,
give Sītā to him, who stands like a daughter of the gods.
O Indra among kings, it was proclaimed that the breaking of the bow would occur at her marriage;
therefore, O lord of men, bring your own bow and worship it.
Having said "So be it," the king indeed restored that wondrous bow of Bhava, which had broken many kings, to its former state.
Then, urged by Viśvāmitra, the lotus-eyed Rāma, son of Daśaratha, rose up from among them.
Having bowed to the brahmins and the gods,
the mighty-armed one then took up that bow, strung it, and produced the sound of its twanging string.
But as it was being pulled with force by him, the great bow broke;
and Sītā took a beautiful garland and placed it upon Rāma’s head.
Having cast [the challenge], he made a vow in the presence of all the kṣatriyas;
then those kṣatriyas, filled with rage, assailed Rāma from all sides.
Roaring, those of great strength released nets of arrows;
then Rāma, beholding them, took up his bow with speed.
With the sound of his bowstring and the clatter of his palms, he made those kings tremble;
then, with his own weapons, he cut through their nets of arrows and destroyed their chariots.
Then Rāma, with effortless ease, cut down the bows and banners;
thereupon the Lord of Mithilā arrayed his entire army.
Protecting his son-in-law in battle, he indeed became the one who guards the rear;
and the great hero Lakṣmaṇa, having put those kings to flight in the fray, [remained there].
He seized their elephants, horses, and many chariots,
as the kings, having abandoned their mounts, were intent on flight.
Then Lakṣmaṇa ran after them to strike them down,
but Kauśika, the lord of Mithilā, restrained him.
Then Janaka, taking with him the great hero Rāma, who had conquered his senses, along with his brother, went to his own auspicious residence.
And then he dispatched a messenger to Daśaratha;
having heard everything from the mouth of the messenger, that king understood the matter.
Accompanied by his wife and sons, the illustrious one, with elephants, horses, chariots, and mounts,
quickly arrived at Mithilā together with his own army.
Then King Janaka, having performed the honors for him, gave his own daughter to Rāma according to the prescribed rites, after the bride-price had been paid, O monarch.
Furthermore, he gave his three other beautiful daughters, well-adorned,
to Lakṣmaṇa and the others according to the prescribed rites.
Having thus performed the marriage, that lotus-eyed Rāma,
together with his brothers, his mothers, and his powerful father, [departed].
Having stayed there for some days with various kinds of food,
the king saw King Daśaratha, who was eager to go to the city of Ayodhyā along with his son; the king then bestowed wealth upon Sītā.
Having given many divine jewels and most splendid garments to Rāma,
he also gave elephants, horses, and slaves fit for work, as well as female servants and excellent women.
Having placed the virtuous Sītā, adorned with many jewels and beautiful in form, upon the chariot,
that powerful king sent her forth amidst the sounds of the Vedas and many auspicious rites.
Having sent his daughter Diśā away, having bowed to King Daśaratha,
and having paid homage to Viśvāmitra, Janaka returned.
Then his highly fortunate wives, having instructed their daughter, said:
"O auspicious one, practice devotion toward your husband, and likewise toward your mother-in-law and father-in-law."
Having entrusted her to their mothers-in-law, they returned and entered the city;
meanwhile, Rāma, accompanied by his powerful [brother], was proceeding toward Ayodhyā.
Upon hearing this, Paraśurāma indeed blocked the path;
seeing him, all those royal officers became dejected in spirit.
And King Daśaratha, along with his wife and his retinue, was overwhelmed by pain and grief due to the fear of Bhārgava, O monarch.
Then Vasiṣṭha, the great sage of powerful asceticism and a lifelong celibate, spoke to all the people and to the deeply distressed king.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this matter, you should not feel even the slightest bit of sorrow on account of Rāma."
O King, this Rāma in your house is indeed Viṣṇu himself, [honored] by your father, your mothers, and even by your other servants.
He has taken birth for the sake of protecting the world, of this there is no doubt;
by merely chanting his name, the fear of worldly existence is destroyed.
If even the mere recitation of the story of Rāma, O Lord, is itself the personified Brahman, what need is there to speak of fear and the like?
"There shall be no fear of calamities there, nor untimely death for men.
When this had been said, Rāma Bhārgava spoke to Rāma, who stood before him.
"Abandon your identity as Rāma, or else engage in combat with me.
When this was said, Rāghava spoke to that descendant of Bhṛgu who stood upon the path.
"How can I abandon the name of Rāma? I shall fight with you; stand firm!
Having spoken thus to him and standing apart, the lotus-eyed Rāma [prepared for battle].
Then the hero made the twang of his bowstring right before that other hero;
thereupon, the Vaiṣṇava [power] indeed emerged from the body of Paraśurāma.
While all beings were looking on, his splendor entered the mouth of Rāma;
seeing him, Bhārgava Rāma spoke with a serene countenance.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! You are Rāma; there is no doubt about this.
You are indeed Viṣṇu who has been born; today you have been recognized by me, O Lord."
Go, O hero, as you desire, and truly perform the work of the gods;
having brought about the destruction of the wicked, protect those who are righteous.
"O Rāma, go wherever you wish; I shall go to the forest of asceticism.
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Bhṛgu was honored by them with the devotion due to a sage.
Then, with his mind firmly resolved upon asceticism, he went to Mount Mahendra;
thereupon those people and Daśaratha were filled with joy.
Having reached the city of Ayodhyā together with Rāma,
the king made that city possess divine splendor and auspicious on every side.
Then, having risen up with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
the citizens approached Rāma as he entered, now married and undefeated in battle.
Beholding him, they were filled with joy and entered the city by that very path;
seeing them arrived nearby, the sage approached Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having entrusted them to his father Daśaratha and especially to his mothers, that best of sages Viśvāmitra, honored by the king,
set his mind upon departing immediately.
Having entrusted Rāma— along with his younger brother and his wife, who was his father’s sole beloved— to the presence of his father,
that great-minded sage, laughing, went back again and again to his own Siddhāśrama after making him hear [the instructions] repeatedly.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Rāma," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 47)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having taken a wife, the lotus-eyed Rāma of great splendor brought immense joy to his father and to the people.
O King, while Rāma, the lord of the Raghus, remained in Ayodhyā endowed with all enjoyments,
the people rejoiced in Ayodhyā out of affection for Rāma.
Accompanied by his brother Śatrughna, Bharata went to his maternal uncle;
then King Daśaratha, having observed that most auspicious sight, [was filled with joy].
Having consecrated his son Rāma— a youth, strong, capable, a poet, and a devotee of Viṣṇu— for the sake of attaining royal success, he entrusted the burden of the kingdom to him.
"I shall exert great effort to attain that supreme state," he thought;
having reflected thus, the king, intent on that goal, issued commands in all directions.
The ministers, along with the circle of counselors, quickly assembled wise servants and the kings,
as well as all those materials for Rāma’s consecration that had been prescribed by the sages.
"Having gathered those [treasures], you servants must return quickly;
messengers and ministers, by my command, [go] to the lords of men in all directions."
"Having summoned them and gathered them together, you must return quickly to the city of Ayodhyā, which is exceedingly endowed with every splendor."
O people, everywhere perform celebrations such as dance and song,
which bring joy to the city-dwellers and are pleasing to the hearts of those living in the countryside.
"Know that tomorrow the grand consecration of Rāma will take place.
Having heard this, the ministers bowed down to the king and spoke.
"O King, your thought is excellent, as is this which you have spoken;
the consecration of Rāma will bring joy to all of us."
Thus addressed by them, Daśaratha spoke to them all again:
"Let all the necessary materials be brought quickly at my command."
And this city, which is the essence of all things on every side, must today be made resplendent; the sacrificial mandala must be prepared.
Thus addressed by the king, those swift-acting ministers did exactly so, being exhorted again and again.
Filled with joy, that king awaited an auspicious day,
as did Kauśalyā, Lakṣmaṇa, Sumitrā, and the people of the city.
Having heard of Rāma’s consecration, she attained joy and was exceedingly delighted;
she remained entirely devoted to the proper service of her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
Filled with joy, the pure Sītā, having heard the auspicious news regarding the consecration of her husband Rāma, the knower of the self, which was to take place on the following day, [was delighted].
But the maidservant named Mantharā, who was hunchbacked in form, spoke these words to her mistress Kaikeyī: Naiṣadhīyacarita 48.18.
Listen, O illustrious queen, to my auspicious words:
your husband, the great king, is intent upon your destruction.
O auspicious lady, tomorrow that Rāma, the son of Kauśalyā, shall become the sovereign;
he shall possess all the kingdom, including its wealth, vehicles, and treasury.
Today there will be nothing for Rāma;
as for Bharata, he has gone far away toward the house of his maternal uncle.
"Alas, what misery! You are ill-fated and deeply distressed by your co-wifehood.
Having heard this, Kaikeyī then spoke thus to the hunchbacked woman:
"Behold my skill, O wise Kubjā; this very day you shall see how the entire kingdom will come to belong to Bharata."
"I shall likewise make such an effort so that Rāma goes into exile in the forest.
Having said this to Mantharā, she then removed her own bodily ornaments.
Having cast off her garments and flowers, she put on coarse clothing;
wearing withered garlands, she was miserable, her limbs were soiled, and she was disfigured.
Smeared with ashes, dust, and the like, and likewise resting upon ground covered in ashes and dust where the lamp has gone out,
she was deeply distressed at the time of twilight.
Having tied a white cloth upon her forehead and deliberated on all matters of state together with her ministers, the beautiful woman went to sleep.
Having established Rāma within the mandala with auspicious, propitious,
and festive rites, together with the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, he [was seated] in the pavilion of offerings.
While the sound of trumpets resounded on all sides from those keeping the vigil for prosperity,
the air was filled with singing and dancing, and the blare of conchs and trumpets.
Daśaratha himself, having stayed there, returned once more to the door of Kaikeyī’s chamber, which was guarded by elderly men.
Desiring to speak of Rāma’s consecration to Kaikeyī, the king,
seeing Kaikeyī’s palace enveloped in darkness, then spoke.
"O beloved, why is there this darkness today in your palace?
Even the outcastes have considered Rāma’s consecration a cause for joy."
"Today the people are making the house beautifully decorated;
why have you not done so today? having said this, the lord of the earth [spoke].
Having lit the lamps in the house, the king entered his residence to find his wife Kaikeyī, whose limbs were unadorned, fallen upon the ground.
Seeing her, Daśaratha said, "This is indeed dear to her. The king, having embraced her and raised her up, said, "Listen to my supreme words."
"O beautiful one, tomorrow there will be the consecration of Rāma for him who indeed always shows you greater devotion than that shown to his own mother."
Though addressed thus by the king, that auspicious lady said nothing at all;
she only repeatedly released long, hot sighs of rage.
The king embraced her with both hands and spoke to her who was filled with anger:
"O beautiful Kaikeyī, tell me, what is the cause of your sorrow?"
"O beautiful one, whatever you desire— clothing, ornaments, jewels, and so forth—
take that from the treasury without hesitation and be happy."
"O auspicious one, tomorrow my purpose will be accomplished through Bhāṇḍāra,
when the lotus-eyed Rāma has received his consecration."
"The door of my treasury has been opened by me without a bolt;
it shall become full again while Rāma rules the kingdom."
"Honor the consecration of the high-souled Rāma.
Thus addressed by the best of kings, Kaikeyī, who was marked by evil, [replied].
The evil-minded, merciless, and wicked Kubjā, having been instructed, spoke these cruel and exceedingly harsh words to her husband, the king: NsP_48.43.
Whatever jewels and all else you possess belong to me alone; of this there is no doubt, for you granted me two boons out of affection during the great battle between the gods and the asuras.
"O King, give me now that which was given by you previously.
Thus addressed, the monarch then spoke to the inauspicious Kaikeyī.
"O auspicious one, I shall give even what has not been given to you, and to no one else;
for what was promised by me previously has already been given to you."
"O lady of beautiful limbs, be auspicious; abandon this useless anger.
Rejoice in the joy arising from Rāma’s consecration; arise and be happy."
Thus addressed by the best of kings, Kaikeyī, who delighted in strife,
spoke harsh words that were the cause of the king’s death.
"O Lord, if you will grant me the two boons previously given,
then let this Rāma, the son of Kośala, go to the forest tomorrow."
At your word, let him dwell for twelve years in the Daṇḍaka forest;
and the consecration and the kingdom shall belong to Bharata.
Having heard these terrible and unpleasant words of Kaikeyī,
the king fell unconscious upon the ground, as did she too, though she was adorned with ornaments.
Having passed the remainder of the night, at dawn Sumantrāvatī spoke thus to the messenger Sumantra: "Let Rāma be brought here."
Rāma, however, having had the Puṇyāha ceremony performed and having had the Svastyayana rites performed by the twice-born,
stood in the center of the sacrificial pavilion accompanied by the sound of conchs and trumpets.
Having approached him, the messenger then prostrated and stood before him, saying:
"O Rāma, O Rāma of mighty arms, your father commands you."
"Arise quickly and go to where your father stays!
Thus addressed by that messenger, Rāghava rose up swiftly.
Having taken leave of the twice-born, he arrived at the residence of Kaikeyī;
as Rāma was entering the house, the pitiless Kaikeyī spoke to him.
"O child, I shall tell you this, which is the wish of your father:
go, O mighty-armed one, and dwell in the forest for twelve years."
"Go this very day, O hero, with your mind resolved upon asceticism.
Nothing else should be thought of, my child; out of respect for me, carry out my word."
Having heard these words of his father, the lotus-eyed Rāma accepted the command,
saying "So be it," and paid homage to them both.
Having departed from that house and taken up his bow from the dwelling, Rāma paid homage to Kauśalyā and Sumitrā, and prepared to go.
Upon hearing that, the citizens were overwhelmed with pain and grief and were deeply distressed;
then the son of Sumitrā was filled with wrath toward Kaikeyī.
Then, seeing Lakṣmaṇa with blood-red eyes, the high-minded Rāghava,
who knows the Dharma, restrained him with words consistent with righteousness.
Then, having bowed there to the elders and the sages,
Rāma indeed ascended his chariot, whose driver was weary, for the purpose of setting forth.
Having given away his entire personal wealth, as well as various garments, to the brahmins with supreme faith, the prince—
Having addressed his three mothers-in-law and his unconscious father-in-law,
who was shedding streams of tears born of grief from his eyes, he spoke.
Sītā watched from all sides as she thus ascended the chariot;
having mounted the chariot, Rāghava departed together with Sītā.
Seeing this, the sorrowful Sumitrā spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Know Rāma to be Daśaratha; know me to be the daughter of Janaka."
"Know Ayodhyā to be a forest; go there with those two, O mine of virtues.
Thus was the righteous-souled one addressed by his mother, whose body was moist with the milk from her breasts.
Having bowed to her, Lakṣmaṇa ascended that beautiful vehicle;
as they departed, there were his brother Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, devoted to her husband.
O high-minded one, those two heroes followed behind Rāma from the city;
they followed that lotus-eyed Rāma, whose consecration had been interrupted by fate.
The family priests, ministers, and leading citizens followed him as he departed from Ayodhyā, overcome with great sorrow.
And having reached him as he was departing, they spoke these words to Rāma:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, O handsome one, you ought not to go."
"O King, turn back here; leaving us behind, where are you going?
Thus addressed by them, Rāghava, firm in his vows, spoke to them.
"Go, O ministers; go, O citizens; and go, O priests!
I must carry out my father’s command and shall indeed depart for the forest."
Having completed this twelve-year vow in the Daṇḍaka forest,
I shall come to my father’s feet to see my mothers directly.
Having spoken thus, Rāma, who is devoted to truth, then departed;
as he was going, the sorrowful people followed after him once more.
Again that descendant of Kakutstha said: "Go to this city, and [inform] my mothers, my father, and Śatrughna regarding this city."
"O highly fortunate ones, you all, remaining there, must protect the kingdom and Bharata as well; I am going to the forest for asceticism."
Then Rāghava spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Hand Sītā over to King Janaka, the lord of Mithilā."
"Remain under the authority of your father and mother; go, Lakṣmaṇa, for I am departing.
Thus addressed, the righteous Lakṣmaṇa, who was devoted to his brother, replied:
"Do not command me thus today, O Lord, O mine of compassion;
wherever you wish to go, there I shall surely go."
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, that Rāghava said to Sītā:
"O beautiful Sītā, go to my father at my command."
O slender-waisted one, stay now in the house of Sumitrā and also that of Kauśalyā until my return.
Thus addressed by Rāghava, Sītā, with palms joined in reverence, replied:
"O mighty-armed one, wherever you go to dwell in the forest..."
Having gone there, O subduer of enemies, I shall dwell together with you;
for I cannot endure separation from you, who are truthful, at any time, O King.
Therefore, I shall entreat you: show me compassion, O Lord!
Wherever you wish to go, there I shall surely follow.
Seeing the people approaching from various vehicles and the throngs of women following behind, Rāma, the knower of dharma, restrained them.
"O people and women, turn back and remain at your ease in Ayodhyā;
having gone to the Daṇḍaka forest, I shall dwell there with my mind fixed on asceticism."
"In a few years I shall return; this which has been spoken is the truth, not otherwise—along with my brother Lakṣmaṇa and my own wife Vaidehī."
Having turned back the people, Rāma went to the hermitage of Guha;
for that Guha was a devotee of Rāma and, by his very nature, a Vaiṣṇava.
With palms joined in reverence, he stood there, wondering what ought to be done;
for that [knowledge] which was previously brought to you by your Guru through great austerity—[that very thing has arrived].
That auspicious land, which removes all sins, was brought by Bhagīratha;
it is frequented by various holy men and teeming with tortoises and fish.
The Gaṅgā was rich with garlands of lofty waves and carried water clear as crystal;
that one of great splendor [crossed] that Gaṅgā by means of a boat brought by Guha.
Having crossed over to the auspicious hermitage of Bharadvāja, the Blessed One Rāma then bathed according to the prescribed rites at that sacred ford in Prayāga.
Rāghava, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā,
rested there in the hermitage of Bharadvāja, where he was honored by him.
Then, at the clear dawn, Rāghava took leave of him and proceeded slowly toward Citrakūṭa by the path described by Bharadvāja.
Having assumed the guise of an ascetic and having crossed the daughter of Jahnu, he reached that unsurpassed, holy ford filled with various trees and creepers.
When Rāma had departed with his wife, his brother, and his charioteer,
the people dwelt in Ayodhyā, which was bereft of its splendor, deeply afflicted by grief, O King.
Having heard the unpleasant words issuing from Kaikeyī’s mouth, which would cause the exile of Rāma, Daśaratha lost consciousness.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, the king cried out, "Rāma!
Rāma! Kaikeyī said to the monarch, "Consecrate Bharata."
Then Rāmacandra went to the forest accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
while King Daśaratha was consumed by grief for his son.
Then, having abandoned his body with difficulty, he went to the world of the gods;
thereafter, O subduer of enemies, [he was born] in his great city of Ayodhyā.
All the people and the women wept, afflicted by pain and grief—
Kauśalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī, who had caused such hardship.
Then, having surrounded their deceased husband there, they wept;
thereafter, the family priest Vasiṣṭha, who knew all the dharmas, arrived at that place.
Having cast the dead body of the washerman into a vat of oil,
he, remaining with his assembly of ministers, dispatched a messenger.
Having gone to where Bharata was staying together with Śatrughna, he reached that place and, having delivered the news, sent the two princes back.
Having quickly brought those two back from there, Bharata returned once more to Ayodhyā,
having observed cruel omens along the way.
But that king considered Ayodhyā to be the opposite:
a city devoid of splendor, stripped of its glory, and filled with misery and grief.
He entered Ayodhyā, which had been scorched by the fire of Kaikeyī;
seeing those two, all the people, overcome with grief, wept bitterly.
"O father Rāma! O Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa! Bharata and Śatrughna, deeply distressed, wept there again and again.
Upon hearing this from Kaikeyī at that moment, Bharata then became enraged:
"You are wicked and evil-minded, you by whom Rāma has been exiled!"
O wicked woman of meager fortune, what rash deed have you committed against Rāghava, who was with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā in the forest? You have done this instantly.
"Having sent away Rāma along with Sītā and the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,
let him make my own son the king"— this was your intention.
I am the son of a wicked woman whose fortune has perished;
devoid of luck myself and separated from my brother Rāma, I shall certainly not rule the kingdom.
There dwells Rāma, that tiger among men, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals,
who knows the Dharma, is learned in all the scriptures, possessed of wisdom, and affectionate toward his kinsmen.
And there is Sītā, the princess of Videha, who observes vows and restraints,
devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
And Lakṣmaṇa, of great heroism, virtuous, and devoted to his brother—he too shall go there, O Kaikeyī; a great evil has been committed by you.
Rāma alone is my elder brother, the best among the wise;
he alone is the king, O evil-souled one, and I am indeed always his servant.
Having spoken thus to his mother there, he wept, deeply afflicted by grief:
"Alas, O King, protector of the earth! Having abandoned me, who am so miserable..."
"O father, where have you gone today? Tell me, what shall I do here?
Where is my eldest brother, my compassionate one, who is equal to a father?"
"And where has Lakṣmaṇa gone, and Sītā, who is like a mother to me?"—
thus Bharata lamented along with his ministers.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, who knows the distinction between time and karma, said:
"Arise, arise, my child; you ought not to grieve."
"By the very power of karma and time, your father has ascended to heaven; O auspicious one, perform for him the rites of consecration and his funeral ceremonies."
Rāma, the Lord of the World, Mādhava himself, has descended to earth with a portion of his own self for the destruction of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous.
Generally, there is much that must be done by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa wherever that blessed hero is impelled by his task.
"Having performed that, the lotus-eyed Rāma will return again"—
thus was Bharata addressed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.

Having cremated his father’s body according to the prescribed rite with the fire of the *agnihotra*, he caused the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) to be performed through rituals seen in the sacred injunctions.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarayū and performed the water-libation rites for him,
the illustrious one [Rāma] remained together with Śatrughna, his mothers, and his kinsmen.
Having performed the funeral rites for him, the high-minded minister, the leader of ministers, set forth together with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
The most excellent Bharata, following Rāma’s path, set out to search for Rāma;
he encountered that great army coming along, which was hostile toward Rāma.
Then Guha, devoted to Rāma, regarding that Bharata as an enemy,
put on his armor, mounted his chariot, and, fully equipped, drew up his own army in a circular formation.
Surrounded by a great army, he blocked Bharata on the road.
"O wicked one, you now wish to kill my supreme lord Rāma, along with his brother and his wife, by sending them to the forest."
"You shall go, O evil-souled one, together with your army, O wicked-minded one!"—
thus was Bharata, the delight of kings, addressed there by Guha.
Then, with a humble soul and palms joined in reverence, he said to Rāma:
"Just as you are devoted to Rāma, so too am I full of devotion."
"O high-minded one, while I was away, this was done by Kaikeyī;
O high-minded one, I shall go today for the purpose of bringing Rāma back."
"I shall go by the path of truth; give it to me, O Guha," he said, and having thus inspired confidence, he caused the daughter of Jahnu to be ferried across.
Having bathed in the waters of the Ganges with many fleets of boats,
that Bharata reached the hermitage of Bharadvāja and approached that great sage.
Having bowed his head to him, he related exactly what had occurred;
Bharadvāja also said to him, "Such a thing was brought about by time."
You must not cause any grief now, even for the sake of Rāma;
that Rāma of true prowess is currently staying at Citrakūṭa.
Even if you go there, it is likely that he will not come;
nevertheless, go there and do whatever he tells you.
Rāma, however, remained with Sītā in that auspicious grove,
while the immensely powerful Lakṣmaṇa was intent on observing the wicked.
Thus addressed there by the wise son of Bharadvāja,
the great Bharata crossed the Yamunā and went to Citrakūṭa.
Standing there, he saw from afar the northern direction covered in dust;
having reported this to Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa then acted according to his command.
Having climbed a tree and looking with great effort,
the wise man then beheld a vast army approaching joyfully.
Seeing the army equipped with elephants, horses, and chariots, he then said to Rāma:
"O brother, O mighty-armed one, stand firm by Sītā's side."
"There is a certain powerful king [possessed] of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry"—
having heard these words of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
The heroic Rāma, whose prowess is truth, said to that hero Lakṣmaṇa:
"Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata is likely coming here to see us."
While the self-knowing Rāma was speaking thus,
Bharata, endowed with humility, drew up his army at a distance.
Then, weeping along with the Brahmins and ministers, he approached and fell at the feet of Rāma, as well as those of Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the ministers, the group of mothers, and his affectionate kinsmen and friends, having surrounded Rāma, wept, overwhelmed with grief.
Then, having learned that his father had ascended to heaven, the high-minded Rāma,
accompanied by his brother Lakṣmaṇa and by Vaidehī, [proceeded].
Having bathed in the purifying holy ford and offered a handful of water,
Rāma, overcome with grief, then paid his respects to his mother and the others.
Overcome with great sorrow, O King, he said to Bharata:
"O high-minded Bharata, go from here to Ayodhyā quickly."
"Protect this city, which is now leaderless and bereft of its king.
Thus addressed, Bharata spoke to the lotus-eyed Rāma.
"O tiger among men, without you I shall certainly not go from here;
wherever you go, there I shall go, just as Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa do."
Having heard this, he spoke again to Bharata, who stood before him:
"For men who follow their own duty, the eldest brother is like a father."
Just as the word spoken from the mouth of my father must not be transgressed by me,
so too, O best of beings, the word of mine must not be transgressed by you.
"Having gone from here away from my presence, you must protect the subjects;
this twelve-year vow of mine was proclaimed by the mouth of my father."
"After wandering in the forest, I shall return to your presence;
go, stay by my command—you ought not to cause me distress."
Thus addressed, Bharata, his eyes clouded with tears, replied:
"As you are to me, so is my father; there is no need for further deliberation on this point."
"By your command, I must perform my duty; give me your sandals.
I shall dwell in Nandigrāma for twelve years, O sandals."
Your hatred is indeed my hatred; your vow is my great vow.
O best of beings, if you do not come after twelve years have passed, [I shall act].
Then, having made this oath— "I shall consume my body like an oblation in the fire"— Bharata was indeed deeply distressed.
Having performed many circumambulations and paid homage to Rāghava,
Bharata placed the two sandals upon his head and set out slowly.
Carrying out his brother’s command, that self-controlled man remained in Nandigrāma,
practicing austerities with a restricted diet, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
Bearing a mass of matted locks upon his head and wearing the bark of trees, subsisting indeed on forest fare,
that man of blameless soul, out of devotion to Rāma’s word, bore the burden of the earth held within his heart.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Śrī Rāma," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 48)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
After Bharata had departed, the lotus-eyed Rāma,
together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Sītā, [remained there].
Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, the majestic Lord Rāma wandered through the great forest,
sometimes without Lakṣmaṇa.
In the region of the Citrakūṭa forest, resting upon the lap of Vaidehī, he slept for a moment; then that evil-minded crow appeared.
Approaching Sītā, he tore at her breast;
having torn it, that lowest of crows climbed a tree and remained there.
Then, having woken up and seeing the blood between her breasts,
the lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to Sītā, who was overwhelmed with grief.
"Tell me, O blessed lady, the cause of this redness upon your breasts.
Thus addressed, she spoke to her husband with humility.
Behold, O Indra among kings, the crow of wicked conduct upon the treetop;
it was by this very one that the deed was done while you were asleep, O high-minded one.
Rāma also saw the crow and then became enraged;
he concentrated on the *iṣīkā* weapon, which had been consecrated with the *brahmāstra*.
Aiming at a crow, he threw it; that crow, filled with fear, fled, but O King, the son of Indra entered the world of Indra.
The blazing, radiant Rāma-weapon indeed entered after him;
and the Lord of the Gods, having understood the situation, arrived accompanied by the gods.
And having expelled that wicked one who had harmed Rāghava,
he was then cast out from the world of the gods by all the deities.
Again he fell, having sought refuge with King Rāma:
"Protect me, O mighty-armed Rāma, for I have acted wrongly out of ignorance."
To him who was speaking thus, the lotus-eyed Rāma said:
"My weapon is indeed unfailing; give me one of your limbs."
"Therefore you live, O wicked one; a great injury has been committed," he said, and that man offered one of his own eyes for the sake of the weapon.
That weapon, having reduced that single eye to ashes, returned;
from that time forth, all crows have possessed but one eye.
O King, by that very reason they see with only one eye;
for that Rāghava dwelt there on Citrakūṭa for a very long time.
Accompanied by his brother and his wife, and having assumed the garb of an ascetic, he went to the Daṇḍaka forest inhabited by various sages.
With bow, joints [of the fingers], and hand, and equipped with a quiver,
the mighty one then beheld there the great sages subsisting on water.
Many who grind with stones, as well as those who use their teeth as mortars,
others who stand in the midst of five fires, and various others performing fierce austerities.
Having seen them, Rāma bowed down and was greeted by them in turn;
then, having beheld the entire forest, Rāma was Janārdana himself in visible form.
Having shown Sītā the auspicious forest in full bloom, the high-minded one set forth together with his brother and his wife.
Moving slowly, he beheld that which was endowed with various wonders—
a dark-bodied being with red eyes, resembling a massive mountain.
Rāghava, having fixed an arrow upon his bow— possessing white fangs, mighty arms, hair like evening clouds, and a voice like thunder— took aim at the offender.
The Lord, together with Lakṣmaṇa, pierced the Rākṣasa in his rage;
having slain him—who was otherwise incapable of being killed—there in a mountain cave, he whose body was of great size.
Having covered [the area] with stones, he then went to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga;
having bowed to him there and rested, his mind was delighted by that discourse.
Having approached the Tīkṣṇa hermitage, he saw that great sage;
then, proceeding by the path directed by him, he beheld Agastya.
From him, the joy of the Raghus obtained a stainless sword,
as well as a quiver with inexhaustible arrows and the bow of Viṣṇu.
Then, accompanied by his brother and wife, Rāma dwelt at Pañcavaṭī near the Godāvarī river, departing from Agastya’s hermitage.
Then Jaṭāyu, the leader of the vultures, approached the lotus-eyed Rāma; having bowed and announced his own lineage, he stood before him.
Rāma also, having seen him there and having related his own history in detail, said to him: "O high-minded one, protect Sītā."
Thus addressed, Jaṭāyu embraced Rāma with affection;
and when Rāma had departed for the interior of the forest with his brother to attend to his duty, [Jaṭāyu remained].
"I shall protect your wife; stay here, O handsome one.
Having spoken thus, the king of vultures went to his own hermitage to meet Rāma.
There, on the nearby southern side frequented by various birds,
dwelt the beautiful Rāghava together with Sītā.
Having assumed an illusory form endowed with the quality of loveliness, he spoke great tales resembling the very appearance of Manmatha.
Once, the Rākṣasī, the younger sister of Rāvaṇa, her heart overcome by passion,
approached slowly while singing a song in a beautiful voice.
Then the terrible Śūrpaṇakhā, assuming a beautiful illusory form, beheld Rāma seated in the forest together with Sītā.
Free from hesitation and with a wicked mind, she addressed Rāghava:
"O beloved, enjoy me, for I am auspicious and devoted to you as a lover here."
"He who abandons a woman who is devoted to him shall incur a great fault.
Having been addressed thus by Śūrpaṇakhā, King Rāma said to her:
"I am already married, O young girl; resort to my younger brother.
Having heard this, the Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, then spoke.
"O Rāghava, I am exceedingly skilled in the arts of love;
abandoning this Sītā who is ignorant of them, accept me, O handsome one."
Having heard these words, Rāma, who was devoted to righteousness, said to her:
"I do not go to another's wife; you go elsewhere to Lakṣmaṇa."
"He has no wife here in this forest; she will not take you [as a husband].
Having been told this, she spoke again to Rāma, the lotus-eyed one.
"Give me a leaf so that Lakṣmaṇa may become my husband.
Having spoken thus, the wise, lotus-eyed Rāma [acted].
"Cut off her nose"—this was what was to be written; there is no doubt about this.
Thus did the great king Rāma write and deliver the letter.
Having taken that letter, she departed from there filled with joy;
having gone, she gave it likewise to the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing her, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to that Rākṣasī who could assume any form at will: "The word of the descendant of Raghu must not be transgressed by me; stay away from this defilement!"
Then, seizing that sword and raising it, the wise one severed her ears and nose with it as if they were blades of sesame stalks.
Then, her nose severed, she wept, overwhelmed by intense suffering:
"Alas, O ten-faced brother, crusher of all the gods!"
"Alas, what misery! A supreme calamity has come upon me, O Kumbhakarṇa and others!
Alas, alas, what misery, O Vibhīṣaṇa, treasury of virtues and great-minded one!"
Thus, distressed and weeping, she went to Kharadūṣaṇa and Triśiras; having seen them, she reported her own humiliation.
In Janasthāna, having learned that Rāghava was there with his brother, those powerful ones, filled with rage, sent forth [the demons] against the mighty Rāma.
Fourteen thousand powerful rākṣasas marched at the front,
along with three leaders of the rākṣasas by his very side.
Long ago appointed by Rāvaṇa, those exceedingly powerful ones,
accompanied by a vast force, arrived at Janasthāna.
Seeing his sister, Rāvaṇa's own sister, with her nose cut off, weeping and her limbs smeared with tears, she was overcome with great rage.
Rāma too, having seen that force of the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasas,
stationed Lakṣmaṇa there for the protection of Sītā.
Having gone there, fourteen thousand highly powerful Rākṣasas, sent by those Rākṣasas who were arrogant in their strength, [arrived].
In an instant, he was struck down by him with arrows resembling flames of fire;
Khara was slain by him, as was the mighty Dūṣaṇa.
And Triśiras was struck down in battle by Rāma through great wrath;
having slain those wicked rākṣasas, Rāma entered his hermitage.
And Śūrpaṇakhā, weeping, came into the presence of Rāvaṇa;
then Rāvaṇa beheld his sister with her nose cut off.
The evil-minded one said to Mārīca regarding the act of abducting Sītā:
"O uncle, having gone by means of the Puṣpaka chariot, both you and I—"
Having stationed yourself there near Janasthāna by my command,
you must assume the form of a golden deer very slowly.
Go there for the sake of your mission where Sītā resides;
having seen you, O uncle, she will think you are a golden young deer.
He will feel longing for Rāma and will send him to prison;
run after him as he goes there at his word into the deep forest.
In order to bring about Lakṣmaṇa’s downfall, I must utter certain words;
thereafter, I shall ascend the Puṣpaka chariot and assume a deceptive form.
"With my mind fixed upon her, I shall bring that Sītā back;
you too shall come later at your own will, O beautiful one."
When Rāvaṇa had spoken thus, Mārīca then addressed these words:
"Go yourself, O most wicked one; I will certainly not go there."
"When Mārīca said, 'I was already distressed by this Rāma at the sage's sacrifice,' Rāvaṇa was overcome with rage."
He began to slay Mārīca, but Mārīca said to Rāvaṇa:
"O hero, death at the hands of Rāma is better than being killed by your own hand."
"I shall go wherever you wish to lead me.
Then, having ascended the Puṣpaka, he arrived at Janasthāna.
There, Mārīca, assuming the form of a golden deer, went before her to where Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was staying.
Upon seeing the golden deer-cub, the illustrious Sītā,
under the influence of her future destiny, spoke to her husband Rāma.
"O Prince, take this golden fawn and give it to me;
let it be mine for play in my home in Ayodhyā."
Thus addressed by her, Rāma stationed Lakṣmaṇa there for the sake of guarding Sītā, and he himself followed after the deer.
Pursued by Rāma, that deer ran into the forest;
then Rāma pierced that young deer with an arrow.
Crying out "O Lakṣmaṇa!", he fell upon the surface of the earth;
Mārīca, who was as large as a mountain, vanished because of that.
Hearing the sound of weeping, Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Go, O son Lakṣmaṇa, to where this sound has arisen."
"Indeed, that sound of your elder brother weeping is heard;
I perceive a great danger for the high-souled Rāma."
Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa spoke thus to that blameless woman:
"Indeed, there is no doubt regarding Rāma, nor does any fear exist for him anywhere."
To Lakṣmaṇa, who was speaking thus and was possessed by the power of his future karma, Sītā, the princess of Videha, then spoke these contrary words.
"But when Rāma is dead, you shall not go from here while seeking me.
Thus addressed, he of humble soul could not endure those unpleasant words.
Then the prince went forth to search for Rāma;
even the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, having assumed the garb of a wandering mendicant, followed him.
Having approached Sītā’s side, he spoke these words:
"The illustrious and high-minded Bharata has arrived from Ayodhyā."
Having conversed with Rāma, he remained there in that forest;
then Rāma sent me forth, saying, "Ascend this celestial chariot."
Rāma, having been entreated by Bharata, is returning to Ayodhyā;
however, O Vaidehī, he took this young deer for you to play with.
"You have suffered in this great forest for such a long time;
your husband Rāma, with his beautiful countenance, has now attained the kingdom."
"And you, Lakṣmaṇa, of humble soul, ascend this celestial chariot.
Having been addressed thus, she went accordingly and was led away by that great-souled one.
Impelled by deceit, she ascended the celestial chariot;
then that chariot departed swiftly toward the southern direction.
Then Sītā, afflicted by extreme sorrow and deeply distressed, lamented;
even as she wept in the sky within the celestial chariot, the Rākṣasa could not touch her.
Then Rāvaṇa assumed his own form, possessing a massive body;
seeing the ten-necked one of such great stature, Sītā was deeply distressed.
"Alas, Rāma! Today I have been deceived by some demon of terrible form disguised in a deceptive guise; protect me, for I am afflicted by fear! (NsP 49.90)
"O mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, protect me, who am being led away by a wicked Rākṣasa; come quickly and save me as I am overwhelmed with distress."
Hearing that great sound of Sītā as she was thus lamenting,
Jaṭāyu, the king of vultures, arrived there.
"Stay, O Rāvaṇa of evil soul! Release, release Maithilī here!
Having spoken thus, the valiant Jaṭāyu fought with him there.
Jaṭāyu struck him on the chest with his two wings;
however, Rāvaṇa, perceiving that he was striking back, thought, "He is strong."
Severely tormented by him with blows from his beak and snout,
he then rose up with speed and drew the great sword Candrahāsa.
With that [weapon], the evil-minded one struck Jaṭāyu, who was a practitioner of dharma;
Jaṭāyu fell upon the surface of the earth, his consciousness exhausted.
And he said to the ten-necked one: "O evil-souled one, I was not slain by you;
I have been killed by the power of the Candrahāsa sword, O lowest of Rākṣasas!"
"O fool, who other than you, while armed, could kill one who is unarmed?
Know, O wicked Rākṣasa, that the abduction of Sītā is your own death."
"O wicked Rāvaṇa, Rāma will slay you; of this there is no doubt.
Thus spoke Maithilī to Jaṭāyu, weeping and afflicted by pain and grief.
"O best of the twice-born, because you have met death on my account,
you shall therefore attain the world of Viṣṇu through the grace of Rāma."
"O great twice-born one, as long as you have association with Rāma,
so long shall your life-breaths remain"— having spoken thus to the best of birds, [he departed].
Then, having removed those ornaments from her body that had been offered,
she quickly bound them with a cloth, saying, "You shall go to the hand of Rāma."
Having spoken thus, Sītā, deeply distressed, threw herself upon the ground;
and having thus abducted Sītā and struck Jaṭāyu to the earth, he departed.
The wicked night-stalker traveled swiftly by means of the Puṣpaka chariot;
having placed the princess of Mithilā in the midst of the Aśoka grove, he departed.
"O hideous-faced rākṣasīs, guard her right here!
Having thus commanded them, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, went to his home.
And the inhabitants of Laṅkā said to one another in private:
"This has been established by that evil-minded one for the sake of destroying this city."
Guarded on all sides by hideous ogresses,
the sorrowful Sītā remained there, thinking only of Rāma.
Afflicted by great sorrow, she dwelt there in misery, weeping bitterly,
like the goddess Sarasvatī, who rides upon a swan, when she was at Jñānakhaṇḍa.
And Sugrīva’s four monkey servants, by chance,
quickly seized the ornaments that had been cast off by her and were tied in a cloth.
Having informed their own husband, they said to the high-souled Sugrīva:
"In the forest, a great battle took place between Jaṭāyu and Rāvaṇa."
Then Rāma, having slain Mārīca who had arrived through illusion, returned; and seeing Lakṣmaṇa, he went with him to his own hermitage.
Not seeing Sītā, that descendant of Raghu, afflicted by grief, wept aloud;
and Lakṣmaṇa, of great splendor, also wept, being deeply distressed.
Then the wise Lakṣmaṇa, having raised up and comforted Rāghava— who was lying on the ground, weeping, and afflicted in many ways— consoled him.
He then spoke these appropriate words; listen to them from me:
"O Great King, you ought not to indulge in excessive grief. (NsP 49.114)
"Arise, arise quickly, O Lord, to search for Sītā!"—
thus spoke that high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the sorrowful lord of men, having been roused by his grieving brother, went forth with him into the forest to search for Sītā.
Having purified all the forests, Rāghava [searched] all the mountains and the mountain slopes,
as well as the many hermitages of the sages, in lands thick with grass, creepers, and dense thickets.
Though searching on the riverbank, in a hollow in the ground, and in caves, the high-souled king,
not seeing his beloved and beholding Jaṭāyu slain, was then deeply afflicted with grief.

"Alas! By whom have you been struck that you have reached such a state? Are you dead or are you alive? O sir, today everything belongs to me who shares your sorrow, having come here indeed because of my separation from my wife."
As soon as this was said, the bird then spoke these sweet words with great difficulty:
"Listen, O King; I shall tell you what happened here, and what was seen and done by me immediately."

Having removed her by means of illusion and placed that Sītā upon an excellent celestial chariot, the Ten-faced one departed through the sky toward the southern direction; and Sītā’s mother, distressed, lamented.
"O Rāghava, having heard Sītā’s cry, I came with my own army to liberate her;
yet after engaging in a most intense battle with him, I was slain once more by that Rākṣasa with the power of his sword."
"Because of Vaidehī’s words, you have been seen by me while I was still alive; from here I shall go to heaven.
O Rāma, protector of the earth, do not grieve; today abandon this wicked Nairṛta along with his host."
Thus addressed by Jaṭāyus, Rāma spoke to him again out of grief:
"May it be well with you, O best of the twice-born; may you attain the supreme goal."
Then Jaṭāyu, having abandoned his own body, went to heaven by means of a beautiful celestial chariot, being attended by throngs of apsarases.
Rāma, too, having cremated that body and bathed after offering libations of water,
was traveling with his brother when, afflicted by grief, he saw a rākṣasī on the road.

Having struck down that terrifying creature with its gaping mouth, which resembled a great meteor and was vomiting forth flames while bringing living beings to their destruction, he departed in a rage.
As Rāma was proceeding through the forest, he beheld Kabandha,
who was deformed, with a belly for a face, long arms, and thick breasts.
Seeing him blocking Rāma’s path, that scorcher [of enemies] slowly burned him;
having been consumed, he, possessing a divine form, stood in the sky and addressed Rāma.
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, O high-minded one! By you, O hero, my disfigurement—which had long been present due to the sage’s curse—has been destroyed.
"I am going to the third heaven; I am blessed by your grace, there is no doubt.
O friend, please form an alliance with the son of the Sun so that I may regain Sītā."
"O best of kings, having gone to Sugrīva and informed him of your own situation, go to Mount Ṛṣyamūka."
When he had spoken thus and departed, Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa,
entered the hermitage, which was now empty of the perfected ones and the sages.
Having seen the female ascetic staying there and having conversed with her, he remained there;
she was Śabarī, whose impurities had been washed away by the foremost of sages.
Lord Rāma was honored by her with jujube fruits and other offerings;
she too, having worshipped him, indeed informed him of her own condition.
Having said, "You shall regain Sītā," she entered the fire and ascended to heaven;
and having sent her to the celestial realm, Rāghava departed for another place.
Then, accompanied by his disciplined and virtuous brother, that Lord of the World,
King Rāma, whose soul was deeply pained by separation from his beloved, departed toward the southern quarter.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Rāma," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 49)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, who was dwelling in a difficult place after having incurred enmity with Vālin, saw the son of the Wind from afar; having seen him, he spoke.
To whom do these two belong, with bows in their hands and wearing garments of bark and rags,
as they gaze upon this divine lake covered with lotuses and water lilies?
Having ascertained that these two, assuming various forms and clad in the garb of ascetics, had arrived here as messengers of Vālin, the son of the Sun [Rāma]—
Terrified with fear, he leapt from Ṛṣyamūka to another forest,
together with all the monkeys, toward the excellent hermitage of Agastya.
Standing there, Sugrīva spoke again to the son of the Wind:
"Hanumān, go quickly and ask, wearing the guise of an ascetic."
Whose two sons were they born to, and for what purpose did they remain there?
O high-minded son of Vāyu, having ascertained the truth, tell it to me.
Having been addressed thus, Hanumān went to the unsurpassed bank of the Pampā;
disguised as a mendicant, he spoke to Rāma, who was accompanied by his brother.
"Who are you that have arrived here? Tell me the truth, O high-minded one! From where have you come to this desolate, terrible forest, and what is your purpose?"
To him who was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, by his brother’s command, said:
"I shall relate it; listen to you from the beginning regarding the account of Rāma."
There was a king on earth renowned by the name Daśaratha;
his eldest son, O one of great intelligence, is my elder brother Rāma.
His consecration had begun, but it was halted by Kaikeyī;
this Rāma, my elder brother, is now carrying out his father’s command.
Having gone forth together with me and with my wife Sītā,
he entered the Daṇḍaka forest, which was crowded with various sages.
While this high-souled Rāma was dwelling in Janasthāna,
his wife Sītā was carried away from that forest by some wicked person.
"The hero Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, having come here in search of Sītā,
was seen by you"— thus was the account related.
Then, having heard those words of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Hanumān,
the son of the Wind-god, whose true nature was unmanifested, [spoke] out of confidence.
Saying "You are my master," he then comforted Rāma, the lord of the Raghus,
brought Sugrīva forward, and caused a friendship to be established between the two.
Placing the lotus-feet of Rāma, the knower of the self, upon his head,
Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, spoke these sweet words:
"From this day forward, O Indra among kings, you are my master without a doubt;
and I, along with the monkeys, am your servant, O Lord."
O Rāghava, from this day forward, your enemy shall be my enemy, and your friend shall be my true friend; your sorrow is also mine.
Having said, "Your very pleasure is my pleasure," he spoke to him again:
"My elder brother, named Vālin, possesses great strength and prowess."
O tiger among men, that wicked-souled abductor of wives, whose mind is enslaved by passion,
will slay Vālin today, were it not for you.
"O Prince, it has been stated by those who know the Purāṇas that he who shall slay seven palm trees simultaneously will indeed slay him."
Indeed, for the sake of pleasing him, the illustrious Rāma,
the joy of the Raghus, having cut down great trees with a single arrow that was only half-drawn from the bow, [felled them] simultaneously.
Having pierced the great trees, Rāma said to King Sugrīva,
"O son of the Sun, go and fight with Vālin, having made your mark."
Having been addressed thus and marked with the sign, he then engaged in battle with Vālin;
Rāma also went there and [struck] Vālin with a single arrow.
The valiant Vālī pierced him; he fell and died.
But Aṅgada, the son of Vālī, was full of modesty and remained undaunted.
Then Rāghava, having appointed him who was skilled in battle to the position of crown prince,
and Rāma likewise having given Tārā to the son of the Sun;
The righteous and lotus-eyed Rāma said to Sugrīva:
"Seek your own kingdom among the monkeys, and return once more."
"O Lord of Monkeys, exert yourself quickly in the search for Sītā.
Thus addressed, Sugrīva spoke to Rāma, who was accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa.
O descendant of Raghu, the great rainy season has now arrived;
with Indra pouring down rain, the monkeys have no means of moving through the forest.
But once he has departed, O Indra among kings, and the stainless autumn has arrived,
Rāghava, I shall dispatch scouts— monkeys— in all directions.
Having spoken thus to Rāmacandra and having bowed down to him, that lord of monkeys entered the city of Pampā and then took his delight in the company of Tārā.
The high-minded Rāma also, according to the prescribed rites, made his dwelling with his brother on a mountain peak in the great forest, on Mount Nīlakaṇṭha.
When the rainy season had passed with great difficulty and autumn had arrived, Rāghava,
distressed by his separation from Sītā, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā.
Then, his agreement having been transgressed by Sugrīva,
the descendant of Kakutstha, who was devoted to his brother, spoke in anger to his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
"Go, Lakṣmaṇa; that wicked leader of the monkeys has not yet arrived.
When the rainy season has passed, I shall come to your side."
Having said, "I shall go there together with many monkeys," he then departed;
go quickly to that place where the leader of the monkeys resides.
Placing that wicked one at the forefront, accompanied by Hari’s army and sporting with Tārā, bring him quickly before me.
If Sugrīva does not come here despite having attained his prosperity, then you must say this: "Sugrīva is a speaker of falsehood."
"O wicked monkey, the arrow that slew Vālin still remains in my hand even now;
remembering this, act accordingly, for these are the words of Rāma, which are for your own benefit."
Having been addressed thus, Lakṣmaṇa said, "So be it," and after bowing to Rāma,
he went to the city of Pampā where Sugrīva resided;
having seen Sugrīva there, the king of monkeys, he spoke to him.
Attached to the enjoyment of Tārā, you have turned your back on Rāma’s task;
have you forgotten everything, including the oath you made before Rāma?
"O evil-minded one, saying 'I shall find Sītā and give her back wherever she may be,' you have killed Vālī, who formerly gave the kingdom to you."
O lord of monkeys, what evil-minded person would show such contempt for you, having promised [to help] King Rāma, who is bereft of his wife? NsP_50.44.
"I shall provide you assistance," he said in the presence of the gods, fire, and water:
"O King, whoever are your enemies, those very ones are my enemies as well."
"O Lord, those who are your friends are always my friends as well;
O King, surrounded by many monkeys, you must go to search for Sītā."
"Having said, 'I shall go to your side in truth,' who else would have acted otherwise—
save for you, a sinful and wicked man, in the presence of Lord Rāma?"
"O wicked monkey, having thus accomplished your own purpose by that very means,
I have now seen for myself the words of the sages, which are as true as the truth itself."
For the mind of everyone who has accomplished their purpose turns elsewhere;
like a calf that, seeing the exhaustion of the milk, abandons its mother.
Among those great-souled ones in this world who know the ways of people and possess all-encompassing knowledge,
I do not see anyone who returns a favor for what has been done.
In the scriptures, a means of expiation is seen even for those who have committed the greatest sins;
but for an ungrateful person, O wicked monkey, no expiation has been seen since ancient times.
You must not be ungrateful; remember the agreement made by you.
Come, come! Seek refuge with Kakutstha, the protector of those who seek his aid.
If you do not come, O monkey, hear these words of Rāma:
I shall lead you to the abode of death, just as I did Sugrīva and Vālī.
"That arrow by which the monkey Vālin was slain exists with us.
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, the leader of the monkeys, [replied].
Having gone forth, he paid homage to Lakṣmaṇa as prompted by the minister,
and the lord of the monkeys spoke to the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
"You ought to forgive us for the sins committed out of ignorance;
an agreement was made by me with King Rāma of immeasurable splendor."
O illustrious one,
O prince, I shall go today with all the monkeys, for even now I do not transgress that command of his.
O great hero, there is no doubt that you will go to Rāma’s side with me;
and when the descendant of Kakutstha sees me there, he will say something to me.
"I shall accept all of that upon my head and carry it out without a doubt;
for I have heroic monkeys at my disposal for the task of searching for Sītā."
"O King, I shall dispatch them in all directions," said Lakṣmaṇa when he was thus addressed by Sugrīva, the king of monkeys.
"Come, let us go from here this very moment to the side of Rāma;
O hero, let the army of both bears and monkeys be summoned."
"O high-minded one, having seen her, Rāghava has experienced great joy"—
when Lakṣmaṇa had spoken thus, the valiant Sugrīva then [replied].
He spoke by means of a sign to the crown prince Aṅgada, who was standing at his side;
he too, having gone out, then addressed the commander-in-chief of the army.
Summoned by him, tens of millions of bears and monkeys assembled—
monkeys dwelling in caves, on mountains, and in trees.
Then Sugrīva, having arrived quickly with those monkeys of mountainous stature and fearsome prowess, paid homage to Rāghava.
Lakṣmaṇa also, having paid homage to his brother Rāma, said:
"O King, now show favor toward the humble Sugrīva."
Thus addressed by him, Rāghava’s brother spoke to Sugrīva:
"Come here, O great hero Sugrīva; all is well with you."
Having heard these words of Rāma and seeing that the lord of men was pleased,
Sugrīva placed his joined palms upon his head and spoke to Rāma:
Then, O King, my merit shall be realized, O Lord, once Queen Sītā has been found and given back by me; it shall not be otherwise.
When these words had been spoken by him, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
bowed to Rāma and spoke to Sugrīva, the leader of the monkeys.
Listen to my words, Sugrīva: this king is deeply distressed;
because of his separation from Sītā, he never eats fruits or other food.
Because of his suffering, this Lakṣmaṇa is constantly and deeply distressed;
having heard the condition of these two here, Bharata, their younger brother, [will likewise suffer].
A person becomes sorrowful through that sorrow and undergoes further suffering because of it;
therefore, O King, undertake the search for Sītā.
When these words had been spoken there by the wise son of Vāyu,
the exceedingly radiant Jāmbavān bowed to Rāma and stood before him.

"O bulls among monkeys, if we depart without having seen Vaidehī,

He then desired to search for Sītā, who had been carried off by Rāvaṇa,

"Go on a path free from misfortune, frequented by meritorious winds,
so that you may return again," he was thus honored by the monkeys.
Then the heroic one, with his eyes fixed upward, beholding the path from afar, immediately entered into his own inherent vigor.
Having conceived himself as being completely full, the one of great strength leapt from the mountain peak, pressing the mountain against the sky.
As the wise son of Vāyu proceeded along his father’s path,
intent on Rāma’s mission, he was urged forward by the ocean.

Go, O wicked Rāvaṇa, you who are devoted to the wives of others;

Having been told "So be it" and rebuked, the Rākṣasa said to the Rākṣasīs:

Aṅgada. // NsP_52.31 //
"O King,

"O Rākṣasas, go to my city! Bind those two mortals with nooses—you who possess the prowess that destroys enemies—and bring Dhūmrākṣa and Dhūmrapāna here.
Furthermore, let my brother Kumbhakarṇa be awakened by the sounding of musical instruments."
And the mighty Rākṣasas, commanded by Rāvaṇa,
took his order upon their heads and fought with the monkeys.
Fighting to the best of their ability, ten million rākṣasas met their destruction at the hands of the monkeys; then he gave further orders to others.
At the eastern gate was Daśagrīva, along with Rākṣasas of immeasurable power;
they too, while fighting with the monkeys led by Nīla and others, met their destruction.
Then, all those who had been dispatched by Rāvaṇa to the southern quarter were torn apart by the foremost of the monkeys and went to Yama.
In the west, by the exceedingly proud monkeys led by Aṅgada,
Rākṣasas as large as mountains were sent to the abode of Yama.
In the northern quarter, however, those cruel rākṣasas who had been stationed by Rāvaṇa fell,
slain by the monkeys led by Mainda and others.
Then the hosts of monkeys, leaping over the high rampart of Laṅkā,
[attacked] the Rākṣasas stationed within who were arrogant in their strength.
Having slain them, the monkeys quickly returned once more to their own army;
thus, when all the rākṣasas had been killed, the Ten-faced One [Rāvaṇa]...
While those women were weeping, that hero, overwhelmed with rage and surrounded by many rākṣasas, emerged at the western gate.
And where was that powerful one, bow in hand, shouting "O Rāma!",
standing upon his chariot and discharging a rain of arrows upon the monkeys?
Then the monkeys, their limbs mangled by those arrows, fled;
and seeing those monkeys in flight, Rāghava then—
"But why have the monkeys been broken? What fear has come upon them?
Hearing these words of Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa spoke this reply:
Listen, O mighty-armed king, Rāvaṇa has now emerged;
struck by his arrows, O high-minded one, the monkeys are fleeing.
Thus addressed by him, Rāghava, enraged, raised his bow and filled the sky and the quarters with the twang of the string and the slapping of the palm.
Then the lotus-eyed Rāma fought with Rāvaṇa,
as did Sugrīva, Jāmbavat, Hanumān, and likewise Aṅgada.
Vibhīṣaṇa, the monkeys, and the heroic Lakṣmaṇa also approached Rāvaṇa’s army as it was raining down all kinds of arrows.
Those of great strength slaughtered the forces joined with elephants, horses, and chariots;
there too, the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa became terrifying.
Then the mighty Rāghava, having cut down with his own weapons all those missiles and arms indeed discharged by Rāvaṇa, [proceeded].
Having slain the charioteer with one arrow and the great horses with ten,
Rāghava severed Rāvaṇa’s bow with a single broad-headed shaft.
Having severed his crown with fifteen [arrows],
the valiant one then pierced that head again with ten gold-feathered shafts.
Then the ten-faced one, Devamardaka, being deeply pained by Rāma’s arrows,
was led by his ministers into his own city.
Awakened by the sounds of trumpets and the slow, rhythmic tread of elephant herds,
Kumbhakarṇa once again leaped over the wall and went forth.
With a towering and stout body, terrifying eyes, and great strength,
that wicked one roamed about, driven by hunger, devouring the monkeys.
Seeing him, Sugrīva sprang up and struck him in the chest with a spear;
then, with his two hands, he cut off both ears and with his mouth, the nose.
Having caused the lords of the Rākṣasas, who were fighting from all sides and superior in battle,
to be slain by the leaders of the monkeys on every side, Rāghava—
Having personally defeated Indrajit, he arrived with Garuḍa and severed the neck of Kumbhakarṇa with sharp arrows.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and surrounded by the monkeys, Rāma shone resplendent once Indrajit had gone in vain and Kumbhakarṇa had been struck down.
Then the Lord of Laṅkā, enraged, [summoned] his son Triśiras,
as well as Atikāya, Mahākāya, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka.
"Having killed [the others], you must slay those two men in battle, my sons!
Having thus commanded his sons, the Ten-necked One spoke again as follows.
"O Mahodara and Mahāpārśva, together with these mighty ones,
go forth prepared to slay the enemies in this battle."
Seeing those enemies who had arrived and were fighting in the battle,
Lakṣmaṇa dispatched them to the abode of Yama with six sharp arrows.
The host of monkeys and the remaining night-rangers were [protected],
while the Rākṣasa Kumbha, who was arrogant in his strength, was slain by Sugrīva.
Nikumbha, the thorn of the gods, was slain by the son of Vāyu;
and Vibhīṣaṇa struck down Virūpākṣa with his mace as he was fighting.
Bhīma and Mainda slew Śvapati, the lord of monkeys;
then Aṅgada and Jāmbavat killed the other night-stalkers.
O King, while fighting in the battle, Rāma then struck down Mahācala, who was raining down showers of arrows, in that great conflict.
Having once again mounted the chariot obtained through mantras,
Indrajit indeed rained down a shower of arrows upon the monkeys and the bears.
Then, seeing that entire army and all the Raghava-host rendered motionless and pierced by those arrows during the night, Jāmbavat was urged into action.
Having brought the medicinal herb by means of his vigor, Hanumān, the son of the Wind,
raised up Rāma— who was lying upon the ground— as well as the hosts of monkeys.
Together with those very monkeys, who held blazing torches in their hands, he caused that Laṅkā— along with its elephants, horses, chariots, and rākṣasas— to be consumed by fire at night.
Like a rain cloud pouring down masses of arrows in all directions,
that Rāghava caused Meghanāda to be slain by my brother.
Then, when the rākṣasas—along with their sons, friends, and kinsmen—had been slain, and when obstacles to the rites of fire-oblations, recitations, and so forth had been removed; ||| NsP_52.77 |||
Then the enraged Daśagrīva emerged at the gate of Laṅkā and cried out,
"Where is that Rāma, that mere human in the guise of an ascetic?"
Standing in his variegated chariot with swift and well-trained horses, the lord of the rākṣasas cried out loudly, "The warrior is Kapibali!"
Then, seeing him approaching, Rāma said to the Ten-faced one:
"I am Rāma here, O evil-souled one; come toward me, Rāvaṇa!"
When this was said, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa spoke to the lotus-eyed Rāma:
"I shall fight with this rākṣasa; you remain here."
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having advanced, obstructed him with showers of arrows;
