meanwhile, in the battle, [the opponent] assailed Lakṣmaṇa with weapons and missiles discharged from his twenty arms.
That Ten-necked one besieged them; a great battle ensued.
The gods, stationed in their celestial chariots in the sky, stood watching that great conflict.
Then, having cut down Rāvaṇa’s weapons with his own sharp arrows,
Lakṣmaṇa slew his charioteer and also his horses with broad-headed shafts.
Having severed Rāvaṇa’s bow and his banner with sharpened arrows,
the one of great prowess, the slayer of enemy heroes, pierced his chest.
Then, having quickly leaped down from his chariot, the enraged leader of the Rākṣasas seized a spear that resounded with the ringing of its bells.
That spear, with a tongue blazing like a flame of fire and a luster resembling a great meteor,
was hurled by a firm grip into the chest of Lakṣmaṇa.
Then, having split open [the earth] and entered within, the gods became terrified in the sky upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa fallen, while the lords of the monkeys were weeping.
Distressed, Rāghava quickly approached his side and said:
"Where has the heroic Hanumān, my friend and son of the Wind, gone?"
"If my brother, having fallen to the earth, should somehow still live," O King, when this was said, the heroic Hanumān, renowned for his prowess, [replied].
Joining his palms in reverence, he spoke this: "O sir, grant me your permission; I am standing here.
Rāma said, "O great hero, [give me] my *viśalyakaraṇī* herb."
"O friend of great strength, quickly make my younger brother free from pain.
Then, springing up with speed, the monkey went to Mount Drona.
And having bound him, she quickly brought Lakṣmaṇa back, making him free from disease in an instant,
while the Lord of the gods and Rāghava looked on.
Then the lotus-eyed Rāma, the Lord of the World, became enraged at the remaining force of Rāvaṇa, consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and rākṣasas.
Having slain him in an instant with his arrows, Rāma,
surrounded by the monkeys, stood there after having mangled that body with his sharp shafts.
Having regained consciousness slowly after being motionless for eight days,
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa rose up in anger and let out a lion’s roar.
At that very moment, the host of deities in the sky was terrified by the hearing of that roar;
meanwhile, the great sage reached Rāma.
But Agastya, having conceived an enmity toward Rāvaṇa,
gave him the mantra named Ādityahṛdaya, which bestows victory and grants triumph.
Rāma, too, having recited that mantra spoken by Agastya which bestows victory,
took up the incomparable, well-stringed, and firm Vaiṣṇava bow given by him.
Having worshipped it and taken it up, the one of great strength strung it and [pierced him] with sharp,
gold-feathered arrows that tear through the vital organs.
The powerful Lord of the Raghus fought with the lord of the Rākṣasas;
O high-minded one, as those two of terrible power were fighting there, ||| NsP_52.101 |||
O best of kings, the fire released by each other and intensified in the sky rose up in the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
While the battle was raging, the heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha,
whose prowess is beyond description, then fought on foot.
The Lord of the Gods dispatched Mātali along with a divine chariot, renowned throughout the world and drawn by ten thousand celestial horses.
Having ascended that chariot while being honored by the foremost of the gods,
the majestic Rāmacandra followed the instructions given by his maternal uncle.
The powerful Lord Rāma slew his cruel enemy, the wicked Daśānana, who had received a boon from Brahmā, by means of the Brahmāstra weapon.
When Rāvaṇa, the enemy along with his hosts, had been slain there by Rāma,
all the deities, Indra and the others, then spoke to one another:
Since Hari, having become Rāma, slew our enemy Rāvaṇa in battle— even though he was incapable of being killed by others— on the field of combat.
"Therefore, let us descend and worship him who is named Rāma, the infinite and unconquered," having said this, those dwellers of heaven [prepared to descend].
Descending to the surface of the earth from various glorious celestial chariots,
Rudra, Indra, Vasu, Candra, and the others [approached] the eternal Creator.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites Viṣṇu— the victorious one, the embodiment of the universe, the imperishable Rāma together with his younger brothers— they stood surrounding him.
"O gods, behold this Rāma; here stands Lakṣmaṇa;
here is Sugrīva, the son of the Sun; and here is seated the son of the Wind."
"All these, beginning with Aṅgada," said those inhabitants of heaven,
whose fragrance perfumed the guardians of the quarters and who followed in the tracks of swarms of bees.
A rain of flowers, released by the hands of celestial women, fell, adorning the heads of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Brahmā, having arrived by means of his swan-vehicle,
praised Rāma with a hymn called Amogha and spoke to him.
Brahmā said:
You are Viṣṇu, the origin of all beings, the infinite Lord whose vision is knowledge;
you alone are the eternal Brahman, known as the supreme in the Vedānta.
Since Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out, has been slain by you today,
this deed accomplished by you has brought tears to all the worlds and the gods.
When this had been said by the Lotus-born One, Śaṅkara was filled with joy;
having bowed to Rāma, he then [bowed] to that King Daśaratha.
Having shown himself and proclaiming that Sītā was pure, the god departed;
thereafter, he took the auspicious Puṣpaka chariot, which had been acquired through the power of his arms.
Having placed that purified Sītā upon it, the son of the Wind-god was thus commanded;
then he [placed] the goddess Jānakī, free from sorrow and adorned with ornaments.
Having installed Mahādeva in the middle of the bridge, that Rāghava, the brother of great strength, together with the lords of monkeys, paid his respects.
By the grace of Śambhu, he obtained supreme devotion toward Śiva;
he became known as Rāmeśvara, the Great God, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
By the mere sight of him, one is cleansed of all murder;
this Rāma has fulfilled his vow, though his mind remains fixed on Bharata.
Then, having gone to the divine city of Ayodhyā, the majestic Rāma— having been propitiated by Bharata and consecrated there by the best of the twice-born, headed by Vasiṣṭha—
ruled the kingdom righteously for a long time.
Having performed his own duties, such as sacrifices and other rites, Rāma ascended to heaven along with the citizens.
O King, I have related to you in brief the life of the high-souled Rāma upon this earth;
to those who read or hear this with great devotion, Rāma, the Lord of the Universe, grants his own abode.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Rāma," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 52)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe in brief the two auspicious manifestations of the third Rāma and of Kṛṣṇa.
O best of kings, in ancient times the Earth, oppressed by the burden of the Asuras,
spoke to the lotus-seated Brahmā as he sat amidst the gods.
O Lotus-born One, those Daityas and Dānavas who were slain by Viṣṇu in the war between the gods and the asuras have all been born as Kṣatriyas, such as Kaṃsa and others.
O Four-faced One, I am sinking under the weight of this immense burden;
O God, act in such a way that this burden may be removed from me.
Thus addressed by her, Brahmā then went together with the gods to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk to Viṣṇu, who was awakened by devotion.
Having gone there together with the gods, the Creator of the World [worshipped] Janārdana,
the Great God in the form of Narasiṃha, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order.
Having worshipped Govinda with devotion and Keśava even with the flower of speech, O King of kings, he honored him; and by that, the Lord of the World was pleased.
The King said:
"O Brahmin, how did even Brahmā worship Hari with the flower of speech?
Tell me that, O best of sages, the supreme hymn spoken by Brahmā."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim this hymn uttered from the mouth of Brahmā;
it is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu.
Having propitiated that Lord of the World with uplifted arms and becoming single-minded in thought, O King, the Grandfather (Brahmā) uttered this hymn of praise.
Brahmā said:
I bow to the God who is the Lord of Men, the Infallible Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Teacher of the World;
the beginningless, unmanifest, inconceivable, and imperishable Hari, the Supreme Person known through the Vedāntas.

I bow to Mādhava, whose nature is bliss, who is supreme, higher than the highest, whose essence is consciousness, the ultimate goal for those possessed of knowledge, the soul of all, omnipresent and of a single form— the very nature of that which is to be meditated upon.

I bow to Keśava, who is dear to his devotees, exceedingly beautiful, stainless, the lord of the gods, praised by the wise, four-armed, lotus-colored, the sovereign, and who holds a discus in his hand.

I perpetually bow to Viṣṇu, who wears a crown, whose hands hold a mace, a sword, a conch, and a lotus; the Lord of Śrī, the ever-auspicious one, who bears the Śārṅga bow, possesses the radiance of the sun, and has his chest adorned with a necklace and yellow garments.

I bow to that Janārdana, the Lord of Beings, whose cheeks are adorned with deeply red earrings, who illuminates all directions with his own luster, whose Vedic hymns are sung by Gandharvas and Siddhas, and who resounds with the sound of the Rigveda.
Having slain the Asuras age after age, Hari, established upon the earth, protects the gods who abide in their own dharma;
I bow down to that Keśava, Vāsudeva, who effects the creation and the destruction of the world.

I am forever prostrate before Him, who is to be known through the Vedas, who, having assumed the form of a fish, retrieved the Vedas from the subterranean realm and bestowed them upon me, and who, having slain both Madhu and Kaiṭabha in battle.

I bow to that primordial Viṣṇu, the Sun, by whom in ancient times the great mountain was held up when it was cast into the midst of the Ocean of Milk by the gods and asuras; he who assumed the form of a tortoise for the benefit of the world.
I bow to that Boar, the embodiment of the Vedas, the eternal Lord who, assuming the form of a boar, slew the exceedingly arrogant Hiraṇyākṣa and lifted up this entire earth.
I bow to that Narasimha Purusha, the eternal Hari, who for the supreme benefit of the world assumed his own form as a Man-Lion and slew the son of Diti with his sharp claws.
I bow to that primordial Vāmana, the Lord Janārdana, who, having assumed a dwarf form, bound Bali with three powerful strides and, having traversed the three worlds, bestowed them upon Purandara.

I bow forever to that son of Jamadagni, who out of wrath slew Kārtavīrya and even the sons of kings twenty-one times; to him, the destroyer of the earth’s burden, I am ever devoted as Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person.
I perpetually bow down to that eternal Lord Rāma, who built a great bridge across the ocean and, having reached Laṅkā, slew the ten-faced Rāvaṇa along with his hosts by means of his servants.

O Lord Viṣṇu, just as you have brought benefit to the gods through the forms of the Boar and the Man-Lion, so today perform the removal of the earth's burden; be gracious, O Blessed One, salutations to you!
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus praised by the lotus-born Brahmā, the Blessed Lord Śrīdhara, the Master of the World,
manifested himself, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
And Hṛṣīkeśa said to the lotus-born one and to the gods:
"O Grandfather, O denizens of heaven, I am well-pleased by this hymn of praise."
O gods, for the destruction of the sins of those devoted men who recite this,
I, Hari— though difficult even for the gods to attain— have become manifest.
"I have indeed been entreated by the gods, including Indra and Rudra, as well as by the Earth;
O Lotus-born One, speak now so that, having heard it, I may do for you what you desire."
When Viṣṇu had spoken thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said:
"This earth is being severely oppressed by the heavy burden of the Daityas."
O Puruṣottama, I have come here together with the gods for no other reason than to have this [city] made small by you.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: "Go yourselves, O immortals;
all of you, being free from affliction, depart, but let the Lotus-born one go [alone]."
Having descended to the surface of the earth from Vasudeva and Devakī, my two powers,
Śita and Kṛṣṇa, will cause Kaṃsa and the others to be slain.
Having heard these words of Hari and having bowed to Hari, the gods departed;
and when the dwellers of heaven had gone, Janārdana, the god of gods, remained.
O King, for the sake of protecting the virtuous and for the subjugation of the wicked,
you dispatched your two own powers, the white and the black.
Of those two, Sītā was born to Rohiṇī from Vasudeva;
likewise, Kṛṣṇā was born to Devakī from Vasudeva.
Now hear from me the deeds of those two: the virtuous son of Rohiṇī, the great one who took the name Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa, the delight of Devakī.
O King, in Gokula during his childhood, the Rākṣasī Śakunī was slain by Rāma at night, and likewise Pūtanā was slain by Kṛṣṇa.
Dhenuka, along with his followers, was slain by Rāma in the Tāla forest;
likewise, Śakaṭa and the two Arjuna trees were destroyed by Kṛṣṇa.
The Daitya Pralamba was brought to his destruction by Rāma with a single blow of His fist;
Kāliya, the venomous serpent, was subdued in the waters of the Kālindī.
And while Indra was raining down, Govardhana was held up by Kṛṣṇa as he protected Gokula; and Ariṣṭa was struck down by him.
And the great asura Keśin, that wicked horse, was brought to his end;
and those two were led to Mathurā by the high-souled Akrūra.
And as he was submerged, O high-minded one, Akrūra beheld within that water the respective forms of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, which bestow divine power.
O prince, having understood and witnessed the incomparable nature of these two, the Yādavas and Akrūra were indeed filled with joy in their hearts.
Then Kṛṣṇa struck Kaṃsa’s washerman as he was speaking such harsh words, and Rāma gave that garment to a brāhmaṇa.
When they had been worshipped with devotion by the garland-maker with beautiful flowers,
Rāma and Keśava then granted him boons that are difficult to obtain.
As they were walking along the royal road, they were then honored by the hunchback;
she removed that crookedness and that misshapen bow.
The powerful Kṛṣṇa pulled [the elephant] away from Kaṃsa and broke it at that very moment;
then Rāma slew many wicked guards there.
Having killed the elephant named Kuvalaya, both Rāma and Janārdana—
Having entered the arena, the two sons of Vasudeva, with hands like elephant tusks and smeared with ichor, [stood there];
then in the fight, the imperishable-souled Rāma slew the wrestler Muṣṭika, who was like a mountain.

Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the assembly of people, having fought for a long time with Cāṇūra— the world-renowned wrestler of Kaṃsa, renowned for his strength and prowess— then slew that Daitya wrestler in the midst of the crowd.

Furthermore, that heroic Rāma, having risen for the sake of battle, struck with a fist-blow Puṣkaraka, who was a friend of the deceased wrestlers Mallaka and Muṣṭika, as he stood waiting for the encounter.
Kṛṣṇa, having again struck down all of them, seized Kaṃsa and cast him to the ground;
then Kṛṣṇa himself threw himself upon his body, and having killed him, he likewise dragged him along the earth.

But when Kaṃsa had been slain by Hari, his brother, known as Sunābha—who was endowed with great strength and valor—rose up in extreme fury; yet even he was sent to the abode of Yama by Rāma in an instant.
Having paid homage to their parents, the two of them— highly delighted and well-surrounded by all the people and the Yadus—
installed Ugrasena as the king of the Yadus and bestowed upon him the Sudharmā assembly hall, which belonged to the great Indra.
Having obtained the knowledge of weapons from Sāndīpani, even though Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were both omniscient,
he slew Pañcajana for the sake of his teacher and, having conquered Yama, restored the son to his guru.
Having utterly destroyed the entire force of the Lord of Magadha that had assembled in great numbers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
by means of floods of divine weapons, rendered both these cities on the shore of the ocean as secure as the immortals [in heaven].
Having then provided lodging for the people there, slain the jackal, and burned the great Yavana, the Lord of immutable soul bestowed a boon upon the king and departed.
Then Rāma, having completely pacified all hostilities and returned once more to Gokula with Nanda, was greeted with kind words by the cowherds in Vṛndāvana; there, Rāma drew the Yamunā with his plow.
Having obtained Revatī as his wife, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) took his pleasure with her in Dvāravatī;
and having likewise obtained Rukmiṇī through the Kṣatriya rite, the ancient Puruṣa Kṛṣṇa also took his pleasure.
In a gambling match, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) uprooted the teeth of the King of Kaliṅga and slew Rukmin, who was joined by falsehood, with his very foot.
Kṛṣṇa, having slain many Daityas of Prāgjyotiṣa such as Hayagrīva and others,
and having also killed Naraka, seized a vast amount of wealth.
Having given the earrings to Aditi and having defeated Indra along with the gods,
he took the Pārijāta tree and then [departed for] the city of Dvāravatī.
The mighty and heroic Rāma alone,
having instilled fear in the Kurus, liberated Sāmba who had been held captive by them.
The forest of Bāṇa’s arms was severed by the wise Kṛṣṇa in battle;
that army, ten million times greater, was brought to destruction in an instant by Rāma.
A great monkey who had wronged the gods was slain by Rāma,
who was acting as an ally to Arjuna, the enemy of Kaṃsa.
O King, by the slaughter of all those beings, the burden of the earth was removed;
likewise, Rāma undertook a pilgrimage for the sake of the world.
I am not able to enumerate those who were slain by Rāma;
thus, O King, having thus carried out the slaughter of the wicked, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa—
Having removed the burden of the earth, they departed for heaven by their own will.
Thus have these two divine incarnations of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa been described by me to you in brief; now hear from me concerning the Kalkin.
Thus, O King, those two powers of the infinite Hari, white and black in form and endowed with great strength,
having removed the burden of the earth, returned once again to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Kṛṣṇa," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. NarP 53.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, O King, listen with a concentrated mind as I proclaim the meritorious manifestation of Hari known as Kalki, which destroys all sins.
O Indra among kings, when the Dharma has perished from the surface of the earth due to the Kali age,
and when sin has increased and people are tormented by disease;
Requested by the gods with hymns of praise in the Ocean of Milk, Viṣṇu [appeared] in the great village named Sāṃbhala, which was crowded with various people.
A king named Kalkī, the son of Viṣṇuyaśas, will appear;
mounting a horse and wielding a sword, he will exterminate the mlecchas.
Having slain all the Mlecchas, who were the cause of the earth's destruction, that Kalki, an incarnation of Puruṣottama,
performed the sacrifice known as Bahukāñcana, established the Dharma, and ascended to heaven.
O King, I have recounted to you these ten incarnations of Hari, the destroyer of sins.
That devotee of Narasiṃha who always hears this constantly goes to Viṣṇu.
The King said:
"O best of Brahmins, through your grace, I have heard the accounts of the manifestations of the divine Nārāyaṇa, which remove the sins of those who hear them."
O best among all knowers, O most excellent of sages, please explain Kali in detail— [the nature of] the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
What will be their food and what will be their conduct in the Kali age?
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, together with Bharadvāja.
All phenomena perish when Kṛṣṇa has attained his dark state;
therefore, the Kali age is most terrible, the accomplisher of every sin.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras will turn their backs on dharma and become averse to the twice-born and the gods.
All will be devoted to the dharma of hypocrisy, intent on deceitful conduct,
absorbed in envy, and defiled by vain egoism.
All men who pride themselves on being learned diminish the truth;
indeed, everyone says, "I alone am superior."
All will be greedy for unrighteousness and likewise revilers of others;
therefore, in the Kali age, all will become short-lived.
O twice-born ones, because the lifespan of humans is short, there is no acquisition of knowledge;
and due to the absence of the acquisition of knowledge, unrighteousness prevails once again.
Likewise, the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas become intermixed with one another;
deluded and devoted to lust and anger, they are afflicted by the torment of futile distress.
Bound by enmity and desiring to kill one another,
the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will all turn their backs on the Dharma.
Devoid of austerity and truth, they will become equal to Śūdras;
the high-born will fall to a low state, and likewise, the low-born will attain a high state.
Kings are devoted to material wealth and likewise intent on greed;
though clothed in the cloak of dharma, they are destroyers of dharma.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is filled with all manner of unrighteousness,
whoever possesses horses, chariots, and elephants shall become king.
Sons will employ their fathers in menial tasks, and daughters-in-law will employ their mothers-in-law;
deceiving their husbands and sons, women will go elsewhere.
There will be few men and many women, an abundance of dogs, and a decline in cattle; wealth will be considered praiseworthy while the conduct of the virtuous is unhonored;
the rain-cloud will pour in fragments, and the roads will be infested with thieves; and everyone will know everything without having served their elders.
There will be no one called "unpoetic," for the twice-born will become drinkers of wine and expounders of the Veda; and the twice-born will become servants of the Śūdras.
Sons hate their father, disciples hate their teacher,
and wives hate their husbands when the terrible Kali age has arrived.
With minds overcome by greed, all the twice-born will be habituated to evil deeds and will be constantly covetous of the food of others.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, all people will be devoted to the wives of others and intent upon the wealth of others, [while] a man devoted to dharma [will remain].
All will be intent on envy and will engage in derision;
the Brahmins, revilers of the Vedas, will no longer observe their religious vows.
Reviled by those who propound causal theories, they will neither sacrifice nor offer oblations;
instead, the twice-born will perform rites such as ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña) merely for the sake of hypocrisy.
People do not give gifts solely for the sake of the vessels;
likewise, they cultivate affection for cows because of the milk as their motive.
And the king’s servants bind the very twice-born for the sake of wealth;
the twice-born, in turn, sell the fruits of their charity, sacrifices, and recitations.
In the first quarter of the Kali age, the twice-born will accept gifts even from outcasts and the like,
and men will revile Lord Hari.
And at the end of the age, no one at all will remember the name of Hari;
they will be devoted to union with Śūdras and women, and greedy for the company of widows.
In the Kali age, the twice-born will be intent on consuming the food of Śūdras;
they will neither perform service for those of the twice-born nor engage in the practice of their own dharma.
At that time, base Śūdras, wearing the outward marks of renunciation, will embrace the life of wandering ascetics for the sake of pleasure; they will wear matted hair and carry ashes and staffs.
Śūdras, skilled in deceitful intellects, will proclaim the dharmas;
these and many other heretics, O best of Brahmins, [will arise].
In the Kali age, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will come to be;
the Brahmins will be devoted to singing and instrumental music, turning their backs on the discourse of the Vedas.
When the Kali age has arrived, there will be those who follow the path of the Śūdras;
possessing meager wealth, they will bear outward signs in vain, corrupted by useless egoism.
In the Kali age, the twice-born who follow the path of the righteous will always be intent on receiving gifts; they will be takers and not givers.
All men are intent on praising themselves and likewise intent on reviling others;
they are devoid of trust toward the gods, the Vedas, and the twice-born.
Those who speak words they have not heard, those who delight in hatred toward the twice-born, all those who abandon their own duty, the ungrateful, and those of broken conduct; NsP_54.40 //
In the Kali age, there will be beggars and slanderers;
they will be intent on reviling others and devoted solely to praising themselves.
People who always contemplate means of seizing the property of others take great delight in consuming [wealth] there in the houses of others.
On that very day, those who were generally intent on the worship of deities and those devoted to censure gathered together in one place after having eaten.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other castes likewise,
being excessively lustful, become intermingled with one another.
In that state of confusion, there will be no disciple and no teacher, no son and no father, and likewise no wife and no husband.
The twice-born who live by the very livelihood of a Śūdra are destined for the experience of hell;
with their gaze fixed upon the sky, they will be beset by the constant fear of drought.
At that time, all people will be distressed by the fear of hunger;
monks will take on disciples for the sake of and as a pretext for food.
Women who scratch their heads with both hands will disobey the commands of their elders and husbands; they will not be beneficial.
Whenever the twice-born neither perform sacrifices nor offer oblations,
at those times the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
When all phenomena have perished, the world falls into a state of being devoid of splendor.
Sūta said:
Thus, O best of Brahmins, the true nature of Kali has been described.
O twice-born ones, Kali does not afflict those who are solely devoted to Hari;
for austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age, while meditation alone is so in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age they say sacrifice alone is supreme, while in the Kali age, charity is the one thing;
what is accomplished in ten years in the Tretā age is achieved in a single year [in the Kali].
In the Dvāpara age, that [result] is attained in a month, and in the Kali age, it is attained in a single day and night;
for one meditates in the Kṛta age, sacrifices with rituals in the Tretā, and worships in the Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, whatever one desires to attain, one attains it by chanting the name of Keśava,
the support of the entire world and the embodiment of the supreme reality.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, one who meditates upon Viṣṇu does not suffer;
oh, how exceedingly fortunate are those who worship Keśava even once!
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is excluded from all ritual acts,
there shall be no deficiency or excess in the rites prescribed by the Vedas during the Kali age.
In this matter, the remembrance of Hari alone bestows the complete fruit:
"O Hari! O Keśava! O Govinda! O Vāsudeva! O You who pervade the universe!"
"O Janārdana, O Abode of the World, O Acyuta clad in yellow garments"—
those who constantly utter these words are indeed not afflicted by the Kali age.
Oh, how fortunate are those great-souled ones who are devoted to Hari in this Kali age, which causes fear to all beings, and who likewise delight in association with Him!
Those who are devoted to the names of Hari, those intent on the glorification of Hari, and those delighted in the worship of Hari—they have achieved their life's purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has this been declared to you: the glorification of Viṣṇu, which wards off all suffering and bestows the fruit of all merit in the Kali age.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Kali Age," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 54)
The King said:
"O Mārkaṇḍeya, how was Śukra formerly the preceptor at Bali’s sacrifice?
How was his eye pierced by Vāmana, and how did he obtain it back through praise?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having had his eyes pierced by Vāmana at many sacred fords, that descendant of Bhṛgu stayed in the waters of the Ganges and worshipped the god Vāmana.
With his arms raised, he meditated upon the eternal Narasiṃha— the Lord of Gods who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace— and praised him from within his heart.
Śukra said:
I bow to the Lord of the Universe, Vāmana, who takes the form of Viṣṇu;
the peaceful, eternal Supreme Person who destroys the pride of Bali.
I bow to Hari, the infallible Acyuta—the steadfast, the heroic, the Great God, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace; who is utterly pure and endowed with perfect knowledge.
I bow to the god who possesses all powers, who is all-pervading, the source of all beings, without beginning, undecaying, and eternal— the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
I bow to that Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the world, who is always praised by the devoted gods and asuras, and who is worshipped as Hṛṣīkeśa.
I bow to Narasiṃha, whose form yogis always contemplate within their hearts, who is the nature of light and beyond comparison.
I bow to Him whose supreme form the hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, do not know,
yet whose forms of incarnation they worship.
I bow to that Janārdana by whom all this was created in the beginning, who again protected it from the destruction of the wicked, and wherein the world is dissolved.
I bow to that stainless, divine Lord of the universe, who is constantly worshipped by his devotees and who is indeed ever dear to his devotees.
I bow to that eternal Viṣṇu, the witness of all, who, when propitiated, bestows even that which is difficult for devotees to attain.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, having been thus praised by Śukra in the past,
the Lord of the World appeared before him, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa spoke to the one-eyed Śukra:
"For what purpose was I praised on the bank of the Jāhnavī? Tell that to me."
Śukra said:
O God of gods, a great offense was previously committed by me;
now I have offered this praise for the sake of removing the fault of that transgression.
The Blessed One said:
"O Śukra, because of my offense, one of your eyes has now been lost;
nevertheless, O sage, I am well-pleased with this hymn of praise of yours."
Having spoken thus to that sage, Janārdana, the Lord of the gods, as if smiling,
touched his eye with the Pāñcajanya conch.
O best of kings, as soon as he was touched by Śaṅkha, the god of gods who wields the Śārṅga bow, his eye became stainless, just as it was before.
Having thus restored the sage’s sight, Mādhava was honored by him;
he immediately vanished from view, and Śukra also departed for his own hermitage.

Thus was this spoken by the great-souled Sage, obtained in former times through the grace of the best of gods by Śukra. O King, what more shall I tell you? Ask me again regarding the inner workings of the mind.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of the Boon upon Śukra," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 55)
The King said:
"Now I wish to hear the entire supreme procedure for the installation of this Narasiṃha, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the God of gods."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, listen as I describe, according to the scriptures, the procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the wielder of the discus— a rite that bestows merit.
O King, he who desires to perform the consecration of Viṣṇu here should first begin the purification of the ground during a fixed lunar mansion (sthira-nakṣatra).
Having dug a pit measuring one man's height, or even two arm-spans,
one should fill it with pure earth mixed with gravel and moistened with water.
Then, O King, having understood the foundation, one who is learned in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) should have a palace constructed there using stone, brick, or clay.
It should be square, with four corners on all sides along the path of the cord;
it is best if made of stone walls, and in their absence, made of bricks.
But if those are unavailable, one should construct a very beautiful earthen wall with its entrance facing east,
supported by pillars made of *jāti* wood that are firmly fixed and endowed with auspicious fruits.
Having thus caused a most beautiful residence for Hari to be constructed by skilled artisans with fallen blue lotuses and lotus petals, [he should proceed].
O best of kings, the eastern gate should have fine door-panels and be beautifully decorated;
however, one should not have the image of Hari made by those who are too old or too young.
O best of kings, those afflicted by leprosy and other such diseases, or by other chronic ailments,
[should perform it] according to the path taught by Viśvakarman, as described in the Purāṇas.
A wise person should have a divine image fashioned with well-proportioned limbs,
possessing a gentle face, beautiful ears, a fine nose, and lovely eyes.
One should not cast the gaze downward, nor upward, nor askance;
rather, one should maintain an even gaze with eyes as long as lotus petals.
The wise man should have her made with beautiful eyebrows, a lovely forehead, and auspicious, symmetrical cheeks; with lips like the bimba fruit, a well-formed chin, and a graceful neck.
On the upper arm, a wheel should be depicted on the right side like the sun,
with divine spokes attached to the hub and joined all around by a rim.
On the left side— that is, on the upper arm— one should place the auspicious conch shell, radiant as the moon,
known as Pāñcajanya, which destroys the pride of the Daityas.
She is divine, with excellent garlands placed upon her neck, marked by the three folds [of the waist],
possessing beautiful breasts, a lovely heart, a fine belly, and a symmetrical, auspicious form.
Her left hand rests upon her hip and her right hand rests upon a lotus;
she possesses divine armlets on her arms, a beautiful navel, and the folds of her skin.
O best of kings, having thus caused that image to be made— with beautiful hips, shanks, and thighs, and adorned with garments and a girdle— NsP_56.18.
O best of beings, having honored those who performed it with gifts of gold and garments,
the wise man should install the image during an auspicious time in the bright fortnight.
Having constructed an excellent sacrificial pavilion in front of the temple,
it should have four doors in the four directions and be provided with four archways.
The image, provided with sprouts of the seven grains and resounded by the sounds of conchs and drums,
should be washed by the learned with thirty-six jars of water.
Having entered that pavilion, one should then have [the image] bathed there with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), each separately, by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
Likewise, having bathed [the image] with warm water and again with cold water,
one should anoint it with turmeric, saffron, and the like, as well as with sandalwood paste.
Having adorned her again with flower garlands and covered her with garments,
and having performed the *puṇyāha* rite there, he should sprinkle her with water while reciting the *ṛg* verses.
Having bathed it with devoted Brahmins amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums,
one should cause it to dwell for seven nights or three nights in the waters of a river.
O best of kings, having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should likewise protect the deity in a pure and stainless pool or even in a pond within the water.
Then, having raised him up, the brahmins should establish and adorn Keśava as before;
thereafter, with the sounding of kettledrums and the chanting of the Vedas, [they should worship] Keśava.
Having brought [the image] into a pure pavilion constructed in the shape of a lotus,
and having bathed it once again, one should then have it adorned by the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Having fed the Brahmins according to the rules, as well as the sixteen officiating priests,
the study [of the Veda] should be performed by four, and likewise the protection by four.

O King, the wise should perform the fire-oblation in the four directions with the four [substances]; one should offer bali-offerings in the directions with [materials] mixed with flowers, unbroken rice, and cooked food.
One should cause them to be given with the words, "May Indra and the others be pleased," at each individual twilight—
namely, in the evening, at midnight, and likewise at dawn.
And when [the sun] has risen, one should then give [the offering] to the group of Mothers or to the Brahmins,
while repeatedly reciting the Puruṣasūkta alone.
O King, with a single-minded focus, staying within the temple of Viṣṇu and having fasted for a day and a night, the sacrificer, together with the twice-born brahmins, [should perform the rites].
Having entered through the door of the image at an auspicious moment, the wise one,
together with the twice-born, should offer the hymns to the deity and firmly establish it.
Having established [the deity] with the Viṣṇu-sūkta or again with the Pavamāna hymn,
the preceptor should sprinkle the Lord of the gods with water mixed with kuśa grass.
Having established the fire in front of that and having carefully strewn it around,
one should offer oblations for the birth-rite and subsequent ceremonies with the Gāyatrī and the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
The preceptor himself should perform each individual rite with four oblations of clarified butter, and he should also cause the binding [of the site] to be performed with the *astra* mantras.
One should perform the *ājyapraṇunna* rite with the verse "trātāram" in the eastern direction;
with "parodiva" in the southern; and with "niṣa" in the western.
O King, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the verse "yā te rudra," and with the two hymns beginning with "paromātrā," one should offer clarified butter oblations everywhere, O King.
Having offered the oblation, he should recite according to the rule the mantra beginning with "yad asya," followed by the Sviṣṭakṛt offering;
thereafter, he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) as is appropriate.
Then the patron, if he has the means, should give two garments, two earrings, and a ring to the preceptor, as well as gold.
A wise person should perform the ceremonial bathing with eight thousand jars, or eight hundred jars, or even with twenty-one jars.
With the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, with Vedic chants and auspicious hymns, and with vessels filled with barley and rice from which sprouts have been raised and held aloft; NsP_56.43.
Having caused the ceremonial bathing to be performed with lamp-stands, banners, parasols, chowries, and arches, according to the full extent of one's wealth;
There too, O King, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins according to one's ability;
he who thus performs the installation of the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu), O King, [attains the highest reward].
Completely liberated from all evil and adorned with every ornament,
he is surrounded by those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage, traveling in a variegated celestial chariot.
Having received great worship in the worlds of Indra and others in succession,
and having established his kinsmen in those realms, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having attained knowledge right there, one shall reach the station of Viṣṇu.
This procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu has thus been proclaimed by me to you.
It destroys all sins for those who read it and those who hear it.
O Lord of Men, when one has installed Viṣṇu as Nṛsiṃha upon the earth according to this rite,
he indeed goes to the abode of Hari, from which, once situated, he does not return again.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Consecration," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 56)
The King said:
"O twice-born one, O Narasiṃha, tell me the characteristics of those devotees by whose mere association the world of Viṣṇu is no longer distant."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Those who are devotees of Viṣṇu, possessed of great energy, always engaged in the ritual worship of Viṣṇu,
self-controlled, and endowed with righteousness— they accomplish all their goals.
Devoted to helping others and intent on serving their gurus,
they observe the conduct prescribed for their social class and stage of life, and speak very kindly to everyone.
They were knowers of the truth of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas; free from anger and free from desire;
peaceful, with gentle countenances, and eternally devoted to dharma.
They speak what is beneficial and measured at the proper time according to their ability; they are dear to guests, free from hypocrisy and deceit, and devoid of desire and anger.
Such wise men are patient and deeply learned;
their hair stands on end with joy born from the chanting of Viṣṇu’s praises.
Those who are intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu’s image and devoted to his stories—
such as these are proclaimed to be the great-souled devotees of Viṣṇu.
The King said:
"O learned one, O best of the Bhṛgus, O my teacher, you have stated that those who abide by the duties of their social class and stage of life are devotees of Keśava."
You ought to tell me the duty of the social classes and the stages of life,
by the performance of which the eternal god Narasiṃha is pleased.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you an unsurpassed ancient account,
the dialogue between the high-souled Hārīta and the sages.
Having prostrated before Hārīta, who was seated there, knowing the true essence of dharma and possessing great learning, all the sages, desiring to understand dharma, spoke to him.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, impeller of all phenomena,
please proclaim the eternal Dharma of the social classes and the stages of life.
Hārīta said:
In ancient times, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the world,
slept upon the waters upon a serpent-couch as his bed, together with Śrī.
While he was thus asleep, it is said that a divine lotus appeared at his navel;
and in its center arose Brahmā, adorned by the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
And he was told by that god: "He created the Brāhmaṇas from his mouth;
he created the Kṣatriyas from his arms, and he created the Vaiśyas from his thighs."
The Śūdras, however, were created from his feet; and for them, as well as for the others in their proper order, the Lotus-born One proclaimed the Dharmaśāstra and the established codes of conduct.
In the same manner, I shall proclaim everything; listen, O best of the twice-born!
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation.
One born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is traditionally known as a Brāhmaṇa;
I shall now declare his duty as well as the region appropriate for him.
O bull among brahmins, dwell in that region where the black-spotted deer roams by its very nature, and there perform your dharma.
And those six duties which the wise have declared for a Brāhmaṇa—
he who is constantly engaged in them alone prospers in happiness.
Studying and teaching, sacrificing for oneself and officiating at sacrifices for others, as well as giving and receiving gifts— this is said here to be the sixfold set of duties.
Teaching is proclaimed to be threefold, being the cause of dharma, wealth, and pleasure;
likewise, service is proclaimed to be threefold as well.
He should teach worthy disciples and also officiate at the sacrifices of those entitled to perform them;
and he should accept gifts according to the prescribed rule for the sake of fulfilling the duties of a householder.
One should constantly study the Veda with a concentrated mind in a pure place;
one should diligently perform obligatory, occasional, and optional rites at all times.
And the best of the twice-born, being untiring, should attend upon his guru according to the rule, and he should worship the sacred fire with the prescribed ritual in the evening and in the morning.
Having performed his bath, the householder should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite day after day;
and he should honor a guest who has arrived with devotion, according to his ability.
Having seen other Tathāgatas, one should worship them without opposition;
always devoted to one's own wife, one should avoid the wives of others.
One should be a speaker of truth, have conquered anger, and be devoted to one's own duty;
and when one's own task has arrived, one should never allow for negligence.
One should speak words that are pleasant, beneficial, and not contradictory to the next world.
Thus has the duty of a Brahmin been succinctly declared. He who acts in accordance with this very dharma goes to the state of Brahman.
Thus, O brahmins, this dharma which removes all sins of a brahmin has indeed been told by me.
Now I shall declare the dharma for kings and other classes; listen individually, O best of brahmins.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of Brāhmaṇas," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 57)
Hārīta said:
I shall now declare, in due order and according to the facts, the specific rules by which the Kṣatriyas and the other castes conduct themselves.
A Kṣatriya established in sovereignty should protect his subjects according to dharma;
he should study properly and perform sacrifices according to the prescribed rules.
Endowed with a mind fixed on righteousness, he should give gifts to the foremost of the twice-born;
he should always be devoted to his own wife and avoid the wives of others.
He was skilled in the meaning of the treatises on ethics, a knower of the true principles of peace and war,
devoted to the gods and brahmins, and likewise intent upon the ancestral rites.
A Kṣatriya should desire victory through dharma alone and should completely avoid adharma; by acting in this way, he attains the highest state.
A Vaiśya should duly engage in cattle-rearing, agriculture, and trade;
he should also practice the duty of charity according to his ability, as well as service to his teacher.
Free from greed and hypocrisy, truthful in speech, and free from malice;
devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, and avoiding the wives of others.
One should honor the Brahmins with wealth, acting with haste at the time of sacrifice;
one should constantly perform sacrifices, study, and give gifts without weariness.
The ancestral rites at the proper time, as well as the worship of Narasiṃha—
this is declared to be the duty of a Vaiśya who performs his own specific dharma.
By practicing this, he will undoubtedly become a dweller in heaven;
a Śūdra, moreover, should diligently perform service for the three castes.
One should behave especially like a servant toward Brahmins;
one should give what is unasked for and practice agriculture for the sake of a livelihood.
The monthly rite for the planets should be performed according to the principles of justice and dharma;
likewise, one should wear worn-out clothes and wipe away the remnants of food from a Brahmin.
One should take delight in one's own wife, avoiding the wives of others;
one should listen to the Purāṇas, honor the Brahmins, and worship Narasiṃha.
Likewise, one should perform salutation to the Brahmins endowed with faith,
as well as speaking the truth and abandoning passion and hatred.
Acting always in this manner through the actions of mind, speech, and body, the Śūdra,
having destroyed his sins and possessing merit, attains the station of Indra.
I have explained the various duties of the social classes (varṇa) in their proper order, as established by the best of Brahmins.
Now listen, O lords of sages, as I describe in due sequence the primary duty of the stages of life (āśrama), which is being spoken by me.
Hārīta said:
Once initiated, the young student shall always reside in the teacher’s household;
he must perform what is pleasing and beneficial to the teacher through deed, thought, and speech.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, likewise attend upon the sacred fire,
provide a water-pot for the teacher, and likewise fetch fuel.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should first engage in study according to the prescribed rule;
one who performs it while abandoning the rule shall not obtain the fruit of self-study (svādhyāya).
Whatever action one devoid of self performs while disregarding the prescribed rule,
he does not obtain its fruit, for he acts having fallen away from the injunction.
Therefore, one should observe these vows here for the sake of attaining mastery in sacred study;
moreover, one should learn the entirety of pure conduct in the presence of the guru.
A student, being vigilant and composed, should wear the deerskin, the wooden staff, the girdle, and the sacred thread.
Restraining his senses, he should go for alms in the evening and in the morning for his meal;
he should not beg from the family of his guru, nor from the families of his kinsmen or relatives.
If houses of others are not available, one should avoid each preceding [house] in turn;
having sipped water and being purified, one should always eat with the permission of the guru.
Having risen before his bed, he should offer *darbha* grass for cleaning the teeth,
as well as clothing and other items, to his guru.
After the preceptor has bathed, the diligent student should then bathe;
a perpetual celibate observing his vows must never clean his teeth.
One should avoid umbrellas, shoes, ointments, perfumes, and garlands;
and especially dancing, singing, storytelling, conversation, and sexual intercourse.
One should avoid honey, meat, the tasting of savory flavors, as well as women,
desire, anger, greed, and the slandering of men.
He should avoid looking at or touching women and causing injury to others;
he should always sleep alone and never spill his semen.
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and tend the fire, and then mutter the verse beginning with "punar mām."
A believer, established in the vow of celibacy, should daily worship at the three junctions of the day with restrained senses, according to the prescribed rule.
Having saluted the feet of his guru at the conclusion of the twilight rites,
he should perform his duties toward his mother and father with devotion as is appropriate.
When these three are satisfied, all the deities shall be satisfied;
therefore, one should abide by their teaching as a celibate student, free from envy.
Having studied four Vedas, two Vedas, or even one Veda,
and having given the teacher a sacrificial fee, he may then dwell according to his own will.
A wise man who is dispassionate should renounce the world; one who is full of passion should remain a householder.
For if a twice-born man who is still possessed by passion renounces the world, he will certainly go to hell.
A Brahmin who has maintained his celibacy and has not yet married should renounce the world when these— his tongue, genitals, stomach, and speech— are perfectly purified.
Thus, he who, remaining vigilant, should spend his time by adhering to this rule,
shall be born again as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) firm in his vows.
The celibate student who, established in this rule, should practice on earth devoted to service of the guru,
having attained even that knowledge which is difficult to obtain, indeed finds the entire fruit thereof.
Hārīta said:
Having completed the study of the Vedas, knowing the true meaning of the Śrutis and Śāstras,
and having properly received permission from his teacher, he should begin the rite of returning home (samāvartana).
Then, he should marry a maiden who does not share his name or lineage, who has brothers, who is auspicious, endowed with all excellent physical traits, and of virtuous conduct.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is talkative, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one who is deformed, nor one of fearsome appearance.

One should not [marry] a girl whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river; nor one whose name ends with "mountain" (parvata); nor one whose name is that of a bird, a serpent, or a servant; nor one whose name is terrifying.

One should marry a woman whose limbs are free from defects, who has a pleasing name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose lips, hair, and teeth are slender, while her body is soft.

The best of the twice-born should perform the marriage according to the praiseworthy Brāhma rite; indeed, he should do so in this manner, in accordance with the dharma of the social classes as appropriate.
Having risen at the time of dawn and performed his purification, the best of the twice-born,
being wise, should then perform his bath preceded by the cleansing of his teeth.
Since a man remains perpetually impure when his mouth is stale,
he should therefore consume a tooth-stick, whether dry or moist.
Khadira, kadamba, karañja, and likewise vaṭa;
apāmārga and bilva, as well as arka and udumbara.
These have been declared as recommended for the act of cleaning the teeth;
now I shall speak of the tooth-stick and its excellence.
All thorny trees are meritorious, while those that exude milky sap are glorious;
their measurement here is said to be eight finger-breadths.
Or else, O best of beings, one should clean the teeth with that [twig] of the length of a span on the first day,
the new moon, the sixth, and the ninth.
Through contact with a wooden stick, the teeth burn the family up to the seventh generation;
this applies when a tooth-stick is unavailable or when its use is prohibited on that particular day.
The purification of the mouth is prescribed by means of twelve mouthfuls of water;
having bathed and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) with mantras, one should perform the sipping again.
Having sprinkled himself with the mantra, he should cast a handful of water toward the sun in the morning; for at that time, the Rākṣasas known as Mandehas [seek to devour it].
By virtue of the boon granted by Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, they fight;
[this occurs] through the scattering of handfuls of water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra.
He slays all those Rākṣasas, the Mandehas, who are enemies of the Sun;
thereafter, Savitṛ proceeds through the sky, protected by the Brāhmaṇas.
By the highly fortunate Marīci and others, and by Sanaka and other yogis;
therefore, a twice-born man should never neglect the twilight prayers in the evening and in the morning.
He who, out of delusion, transgresses this goes certainly to hell.
Having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with mantras in the evening and having sprinkled himself, he should offer a handful of water to the Sun.
Having offered [the water], performed a circumambulation, and touched water, one becomes purified;
having commenced the morning twilight ritual while the stars are still visible, according to the prescribed rule.
One should practice the Gāyatrī until the stars become visible;
then, having reached his dwelling, the wise man himself should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having reflected upon the means for the maintenance of his circle of dependents,
the wise man should then perform some study of the scriptures for the benefit of his disciples.
The best of the twice-born should approach the Lord for the sake of protection;
having gone a distance away, he should gather kusha grass, flowers, fuel, and other such items.
One should perform the midday rite in a pure place with a concentrated mind.
I shall now describe, in brief, the procedure for bathing that destroys all sins.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite by which one is immediately liberated from sin,
the wise man, for the purpose of bathing, should take white *kuśa* grass together with sesame seeds.
Then one should go to the river Sumanā, which is pure and beautiful;
however, when that river is available, one should not bathe in waters of little depth.
Having sprinkled a clean place with water, one should place kusha grass and clay there;
having diligently washed one's own body with earth and water, [one should proceed].
Having purified his body by bathing, the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
then, having entered auspicious water, he should bow to Varuṇa, the lord of waters.
Meditating on Hari alone in his mind, he should immerse himself in the abundant water;
then, having performed the ritual bath and sipped water according to the mantra, he should proceed.
One should sprinkle the god Varuṇa with those purificatory (pāvamānī) mantras;
having sprinkled oneself with effort using water held on the tips of kuśa grass.
One should apply clay to the body three times with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and then,
recollecting the god Nārāyaṇa, one should enter the water.
Having fully immersed oneself in the water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
likewise, having bathed with kuśa grass and sesame seeds, one should [offer oblations] to the gods and ṛṣis together with the ancestors.
Having offered libations from that water and emerged with a concentrated mind,
he reached the riverbank and put on two washed, white garments.
Having put on the upper garment, one should not shake out one's hair;
nor should one wear clothing that is dyed red or gaudy, for blue is not recommended.
A wise person should avoid clothing that is stained with dirt or has been worn for ten days;
thereafter, the discerning one should wash his feet with earth and water.
One should drink water three times after looking at it, wipe the mouth twice,
sprinkle water on the feet and the head, and having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) three times, one should touch [the various parts of the body].
One should touch the nose with the thumb and the index finger;
the navel and the heart with the thumb and the little finger, and [the heart] with the palm.
Then one should touch the head with all the fingers and likewise the arm;
having sipped water according to this rule, the Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in mind.
On darbha grass, with darbha grass in hand, facing east and well-composed,
one should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the scriptures, without sloth.
Thereafter, one should perform the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) of the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas. The sacrifice of recitation is threefold; learn its divisions.
It is traditionally taught that recitation is threefold: vocal, whispered, and mental;
among these three types of recitation-sacrifices, each subsequent one is more excellent than the preceding.
When one utters sound with speech through syllables that possess clear phonemes and are articulated with high, low, and circumflex tones,
that is the vocal sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*).
One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
when one understands the mantra somewhat for oneself, that is known as the whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa).

When one contemplates the meaning of words through the intellect, moving from syllable to syllable and from word to word along a sequence of phonemes, that meditation is called mental recitation (*mānasajapa*).
When constantly praised with recitation, the deity becomes pleased;
being pleased, she bestows abundant enjoyments and eternal liberation.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and the planetary spirits (grahas) who afflict the sun and other celestial bodies do not approach the practitioner of recitation; they flee far away from him.
Having fully understood the lunar mansions and other such factors,
the twice-born man, untiring and with his mind fixed on that [deity], should bathe daily and recite the Sāvitrī mantra as a sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
He who constantly recites the Gāyatrī, which has a thousand as its maximum, a hundred as its middle, and ten as its minimum, is indeed not tainted by sins.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers to the Sun with arms raised,
one should recite the mantra "Ud u tyam" and also "Citram tat cakṣuḥ."
Having circumambulated [the sun], one should pay homage to the Maker of Day;
with water through his own *tīrtha*, the wise man should satisfy the gods and others.
The wise man should constantly gratify the gods and the hosts of gods, as well as the sages and the hosts of sages, and the ancestors and the hosts of ancestors.
Then, having wrung out the bathing garment, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again;
holding darbha grass in hand upon darbha grass, one should proceed according to the rules for the Brahma-yajña.
Facing the east, one endowed with wisdom should perform the Brahma-yajña;
thereafter, one should offer arghya to the Sun, accompanied by sesame seeds, flowers, and water.
Having risen and paid homage to the God in the water with the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," he then returns home once more.
There, one should worship Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rite with the Puruṣasūkta;
thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering and the ritual of bali-offerings according to the rules.
A householder should indeed wait for a guest for as long as it takes to milk a cow;
he should honor a guest who has arrived before, even if he has never seen him before.
And having arrived, by rising up properly at the door and greeting them with a welcome, the fires become pleased with householders.
By the gift of a seat, the King of the Gods becomes pleased;
and by the washing of his feet, his ancestors attain satisfaction.
By the gift of food and drink, Prajāpati is satisfied in this world;
therefore, the householder must perform the honoring of the guest.
With devotion, the devotee should always worship Viṣṇu and meditate upon Him;
he should also give alms to a mendicant, a wandering ascetic, and a student.
Having taken from prepared food that is joined with all kinds of condiments,
one should always diligently give alms to a mendicant with a focused mind.
If a mendicant arrives seeking alms before the Vaiśvadeva offering has been performed, one must certainly give it; such a gift acts as a staircase to heaven.
Having set aside food for the Vaiśvadeva offering and having given alms, he should dismiss [the guests];
a mendicant is capable of removing the fault incurred by not performing the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Having fed the married women, the maidens, and even the sick,
as well as the children and the elderly, the householder should then eat the remainder himself.
Facing either the east or the north, maintaining silence or speaking sparingly,
one should first pay homage to the food with a joyful inner self.
One should offer the five oblations of breath, each with its respective mantra;
thereafter, being well-composed, one should eat food that is delicious.
Having sipped water, the wise man, touching his belly, should call to mind his chosen deity;
he should then spend some time with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Then, having gone outside, he should perform the twilight worship according to the rule;
having performed the fire-oblation, he should eat and honor any guest during the night.
The twice-born are enjoined by the Vedas to eat in the evening and in the morning;
they should not take food in between, for this rule is equal in importance to the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Likewise, a twice-born man should teach his disciples and avoid all occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya),
both those previously mentioned in the Smṛtis and those declared in the Purāṇas.
On the Mahānavamī, on the twelfth lunar day, on the Bharaṇī asterism,
and likewise on the Akṣayya-tṛtīyā, a wise man should not teach his disciples.
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, one should abandon recitation on the road;
likewise, after anointing the body with oil, one should avoid teaching at the time of bathing.
A householder who desires his own welfare should give gifts according to the prescribed rules,
especially gifts of gold, gifts of cows, and gifts of land.
The best of the twice-born who bestows these upon those learned in the Vedas is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world.
A householder who is endowed with auspicious conduct, pure, and devoted to faith, should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) with faith; he goes to the abode of Brahmā.
O best of beings, through the grace of Narasiṃha, he attains excellence in his birth;
therefore, he attains liberation along with Brahmā.
Thus, O Brahmins, this eternal mass of dharma has been recounted by me to you in brief.
For a householder who practices dharma with diligence, being liberated, he attains Hari.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Duties of the Householder," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 58)
Hārīta said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the characteristics of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*);
O highly fortunate ones, understand the supreme dharma as it is being told.
Having seen his sons, grandsons, and others, and observing his own grey hair,
the householder should establish his wife with his sons and enter the forest accompanied by his disciples.
Wearing a mass of matted hair and rags, or allowing his nails and body hair to grow long,
he should offer oblations into the fire while remaining established in the ritual procedure for the three sacred fires.
A wise man, remaining untiring, should perform his daily rites with gathered leaves, earth-born grains such as wild rice (nīvāra), or even with tubers, roots, and fruits.
Engaged in bathing three times a day, he should always perform intense austerity;
having passed a fortnight, or at the end of a month, he may eat, having performed the *parāka* penance.
One may eat at four times a day, or likewise at the eighth mealtime;
or indeed at the sixth mealtime, or else subsist on air alone.
In the heat, he should spend his time standing amidst five fires; during the rainy season with its downpours, he should pass the time;
and in the winter, he should spend his time remaining in water while practicing austerity.
Having thus purified oneself by means of the enjoyment of one's own karma,
and having indeed internalized the fire within oneself, one should then depart toward the northern direction.
Remaining in the forest until the fall of the body, the ascetic, having adopted silence and remembering the Brahman that transcends the senses, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

For that best of the twice-born who, dwelling in the forest, practices austerity and abides endowed with great being and meditative concentration— freed from evil and with a tranquil mind— goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Duties of the Forest-Dweller," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 59)
Hārīta said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed duty of the ascetic (yati),
by performing which with faith an ascetic is liberated from bondage.
Thus, while dwelling in the forest hermitage, having burnt away his sins through austerity,
the twice-born man should enter the fourth stage of life after renouncing according to the prescribed rule.
Having diligently offered the divine *śrāddha* to the sages, the gods, and his own ancestors, as well as to the sages, human beings, and himself; 60.3.
Having performed either the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi or the Prājāpatya sacrifice,
and having established the fire within his own self according to the mantras, he may then go forth as a wandering mendicant once more.
From that time forward, one should avoid attachment to the pleasure of children and the like;
and one should offer water upon the ground, granting fearlessness to all living beings.
The triple staff (tridaṇḍa) should be made of bamboo, pleasing to the eye, with its bark intact, with joints of equal length,
four finger-breadths in thickness, and wrapped with a cord made from the hair of a black cow.
One who knows the mantra should wear it, purified by water and bound with three knots,
having taken it up with the right hand while reciting the mantra itself.
He may accept a garment to cover his loins, a rug to ward off the cold, and sandals; he should not make a collection of anything else.
These signs of that ascetic have been declared according to dharma;
having embraced them and performed the renunciation of worldly ties, he went to a supreme sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, indeed with a garment moistened with water,
and having offered libations with water while reciting the mantra, one should bow to the Sun.
Seated facing east, observing silence, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas);
having recited the Gāyatrī according to one's ability, one should meditate upon the supreme state.
For the sake of his own sustenance, he should always practice the wandering for alms;
at the time of evening, the ascetic should go from house to house among the Brahmins.
A seeker of food should practice begging for as much alms as is required;
then, having desisted, the self-controlled one should sprinkle that bowl with water and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having offered food to the deities beginning with Sūrya and having sprinkled it with water,
the ascetic (yati) should eat from a leaf-cup or a vessel while remaining silent.
One should never eat food placed upon leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *kumbhī*, *tinduka*, *kovidāra*, or *karañja* trees.
Having eaten and sipped water, and having restrained his breath, he should worship the Sun;
the ascetic should spend the remainder of the day in recitation, meditation, and the study of ancient histories.
All ascetics who eat from bell-metal vessels are called *palāśas*;
likewise, the householder’s vessel is just like that of the bell-metal [ascetic].
A mendicant who eats from a bell-metal vessel shall incur all sin once again;
therefore, a mendicant should always eat from his own eating-bowl, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
His vessel does not become defiled, like the chalices used in sacrifices;
having performed the twilight rituals, he should then pass the night in temples or similar sacred places.
Meditating upon Hari, Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the lotus of the heart,
one attains that state, reaching which one does not return.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Duties of Ascetics," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 60)
Hārīta said:
The defining characteristics of the duties of the social classes and the stages of life have been declared,
by which those beginning with the twice-born may attain both heaven and liberation.
I shall declare, in brief, the supreme essence of the Yogaśāstra,
by the power of practicing which seekers of liberation attain emancipation even in this world.
And for one who delights here in the practice of yoga, even sins shall perish.
Therefore, becoming devoted to yoga, one should constantly meditate during the intervals between ritual acts.
Having brought the speech under control by means of breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma), the senses by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
and the mind— which is otherwise difficult to subdue— by means of concentrations (dhāraṇās), [one attains mastery].
One should meditate upon that single cause, which is blissful consciousness, free from disease,
subtler than the subtlest, the support of the universe, and immutable.
In a secret, solitary place, one should sit and meditate upon the Self, which has the luster of molten gold and resides within the lotus of the heart.
One should reflect: "I am he who knows the minds of all living beings, who dwells in the hearts of all, and who is to be known by all people."
Meditation is said to last as long as there is the bliss of attaining the Self;
thereafter, one should perform those various actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Just as horses are useless without a chariot, and chariots are useless without horses, so too are both austerity and knowledge useless for one who possesses neither austerity nor knowledge.
Just as food mixed with honey and honey mixed with food,
so too austerity and knowledge, when combined, constitute a great medicine.
For just as the flight of birds depends upon two wings alone,
even so is the eternal Brahman attained through both knowledge and action.
A Brahmin endowed with knowledge and austerity, devoted to yoga,
quickly casts off the pair of bodies and becomes liberated from bondage.
As long as the supreme state has not been attained by way of the path of the gods,
the destruction of the body-liṅga does not occur anywhere.
O best of the twice-born, I have thus related to you in brief the entire eternal dharma of those [castes], according to the divisions of social classes and stages of life.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus heard the dharma that bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation,
those sages bowed to that ṛṣi and departed for their own abodes, filled with joy.
But he who, having heard this Dharmaśāstra issued from the mouth of Hārīta, performs his duty, attains the supreme goal.
O King, such is the duty of one born from the mouth, such is the duty of one born from the arms, and such is the duty of those born from the thighs and likewise from the feet.
Performing their respective duties, the Brahmins and others attain a good rebirth;
for by acting otherwise, one falls immediately and goes downwards.
A person is established by those very duties which have been prescribed for him;
therefore, one should always perform one's own duty in this way, except in times of distress.
O Indra among kings, those of the four castes and those in the four stages of life who perform their own respective duties attain the supreme goal.
Just as Narasiṃha is well-pleased with men through their own specific duties,
so too should one worship Narasiṃha in accordance with the duties of one's social class.

Through the practice of yoga by the power of the detachment already arisen, the practitioner of rites should always meditate upon the Supreme Brahman—the primordial, whose nature is truth and whose form is consciousness and bliss; having abandoned the body, he attains the station of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Yoga," in the glorious *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*. (NarP 61)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The characteristics of the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas) have been told to you.
Speak further, O Indra among kings; what, O King, is the duty of service in that regard?"
Sahasrānīka said:
"O best of brahmins, you have told me that one should bathe and worship Acyuta, the Lord of Gods, within one's own home; how, then, should that worship be performed?"
O Sage, O Great Sage, tell me those places and those mantras by which Viṣṇu is worshipped.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now fully describe the worship of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable,
by performing which all sages attained supreme liberation.
The Lord is in the fire for those who perform ritual acts; He is in the heart for the wise;
He is in images for those of small intellect; and Hari dwells in the hearts of yogis.
Therefore, the sages have declared that the proper worship of Hari is performed in these: in the fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial ground, and in images.
And because he consists of everything, Viṣṇu is the deity of that *ānuṣṭubha* hymn on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and in the images (*pratimā*).
The Puruṣa who is known as the seed of the universe and the seer Nārāyaṇa—
whosoever should offer flowers and even water with the Puruṣasūkta [to him].
By him indeed the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, becomes honored.
One should invoke the God Puruṣottama with the first *ṛc*.
One should offer a seat with the second [verse], offer water for the feet with the third,
the arghya offering should be given with the fourth, and the water for sipping with the fifth.
One should perform the bath on the sixth day, the clothing on the seventh,
the sacred thread on the eighth, and the perfume on the ninth.
On the tenth day there should be the offering of flowers; on the eleventh, incense;
on the twelfth, likewise a lamp; and on the thirteenth, likewise worship.
Having performed the praise on the fourteenth [day], the circumambulation on the fifteenth,
and the dismissal on the sixteenth, one should perform the remaining rites as before.
One should offer a bath, clothing, and food offerings, as well as the *ācamanīyaka*;
by worshipping the God of gods in this way, one attains perfection within six months.
In that very year, one attains union with Him:
by means of oblation in the fire, by flowers in the water, and by meditation in the heart, [one worships] Hari.
The wise ones constantly worship with recitation within the solar disc;
having meditated upon the divine God of gods, the stainless Viṣṇu, who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, they pay homage to him within the orb of the sun.

Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, a crown, and necklaces, possessing a golden body and bearing the conch and the discus— He is to be meditated upon always.
A man who, having cultivated a mind fixed on Viṣṇu, recites this hymn alone day after day,
casts off all sin and attains the station of Viṣṇu, bringing satisfaction to the Imperishable One.
Since leaves, flowers, fruits, and water are always available without being purchased,
why is no effort made for the sake of liberation toward the Ancient Puruṣa, who is attainable through devotion alone?
Thus has the ritual for the worship of the Person Viṣṇu been described by me today, O lord of men.
Perform this worship of Viṣṇu constantly, if you indeed desire to attain the beloved station of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Viṣṇu," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 62)
Sahasrānīka said:
"O Brahmin, you have spoken the truth; this is the supreme Vedic injunction regarding the worship of Viṣṇu, the god beyond all gods, for me now."
O Brahmin, by this rite Madhusūdana is worshipped only by those who know the Vedas, and not by others; therefore, speak that which is beneficial for all.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: A person should constantly worship the Lord of Gods, Narasiṃha, the healthy and infallible Acyuta, with the eight-syllable mantra using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
O King, this eight-syllable mantra is supreme, removing all sins;
it bestows the fruit of all sacrifices, brings about all peace, and is auspicious.
Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa!
With this [mantra], one should indeed present all things such as perfumes and flowers;
when the God is worshipped with this, he becomes pleased at that very moment.
What need has he for many mantras, what need has he for many vows?
The mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all purposes.
