Whoever, having become pure and composed, should recite this mantra,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with Viṣṇu.
For this, O King, is the fruit of all sacred fords; it is the best of all sacred fords.
The undistracted worship of Hari, O King, yields the fruit of all sacrifices.
Therefore, O best of kings, perform worship through images and the like, and bestow gifts upon the mouths of Brahmins according to the prescribed rite, O King.
When this is done, O best of kings, one attains through the grace of Narasiṃha that Vaiṣṇava splendor which those seeking liberation desire.
O King, in ancient times Purandara attained womanhood through unrighteous conduct;
he was indeed liberated from the curse of the sage Tṛṇabindu by chanting the eight-syllable mantra.
Sahasrānīka said:
O god among the earth-dwellers, tell me this: what was the transgression that led to the liberation from sin for the Lord of the Gods?
What was the improper act, and how did he attain womanhood? Tell me the cause.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Indra among kings, listen to this great narrative filled with wonder,
which generates devotion to Viṣṇu for those who hear or recite it.
Long ago, while Purandara himself was exercising the sovereignty of the gods,
a sense of detachment toward external objects also arose within him.
At that time, Indra became despondent in nature regarding both kingdoms and enjoyments, and he thought:
"Surely, for those whose minds have been made dispassionate, even the sovereignty of heaven is nothing at all."
The essence of sovereignty is the enjoyment of sense objects, yet at the end of that enjoyment, nothing remains;
having reflected upon this, even sages constantly contemplate the pursuit of liberation.
The practice of austerity is always for the sake of enjoyment, for when enjoyment ends, the austerity is lost;
for those who partake in liberation and are turned away from attachment to friendliness and the like, there is neither austerity nor enjoyment.
Having reflected upon this, that lord of the gods, desiring liberation, mounted his chariot adorned with small bells and surely approached Kailāsa for the sake of propitiating Hara.

Once, having arrived at Mānasa, he beheld that beloved wife of the lord of the Yakṣas as she was worshipping the pair of feet of the Daughter of the Mountain— she who was like a banner for the great chariot of the Bodiless One (Kāmadeva).
Her complexion was as pure as the finest Jambūnada gold; her beautiful eyes reached to her ears;
and her limbs were visible through her very fine garments, like the crescent moon appearing from amidst the mist.
Beholding her with a gaze filled with a thousand glances, his mind utterly deluded by passion for the body of Kāma, he did not depart at that time;
having returned to his own home after a long journey, the Lord of the Gods remained there, desiring sensual pleasures, though he possessed well-accumulated wealth.
First, there would be birth in a noble family as the foremost boon; from that, indeed, comes the beauty of a body with all its limbs intact.
After that, wealth is truly difficult to obtain; thereafter, the mastery of wealth is attained through meritorious deeds.
I have indeed attained sovereignty over heaven, yet I lack the fortune for enjoyment;
having abandoned my own [kingdom] out of a desire for liberation, there remains a wicked thought in my mind.
Even if liberation is to be attained through this [kingdom], which deludes one, what cause for liberation is there even in sovereignty?
Having abandoned a field that is fully ripe, why indeed would one practice forest-farming at the gate?
Those men who are afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra, who are incapable of doing anything at all,
and who are inactive and devoid of fortune— those deluded ones desire the path to liberation.

Having reflected upon this in many ways, the wise and heroic one, whose mind was deluded by the beauty of the Giver of Wealth’s daughter, became overwhelmed by all his passions; with his composure utterly abandoned and his intellect agitated, he called to mind Māra, the universal monarch of the lords of the immortals.
Having encountered him, Kāma, whose mental state was agitated by excessive passion, approached very slowly;
for who would fearlessly succumb to dissolution out of fortitude when his own destruction as a woman had been brought about by Maheśa in the past?
"O Lord, let it be commanded what task remains; who indeed is now your enemy?
Give your order quickly, do not delay; I shall now provide for his downfall."

Having heard those delightful words which expressed his innermost thought, the hero was supremely pleased; considering the goal to have been accomplished all at once, he spoke these words with a smile: śrutvā tadā tasya vaco abhirāmaṃ manogataṃ tat paramaṃ tutoṣa / niṣpannam arthaṃ sahasaiva matvā jagāda vākyaṃ sa vihasya vīraḥ // NsP_63.28 //
Even Rudra, by whom [the god of love] was reduced to being merely half a body and rendered bodiless even while remaining in the mind—
what other person in this world, O Māra, is capable of enduring the strike of your arrows?
"She whose mind is one-pointedly fixed even upon the worship of the Daughter of the Mountain utterly deludes my heart here;
make her—she who is known as Anaṅgāyatalocanā and whose sole essence is the touch of my limbs—your own."
Thus addressed by the beloved of the gods, with a gravity exceeding that of his own task,
the wise Māra, the flower-armed god, fixed an arrow and called to mind his power of enchantment.
Deluded by the flower-arrowed Kāma, the young woman, her limbs overwhelmed with intoxication, abandoned the worship and laughed at the Lord of the Gods; for who could endure the sound of Kāma’s bow?
"O girl with tremulous eyes, who are you? The Lord of the Gods spoke these words to her:
'You seem to bewitch the minds of men; tell me, whose beloved are you here, O fortunate one?'"
Though thus addressed, the young woman, her limbs overwhelmed by intoxication, her body trembling with horripilation and perspiration,
agitated by the arrow of desire, spoke these words slowly and with a faltering voice.
"The beloved Yakṣa maiden of the Lord of Wealth has arrived to worship the feet of Gaurī.
Tell me, O Lord, what is your business? Who are you that stands here, able to assume any form at will?"
Indra said:
Therefore, come to me; enjoy me, for you have long been eager for union with my body—attain it quickly.
Without you, even this vast life of mine, as well as the sovereignty of heaven, would be fruitless.
Thus addressed by him in sweet words, she, whose beautiful body was tormented by the god of love,
ascended a celestial chariot with fluttering banners and embraced the neck of the Lord of the Gods.
For that lord of heaven went quickly with her to the caves of Mount Mandara,
which were inaccessible to the movement of gods and asuras, and radiant with sprouts of various jewels.
Though he possessed noble prowess and was indifferent even to the sovereignty of the gods, that treasury of artfulness took delight with her,
full of desire, as he himself prepared for her a wonderful bed of light flowers.
Born with his purpose fulfilled as the lord of the hosts of immortals, he was ever skilled in the enjoyments of desire;
yet he found the pleasure of embracing another’s wife—polished by the essence of affection—to be superior even to liberation.
Then those women, having approached the presence of the Lord of Yakṣas while showing due respect to Citrasena,
spoke with faltering voices, full of agitation, their limbs distressed by that agitation, yet mindful of the prohibition against rashness.
"O Lord of Yakṣas, listen surely!
A certain thief has boarded a celestial chariot and departed, looking back toward the lovely quarters of the sky while clutching his beloved with haste."
Then, having heard those words which were like poison, the Lord of Wealth, his face turning the color of soot with rage, said nothing further; he remained as if a tree consumed by fire.
Having had his purpose made known by the excellent maidens who were the companions of Citrasenā,
Kaṇṭhakubja also arrived, applying his mind toward the removal of [the king's] delusion.
Hearing that he had arrived and seeing him, the king of kings opened his eyes and spoke these words;
sighing deeply with his limbs trembling violently, the wretched man quickly steadied his mind.
That is true youth which is the delight of young women; that is true wealth which benefits one's own kin;
that is true life which is spent in the practice of the sublime Dharma; and that is true sovereignty which is free from conflict.
"Shame on my wealth, my life, my no small fortune, and now this vast kingdom of the Guhyakas!
I shall enter the fire, yet no one knows that such a defeat exists—even for the dead. (NsP 63.47)
"Though standing by my side while I was alive, she went to the lake to worship the Daughter of the Mountain;
and we do not know by whom we have been carried off—surely he has no fear of death."
And that minister, Kaṇṭhakubja, spoke these words to dispel the Lord’s delusion:
"Listen, O Master; the destruction of one's own body is not appropriate when separated from a beloved."
In the past, a single wife of Rāma was abducted by a night-stalker, yet even he did not die;
here you have many women, so why indeed do you harbor despair in your heart?
O King of Yakṣas, cast off your grief and set your mind on valor; take hold of steadfastness.
The virtuous do not lament excessively nor weep; they endure the defeat inflicted by others.
For they show that the task has indeed been accomplished when one has an ally; O Lord of Wealth, why are you so timid?
For now Vibhīṣaṇa, his younger brother, is himself performing the work of an ally.
Dhanada said: "Vibhīṣaṇa has become my adversary and does not relinquish his status as my heir.
Indeed, wicked people do not remain grateful; they are as harsh as Hari’s thunderbolt, even when they have been shown kindness."
"For the mind of one born of noble lineage does not become gracious through favors, nor through virtues, nor through acts of friendship.
And Kaṇṭhakubja spoke these words: "O Lord of Wealth, what you have said is indeed fitting."
Though they strike one another and are thus at odds, there is nevertheless no defeat in the world;
they do not tolerate a defeat inflicted by another, just as water does not burn with heat nor does it set fire to grass.
Therefore, O Lord of Wealth, come to the side of Vibhīṣaṇa without haste;
for what opposition can there be among one's own kinsmen between those who enjoy wealth acquired through the strength of their own arms?
Thus addressed at that time by the minister Kaṇṭhakubja,
he quickly went into the presence of Vibhīṣaṇa, reflecting deeply.
Then, having heard that his kinsman and elder brother had arrived, the Lord of Laṅkā quickly returned, endowed with humility.

Then, O King, having seen his kinsman so dejected, Vibhīṣaṇa, with a deeply distressed mind, spoke these significant words: NsP_63.59: "Then, O King, having seen his kinsman so dejected, Vibhīṣaṇa, with a deeply distressed mind, spoke these significant words."
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"O Lord of Yakṣas, why are you dejected? What distress is in your mind?
Tell it to us now; I shall resolve it with certainty."
Then, having retired to a secluded place, she spoke of her suffering.
Dhanada said:
"Was she captured by herself, or did she go of her own accord, or was she slain by some enemy?"
"Brother, I do not see my beloved Citrasenā, who is so enchanting;
O kinsman, this great misery of mine has arisen from a woman."
I shall surely give up my life if I do not find my beloved.
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"O Lord, I shall bring back your beloved, wherever she may be staying."
"O Lord, who is now capable of taking even a blade of grass from us?
Then Vibhīṣaṇa [spoke] there to the night-stalker Nāḍījaṅghā.
She spoke at great length concerning her various and extensive magical powers,
as well as the beloved wife of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), who had been fashioned according to the design of Citrasena.
And by whom was she carried away from the world while she was staying at Lake Mānasa?
Having searched through the abodes of the king of the gods and others, you must recognize her.
Then, O King, the night-stalker, having assumed a body composed of illusion,
quickly went to the heavens, to the abodes of the king of the gods and others.
By that vision, even a stone, if seen for a moment, will fall into delusion;
for its form is eternally uniform and exists nowhere among the moving or the unmoving.
And at that very time, O King, the king of the gods also arrived swiftly from Mount Mandara, having been dispatched by Citrasenā.
While there, as he was gathering divine flowers produced in the Nandana grove,
he saw that slender woman arrived at her own place in the assembly hall.
Beholding her, who was endowed with exceeding beauty and devoted to the singing of songs, even the King of the Gods fell under the sway of desire.
Then the lord of the gods dispatched the two physicians of the gods to bring her certainly to his side within the inner apartments.
Then the two physicians of the gods arrived, spoke [to her], and stood before her:
"Come, O slender-limbed one, and become the consort of the King of the Gods."
Thus addressed by those two, she then spoke in sweet syllables.
Nāḍījaṅgha said:
"The King of the Gods himself will come here to my side."
"His word must be carried out by me in every way and not otherwise.
Then those two, having approached Vāsava, spoke these auspicious words.
Vāsava said:
"Command me, O slender-limbed one; what must be done by me now? I am always your servant; whatever you ask for, I shall give it."
The slender-limbed one said:
"O Lord, if you will grant what I have asked, there is no doubt;
then, O God, I shall come under your control, of this there is no doubt."
Today, show us all your consorts;
do you have a beloved woman whose beauty is equal to mine, or not?
And when those words had been spoken by her, Vāsava spoke again:
"O Goddess, I shall show you the entire collection of your beloved."
Then Vāsava showed him the entire inner apartment;
thereafter he spoke again: "Something remains hidden from me."
Having released one young woman, everything has been shown to you by me.
Indra said:
That beautiful woman is on Mount Mandara, unknown to the gods and asuras.
"And I shall show her to you; you must not tell this to anyone.
Then, O King, even that lord of the gods [appeared] together with her.
O King, as he traveled toward Mount Mandara through the sky in that celestial chariot possessing the brilliance of the sun, he proceeded along his way.
Then, the sight of Nārada also appeared to him in the sky;
seeing that Nārada, the heroic Vāsava felt ashamed.
Having paid homage, he spoke aloud: "Where will you go, O great sage?
Then, having offered his blessing, that sage replied to the Lord of the Three Gods:
"I am going to the Mānasa lake to bathe; O King of the Gods, may you be happy.
There is no welfare for the great-souled Rākṣasas in Nāḍījaṅgha."
"Your brother Vibhīṣaṇa also remains happy at all times.
When addressed thus by the sage, she became dark-faced.
Even the King of the Gods was astonished, deceived by this wicked woman;
and Nārada too went to bathe at Lake Mānasa on Kailāsa.
Indra, though desiring to slay her, went toward Mount Mandara,
where the hermitage of the high-souled Tṛṇabindu was surely located.
Having rested for a moment right there, the Lord of Gods seized the night-stalking Rākṣasī Nāḍījaṅghā by the hair and desired to kill her.
Just then, O King, Tṛṇabindu arrived there from his own hermitage; that night-stalker woman was being held captive and was crying out even before Indra.
"The virtuous soul is protecting me as I am being struck right now;
then the best of sages, Tṛṇabindu of great asceticism, arrived."
Standing before him, he said, "Release this woman in the forest";
while the sage was thus speaking, Mahendra [acted] toward the night-stalker woman.
Struck again by the thunderbolt with a mind full of wrath,
that best of sages grew enraged as he gazed at him repeatedly.
"Since this young woman was wickedly slain by me in my ascetic grove,
you shall therefore certainly become a woman by my curse."
Indra said:
"O Lord, this most wicked Rākṣasī has been slain by me.
I am the lord of the gods; do not cast a curse upon me now."
The sage said:
"Surely there dwell among us in this penance grove virtuous ones who are wicked; because of the power of my asceticism here, they do not slay one another."
Thus addressed, O King, Indra then undoubtedly attained womanhood;
with his power and prowess destroyed, he departed for the third heaven.
For he was never indeed seated in the assembly of the gods;
the gods fell into distress upon seeing Hari transformed into a woman.
Then all the hosts of gods, accompanied by Vāsava,
went to the abode of Brahmā, and Śacī likewise departed in a state of distress.
And Brahmā, his meditative absorption shattered, remained right there;
and all those gods, accompanied by Vāsava, spoke.
O Brahmin, due to the curse of the sage Tṛṇabindu, the lord of the gods has undergone the state of womanhood;
that sage, being full of wrath, does not at all grant his favor.
He has come to this state of womanhood through his own karma, on account of having killed a woman.
The gods and even the king of the gods, intoxicated with pride, committed a wicked deed;
he carried off Citrasenā, the well-guarded wife of the Giver of Wealth.
Likewise, he killed a young woman in the penance grove of Tṛṇabindu;
by the ripening of that karma, Vāsava underwent the state of being a woman.
The gods said:
"O Lord, whatever misconduct that evil-minded one has committed against Śambhu,
we shall accomplish all of that together with Śacī."
O Lord, that beloved wife of the Lord of Wealth who remains hidden—
we shall all give her to him, having formed a supreme resolve.
On the thirteenth and fourteenth [lunar days], the King of the Gods, accompanied by Śacī,
shall always perform worship in the Nandana grove for the sake of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
Then Śacī, having secretly seized Citrasenā—
who was following her beloved through his hardships— released her from the abode of the Yakṣas.
In the meantime, a messenger arrived in Laṅkā at an improper time and informed the Lord of Wealth of his meeting with Citrasena.
O Lord of Wealth, your beloved has arrived together with Śacī;
having obtained her peerless friend, she has achieved her life's purpose.
The Lord of Wealth also, having accomplished his purpose, returned to his own abode;
and just as a woman is without her husband, or an army without its leader,
so was Gokula bereft of Kṛṣṇa, while Amarāvatī was likewise deprived of Indra.
O Lord, tell me of recitation, ritual action, austerity, charity, knowledge,
and pilgrimage sites belonging to Vāsava, by means of which one is liberated from womanhood.
Brahmā said:
"Neither I nor Śaṅkara am capable of nullifying the sage’s curse;
I see no other means of liberation except for the singular worship of Viṣṇu."
Let Śakra perform worship and likewise recitation with the eight-syllable mantra according to the prescribed rule, so that he may be liberated from his state as a woman.
O Śakra, having bathed with a one-pointed mind and endowed with faith,
recite "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" for the sake of self-purification.
"O Hari, when two hundred thousand recitations have been performed, you shall be released from this female state.
Having heard these words spoken by Brahmā, Hari acted accordingly;
and then, through the grace of Viṣṇu, he was completely liberated from his female form.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus I have related to you in its entirety this supreme majesty of Viṣṇu; being commissioned by Bhṛgu, perform all [this] without indolence.

Those who, being stainless, hear the stories of Viṣṇu—the heroic power of Viṣṇu, the cause of all—become freed from sin; even those who have gone to another's wife enter the eternal, supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by Mārkaṇḍeya, the king,
having propitiated Narasiṃha, indeed attained the station of Viṣṇu.
All this has been told to you by me, O sage Bharadvāja—the life of Sahasrānīka; what else shall I tell you?
That person who hears this ancient tale, which grants complete liberation,
shall attain exceedingly pure knowledge and, by that very means, reach Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Eight-Syllable Mantra," in the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa*, within the account of Sahasrānīka.
The venerable Bharadvāja said:
Some praise truth, while others likewise praise austerity and purity;
some praise Sāṃkhya, and others proclaim Yoga.
Some who regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal praise wisdom;
others praise forbearance, as well as compassion and uprightness.
Some praise generosity; some say that supreme purity is best;
some say right knowledge is supreme; and some say dispassion is the highest.
Some know ritual acts such as the Agniṣṭoma and others to be supreme;
others, who know the true meaning of the principles of Sāṃkhya, consider meditation on the Self to be supreme.
In this world, the sole means for attaining the four goals— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—
is thus explained in many ways through various divisions of its constituent parts.
When the world stands thus in the matter of what ought and ought not to be done,
men fall into sheer delusion, even though they are freed from evil deeds.
O Omniscient One, you ought to tell me that supreme duty which is to be performed by the great-souled ones among these [teachings], which accomplishes all my goals.
Sūta said: Listen to this which is extremely secret and liberates one from the cycle of existence;
in this very context, they cite this ancient history.
The conversation between Puṇḍarīka and the celestial sage Nārada;
[it concerns] the Brahmin Puṇḍarīka, who was endowed with sacred learning and possessed of great intelligence.
Abiding in the first stage of life, always remaining under the control of his teachers,
with his senses conquered and his anger subdued, he should be established in the performance of the twilight devotions.
Skilled in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and proficient in the treatises,
he [should] diligently offer oblations into the fire with sacrificial fuel both morning and evening.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, he properly worshipped the omnipresent one,
devoted to austerity and sacred study, like the son of Brahmā himself.
Constantly satisfying his gurus with offerings of water, fuel, and flowers,
he served his mother and father, subsisted on alms, and was beloved by the people.

O Great King, as he was studying the knowledge of Brahman and was devoted to the practice of breath control, his intellect—having become indifferent to all worldly objects—became utterly free from desire for the cycle of existence and served as a means of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra; [he then reflected upon] his father, mother, brothers, and grandfathers.
The most noble one, having cast aside his paternal uncles, maternal uncles, friends, kinsmen, and relatives as easily as blades of grass, according to his pleasure; NsP_64.16.
Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he wandered this earth,
[reflecting upon] the impermanence of youth, beauty, lifespan, and the accumulation of wealth.
Reflecting thus, O Sage, he regarded the three worlds as mere clods of earth,
and all sacred fords according to the path proclaimed in the Purāṇas.
With his mind firmly resolved, "I shall go at the proper time," [he visited] the Gaṅgā,
the Yamunā, the Gomatī, and the Gaṇḍakī.
The Śatadrū, the Payoṣṇī, the Sarayū, and the Sarasvatī;
Prayāga and the Narmadā—these great rivers and also the streams.
And Gayā, the sacred fords of the Vindhya mountains, those originating from the Himalayas, and other holy sites as well— the one of great splendor and firm vows traversed them all.
The mighty-armed hero, whose wealth was his asceticism, wandered about according to the time and according to the prescribed rule; at one point, he reached Śālagrāma.
The illustrious Puṇḍarīka, who follows the power of his meritorious deeds,
was attended by sages rich in austerity who were knowers of reality.
The delightful hermitage of the sages, renowned in the Purāṇas,
was adorned by the Cakranadī river, its rocky floor marked with wheel-shaped impressions.
Delightful, secluded, and vast, it always inspires clarity of mind;
some living beings there, marked with wheels, are of auspicious appearance.
In that highly meritorious field of Śālagrāma, the high-minded one wanders at will, devoted to sacred fords.
Puṇḍarīka, serene in soul and firm in his vows, visited various sacred fords;
having bathed in the Devahrada and at the Tīrtha of the Sarasvatī, he performed his rites.
He wandered through Jātismaryā, Cakrakuṇḍa, and the confluences of the Cakranadī, as well as various other sacred fords (tīrthas) located in that very place.
Then, by the power of the sacred field and by the splendor of the holy fords,
the mind of that great-souled one attained serenity.
He too, having purified his soul at that sacred ford and being devoted to the yoga of meditation,
remained there desiring spiritual perfection while propitiating the Lord of the World.
Endowed with supreme devotion, he dwelt for a long time alone, free from the pairs of opposites, with his senses restrained, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, contented, and possessing equal vision,
he is likewise established through the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), and the postures (āsanas).
Through extremely sharp breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), through constant withdrawals of the senses (pratyāhāra),
as well as through concentrations (dhāraṇā), meditations (dhyāna), and absorptions (samādhi), he remains unwearied.
Then, with his impurities removed, he practiced yoga correctly,
having propitiated the Lord of the gods with an inner self entirely absorbed in Him.
The highly fortunate Puṇḍarīka, who was proficient in the goals of human endeavor,
with his mind fixed upon Viṣṇu, longed for the supreme grace of the Lord.
O king of kings, as that high-souled Puṇḍarīka was dwelling there in Śālagrāma, a great length of time passed by.
O Sage, once Nārada, the knower of the supreme truth,
possessed of great splendor and resembling the sun itself in person, went to that region.
Desiring to see that Puṇḍarīka, a treasure-house of asceticism, the celestial sage—
whose soul was permeated with devotion to Viṣṇu and who was intent on the welfare of the Vaiṣṇavas— [approached him].
He saw that Nārada had arrived, endowed with the splendor of all radiance,
possessed of great intelligence and great wisdom, and proficient in all the scriptures.
With palms joined in reverence and bowing down with a joyful inner soul,
he then offered the guest-offering (argha) as was appropriate and performed a prostration.
Who is this person of such wondrous form, radiant, wearing a charming garment,
with a musical instrument in hand, possessing a beautiful face, and adorned with a circle of matted locks?
"Is it Vivasvat, or perhaps Agni, Indra, or even Varuṇa?"— thus reflecting, the most radiant sage inquired.
Puṇḍarīka said: Who are you that have arrived here, and from where, O you of supreme luster?
For the sight of you is generally difficult to obtain for those without merit on this earth.
Nārada said:
"O twice-born Puṇḍarīka, I am Nārada, arrived out of a desire to see you; you are a constant devotee of Hari like him, O brāhmaṇa."
O best of the twice-born, even a devotee of the Blessed One who is a caṇḍāla purifies by chance— whether remembered, addressed, or even worshipped.
"I am the servant of Vāsudeva, the god of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow"—
thus was he addressed by Nārada, whose soul was overwhelmed with devotion.
Greatly amazed by the sight of him, the brahmin spoke sweetly.
Puṇḍarīka said:
"I am blessed among embodied beings today; I am worthy of worship even by the gods."
My ancestors have today achieved their purpose; the fruit of my birth has been fully attained.
O divine sage, show your favor especially to me, your devotee.
O learned one, what should I do, wandering about as I am by my own karmas?
You ought to instruct me in that which is the supreme secret to be performed.
You are the refuge of all the worlds, and especially of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Nārada said:
"O twice-born one, there are many scriptures here, as well as various ritual actions."
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, the paths of dharma and living beings are manifold; it is from that very source that the diversity of the world arises.
"From the unmanifest, this entire world, which consists of all things, is born;
thus say others, and that therein [it] also undergoes dissolution. (NsP 64.52)
O best among the wise, others who are intent on perceiving the truth have declared that there are many selves, and that they are likewise eternal and all-pervading. (NsP 64.53)
Having reflected thus and so forth, according to their own understanding and according to what they have heard,
all the sages, who are experts in various philosophical systems, speak.
Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall tell you, O sinless one, this supreme secret of ultimate reality which liberates from the terrible cycle of saṃsāra.
The vision of humans, which is restricted to determining objects of the present, does not grasp what is future or past, nor that which is exceedingly remote. (NsP 64.56)
Listen attentively, my dear son; O sinless one of noble vows, I shall tell you that which was previously spoken by Brahmā to me when I questioned him.
Once, having prostrated according to the prescribed rule before the imperishable Grandfather, the lotus-born Brahmā, who was residing in the world of Brahmā, I questioned him.
Nārada said:
O God, what is that supreme knowledge, and likewise, what is the supreme yoga?
O Grandfather, explain all of this to me in accordance with reality.
Brahmā said: That Supreme Being who is declared to be beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the twenty-fifth principle (puruṣa),
he alone is designated as "Nara" among all beings.
The principles born from Nara are known as "Nārāṇi";
since they are his path (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
At the time of creation, the entire world is born from Nārāyaṇa;
and at the time of dissolution, it is completely absorbed back into him alone.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Self.
O Sage, he is even beyond the beyond; therefore, there is nothing higher than him, whether it be seen or even heard anywhere in this world.
"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without;
having known him thus, the gods repeatedly proclaimed him in his embodied form."
Having meditated with undistracted minds upon "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," what need has he for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
He who constantly meditates upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with undivided mind—this is the supreme knowledge; there is no yoga higher than this.
What is the use of other extensive treatises whose contents are mutually contradictory?
Just as many different paths enter into a single great city, so too do [all these teachings] lead to the same goal.
In that same way, all forms of knowledge enter into that Lord;
for He is the omnipresent God, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal.
The origin of the world, without beginning or end, the self-existent, the creator of beings,
Viṣṇu, the all-pervading, whose nature is inconceivable, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being.
Vāsudeva is the abode of the universe, the ancient, the seer, and the imperishable;
from him the entire triple world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, has obtained its stability.
Therefore, that Blessed One is designated as the god Viṣṇu,
because at the end of the age, he [is the source] of all beings, beginning with the principles (tattva).
Because he dwells within that [universe] through association, he is called Vāsudeva;
some call him Puruṣa, while others call him the immutable Īśvara.
Some [hold] that there is consciousness alone; others likewise [hold] that there is the supreme Brahman;
some [hold] that there is time, without beginning or end; and others [hold] that there is the eternal individual soul.
Some call him the Supreme Self (paramātman), some the Untainted (anāmaya), some the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and others likewise the Twenty-sixth (ṣaḍviṃśaka).
Some [describe it] as the size of a thumb, and others as being like a particle of lotus-pollen;
these and other various distinct designations have been made by the sages.
In the scriptures, [various doctrines] have been proclaimed that cause delusion in the world regarding Viṣṇu;
if there were only one scripture, knowledge would be free from doubt.
Because of the great number of treatises here, the reality of knowledge is very difficult to attain;
having churned all the scriptures and investigated them again and again—
This one thing is perfectly established: Nārāyaṇa is always to be meditated upon, having abandoned all delusive elaborations of the meaning of the scriptures.
Meditate on Nārāyaṇa with an undistracted mind and without weariness;
having thus constantly known that imperishable God of gods.
Having heard this most difficult-to-attain yoga of knowledge proclaimed by Brahmā, you will quickly attain union (*sāyujya*) right there; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, O best of Brahmins, I became devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
for those who know "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" know the eternal Brahman.
Chanting at the time of death, they go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O dear one, Nārāyaṇa is the eternal Supreme Self.
Nārāyaṇa, the all-pervading, eternal Supreme Self, should always be meditated upon with undistracted minds by those who contemplate the ultimate reality.
He is intent upon the creation, destruction, and preservation of the worlds;
[he is attained] by those devoted to hearing, reciting, and meditating [upon him].
O Brahmin, a person who desires their own welfare must by all means propitiate those who are free from desire, eternally contented, wise, and have their senses fully restrained.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, devoid of passion and hatred, impartial, peaceful, and free from all conceptual constructions.
O Brahmin, those great-souled ones who are devoted to the yoga of meditation, having abandoned the three [qualities], behold Vāsudeva, Hari, the Lord of the World and their Guru.
Those who glorify the Lord of the World behold the Master of the Universe;
therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too should be devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
O twice-born one, who else besides him is so magnanimous as to be capable of granting what is requested? Indeed, he who bestows his own station with ease upon being merely praised.
Furthermore, you must perform recitation and the study of sacred texts;
directed toward that very Lord of Gods, perform these daily without weariness.
What is the use there of many mantras, what is the use there of many vows?
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" is the accomplisher of all aims.

O best of the twice-born, whether one is clothed in bark, wears matted hair, carries the triple staff, or is even shaven-headed— or even if adorned with ornaments— the external mark is not the cause of dharma.
Even those men who are cruel, evil-minded, and always devoted to sinful conduct go to the supreme abode if they take refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
Only after thousands of other births would one possess such an understanding as this:
"I am the servant of Vāsudeva, the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow."
A person attains the same world as Viṣṇu; there is no doubt about this.
How much more so, then, a man who has offered his life-breaths to Him and whose senses are restrained?
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the god and celestial sage,
who is devoted to the welfare of others and the sole ornament of the three worlds, vanished right there.
The righteous Puṇḍarīka as well, being devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, repeatedly uttered: "Obeisance be to Keśava!"
"Be gracious, O Great Yogin! Having always recited this, one should establish Govinda Janārdana within the lotus of the heart."
In the forest of Śālagrāma, which brings about the perfection of asceticism, the one whose wealth is penance,
skilled in the goals of human existence, dwelt alone for a long time.
Even in his dreams, that man of great asceticism saw nothing other than Keśava;
even sleep did not oppose his pursuit of the goals of human life.
Through austerity, celibacy, and especially through purity,
as well as by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) accumulated over the course of many successive births, that twice-born man [attains his goal].
Through the grace of the God of gods, the sole witness of all the worlds, he,
cleansed of all impurity, attained the supreme Vaiṣṇava perfection.
O best of the twice-born, lions, tigers, and other predatory beasts, having abandoned their innate hostility, gathered together in his presence and dwelt there with their senses fully pacified.
Then, at one time, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, appeared before the wise Puṇḍarīka.

Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments and radiant with a garland, he has the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest; he is the abode of prosperity, adorned with the Kaustubha gem.
Having mounted Garuḍa, the glorious one, who resembled a mountain of collyrium,
appeared like a dark cloud flashing with lightning that had ascended the peak of Mount Meru.
The Lord of the Gods shone forth, resplendent with a silver parasol from which hung strings of pearls, and with yak-tail fans and other such regalia.
Having seen that Lord of the Gods of gods, the twice-born Puṇḍarīka, with palms joined in reverence,
fell prostrate upon the ground with his head bowed in awe.
Then the sinless Puṇḍarīka, his eyes agitated as if drinking in Hṛṣīkeśa, attained great satisfaction.
Gazing upon him, whose sight he had long desired,
the heroic Lord Padmanābha Trivikrama then spoke to him:
"I am pleased, my child; may it be well with you, O high-minded Puṇḍarīka!
Choose a boon, and I shall grant whatever dwells in your heart."
Sūta said:
Having heard these words spoken by the God of gods, the high-minded Puṇḍarīka made this request: *Nārasiṃhapurāṇa* 64.113.
Puṇḍarīka said:
Where am I, possessed of such extreme folly, and where is the discernment of one's own welfare?
O Lord of Gods, O Mādhava, command me as to what is beneficial for me.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, being well-pleased, spoke again to the illustrious Puṇḍarīka, who stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One said:
"Come, may it be well with you, O observer of noble vows; together with me, become my constant attendant, assuming my form and possessing my very self."
Sūta said:
When Śrīdhara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, had spoken thus with love,
the celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Then the gods, together with Indra, as well as the Siddhas, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
And the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and especially the Kinnaras sang.
Then, having taken him up, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World,
honored by all the gods, departed mounted upon Garuḍa.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too, endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu,
with your mind fixed on Him, your life-breath dedicated to Him, and delighting in the welfare of His devotees, [should act accordingly].
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed method, devote yourself to the Supreme Person;
listen to his meritorious stories, which destroy all sins.
O best of Brahmins, perform in great detail that means by which Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe and the Lord of all lords, becomes pleased.
Even by means of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices,
those who are averse to Nārāyaṇa do not attain that meritorious state.

O Viṣṇu, I have taken refuge in You—the Lord, the teacher of the three worlds; who are ageless, immortal, and singular; the object of meditation, devoid of beginning or end; possessed of attributes yet beyond attributes; the primordial, the gross, and the exceedingly subtle; incomparable, yet the very standard of comparison; and accessible through the knowledge of yogis.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Puṇḍarīka and Nārada. (NarP 64)
Bhāradvāja said:
"Indeed, I wish to hear from you about the secret sacred sites of Hari;
tell me also his most secret names, which remove all sins."
Sūta said: Brahmā questioned Keśava, the Lord Hari,
the God of gods, who dwells on Mount Mandara and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Brahmā said:
O Hari, O best of gods, in which various sacred fields (kṣetra) are you to be seen by me, and especially by other devotees who desire liberation?
O Lord of the World, O lotus-eyed one, I desire to hear from you those secret names and fields of yours.
"O Lord of the Gods, for the benefit of those devoted to you, tell me this: what should a man constantly and tirelessly recite so that he goes to a happy destiny?"
The Blessed One said: Listen attentively, O Brahmin, to my secret names now;
I shall also tell you truly of my secret sacred fields (kṣetra).
One should worship Vārāha at Kokāmukha, Madhusūdana on Mount Mandara,
Ananta at Kapiladvīpa, and the Son of the Sun (Yama) at Prabhāsa.
One should worship Vaikuṇṭha at Mālyodapāna, the Son of Nṛpa at Mahendra,
Mahāviṣṇu at Ṛṣabha, and Bhūpati at Dvārakā.
At Pāṇḍusāhya, one should worship Deveśa; at Vāsurūḍha, Jagatpati;
at Vallīvaṭa, Mahāyoga; and at Citrakūṭa, Narādhipa.
One should meditate on Hari wearing yellow garments at Nimiṣa, at the departure of the cows;
on his dwelling in ascetic penance at Śālagrāma, and his inconceivable state on Gandhamādana.
One should worship Hṛṣīkeśa in the house of the hunchbacked woman (Kubjā), Payodhara at Gandhadvāra, Garuḍadhvaja in Sakala, and Govinda in Sāyaka.
One should know Gopāla to be in Vṛndāvana, Svayaṃbhū in Mathurā,
Mādhava in Kedāra, and Keśava in Vārāṇasī.
One should worship Puṣkarākṣa at Puṣkara, Jayadhvaja at Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
the hero Aśoka in the Tṛṇabindu forest, and [Aśoka] at the Sindhusāgara.
In Kaseraṭa, [he saw] the mighty-armed one; in the Taijasa forest, the immortal;
at Viśvāsayūpa, the Lord of the Universe; and in the great forest, Narasiṃha.
They know Halāṅga as the destroyer of enemies, Devaśālā as Trivikrama, Puruṣottama as [the deity] in Daśapura, and Vāmana as being at Kubjaka.
One should worship Vidyādhara at the Vitastā, Dharaṇīdhara at Vārāha,
Guhya in the Devadāru forest, and Nāgaśāyin at the Kāverī.
At Prayāga he is Yogamūrti, at Payoṣṇī he is Sudarśana,
at Kumāratīrtha he is Kaumāra, and at Lohita he is Hayaśīrṣaka.
Having seen Trivikrama at Liṅgakūṭa in Ujjayinī,
and Harihara at Bhadrā, one is liberated from sin.
One should worship Viśvarūpa at Kurukṣetra, Halāyudha at Maṇikuṇḍa,
Lokanātha at Ayodhyā, and Kuṇḍineśvara at Kuṇḍina.
One should know Vāsudeva to be in Bhāṇḍāra, Sudarśana at Cakratīrtha,
Viṣṇupada in Āḍhya, and they know Śūkara to be in Śūkara.
They know Brahmeśa to be at the Mānasa-tīrtha, Śyāmala in Daṇḍaka,
Nāgamokṣa on Trikūṭa, and Bhāskara on the summit of Meru.
They know Viraja to be in Puṣpabhadrā, Bāla in Kerala,
Yaśaskara in Vipāśā, and Hutāśana in Māhiṣmatī.
One should worship Padmanābha in the Ocean of Milk, the eternal one in Vimala,
Śivakara in the Śivanadī, and Gadādhara in Gayā.
He who perceives the Supreme Self everywhere is liberated;
and sixty-eight names have been recounted by me to you.
And these secret fields have been specifically described;
these are my secret names, O Prajāpati.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should recite this or listen to it constantly,
shall obtain the fruit of giving away a hundred thousand cows.
Whoever, having become pure day by day, should recite these names, for him no bad dream shall occur through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
The man who recites these sixty-eight names at the three times of day,
being liberated from all sins, rejoices in my world.
These sacred fields should be visited by men according to their ability, especially by Vaiṣṇavas; to them, I grant liberation.
Sūta said: Having worshipped Hari and standing before Him while remembering Hari, especially on the day of Viṣṇu (Ekādaśī),
that man who recites this hymn attains the immortal state of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa, which bestows dharma, artha, and mokṣa in its beginning, and is beloved by Viṣṇu. NarP 65.
Sūta said: O Brahmin, this meritorious hymn of praise for Hari has been recited by means of these names;
now learn from me those other names as well.
First, the Gaṅgā is meritorious, followed by the Yamunā and the Gomatī;
then the Sarayū, the Sarasvatī, the Candrabhāgā, and the Carmaṇvatī.
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Puṣkara lakes, as well as Arbuda,
and the highly meritorious Narmadā— these are the sacred fords (tīrthas) in the north.
The Tāpī and Payoṣṇī are two holy rivers; through their confluence, it is an excellent sacred site (tīrtha).
Likewise, it is endowed with the ridges of Brahmagiri.
Likewise, O Four-faced One, there is the holy ford Viraja which causes the destruction of all sins, and the highly meritorious Godāvarī, which exists everywhere.
O Lotus-born One, there is the highly meritorious Tuṅgabhadrā,
where I dwell with affection together with Hara, honored by the sages.
O Lotus-born One, the Dakṣiṇagaṅgā, the Kṛṣṇā, and especially the Kāverī [flow there]; and I myself am stationed at Āmalakagrāma on Mount Sahya.
O Brahmin, you have always worshipped the God of gods by his name;
in that place there are indeed many sacred fords (tīrthas) that remove all sins,
by bathing in which and drinking from which a human being is liberated from evil.
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, having thus described the sacred fords to Brahmā, Madhusūdana departed; and Brahmā, too, returned to his own city.
Bharadvāja said:
O knower of dharma, tell me in detail and according to the truth about those holy pilgrimage sites (*puṇyatīrtha*) that are indeed located in that village of Āmalaka.
Regarding the origin of the sacred field, its majesty, and the festival of pilgrimage held there,
it is said that the Lord of the Gods is worshipped there by Brahmā himself.
Sūta said: Listen, O Brahmin, great sage; I shall proclaim the meritorious origin and other details of Sahyāmalaka-tīrtha, which destroys all sins.
O Brahmin, formerly in the region of Sahyavana there was a great Āmalaka tree; this formidable one is called by that name by the wise.
The fruits of that tree, O great sage, are large, delicious,
beautiful, divine, and difficult to obtain.
In former times, that great tree, endowed with large fruits, was seen by another Brāhmaṇa who was himself beyond the Brahman.
"O best of Brahmins, wondering what this was, he became intent on seeing with his vision of meditation;
through meditation, he saw there once again an *āmalaka* tree."
Above that, however, one should see the Lord of Gods, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
and rising up again, one should behold only the image itself.
That great tree, a deity, entered the earth at that spot;
thereupon, he propitiated the imperishable Lord of the gods of gods.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, constantly worships Hari with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
likewise, Hari is worshipped by twelve and seven [classes of beings].
O best of sages, who could describe the majesty of that Lord of the God of Gods, the Imperishable One, in that field at the village of Sahyāmalaka?
Having propitiated the twelve [deities] at the sacred ford, they reached the presence of the Four-faced One;
from the sole of his foot, a sacred ford issued forth facing the west.
That became the holy Cakratīrtha, which destroys all sins;
having bathed in Cakratīrtha, a man is liberated from all evils.
For many thousands of years he is honored in the world of Brahmā;
having bathed at Śaṅkhatīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
O Sage, on the day of the pilgrimage in the month of Pauṣa under the Puṣya asterism,
Brahmā’s water-pot was formerly filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
O Brahmin, having fallen upon that mountain, it removes inauspiciousness at that sacred site;
by name, that is the Kuṇḍikā Tīrtha, which is endowed with a stone house.
Having bathed at that sacred ford at that time, a person shall attain perfection;
so too the man who, having fasted for three nights, bathes there.
Completely liberated from all evil, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā,
located to the north of Kuṇḍikātīrtha and to the south of Piṇḍasthāna.
For the Ṛṇamocana-tīrtha is the supreme secret among all sacred fords;
whoever stays there for three nights and performs an ablution, [is liberated from debt].
O Brahmin, that man who, having performed a śrāddha for his ancestors at the places where the pindas are offered, is liberated from the three debts; of this there is no doubt.
Having offered rice-balls (piṇḍas) according to the rule for the sake of the ancestors, the ancestors, being fully satisfied, go to the world of the ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed at the Pāpamocana tīrtha after fasting for five nights,
one attains the destruction of all sins and rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who bears that very great stream upon his head,
having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, is glorified in the vault of heaven.
Whoever performs a bath with devotion at the great holy site of Dhanuṣpāta,
having obtained the fruit of long life and enjoyment, is glorified in the heavenly world.
O best of Brahmins, a man who bathes at Śarabindu goes to the city of Indra;
and he who performs a ritual bath at Vārāhatīrtha on Mount Sahya [attains the same].
Having fasted for a day and a night, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
and there is an excellent sacred site (tīrtha) on the peak of Sahya known as Ākāśagaṅgā.
Then, O Brahmin, white clay emerged from the surface of the stone;
the man who bathes with devotion in that clay, O best of the foremost twice-born, [attains the highest merit].
Having attained the fruit of all sacrifices, O Brahmin, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; such is the case for whatever water flows forth from the stainless Sahya mountain.
Know that there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) there; by bathing, one is liberated from sin.
Having gone to the Sahya mountain, one is constantly liberated from sin by bathing.

O best of the twice-born, a man who, having offered beautiful flowers with devotion to Hari at these meritorious holy sites originating from the Sahya mountain, shall cast off his sins and enter into Viṣṇu.
One should bathe once in the waters of other sacred sites and mountains, but repeatedly in the Gaṅgā;
for the Gaṅgā embodies all sacred sites, and Hari embodies all the gods.
The Gītā consists of all the scriptures, and compassion is the essence of all dharma;
thus, O Brahmin, has this supreme majesty of the sacred field been described to you.
O best of the twice-born, having bathed at the shrine in the village of Śrīsahyāmalaka and [eaten] its fruits— that which is the shrine among all shrines—
is the shrine that has emerged upon the earth from beneath the feet of the God of gods.
Those learned in the Vedas declare that Ambhoyuga is equal to a thousand horse sacrifices;
it is called Cakratīrtha, and by bathing there and bowing one’s head at the feet of Madhusūdana, men are not born again.

The Gaṅgā, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, the ten thousand holy sites, Kurujāṅgala, and the Yamunā—these waters of sacred fords purify one from sin over time; but the water from the feet of the Blessed One purifies instantly.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Praise of the Tīrthas," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 66)
Sūta said: Thus, O best of the twice-born, the terrestrial holy places have been described;
for the mental holy places are especially fruitful.
The purity of the mind is a sacred ford, undisturbed by passion and the like;
truth is a sacred ford, compassion is a sacred ford, and the restraint of the senses is a sacred ford.
Service to the guru is a sacred ford, as is service to one’s mother;
the practice of one’s own dharma is a sacred ford, and the worship of the sacred fire is a sacred ford.
These are the meritorious sacred sites; now hear from me, O Sage, concerning the vows: namely, eating once a day, eating only at night, and fasting.
On the full moon and the new moon days, one should practice eating only once a day;
by practicing this single meal there, one shall attain a meritorious state.
On the fourth, the fourteenth, and the seventh lunar days, one should observe the *nakta* fast;
on the eighth and the thirteenth, he obtains his desired goal.
O best of men, the fast on the eleventh day is ordained;
by worshipping Narasiṃha, one is liberated from all sins.
On a Sunday when the moon is in conjunction with the Hasta nakṣatra, one should perform the saura-nakta rite;
having bathed and meditated upon Viṣṇu in the midst of the sun, one is liberated from disease.
When the sun stands so that its shadow is twice the length of one's own body, one should know that it is the solar night; this is not the "night" for eating.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the fortnight, on Thursday, in the afternoon,
one should offer libations to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages with sesame seeds and rice in the water.
Having worshipped Narasiṃha and observed a fast,
one who does so is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O great sage, when the rising of Agastya has occurred, one should offer the *arghya* oblation after duly worshipping Agastya for seven nights.
Having poured water into a conch shell, joined with white flowers and unbroken rice grains,
one should indeed offer it with this mantra while worshiping with cut flowers and other offerings.
O you who resemble the kāśa flower, born from fire and wind,
son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O pot-born one, homage be to you!
May Agastya, by whom the great asura Vātāpi was devoured while he was still alive and by whom the ocean was dried up, be pleased with me.
He who gives all this to Agastya in every direction,
being liberated from all sins, crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
Thus, O great sage Bharadvāja, I have related to you in the presence of the sages the entire ancient narrative of Nārasiṃha.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— all of this has indeed been proclaimed.
O sage, this was indeed proclaimed by Brahmā in ancient times to Marīci and the others;
and from them it was proclaimed by Bhṛgu to Mārkaṇḍeya.
This was indeed proclaimed by Mārkaṇḍeya to the king of the Nāga clan;
through the grace of Narasiṃha, it was obtained by the wise Vyāsa.
Through his grace, I have obtained this Purāṇa of Narasiṃha, which destroys all sins; and it has now been narrated by me to you.
In the presence of the sages, may there be merit; may it be well with you, for I am now departing.
Whoever, having become pure, listens to this supreme Purāṇa, [attains the highest goal].
He who daily recites this [account] of Narahari with devotion to his devotees shall obtain the fruit of bathing at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
having heard this, the high-minded Bharadvāja [departed] together with those who had completed their ritual ablutions.
Having honored the Sūta, he remained right there while the sages departed;
[he heard] the meritorious Purāṇa concerning the essence of Nṛsiṃha, which removes all sins.
Narasiṃha is pleased with those men who read or hear [this];
when the Lord of the gods is pleased, the destruction of all sins occurs.
Those men whose bonds of sin have been destroyed attain liberation.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Vow of the Mental Pilgrimage," in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 67)
Sūta said: Thus has this entire Purāṇa of Nṛsiṃha been narrated;
it is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and the warder-off of all sufferings.
Those who read or even hear a single verse, or even half a verse, which bestows the fruit of all merit and grants the fruit of all sacrifices; NsP_68.2 //
For them, no bond of sin ever arises;
this meritorious Purāṇa, dedicated to Viṣṇu, grants all desires.
And listen to the fruit for those who speak this with devotion and those who hear it:
they are instantly liberated from the sins accumulated over a hundred lifetimes.
Accompanied by a thousand kinsmen, they go to the supreme state;
what need is there for sacred fords, gifts of cows, austerities, or sacrifices?
For those who listen to Govinda day after day with single-minded devotion,
Having obtained the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
This [text] is purifying and worthy of worship, and it should not be spoken to those of undisciplined soul.
This is to be heard by the twice-born who are devotees of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
This listening to the Purāṇa bestows happiness both in this world and the next.
For those who speak and for those who listen, it instantly destroys all sins;
O lords of sages, what is the use of saying more on this matter again and again?
Whether with faith or even without faith, this supreme [teaching] should be heard;
all these best of the twice-born, headed by Bhāradvāja, have accomplished their purpose.
Then, having joyfully honored the charioteer, they all departed for their respective hermitages.
Thus ends the majesty of the Śrīnarasiṃha Purāṇa, which removes all suffering, within the dialogue between Sūta, Bharadvāja, and others, in the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa. (NarP 68)
